Can this $77 million state initiative bolster Ukraine's cultural sphere?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

Can this $77 million state initiative bolster Ukraine's cultural sphere?
The "The Future Remembers" light installation is projected onto the Mother Ukraine Monument in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 20, 2026. (Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
With Ukraine's cultural heritage threatened by Russia's all-out war of annihilation, Kyiv is ramping up its efforts to support Ukrainian artists at the state level.
"Tysiachovesna," or "1,000 Springs," is a project originally proposed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in the fall of 2025 to use Hr 4 billion ($76.7 million) of the state budget to support the creation of 1,000 hours of Ukrainian-language content.
The Culture Ministry formally launched the initiative earlier this spring, encouraging artists to submit funding proposals.
According to the government, the goal of "1,000 Springs" is not just to support Ukrainian culture during wartime, but also to boost the presence of Ukrainian-language content and reduce the influence of Russian-language material in the country.
The hope is that the initiative will generate more stories about Ukraine told through a distinctly Ukrainian lens, while cultivating a competitive landscape among artists.
Culture Minister Tetiana Berezhna has frequently emphasized the need to promote Ukrainian culture as a matter of national interest. Speaking to the Kyiv Independent back in early May, the minister said that culture should be seen not just as a form of entertainment but "a vital part of our economy."
read also
A test for the judges
The "1,000 Springs" website encourages artists to submit projects across a broad range of subjects, from Ukraine's history, folklore, and natural heritage to life during the war, mental health, and preservation and development of the Ukrainian language.
Applicants faced three stages of review, with the final round of presentations to expert panels of judges concluding on Aug. 19. However, given the size and scope of the initiative in its first year, this process was not without its setbacks.
A number of people from across Ukraine's cultural sphere raised concerns about whether the application criteria were adequate to fairly evaluate such a diverse range of projects.
"I was surprised that short films, features, and series could all be placed in the same category, along with films for children and adults, live-action and animation, auteur films and films aimed at a broad audience," filmmaker Iryna Tsilyk, whose animated film "Red Zone" was among the selected applicants, wrote.
"In other words, they all belong on very different shelves, and I wouldn't want to be the expert who had to evaluate, say, a live-action film for toddlers and an auteur animated documentary for adults at the same time."
The experts assigned to judge applicants' projects in the final stages reportedly included both people familiar with the project and those engaging with it for the first time.
With just five minutes to present a film and three minutes for a question-and-answer session, Tsilyk worried the time was too short and that certain valuable projects could have gone unnoticed.
Ninety-two projects were selected in the "Feature Film and TV" category from 404 proposals in the third stage; 70 of 354 in "Documentary TV and Film"; and 30 of 170 in "Children's TV and Film."
Furthermore, 144 were selected from 293 for "Contemporary Music," 133 from 282 for "Performative Arts," 77 from 191 for "Visual Arts," and 135 from 465 for "Audiovisual Shows and Video Clips for Social Media."
The judging process also came under scrutiny for potential conflicts of interest, although the Culture Ministry said it took significant steps to address the issue.
"Understanding this situation, my team and I worked out a system for identifying and preventing conflicts of interest, which operated at every stage of the program," Berezhna said at a press event on Aug. 20.
Projects were reportedly assigned to experts for evaluation through a closed lottery system, where balls were drawn at random, so no one knew which expert was judging which project. If an expert had a conflict of interest, they submitted a statement, and the project would be reassigned to a "reserve" expert, also chosen by lottery.
"A great many people who make decisions about allocating funding for the following year are watching the discussion around '1,000 Springs.' So, as people who care about Ukrainian culture, we simply need to sit down and have a serious discussion together about what we can improve in the competition so that it can be perfected for next year," Berezhna added.
read also
Lessons for the next year
Reflecting on the outcome of the first "1,000 Springs," writer Oksana Moroz, who served as one of the experts for the "Audiovisual Shows and Video Clips for Social Media" category, advocated for a stronger emphasis on promotion and distribution in future competitions.
"Applicants described the idea, its advantages, how it would be filmed and edited in great detail. But only about a third (of candidates in the category) wrote about distribution and promotion or provided projected viewership figures," Moroz wrote.
"Another particular headache was (calculating projected viewer) reach instead of (just) views. A typical example would read: 'This project will have a reach of 800,000 views on Channel X.' You'd go to the channel and see that its typical videos had 400–500 views."
Moroz also proposed creating an "online school" for future applicants so they can better understand not only how to plan the distribution, promotion, and budgeting of their projects, but also their concepts — namely, the value they bring to society and what makes them stand out from preexisting work.
The idea is not unprecedented. The Ukrainian Book Institute, a state agency under the Culture Ministry, holds online seminars for prospective applicants to its Translate Ukraine program, which provides financial support to publishers worldwide for publishing translations of Ukrainian books.
As participants, organizers, and observers alike engage in candid public discussions about what worked — and what did not — in the inaugural "1,000 Springs," it is apparent that there is a collective will for the project to evolve.
During the final stage of judging, held in the western Ukrainian city of Ivano-Frankivsk from Aug. 12 to 19, Zelensky expressed his hope that "1,000 Springs" would become an important tradition.
"I am convinced that we need to maintain this pace (of supporting culture at the state level) for at least five to 10 years. Today we are already seeing the capacity of the industry, while the state, accordingly, is providing its support," Zelensky said.

As schools re-open, Congo drops remote learning plan in Ebola red zone
BENI, Democratic Republic of Congo, Sept 2 - Schools reopened this week in areas of Democratic Republic of Congo hardest hit by Ebola, after authorities decided the risk of transmission was outweighed by the risk of pupils struggling with remote learning, an official told Reuters on Wednesday.
The death toll from the outbreak - the worst in Congo's long history with the disease - has exceeded 3,000, according to government data published on Wednesday, with cases spread across six provinces and a mortality rate of 48.6%.
More than 1,000 schools in Ituri are classified as being in the "red zone", meaning a high-risk zone or zone of active transmission, according to an education ministry document seen this week by Reuters.
Ministry regulations published on August 19 stipulated that schools in the red zone would temporarily replace in-person classes with "distance learning" involving worksheets distributed every two weeks and programmes broadcast on the radio and television.
But schools opened as usual this week in Ituri, an education ministry official said.
"The government reviewed its initial decision at the request of provincial authorities who wanted to ensure that students living even in red zones would not fall behind in the school curriculum compared to others," said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
"At the first sign of a case, we will close and implement distance learning, but for now, that's not the case."
Schools also reopened in areas of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces controlled by the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebels, who staged a lightning offensive in the region last year, according to a rebel official. Authorities are requiring hand-washing and social distancing in classrooms, the official said.
PARENTS ON HIGH ALERT
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo species, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
Anxiety about Ebola was evident this week well beyond the epicentre.
La Reine Vahwere stocked her three young children's backpacks with bottles of disinfectant before sending them off to school in the city of Beni, in North Kivu province, which accounts for 868 of Congo's 6,186 confirmed cases.
"I told them to avoid touching each other, physically touching their classmates," she said.
"Also, as I am accompanying them to school, I am going to ask the authorities to apply the protective measure of distancing within the classrooms. Because it would really be sad to see a child affected at school when at home the child is respecting the protective measures."
As students entered the school compound, a staff member instructed them to wash their hands with hand sanitiser and explained to them where to find wash basins and toilet paper.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The education ministry official said hygiene kits had been installed in red zone schools. REUTERS

Founder of Russian children’s hospice charged with spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
Investigators have charged Lida Moniava, founder of the children’s hospice “House with a Lighthouse,” with spreading “false information” about the Russian military motivated by political hatred — a charge under Article 207.3, Part 2, Clause “d” of Russia’s Criminal Code — and detained her, according to her defense attorney, Mikhail Biryukov, who told the Russian business news outlet RBC.
The statute carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

Investigators searched Moniava’s home on the morning of September 2 and then took her to the Investigative Committee, Russia’s federal investigating authority, for questioning.
A Moscow court fined Moniava 45,000 rubles in February 2026 on an administrative charge of “discrediting” the Russian military, stemming from three posts on her Telegram channel. In one, she linked to a “Christmas Message to Friends” by Orthodox Christians living in emigration, published by The Moscow Times, which spoke of “the terrible war unleashed by the Russian state.” Another described the deaths of children after a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih. A third recounted the deaths of the Martynenko family in a Russian strike on Sumy.
After being fined on the “discrediting” charge, Moniava said she had no plans to leave Russia, despite advice from many people that she do so.
Moniava founded the children’s hospice “House with a Lighthouse” and in 2018 became head of the charitable foundation of the same name, which supports critically ill children and young adults up to age 30. After the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine, she launched a separate fund to help refugees from Ukraine, Russia’s border regions, and Nagorno-Karabakh; it suspended operations in September 2025.

India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?
September 2, 2026
The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force.
Pakistan has welcomed the decision and says India remains bound by the treaty.
India's Ministry of External Affairs described the tribunal as a "so-called Court of Arbitration" that was "illegally constituted."
It said the body had been established by the World Bank in breach of the treaty and that India "categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body."
"The Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions," the ministry said.
What to know about the treaty
The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan.
The agreement largely gives India rights over three eastern rivers while Pakistan has rights over the western Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India is allowed to use the western rivers for specified purposes including certain hydroelectric projects.
The treaty had endured wars and prolonged periods of intense hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.
But India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 as part of a package of diplomatic and economic measures announced after a deadly attack in India-administered Kashmir killed 26 people, mostly tourists.
New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack. Pakistan denied the charges.
High stakes for Pakistan
Millions of people in Pakistan depend on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers for drinking water, farming and daily life.
The rivers are particularly important to Punjab and Sindh provinces, whose agriculture is central to the country's food supply and rural economy.
After India's move to suspend the treaty, Pakistan approached the court in The Hague over the status of the accord.
Pakistani officials have repeatedly warned that any attempt to deny the country its share of the waters of rivers flowing across the border would be treated as an act of war.
Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said India had challenged the treaty on both political and legal grounds.
"Politically, abeyance hands India a new point of leverage, one more lever to press Pakistan into changing its behavior on cross-border terrorism," Bisaria told DW.
He also pointed to India's earlier requests to renegotiate the treaty, citing climate change, new dam-building technology and the deterioration of relations between the two countries.
India chose to put the treaty in abeyance rather than formally abrogate it. Bisaria said the Hague ruling would not change that course.
"The tribunal will not alter this trajectory," he said. "India's course on the Indus Waters Treaty is set. The treaty will not be revived in its present form."
Legal battle over water
Pakistan has taken the opposite view.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the ruling "decisively rejects" India's attempt to place the treaty in abeyance and reaffirmed that it remains "fully in force and binding on both parties."
"The Award vindicates Pakistan's consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside," Dar said in a post on X.
He added that India must comply with its obligations under the treaty and with binding decisions arising from its dispute settlement mechanisms.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and defense analyst, said the ruling may be difficult to implement if India refuses to accept it.
"The arbitration court's ruling may not be implementable because the court doesn't have the force to do so," Siddiqa told DW.
But she said the decision gave Pakistan an advantage as a lower riparian state.
"It does give Pakistan a moral edge," said Siddiqa, a senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King's College London.
She also questioned what India's rejection of the ruling could mean for its international position, particularly given that India has accepted international legal decisions in other disputes.
"This is not just an issue of pure military power but an international standing where India will not be able to justify its position to the world any longer," she said.
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, a South Asia analyst and founder of the Mantraya think tank, said the ruling did not materially change India's position.
"The Permanent Court of Arbitration is an administrative body, not a conventional sovereign court with enforcement capabilities," D'Souza told DW.
"In this particular case, India chose not to participate in the proceedings. This allows it not to recognize the tribunal's rulings. Therefore, it has no enforceable constraint on India and nothing changes materially for New Delhi," she said.
A dispute over the rules
India and Pakistan have disagreed for years over the interpretation of the treaty, particularly over Indian hydropower projects on rivers allocated primarily to Pakistan.
Uttam Kumar Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and author of "Trial by Water," said India is now no longer merely contesting the interpretation of the treaty, but rather "contesting the authority of the treaty's dispute-settlement mechanism itself."
New Delhi maintains that the tribunal was improperly constituted and that its decisions have no legal effect on India.
Sinha describes the emerging contest as "lawfare," with Pakistan likely to use the ruling in international forums and frame the dispute around treaty obligations and international law.
The limits of India's leverage
The practical implications will also depend on what India does with its infrastructure on the western rivers.
D'Souza said the treaty's abeyance gave India more political and psychological leverage than an immediate ability to alter the flow of the rivers.
"To effectively stop or significantly alter the flows of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, substantial infrastructure like dams, canals and large storage systems would be required, and such structures do not currently exist," said D'Souza.
"Furthermore, geographical and technical constraints limit India's capacity to block these rivers."
Sinha echoed this view.
"India cannot simply 'turn off' the western rivers," he said.
Large storage and diversion projects would take years or decades, require substantial investment and involve difficult construction in the mountainous Himalayan region, as well as environmental and domestic approvals.
"There is a significant gap between India's potential strategic freedom on the western rivers and its actual physical capacity to change water flows," Sinha said.

UN warns global warming likely to exceed 1.5C within next few years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:39:42 UTC
22:39:42 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Global warming is likely to exceed 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels within the next few years, but temperatures could still be brought back down through rapid emissions cuts and sustained net-negative emissions, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) said Wednesday.
“Global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5C, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights, but it is still possible to bring temperatures down and achieve global goals in the Paris Agreement,” a new UNEP report said.
The report identified an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway as the best option to minimize both the scale and duration of warming above 1.5C before eventually returning below that threshold.
The pathway seeks to limit peak warming through deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions and subsequently lower temperatures through sustained net-negative emissions.
“There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C. Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer - costing more lives and causing deeper disruption,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.
The report said even the most optimistic scenario would see global temperatures peak at 1.8C above pre-industrial levels, exceeding the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5C.
Most other scenarios project even higher peaks.
Risks would intensify with every additional fraction of a degree of warming and every year temperatures remain above 1.5C, the report said, including through more severe extreme weather and ecosystem losses.
“Severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure, and economies is expected,” it added.
The report also warned that the likelihood of crossing irreversible tipping points rises with both the magnitude and duration of higher temperatures.
“These include the destabilization of major ice sheets, degradation of the Amazon rainforest and disruption of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of currents that moves warm surface water north and cold deep water south, playing a key role in regulating the climate),” it added.
Some impacts are likely to emerge abruptly, while others will accumulate over time, the report said.

The book of poetry I wrote for the home I lost in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:38:27 UTC
22:38:27 KST

Share & more
Almost three years after the beginning of the Gaza genocide, I am publishing a book of poetry about a house that no longer exists, in a language my mother cannot read, in a country where my family cannot follow.
The first two poems I wrote in my life were called Lemon Tree and Hope. I wrote them two or three months after the genocide began in a purple notebook that my sister gave me as a gift, in my now destroyed childhood home, about a tree I will not see again.
The book is named for that house, and it will be published in French on 9 September. When the collection comes out, I will be asked to sign copies of it in a city where nothing that belonged to me has ever been demolished.
The book is called This is My House – in French, Ceci est ma maison. The title has a double meaning. It refers to the house in the north of Gaza where my brothers were married, where my older sisters gave birth, and where their children learned to walk on a rooftop that I could describe to you tile by tile. It also refers to Gaza, my home and the home of more than two million other people. Both have been reduced to rubble.
I want to tell you how I learned that my childhood home had been destroyed because the shape of that experience is the shape of exile: It was at the end of September or early October last year when our neighbours saw the destruction. They told my family, and my family told me. That was the order. The people standing in the street knew before its owners, and I – writing a book about it – was the last to be told.
Distance is not a feeling. It is a delay measurable in hours, and I have been at the far end of that delay since I crossed the border and left Gaza in July 2025. Perhaps I will be at the far end of it for the rest of my life.
I was the last to find out about the destruction of my own house, where I lived since I was five. I was in my room studying when I found out, the French daylight filtering through the window in a country where the electricity does not go off, from a voice on a phone that had already said it out loud to someone else first.
◇◇◇
Everything that was in the house was lost. The oil paintings I had made and never showed to anyone – some of them finished, some still works in progress. My books in three languages, Arabic, English, and French. The room I wrote in. The walls that held space for weddings and births. The rooftop. The particular way the afternoon light came into the kitchen.
A house is not just a structure. It is a set of instructions for where the light falls in space, and those instructions have been deleted from the world. There is no copy. Except one. It is not a good copy, but it is what remains, consisting of over 50 poems in a language I was not born into.
The poems are not gentle memories. I have not been able to write about anything except this: the house; the yearning for what no longer exists; what has been done to the people who called it home; the children killed in numbers that stopped being numbers; massacres that have names in Arabic and no names at all in the papers here; a boy who is now alone in the world because everyone who knew his name was killed on the same afternoon and who is expected to keep waking up.
I did not choose these subjects. There was nothing else in the room.
I wrote the poems for myself and for my family. That was the readership I imagined. I did not intend to create a manuscript. The poems were phrases in notebooks I already owned and that I was already using for something else. There are French verb tables in those notebooks and lecture notes.
I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else.
When I started writing the poems I was a student of English and French literature. My university’s campus was destroyed, like virtually all the university campuses in Gaza. The university continued teaching online throughout the genocide, and I continued attending – which sounds absurd. So was scrawling half a line of a poem about a dead child at the top of a page about the subjunctive. I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else.
I wrote the poems in English even though Arabic is my first language. I’ve never been able to fully account for that. Maybe writing in a foreign language allows for more emotional distance. The words land with less force. The pictures they summon are dimmer.
English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud.
Dimmer is what I needed. English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud. In English, I could stand on the other side and look in.
Every poem in this book was written through that pane of glass by a woman who could not have written a word of it without that separation. But that pane of glass also disappears, even in a second language, when I write about my mother or my younger sister. I can write in English about a child I never met, but I cannot say my own address out loud.
◇◇◇
The poems left me before any publisher was interested. I started reciting them on Instagram while I was still in Gaza. People responded, and I liked that they responded.
Some of the notebooks I wrote the poems in were destroyed with the house. Some stayed behind with my sister. What is being published is what escaped from a fire and across the borders. My first book is the surviving portion of something that was never assembled.
There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer.
Then it was translated, and the translation is extraordinary. Lisa Ducasse did what I would have told you could not be done. Writers I know and trust, Karim Kattan among them, have said so too, and they are right. I want to state my admiration without a single qualifier attached to it. And still, reading it, I meet a stranger who knows everything about me.
Now, I sit down for interviews to talk about the book. There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer. I stop. The kind person across from me waits. The waiting becomes its own weather in the room because now I have made them uncomfortable, and I find myself apologising to someone for the destruction of my own street.
At the launch event in Paris, there will be a table with volumes of the book piled high. My name will be said into a microphone. People will be genuinely moved, and then they will go home, which is the correct thing for them to do and I hold it against nobody. There will be a picture of me smiling, and the smile will be real because this is the thing every writer is supposed to want, and there was a girl in that house who wanted it more than she wanted almost anything else.
At the same time, my mother will not be in the room, nor will my younger sister. Neither can read the language the book is printed in.
Both of these things are true at once, and neither cancels out the other: This is my dream, and it has been handed to me in exchange for everything I had. Nobody consulted me on the rate.
◇◇◇
There is one more thing – the worst of all – which I am going to set down rather than continue to carry: The book matters because Gaza is still happening. Its relevance is my family’s ongoing danger. I wrote the poems because I wanted people to look and see what was happening. That was always the whole of it. I didn’t want people to look away.
In Paris, when they look at me they might see a woman who evacuated from Gaza to continue her studies at one of the best universities in Europe. But it turns out that being looked at and being read are not the same thing. When people read, they might understand the pain and agony of what we have gone through.
The book matters because Gaza is still happening.
If you pick up the book, know that these poems were written by a student who still had French homework, in notebooks that mostly no longer exist, for an audience of her mother, her sister, and herself. And notice the tense of the title – This is My House. The house is gone, but the sentence is in the present tense.
A demolition takes an afternoon, but a house can be kept somewhere else, in a borrowed language, between two covers, as long as someone is still reading the words.

EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:36:36 UTC
22:36:36 KST

EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
Relations between Russia and Armenia have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West.
Russia President Vladimir Putin has warned Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan that Yerevan’s bid to join the European Union could disrupt trade with Moscow.
Relations between the two countries have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West, prompting sharp economic and political retaliation from Moscow.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why?
- list 2 of 3Iran and Russia vow to stand against US ‘unilateralism’
- list 3 of 3Germany says Russia preparing ‘hybrid’ attacks over Ukraine support
In a tense meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital on Tuesday, Putin said that Moscow needs clarity on whether Yerevan wants to join the EU so it can decide on the future of bilateral trade with Armenia.
Putin also said that Armenia joining the EU would be tantamount to declaring a break from the Eurasian Economic Union (EEU) – a Russia-led grouping of several post-Soviet states.
Last April, Yerevan decided to adopt a law to launch the process of EU accession – a sticking point for Russia, which views its neighbouring post-Soviet countries as a vital security shield between its borders and the European Union.
In Bishkek, Armenia’s Pashinyan stressed that Yerevan has not violated any of its obligations towards Russia through its EU accession process and did not want to leave the EEU.
What happened at the meeting? Here’s what we know:
What did Putin tell Pashinyan?
At their meeting on Tuesday, according to the Kremlin, Putin told Pashinyan that while Russia is a key economic and trade partner to Armenia, Yerevan’s EU aspirations could create complications for its EEU membership.
“Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU is the natural and legitimate right of the country and its people. Armenia is a sovereign state, and it is for the Armenian people to determine the trajectory of their own development,” Putin said.
“Nevertheless, this unquestionably creates complications for Armenia’s continued membership in the Eurasian Economic Union, and threatens to erode the advantages the Republic enjoys on the EEU market and to sever established trade links,” he added.
Pashinyan, however, said Armenia’s decision last year to adopt a law launching the process of EU accession did not violate its obligations to Russia or the EEU and that it was only an alternative his government had given to the people of Armenia.
What are Armenia and Russia’s relations like?
After the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, Armenia became Russia’s closest ally in the South Caucasus, with the two nations developing their trade, economic and political ties. Armenia has also long been Russia’s closest regional ally, a Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) member, host to a Russian military base and is dependent on Russian gas.
Currently, Russia is Armenia’s key trade and economic partner, accounting for roughly 30 percent of its trade, and an investor in Armenia’s economy. In the first half of this year, bilateral trade also reached $2.5bn.
But despite economic ties, relations between the two countries have been tense since 2023, after the historical conflict in the Nagorno-Karabakh region of Azerbaijan erupted again.
Russia, which is fighting its own war in Ukraine, did not intervene militarily when Azerbaijan launched a major military offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh, which had a large Armenian population and had been de facto independent since the 1990s.
Laurentiu Plesca, a political analyst and researcher focusing on EU enlargement and European security at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that Moscow decision not to support Yerevan during the Karabakh war in 2023 led to Armenia’s pivot towards the West.
He said that this, in turn, upset Moscow, further souring relations.
“Russia started blocking imports of Armenian goods and is threatening to suspend the duty-free supply of gas, oil products, and diamonds to Armenia,” he said.
“The EU, in turn, has pledged economic support to offset that pressure,” he added.
In early July, the European Commission’s President Ursula von der Leyen also told Yerevan that it could count on the EU amid any economic pressure from Russia and pledged an additional 18 million euros (about $20m) as part of a broader 52 million euros (about $60m) economic support package.
What are Armenia’s EU plans?
Last April, Armenia’s president signed into law a bill that set the legal foundation for the country to move towards joining the EU.
Pashinyan, who took power in 2018 and was part of launching the EU bid, has repeatedly stressed that the bill did not represent an application to join the EU, but the start of a broader process of integration.
However, in July this year, Pashinyan told lawmakers in the country that Armenia would decide its future EU membership by holding a referendum “in the near future”.
Yerevan has significantly deepened its European ties, hosting its first official EU summit last month alongside a wider European gathering attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Armenia also hosted French President Emmanuel Macron for a high-profile state visit, which provoked sharp criticism from the Kremlin after a video emerged of Macron singing while Pashinyan played the drums.
What is the EEU?
Putin has previously warned Armenia that it views membership in the EU as incompatible with the EEU, and Armenia would have to leave if it joins the EU.
The EEU is a group of former Soviet Union countries that coordinate economic and trade policies. Its members are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The group’s treaty was established in May 2014, and it began its operations in January 2015.
According to a 2022 Chatham House report, the EEU is in effect a Russian-led effort to create a Eurasian counterpart to the EU.
So why is Armenia’s EU bid a point of tension for Russia and the EEU?
According to the Chatham House report, the EEU serves an important geopolitical purpose for Russia.
“Putin sees it as part of his drive to re-establish the Russian sphere of influence lost by the dissolution of the Soviet Union,” the report’s writers emphasised.
That’s why Armenia seeking closer ties with the EU represents an attempt to break from Russia’s dominance of its neighbourhood, in the eyes of the Kremlin.
In June, Pashinyan rejected a call from Moscow to hold an immediate referendum on leaving the EEU to join the European Union.
Tensions had boiled over at the EEU summit in Kazakhstan on May 29, as Putin and fellow bloc members Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement urging Armenia to hold the referendum “as soon as possible”.
Putin also appeared to make a barely veiled threat at the EEU summit, warning Armenia against pursuing its Western ambitions, and referring to Russia’s war in Ukraine, said that the “Ukrainian scenario” had also begun with Kyiv’s EU aspirations.
In a video address broadcast on social media, Pashinyan had responded to Putin and stated that his government would continue working within the EEU until a choice between the two blocs “becomes unavoidable”, noting that any referendum before Armenia formally applies for EU candidate status remains purely theoretical.
“Putting a theoretical choice to a referendum is, of course, neither very sensible nor justified,” Pashinyan had said.
At the SCO summit, however, he reiterated that Yerevan had no plans to leave the EEU and said that Moscow has always supported the development of friendly and mutually beneficial relations with Yerevan.
Plesca, the political analyst, said that at its core, there is a tug-of-war over Armenia’s strategic alignment, playing out on two fronts.
“But the pro-EU stance is already clear, and Moscow wants to reverse it. Having failed to do so at the ballot box in the recent parliamentary elections in June, it is now compensating with economic blackmail,” he said. During Armenia’s parliamentary elections in June, Moscow was accused of seeking to tip the scales by exerting economic and diplomatic pressure on Pashinyan’s government.
He noted that while Armenia does have the legal right to join the EU, doing so while still inside the EEU customs union would be legally ambiguous.
“There’s no mechanism to expel a member, and Armenia hasn’t triggered the six-month exit notice, so an EU bid doesn’t automatically breach” its obligations towards the EEU, Plesca said. “That’s exactly the trap Yerevan is navigating, keeping a foot in both camps for now, while Moscow insists that’s not possible.”
He added that for Russia, Armenia’s EU bid is also more about losing a foothold in the South Caucasus region.

====================================================================================================

Life in Kyiv amid constant air-raid warnings as Russia shifts to jet-powered drones
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:36:00 EEST
22:36:00 KST

Life in Kyiv amid constant air-raid warnings as Russia shifts to jet-powered drones
Russia spent the summer terrorising Ukraine with large-scale attacks, only increasing their intensity. Cruise and ballistic missiles, Shahed drones, guided aerial bombs and Banderol missiles have been deployed en masse along with jet-powered strike UAVs from the Geran family. And the number of these drones keeps growing in the reports issued by Ukraine's Air Force.
Western media reports say that the Russians are preparing to further intensify their massive attacks on Kyiv and other regions. Plans to continue the terror have also been voiced openly in Russia's State Duma [parliament]: Deputy Chairman Pyotr Tolstoy called for Ukrainian cities to be bombed to force Ukrainians to surrender. Following this statement, Russia's Defence Ministry stressed that it is preparing to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Which weapons does Russia plan to use most extensively, does Ukraine have the means to counter them, and what should be expected as the cold season approaches? Read about these issues in the new Ukrainska Pravda.In Brief format.
Tactics of attacks are changing
Back in 2025, Russia's main long-range strike tactic was to launch massive attacks against the whole of Ukraine simultaneously using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. Now the Russians are developing a new approach, and a different pattern has emerged over the past two months:
- Infrequent large-scale combined attacks involving cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as jet-powered drones. Kyiv Oblast has recently been one of the main targets of such strikes.
- Regular localised attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, primarily involving large numbers of jet-powered UAVs.
- A major focus on Odesa Oblast, which Russia has been attacking using tactical aircraft and jet-powered drones.
In July 2026, Ukraine's Air Force reported intercepting more than 5,300 aerial assets. The number of interceptions in June was roughly the same, but the nature of the attacks was different. Yurii Ihnat, head of the communications department of Ukraine's Air Force, told Ukrainska Pravda that Russia is placing increasing emphasis on jet-powered UAVs every month.
Ihnat said: "There were five times more jet-powered drones in July than in June. That is the trend. Obviously, there will be no fewer of them in August [according to the statistics – ed.] than there were in July."
Russia is launching high-speed drones straight from the factory, said Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. He estimates that the number of these UAVs has increased by at least 67% over the past month – from around 1,500 to more than 2,500.
Banderols are also becoming a new element of the attacks. They are a type of weapon fitted with a turbojet engine, also known as a missile drone. Banderols are launched from Orion strike-reconnaissance UAVs and attack helicopters. Ihnat does not rule out the possibility that Russian tactical aircraft will also begin using these UAVs soon.
Aviation expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi told Ukrainska Pravda that the increase in the number of jet-powered drones and combined missile drones was an entirely predictable step by Russia. The Russians have long been trying to reduce their dependence on costly missile weapons, replacing them with weapons that are much cheaper but can be deployed in large numbers and travel at high speeds.
How jet-powered drones differ from conventional ones
The main difference between these UAVs is their speed, which changes the rules of the game:
- conventional Shahed drones – 150-170 km/h
- jet-powered drones – around 400-500 km/h
- Banderol missiles – up to 600 km/h.
Khrapchynskyi says the impact of a conventional UAV and a jet-powered one is broadly similar, as the weight of their warheads is the same. However, their speed can have some effect on their destructive power.
Khrapchynskyi said: "Because of its high speed, a jet-powered drone has significantly greater kinetic energy. This increases its penetrating effect when hitting buildings. Residual aviation fuel also produces a more extensive and higher-temperature thermal effect."
It is too early to talk about Russia's stockpiles of jet-powered drones, as the country is still only at the stage of ramping up production. Khrapchynskyi explained that high-speed drones are considerably more expensive to produce than piston-powered Shaheds because of the higher cost of their engines. However, producing jet-powered drones is still cheaper for Russia than producing full-fledged tactical- or strategic-class cruise missiles.
The main factor that could constrain Russia's production of such drones is its almost complete dependence on external supplies, particularly from China. The aviation expert said this primarily concerns heat-resistant structural materials and electronics for control systems.
Russia also depends on supplies of compact, small-sized turbojet engines, most of which are either manufactured in China or brought in through grey imports.
By increasing the number of jet-powered drones, the Russians are reducing the proportion of conventional Shaheds they use. This indicates that they understand Ukraine's weak spot – its difficulty in intercepting high-speed UAVs.
The Air Force told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian interceptor drones, mobile fire groups and electronic warfare systems are effective against conventional Shaheds, allowing nearly 90% of petrol-powered drones to be shot down.
Meanwhile, Ukraine currently uses only aircraft and ground-based air defence against jet-powered drones. The flight characteristics of these UAVs are similar to those of cruise missiles, meaning that interception systems are also considerably more expensive. It should be noted that Ukraine is currently critically short of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
Our country is currently actively working to find effective ways of countering Russian jet-powered drones. On 30 August, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that four potential interceptors had already undergone field tests and were capable of shooting down high-speed drones. The priority at present is to finalise the relevant solutions and scale up their production to thousands of units.
How far can high-speed UAVs fly?
The maximum range of Russian jet-powered drones is not officially known. However, experience shows that they can cover distances of up to 1,000 kilometres. For example, on 18 August, a high-speed UAV reached Rivne Oblast for the first time, having travelled around 900 kilometres from occupied Crimea. And on 28 August, radars detected a jet-powered drone over Volyn Oblast. The drone had covered approximately 960 kilometres.
Khrapchynskyi explained that the Russians can significantly increase their flight range by reducing the weight of the warhead and adjusting the fuel balance.
This would allow them to reach deeper rear areas of western Ukraine, but the accuracy of strikes could deteriorate significantly, Vadym Hlushko, founder of the Cyberboroshno OSINT community, explained to Ukrainska Pravda.
Quote from Hlushko: "When drones fly over the Kyiv-Zhytomyr logistics routes and destroy petrol stations, they are being controlled. Strikes on the west of Ukraine cannot be controlled. But the fact remains: jet-powered UAVs are capable of reaching there, and Russia has plans to attack one of the cities in the west of Ukraine."
Drones are launched in small waves
The terror tactics have changed somewhat compared with previous months. Whereas previously the Russians would accumulate weapons and then launch everything at once, they are now spreading attacks throughout the course of a day, keeping Ukrainians under constant pressure. For example, on 27 August, the capital recorded its highest number of air-raid warnings since 1 March 2022 – 13 warnings were issued within 24 hours.
Jet-powered drones often fly in waves of four or five UAVs. Only after the Ukrainian Air Force repels the attack do the Russians launch the next batch.
According to Khrapchynskyi, the change in tactics can be explained by Russia's capabilities – the number of launchers is limited. There may also be insufficient time to reload them and enter new flight missions. However, there is another side to this strategy.
Quote from Khrapchynskyi: "Russia is exerting continuous pressure on our defences [by launching drones in small batches – ed.]. Fighter aircraft are being drawn onto an exhausting conveyor belt: take-off, interception of a high-speed target, landing, refuelling and rearming. This rapidly wears down the aircraft's resources, while ground-based air-defence systems remain under constant strain.
The Russians are counting on the simple human factor of operator fatigue."
Updated Iskander-1000 ballistic missile
In addition to drones, Russia is placing a major emphasis on ballistic missiles, which Ukraine also struggles to intercept due to a shortage of interceptor missiles.
As Defence Intelligence of Ukraine reported, in summer 2026 Russia used the updated Iskander-1000 ballistic missile against the capital for the first time.
The 1000 in the name is more frightening than realistic, Khrapchynskyi said. He describes the figure merely as a "design ceiling and target" for the Russian defence industry. In reality, the available technical data on the Iskander-1000 indicate it has a range of around 550 kilometres.
Quote from Khrapchynskyi: "They are seeking to achieve a greater range [1,000 kilometres – ed.]. To do this, they are using more energy-dense solid propellant, optimising the engine and significantly reducing the warhead's weight – to approximately 300-350 kilograms.
The main difference between this modification and conventional Iskanders lies in alterations to the ballistic profile and fuel balance."
In reality, the Russians are modifying these missiles because they have a strategic objective – Russia is trying to maximise their range in order to move its scarce launchers as far away from the Ukrainian border as possible, Khrapchynskyi believes.
The Russians now realise that Ukraine's long-range capabilities are expanding. Ukraine also has no shortage of intelligence capabilities, meaning that Russian positions near the line of contact are becoming priority and extremely vulnerable targets for strikes.
***
There is no doubt that Russia's latest attacks and Ukrainian intelligence data indicate that the Russians are working on large-scale production of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. However, with the onset of the cold season, the Russians will not rely exclusively on a single type of weapon, Khrapchynskyi emphasises. Instead, Russia is building a complex synergy in which each weapon will have its own purpose.
"Classic piston-engined drones and cheap decoys overload our radar detection systems and exhaust mobile fire teams. Jet-powered UAVs reduce reaction times and force us to scramble fighter aircraft and deploy medium-range surface-to-air missile systems. Ballistic missiles attempt to strike at moments when the system is under the greatest strain.
This is a carefully calculated layered tactic in which each wave has its own functional task," Khrapchynskyi concluded.
Ukraine is already preparing for the new challenges that Russian attacks may bring in the autumn. The frequent alerts about threats are already hurting Ukraine's economy, as businesses effectively have to halt their operations. If the attacks intensify as the cold weather sets in, the situation will become even more difficult. Therefore, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that the government is already preparing changes to how institutions and transport operate during air-raid warnings so that the country can adapt to the new reality.
Tetiana Kryvishyn

The deal covers the David’s Sling, Spyder, and Barak MX systems, which are expected to be incorporated into Greece’s planned multi-layered Achilles Shield air defense network.
Israel’s Rafael is expected to receive the largest share of the contract, supplying David’s Sling, designed to counter ballistic and other heavy missile threats, as well as the mobile Spyder system for drones and other airborne threats.
Israel Aerospace Industries will supply the Barak MX system, designed to intercept aircraft and missiles, according to the newspaper.
The project also includes a nationwide command-and-control network linking the systems and coordinating interceptions.
The network is expected to use artificial intelligence to process information from radar and sensors, classify threats and select the appropriate interception system.
Spyder batteries are expected to be deployed on Greek islands, while Greek defense companies are set to receive around €700 million ($820 million) in work under the project.
 
Israeli financial daily Calcalist and news website Yedioth Ahronoth reported Friday that the €3.1 billion ($3.6 billion) project would be implemented in stages over roughly 35 months.
The Achilles Shield network is expected to connect Greece’s existing air defenses, including Patriot systems, with David’s Sling, Spyder, and Barak MX under a unified network.
Calcalist said 12 Greek companies would account for at least 25% of the project after Athens sought greater domestic participation and technology transfer during negotiations.
The talks also covered Greek access to the systems’ software source code, which would give Athens greater autonomy in future maintenance and upgrades, according to the newspaper.
Greek daily Kathimerini also reported Friday that the deal is worth around $3.6 billion and is expected to be signed Monday.
If signed at the reported value, the deal would exceed Israel’s $3.5 billion sale of the Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany in 2023.
Neither Greece nor Israel had officially confirmed the agreement as of Sunday evening.

Jo Harper
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Meta said Tuesday it is rolling out an upgraded artificial intelligence system to detect online scams in Poland and will require all financial-services advertisers targeting Polish users to verify their identities following government pressure over fraudulent advertising on Facebook and Instagram.
Poland is among the first European countries where the US technology company is deploying the enhanced AI system, which is designed to detect scams and identify and block accounts impersonating celebrities, politicians, business figures and other public personalities.
Meta said it would also extend identity checks to all advertisers promoting financial services to users in Poland, with implementation expected to be completed within weeks.
The measures come after Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski asked the European Commission to fine Meta €250 million ($291 million) under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA).
The Polish government accused the company of failing to act effectively against fraudulent advertisements and deepfake content used to deceive users and obtain money.
Gawkowski’s request cited tests conducted by CERT Polska, the country’s computer emergency response team operated by state research institute NASK.
Researchers reported 122 advertisements they considered clearly fraudulent to Meta. According to the ministry, 106, or 86.8%, were not removed following the reports.
The Commission has said it will examine evidence provided by Polish authorities.
Meta, however, says its existing anti-fraud measures are producing substantial results. The company said reports by Polish users of scam advertisements fell 83% between July 2024 and June 2026.
The dispute has intensified amid growing concern in Poland over advertisements using artificially generated images and videos of well-known figures to promote fraudulent investments and other scams.
Polish entrepreneur and InPost chief executive Rafal Brzoska, whose image has repeatedly appeared in fake advertisements, has also campaigned for tougher action against online platforms.

Germany Accuses Russia of Leipzig Airport Drone Sabotage Attempt. Here’s Everything We Know
Germany has formally accused the Russian government for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport last month, describing the incident as “dangerous behavior” and part of a concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through hybrid warfare, The Guardian reported on September 2.
A US intelligence assessment conducted with German security agencies previously determined that the device used in the plot showed characteristics typical of Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU). German investigators subsequently recovered multiple drones and traces of military-grade explosives around the airport perimeter during their search.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul confirmed that all indications pointed to the Russian state providing the equipment and recruiting “low-level agents” to carry out the sabotage.
The incident occurred on August 4, when a drone carrying 600 grams of explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The detonator failed to ignite, preventing a catastrophe. In response, Berlin announced a package of retaliatory measures.
As reported by The Guardian, Wadephul stated that Germany saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation” and would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action.” He added: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”
Wadephul further characterized the attack as part of broader “attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression”.
Germany’s retaliatory measures include closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, shuttering the Russian House in Berlin, tightening border controls, and cracking down on Russia’s shadow fleet. According to The Guardian, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s proposed 22nd sanctions package targeting 1,600 additional Russian entities.
In addition to sanctions, Berlin will reportedly deliver extra IRIS-T surface-to-air missiles and “several thousand attack drones” to Ukraine in September while strengthening intelligence sharing, Handelsblatt reported, citing government sources.
German officials noted that “Ukraine has been very successful militarily in recent months, largely thanks to German assistance,” leaving Moscow with no strategic response on the battlefield except escalation. “We must prepare for further, escalating hybrid attacks from Russia,” the government warned.
International leaders, including the French and Italian prime ministers, expressed full solidarity. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney stated: “Attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence–and it will fail. Our support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s aggression is unshakeable,” The Guardian wrote.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin dismissed the sanctions, calling them “another mistake, a serious one” that “runs counter to the interests of the German people,” according to The Guardian.
Domestically, the government had faced pressure to act decisively against Russian threats. As The Guardian noted, Konstantin von Notz, a German Green party security policy expert, previously criticized the government’s approach, stating: “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken”.
In response to Germany’s official attribution, Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev threatened direct military strikes against German infrastructure.
“They deserve a direct strike on all German military equipment production facilities for the Bandera clique. And quite possibly on several other locations in Berlin as well,” Medvedev wrote on Telegram social media, claiming without evidence that Berlin had fabricated the Leipzig incident.

Where is the best bar in Europe? It’s in Budapest according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:31:27 UTC
22:31:27 KST

From Budapest’s famous ruins to centuries-old Belgian boozers and wonderfully eccentric drinking dens, these are the European bars where atmosphere, character and local culture matter more than polish, according to a new ranking.
You can learn a lot about a city by ticking off its top landmarks, museums and monuments, but if you really want to get under its skin, there’s arguably no better place to start than at the bar.
From centuries-old pubs to gloriously chaotic drinking dens, Europe’s best watering holes offer a glimpse into local life that you won’t find in your usual guidebook.
Now, the European Bar Guide, an independent website which publishes reviews of the best pubs and bars across the continent, has revealed its annual ranking of Europe’s 100 best bars.
On its website, the guide says it rates venues “simply on how well they do what they’re trying to do”, with a focus on “spectacle, atmosphere, social scene, intriguing customs, local culture and yes, the quality and choice of drinks”. It also adds that “sometimes a bar’s deficiencies can be handsomely compensated for in other ways”.
That means that, unlike other rankings, glitz and glamour are not the most important thing, so it’s little surprise that Szimpla Kert, Budapest’s original ruin bar, topped the list.
These are the top 10 best bars in Europe, according to the ranking.
The 10 best bars in Europe
Szimpla Kert, Budapest, Hungary
The Hungarian capital is well-known for its ruin bars – spots that are housed inside abandoned or “ruined’ buildings, and Szimpla Kert was the first, launching in 2002.
Located inside an abandoned factory, the bar guide calls a visit here “like entering a portal to another dimension”.
It’s a maze of graffiti-covered rooms, mismatched furniture, fairy lights and wonderfully random objects, all arranged around a leafy courtyard.
Throughout the week, you can drink pálinka, a traditional fruit spirit, or smoke shisha while sitting in a converted car or a bathtub chopped in half.
On Sundays, though, the chaos takes a more wholesome turn as local producers fill the space with cheese, bread, honey and Hungarian treats, often accompanied by live films and music.
Retsins Lucifernum, Bruges, Belgium
Famous for its vast array of beers, Belgium appears five times in the top 10 and Retsins Lucifernum is in second place, with the guide calling this spot in Bruges “a departure into another world entirely” and “simply unmissable”.
This quirky bar is actually the home of a local celebrity named Don "Willy" Retsin, who introduces himself at the door as the "butler" and claims to be a vampire.
The space is packed full of antiques, gothic art and ephemera which leads to a downstairs bar and courtyard garden.
The bar seats just 20 guests, so advance planning is a must if you want to sample unusual cocktails and speak to others experiencing the madness too.
La Fleur en Papier Doré, Brussels, Belgium
La Fleur en Papier Doré is a wonderfully atmospheric Brussels brown café - a traditional, cosy neighborhood pub named for its dark wood interiors and warm lighting – with frosted windows, stained glass, wood, old tiled floors and walls crowded with medieval-style artwork and floral curiosities.
Once a favourite meeting place for Magritte and Brussels’ surrealist crowd, it now draws a cosmopolitan mix of locals and curious travellers.
The Belgian beer list is reasonably priced, while music and local events add to the cosy, lived-in atmosphere.
Goupil Le Fol, Brussels, Belgium
Goupil Le Fol is a candle-lit rabbit hole of low ceilings, vinyl records, old books, portraits and 1950s jazz memorabilia, hidden just off Brussels’ tourist trail.
Follow the narrow passage past the original Wurlitzer jukebox and into its cosy upholstered rooms, where records hang from the ceiling and books cover the walls.
The Belgian beer selection is solid, but fruity wines laced with Cassis and Cognac are the real draw.
Zlatna Ribica, Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina
According to the guide, many bars in Bosnia and Herzegovina are a little too western-influenced, but this must-visit place in the capital Sarajevo is a true tribute to what makes the country special.
Zlatna Ribica, which translates as gold fish, is described as wonderfully eccentric and like a mad professor’s study, crammed with antiques, ornate lampshades, waxed sideboards and books, with the clutter spilling out onto the street.
Every surface seems to hide another oddity, from crenellated furniture to a tiny black-and-white TV in the bathroom showing lions mating in the Savannah.
Recline among the chaos with a cocktail or local beer and enjoy one of Europe’s most quirky drinking spots.
Papa Joe’s Jazz Lokal, Cologne, Germany
The ranking’s authors say Papa Joe’s is “one of the ultimate jazz bars on the globe”, and it’s actually one of Germany’s oldest jazz bars.
This wonderfully unpretentious watering hole is all about fun, with stage-like seating facing daily live concerts, a scoreboard announcing the evening’s line-up and mechanical puppets seemingly playing instruments behind the bar.
There’s even a cocktail machine and Roman ruins tucked beneath the entrance.
Friendly, loud and very unrefined, it’s the kind of place that sweeps you up in the action.
t’Brugse Beertje, Bruges, Belgium
Despite not being the first pub in Bruges in this list, the ranking hails t’Brugs Beertje as “the best pub” in the city.
A cosy, wood-panelled brown café, it boasts an enormous Belgian beer menu which comes in an almanac-style book that takes time to work through, while shelves of gleaming glasses hang above the bar.
Pair a Flemish red or Oud Bruin with Gouda, meat platters or other simple snacks, then settle into the snug, communal atmosphere. It’s hugely popular, but the wait is worth it.
Bar Marsella, Barcelona
Bar Marsella has welcomed plenty of famous names over the past two centuries, with the likes of Ernest Hemingway, Pablo Picasso and Salvador Dalí all said to have drunk here.
Today, you can order the same famous absinthe and imagine the artists and writers who once soaked up the bar’s wonderfully bohemian atmosphere.
Barcelona’s Bar Marsella looks as though it has barely changed in two centuries – and that’s exactly the appeal.
Behind its faded façade are cracked plaster walls, dark wood panelling, dusty bottles and a wonderfully decaying old-world atmosphere. Order the famous absinthe, settle in and soak up one of the city’s most atmospheric drinking institutions.
U Hrocha, Prague, Czechia
Described as “the epitome of a traditional Czech boozer” in the ranking, U Hrocha – or ‘the hippo’ – is a wonderfully old-fashioned Czech pivnice in the Malá Strana district, with five communal tables, leaning posts, a tiny bar and plenty of atmosphere.
Though opened as a pub in 1994, it feels far older.
Try well-priced Czech beer as the room fills with locals and visitors. Intimate, traditional and unpolished, it’s Czech pub culture at its best.
Le Pot au Lait, Liège, Belgium
Le Pot au Lait is one of those bars where the décor is almost as much of a draw as the drinks.
Hidden behind a narrow courtyard in the heart of Liège, this 19th-century former house is filled with bizarre artwork, cartoon gorillas, carnival scenes, macabre taxidermy, graffiti and huge plants, creating a wonderfully surreal, slightly spooky atmosphere.
It began life as a student meeting place in the 1970s and has since become a much-loved local institution, with communal tables, a terrace and plenty of strange little corners to settle into.
Expect Belgian beers, a lively crowd and the feeling that you’ve stumbled into a bar, art gallery and funfair all at once.

Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks stall

Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks remain stalled
Israeli strikes killed one person and wounded another in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh on Wednesday, according to Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency, after the Israeli military said it had struck the area in response to an alleged Hezbollah drone attack on its forces.
The NNA said the casualties resulted from an Israeli drone strike on the al-Ruwaiss and al-Maasouma Garden neighbourhoods of Nabatieh. Further Israeli strikes later hit the Nabatieh area, with local media reporting heavy explosions around Kfar Tebnit and circulating footage of a large column of smoke.
The Israeli military claimed that Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards soldiers operating near the Ali al-Taher Ridge, close to Nabatieh. It said troops fired at and intercepted one of the drones and that no Israeli personnel were injured. Israel said it subsequently targeted what it alleged to be "Hezbollah infrastructure" used to plan attacks on its troops and civilians.
Hezbollah had not publicly commented on the Israeli allegation by Wednesday afternoon. The group has not claimed responsibility for attacks on Israeli targets in recent weeks.
Air raid sirens sounded briefly on Tuesday night in Tuval and Ma’ayan Baruch in northern Israel, near the Lebanese border, amid the alleged drone incident. Lebanese media later reported additional Israeli attacks across the south, including in Mansouri, Houla and Qantara.
The Ali al-Taher Ridge, a high point near Nabatieh overlooking areas of south Lebanon and northern Israel, has become a particular focus of Israeli operations. Israel has alleged that Hezbollah maintains underground military infrastructure in the area, while the elevation gives forces operating there a wide view of the surrounding border region.
Rome talks remain deadlocked
The attacks came a day after US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. Israeli National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra also attended the meeting, according to images issued by Netanyahu’s office, which did not disclose the substance of the discussion.
The meeting took place before an anticipated eighth round of US-mediated Lebanese-Israeli talks in Rome. No official date has been announced, though Lebanese broadcaster MTV reported that the next session could be held on 15-16 September. In a statement on X, Huckabee claimed Hezbollah was the only obstacle to progress in the negotiations.
The talks are based on a US-brokered framework agreed on 26 June, under which Israeli forces would withdraw in phases from southern Lebanon while the Lebanese army deploys to designated areas and non-state armed infrastructure is dismantled. The arrangement has been slowed by disagreements over the sequencing of any Israeli withdrawal, the scope and pace of the Lebanese army’s deployment, and how compliance would be independently verified.
Israel has demanded assurances that areas transferred to Lebanese state control are clear of Hezbollah weapons and military positions. Lebanon, meanwhile, has sought a further Israeli withdrawal and resisted proposals that could amount to a permanent "security belt" or buffer zone inside its territory. Hezbollah has rejected arrangements affecting its weapons, leaving the army’s role in any eventual implementation politically sensitive.
Separately, the Lebanese Armed Forces said it was responding to what it described as "fabricated claims" by Israeli media concerning the army’s positions and operational role in southern Lebanon. In a statement issued on Wednesday, it said the reports sought to undermine internal cohesion and public confidence in the institution and its leadership.
The statement did not identify a specific report or outlets. But it appears to be intended to counter claims often by Israeli media outlets to cast doubt on the Lebanon army’s performance, loyalties or ability to carry out its southern missions at a moment when it is expected to be central to any eventual Israeli withdrawal and security arrangement. The army said its personnel remained committed to the command’s directives and to defending Lebanese sovereignty, security and stability.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities erupted in October 2023.

Introducing TIME Trailblazers: Designing and Making the Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:37 UTC
22:30:37 KST

In 2005, following Hurricane Katrina’s devastating August landfall, Resilience Force founder and executive director Saket Soni moved to Louisiana to help the workers facilitating the state’s recovery. Confronted by the realities of the storm’s aftermath, Soni had a clarifying conversation with his mentor, historian Vincent Harding, who, he said, told him that the country they lived in was a work in progress: "This is a place that's still being built, and you're part of building it.”
To this day, it’s this ethos that underpins Soni’s advocacy, in which he supports and protects the crews who rebuild after disaster. It also provides a powerful shorthand for the apparent mission of every innovator featured on our inaugural TIME Trailblazers list, which recognizes those leaders who, across the world, are designing and making the future.
Among them: Aicha Evans of Zoox, who imagines a future where our roads are dotted by safe, and time-efficient, robotaxis. Bjarke Ingels, a visionary architect who helped design The Dryline, the U.S.’s largest urban climate adaptation project. Mike Schultz, a gold-medalist whose company, BioDapt, creates prosthetics used by many athletes in the Paralympics. And Jason Ballard, the CEO of Icon, which 3D prints homes he hopes “will become a part of humanity’s toolkit”—and potentially help solve the growing housing crisis.
This is a world full of potential, promise, and problems to solve. This is a world that is still being built. These 14 Trailblazers are standout examples of the many committed to building it.

Kaushik Kappagantulu’s Greenhouse in a Box Is Aiding India’s Farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:37 UTC
22:30:37 KST

Kaushik Kappagantulu’s grandmother raised eight kids and 20 grandkids, including him, mostly by herself in the bustling Indian city of Hyderabad. An educated woman, she taught Kappagantulu that if you work hard, you will succeed. But after graduating from engineering college and doing a volunteer program teaching homeless kids, Kappagantulu realized this was not the case for everyone. “In rural India, most of the people work really hard, but because of a lack of access to different things, their hard work does not convert into success,” he tells TIME.
This revelation prompted Kappagantulu to dedicate himself to uplifting others. For six years he worked with school dropouts, helping them access jobs through vocational training. “Every single one of those kids was from a farming family and they were coming to us because farming was failing,” he says.
Sensing a systemic problem that needed addressing, Kappagantulu pivoted to agriculture. In 2015, he launched an agri-tech enterprise called Kheyti, which means farming in Hindi. The goal was to help the more than 100 million smallholder farmers who produce the bulk of India’s staple foods like rice, wheat, and pulses. And one of the biggest challenges facing farmers today is the changing climate.
In India, the combination of extreme heat, unseasonable rain, and depleting groundwater is making it difficult for farmers to grow during the summer season from March to June. During a heatwave this April, sensors installed by Kheyti recorded ground temperatures on multiple farms hitting 125 degrees Fahrenheit. “Climate change is wiping out their hard work,” says Kappagantulu, adding that the average Indian farmer earns about $1,000 a year. “It is not even enough for them to make ends meet,” he says.
Kheyti’s solution was a low-cost modular “greenhouse-in-a-box.” These net houses are designed to be smaller than conventional greenhouses, suitable for the one-acre farmer. They have shade cloth on top, which reduces internal temperatures by about 9 degrees Fahrenheit, and drip irrigation. Each greenhouse is also paired with an AI-powered tool that offers farmers advice on things like choosing the best crops and managing pests. This model works: Farmers reduce their crop losses by 58% while using 67% less water and 70% less fertilizer. Farmers using Kheyti’s structures also increased their net income, earning three times what non-Kheti farmers did on the same amount of land. And thanks to Kheyti’s partnerships with local governments, subsidies and low-cost loans mean the greenhouses are relatively affordable, each costing between $200 to $300. “We have to be the bridge that makes high tech agriculture accessible to the poorest farmer,” Kappagantulu says.
The greenhouse-in-a-box concept won the Earthshot Prize in 2022. It’s been growing ever since, with Kheyti now working with roughly 7,000 farmers across eight Indian states. Kappagantulu aims to double this over the next 12 months with the support of the Indian government, which has recommended states partner with the company.
Kappagantulu hopes to take the greenhouses global in the next three years and has a pipeline of other products, including flexible solar panels that can be installed on top of the greenhouses. His aim is to help one million farmers build secure, climate-smart livelihoods by 2033. But he knows he can’t do it alone. “Long-term change in the climate sector for agriculture doesn’t happen through one solution or one organization,” he says, “but through forming coalitions.”
