Chinese President Xi Jinping has backed Middle Eastern nations in building a new security architecture and said the Palestinian issue should not be marginalised.
Xi made the remarks during summit-level talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el Sisi in Cairo, China's state-run Xinhua News Agency reported on Wednesday.
"China supports regional countries in building a new security architecture for the Middle East," Xi said, opposing external interference in the region.
"Middle East people should remain masters of their own affairs, and external interference should be rejected," he said, calling on China and Egypt to "jointly oppose unilateralism and acts of bullying."
Xi called for a "comprehensive solution for common security" in the region and said the Palestinian issue "remains the core of the Middle East question and should never be overlooked or marginalised."
He also called for support for the UN's "effective role" in the region and urged external powers to abandon "double standards" in the Middle East.
Amid tensions in the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Iran war, Xi said China was "ready to work” with the Middle East countries to “safeguard the security of international shipping lanes".
Xi arrived in Cairo on Tuesday for a two-day state visit, his first to Egypt in 10 years.
The Chinese president and Sisi discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation and regional developments during their talks at Al-Ittihadiya Palace in Cairo.
Xi called on China and Egypt to "create new highlights for cooperation in green energy, electric vehicles, aerospace, the digital economy and modern agricultural technology."
Egypt became the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China in 1956.
The two countries established a strategic partnership in 1999 and upgraded ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership in December 2014.

LUCKNOW: The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust has appointed three new trustees, bringing into its governing body a philanthropist associated with the legacy of late VHP leader Ashok Singhal, a former public representative from Ayodhya and an educationist from Shikohabad whose family has links with the Indian Air Force, the RSS and the erstwhile Jana Sangh.The appointments of Mahesh Bhagchandka, Madan Mohan Pandey and Nirmala Yadav were announced after the Trust’s meeting in Ayodhya on Wednesday. The three have filled vacancies in the Trust’s governing body.Mahesh Bhagchandka, 68, is founder-trustee of the Ashok Singhal Foundation, is related to Ashok Singhal, one of the prominent figures associated with the Ram Janmabhoomi movement. Bhagchandka is also a graduate, businessman based in New Delhi. He is also the author of Hindutva ke Purodha, a book on prominent figures associated with the Hindutva movement.He participated in the rituals as a yajman during both the bhoomi pujan ceremony for the construction of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi temple and the temple’s pran pratishtha programme. His association with Ram-related cultural initiatives also includes work connected with the Shri Ram Van Gaman Yatra.Bhagchandka has been involved in the installation of Shri Ram Stambhs at 292 sacred sites associated with the route believed to have been taken by Lord Ram during his exile.
He is also a member of the executive committee of the World Hindu Economic Forum.
His appointment gives the Trust a member with experience in social and cultural initiatives as well as temple-related programmes. He is also related to late Vishwa Hindu Parishad leader Ashok Singhal and is a founder-trustee of the Ashok Singhal Foundation.Madan Mohan Pandey 74, is a law graduate and advocate based in Ayodhya Cantonment. He represented Shri Ram Lalla Virajman and late Mahant Ramchandra Paramhans Das in the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi legal dispute from 1990 to 2019 before the Allahabad High Court and the Supreme Court.His long association with the temple case places him among those who were directly involved in the legal proceedings that culminated in the Supreme Court judgment paving the way for the construction of the Ram temple at Ayodhya.Pandey also served as Uttar Pradesh’s additional advocate general for six years. Besides his legal practice, he is associated with religious and educational activities. He is the vice-president of the Shri Hari Satsang Samiti and the patron of the Kathakar Yojana training centre in Ayodhya.The third appointee, Nirmala Yadav, comes from a family with a long association with education and public life in Firozabad district. Yadav herself originally hailed from Etah and moved to Shikohabad after her marriage.

Priyadarshini Upadhaya, the present principal of Mahatma Gandhi Vidyalaya and a former colleague of Yadav, described her as a highly capable administrator. She said Yadav had a strong command over institutional management and was particularly efficient in handling administrative and desk responsibilities.Yadav’s late husband, advocate Harendra Yadav, had served as an RSS district chief. Her father-in-law, Squadron Leader Surya Kumar Yadav, served in the Indian Air Force and was later associated with the Jan Sangh.According to her nephew Sachin Yadav, the family’s association with education dates back to 1916, when his great-grandfather, Chaudhary Shyam Singh Yadav, founded Kanhai College in Shikohabad. The family also produced a former MLA, Captain Nihal Singh and Squadron Leader Surya Kumar Yadav.

Scarcity of women directors at Venice due to 'systemic issue' says Gyllenhaal
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:50:04 CEST
21:50:04 KST

The under-representation of female
directors in Venice and at other international film festivals is
due to a "systemic issue",  jury chair Maggie Gyllenhaal told a
press conference before the 83rd edition of the world's oldest
film fest Wednesday, noting that only two women are up for the
Golden Lion this year compared to six last year.
                                    
                                       
				 "I think it's finally become clear that men make better films
than women," Gyllenhaal initially responded with a quip that got
the audience laughing when asked about the lack of female
directorial talent on show.
                                    
                                       
				"I'll answer seriously, there's a systemic problem," Gyllenhaal
added during the press conference with festival director Alberto
Barbera and the chairs of this year's other juries.
                                    
                                       
				"I think it's much more difficult for women than men to get
funding for their films. Furthermore, it's possible that the
themes women tackle, having had a different life experience,
aren't always considered high-level art.
                                    
                                       
				"But who decides what's good? Who decides what has value?
"I must also say, sitting next to one of the people who make
these decisions, that there are a lot of women on this panel and
that my jury also includes incredible female directors. "In any
case, it's a question I ask myself, too, and it's a legitimate
question."
When asked if Barbera thinks it's true that female filmmakers
are penalized for the themes they tackle, the director clarified
that "in the very long selection process, there's no bias
regarding form or content; the only criterion is the quality of
the film."
For Gyllenhaal, however, "there's a lot of confusion about
what's being valued.
                                    
                                       
				"I think it's still been a short time since women had the
opportunity to make films, and it will take time to get used to
the fact that many of them make them very differently from men."
Among the other questions for the Venice 83 jury president was
one about a festival taking place in the midst of a period of
conflict.
                                    
                                       
				"I'll talk about it more in depth tonight (on opening night,
ed.), but we could ask ourselves: 'How is it possible that we're
talking about cinema right now, when the world is in a state of
emergency?'
"For me, the answer has to do with empathy. I believe cinema
offers the opportunity to find empathy within ourselves.
                                    
                                       
				"Personally, I don't think there's a topic, for any filmmaker,
that doesn't deserve to be told.
                                    
                                       
				"I believe we can challenge ourselves by listening to stories
about the most corrupt and perverse people, because it offers us
the opportunity to feel empathy for them and even to reflect on
how we might have a dark side, a perversion, a corruption within
ourselves, and try to fight it, as much as we can.
                                    
                                       
				Gyllenhaal said she believes that "if films truly offer an
honest look at other people's experiences, then they are
fundamentally and inevitably political, among many other
things."
As for her career, "I think I've probably always been a
director, but I didn't see any women around me who were. There
were some, of course, but I just wasn't cool enough to know
Agnès Varda when I was a 16-year-old living in California,"
observes the actress and filmmaker, who directed The Dark
Daughter, which premiered in 2021 at Venice, and this year's
Bride!.
                                    
                                       
				"The people I admired were actresses who had a point of view,
who had an artistic impact on the film they were making, who
were co-narrators with their directors, and there were several,
like Gena Rowlands with her husband (John) Cassavetes.
                                    
                                       
				"I'm thinking of Ingrid Bergman, of Ellen Burstyn, who is the
protagonist of the short film I shot (debuting on the Lido in
the next few days, ed.).
                                    
                                       
				"In reality, however, I then realized that acting wasn't the
right job for me."
Even when making a beloved film like cult S&M classic Secretary,
she said, "I felt like I was pushing a boundary that I didn't
know how much I could express."

Ukraine officially notifies ICAO that Russian airspace is unsafe – Foreign Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:49:45 EEST
21:49:45 KST

Ukraine has officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) that Russian airspace is unsafe for civil aviation due to intensified military activity, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andriy Sybiha reported.
"We urge everyone to avoid it. Russia has been deliberately ignoring the existing threats as a result of its aggression against Ukraine, which has already led to several incidents in the past years. Against the backdrop of Russia’s drastic escalation of terror against Ukraine, Russian airspace is becoming increasingly unsafe," Sybiha wrote on X on Wednesday.
At the same time, he emphasized that Ukraine is exercising its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter, and the war is "coming home to Russia."
"This is our responsible decision to notify ICAO and all airlines, and governments to take caution — even if Russia refuses to fulfill its responsibility to inform them. We want to prevent unintended incidents," Sybiha stressed.
As reported, in an evening video address on September 1, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine is warning every airline using Russian airspace, as well as everyone using key Russian airports, that Russian skies are becoming completely unsafe, while Ukraine does not threaten civil aviation. The President noted that although the Russian authorities do not report this as required, "Russian skies will de facto close: the war unleashed by Russia is closing its skies."
Head of the Presidential Office of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov supported Zelenskyy on the same day, stating: "Russian skies are no longer safe. This is a new reality about which we are officially warning international airlines, insurers, and partners."

One of the largest in the Baltic: the Defense Forces struck an oil refinery in Ust-Luga
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:48:18 EEST
21:48:18 KST

One of the largest in the Baltic: the Defense Forces struck an oil refinery in Ust-Luga
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian forces struck the NOVATEK-Ust-Luga complex, with a capacity of more than 6 million tonnes per year. The facility meets the needs of the Russian army.
On Tuesday, September 1, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the NOVATEK-Ust-Luga oil refinery in the settlement of the Leningrad Region of the Russian Federation, which is one of the largest on the Baltic Sea. The facility’s design capacity for processing stable gas condensate is more than 6 million tonnes per year, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports, UNN reports.
Details
The NOVATEK production complex in Ust-Luga is a complex for the fractionation and transshipment of stable gas condensate, located in the port of Ust-Luga. This enterprise produces oil (light and heavy), kerosene, a diesel fraction, and a marine fuel component (fuel oil).
The complex is part of NOVATEK’s production and logistics infrastructure at the port of Ust-Luga. It is also involved in meeting the needs of the Russian occupying army.

MiG-29 Shoots Down Russian Bandеrol with an R-60 Missile at Extremely Low Altitude
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:48:12 UTC
21:48:12 KST

The Ukrainian Air Force MiG-29 fighter jet, flying at extremely low altitude, shot down a Russian Bandеrol lightweight cruise missile using an R-60 missile.
The Telegram channel Sonyashnyk, affiliated with Ukraine’s Air Force, reported this.
The channel also published footage of the Ukrainian fighter conducting the interception.
The channel said a pilot flying a modernized MiG-29MU1 performed the air defense mission.
“Only a couple of seconds to make a decision: retreat or do everything possible to protect your loved ones?!” the channel wrote.
Using air-launched weapons at such low altitudes requires the pilot to make quick, well-considered decisions.
The R-60 is a Soviet lightweight guided air-to-air missile that entered service in late 1973. It is equipped with an infrared homing seeker that detects the heat radiation of an enemy aircraft or helicopter’s engines and is designed to engage maneuvering aerial targets at short distances.
By the beginning of the full-scale war with Russia, R-60 missiles were considered obsolete, as the Ukrainian arsenal had sufficient stocks of the newer R-73 missiles with better combat capabilities. However, the Ukrainian Air Force’s continuous interception of Russian cruise missiles and Shahed/Geran-2 kamikaze drones depleted missile stocks, necessitating the use of older short-range missiles.
In November 2025, Ihor Fedirko, Executive Director of the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry, discussed modernizing the R-60 air-to-air missile and adapting it for launch from ground-based systems in Militarnyi’s ZBROYA project. He emphasized that this is strictly a temporary solution that allows otherwise unusable old air-to-air missiles to be put to use.
When modernizing the R-60MK and other variants of the missile, analog components are replaced with digital ones, significantly increasing the sensitivity of the older infrared homing seekers. It has been reported that “some companies have achieved nearly a tenfold improvement in sensor sensitivity.”
Russian forces are increasingly attacking Ukrainian cities with S8000 Banderol lightweight cruise missiles, production of which is ramping up.
Banderol was designed and manufactured by JSC Kronstadt. The missile has a maximum speed of 620–650 km/h and a cruising speed of 520–560 km/h. It carries an OFBCh-150 high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing 114.3 kg, of which 49.5 kg is explosive. When launched from airborne platforms, the missile can travel up to 500 kilometers.

Katz: Gaza emigration plan is frozen after Arab states pressured Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:48:05 UTC
21:48:05 KST

Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that plans to facilitate the departure of Palestinians from Gaza remain under consideration despite being frozen for now, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu toured IDF positions inside the enclave and said Israel intended to maintain its hold along the Yellow Line.
Speaking at the “Decision Time: Democracy and Society” conference hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in cooperation with the Israel Democracy Institute, Katz said Israel was prepared to enable Gazans to leave by sea, air or other routes, but that Egypt was unwilling to allow such movement through its territory.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end. The Migration Directorate is ready to do this by sea, by air and by any means. Egypt is not willing for it to go through its territory,” Katz said.
Katz raised the issue after Ofer Winter, chairman of Amcha Yisrael, expressed support for emigration from the Gaza Strip and described it as the solution.
“Eighty percent want to emigrate. We are constantly checking this in surveys,” Katz said. “Hamas does not allow it and there are no countries in the world willing to take them in. What is delaying this is that the countries willing to take them in want US support.”
Katz said countries potentially willing to receive Palestinians from Gaza were seeking American backing before moving forward.
“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing. Trump has not canceled this at the moment — he has frozen it,” he said.
Katz claimed Arab governments had pressured US President Donald Trump to halt the initiative.
“All the Arab countries came to him, pressured him on this issue and said, ‘We will give you whatever you want — investments. We will agree to Hamas being disarmed in exchange for freezing this,’” he said.
“It has not been canceled. It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”
Katz said advancing the plan would ultimately require US support and argued that a future failure by Hamas to uphold its commitments could open the way for broader Israeli action.
“For this to happen, we need the United States — and the moment will come when it becomes clear that Hamas is not honoring its commitment. Then we will get the green light to advance militarily, territorially and in other areas as well,” he said.
At the same time, Netanyahu visited an IDF post inside the Gaza Strip near the Yellow Line, which separates territory controlled by the Israeli military from areas under Hamas control.
He was accompanied by IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Southern Command chief Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor and Brig. Gen. Elad Tzuri, commander of the 99th Division.
Netanyahu received a briefing from commanders on IDF activity along the line, operational missions in the area and efforts to remove threats.
“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal — disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”
Standing at the military position, Netanyahu pointed toward Israeli communities visible from the area.
“We control the territory here — you can see Ashkelon there, you can see all our communities in every direction: Sderot, Netivot and the kibbutzim,” he said.
Katz also described Israel as holding what he called “strategic control” over Gaza, while acknowledging that Hamas continued to operate in parts of the enclave.
“There is still work to do, but about 70% of the territory is essentially deserted. There are no residents, no homes and no tunnels,” he said.
“Ninety percent [of it] had an astonishing scale of tunnels that no one knew about. Day and night, we are thwarting the tunnels according to our directives and defending the borders, including the Philadelphi Corridor, where we prevent weapons from being smuggled.”
“Therefore, we have strategic control over Gaza,” Katz said. “Hamas still exists in the enclave covering 30-something percent [of the territory], but we have strategic control there. The policy is to act forcefully — we thwart [threats] every day.”

New team joins competition for UK’s Land Rover replacement program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:47:51 UTC
21:47:51 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems, Ford and Ricardo are teaming up to compete for the UK's Light Mobility Vehicle program, based on the Ford Ranger platform.
- The LMV requirement is part of the UK's broader Land Mobility Programme, valued at more than £4.8 billion over its first decade, aimed at replacing the Land Rover and Pinzgauer fleets by 2030.
General Dynamics Land Systems has teamed up with Ford Motor Company and Ricardo to compete for the UK Ministry of Defence’s Light Mobility Vehicle program, the companies announced.
The team’s proposal is built on the Ford Ranger platform, which General Dynamics UK described as Europe’s best-selling pickup truck for 11 consecutive years.
“Combining the strengths of three industry leaders, the team will deliver a proven, scalable, and cost-effective solution built on the Ford Ranger platform,” General Dynamics UK said. “Together, General Dynamics Land Systems, Ford and Ricardo bring a credible, low-risk and highly scalable proposition that meets the British Army’s needs while creating significant export opportunities and maximising value for the UK taxpayer.”
The Light Mobility Vehicle program is intended to replace the British Army’s aging Land Rover and Pinzgauer utility vehicle fleets, both of which are due to leave service by 2030. The LMV requirement forms one strand of the UK’s wider Land Mobility Programme, a modernization effort covering more than 11,000 vehicles across multiple weight classes that the Ministry of Defence launched to consolidate a patchwork of legacy fleets built up over decades, some dating back to operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.
The Land Mobility Programme is structured around several vehicle categories. The Light Mobility Vehicle segment alone is expected to cover roughly 2,500 vehicles, part of a broader program the Ministry of Defence has said could exceed £4.8 billion ($6.1 billion) in total value across its first decade. The program also includes a Light Protected Mobility category for vehicles up to 10,000 kilograms (22,046 pounds), and a Heavy Protected Mobility requirement covering platforms in the 20 to 30 tonne range, which replaced an earlier “medium” category the Ministry of Defence dropped from the program’s structure in January.
The Ministry of Defence first sought industry input on the LMV requirement through a Request for Information issued in January 2025, seeking a wheeled utility platform built on a common base to modernize roles currently filled by the Land Rover and Pinzgauer. That process specifically explored the potential for an off-the-shelf solution, rather than a bespoke design, to meet the requirement quickly. A formal tender notice for the LMV competition was expected imminently as of late July, according to trade publication Army Technology, with vehicle trials tentatively planned to run from October 2026 through January 2027.
General Dynamics Land Systems joins a competitive field for the LMV requirement that has already drawn interest from other established suppliers, including UK vehicle maker Supacat, which unveiled its own tactical Light Mobility Vehicle in late 2024 aimed at high-readiness units such as the Royal Marines’ 3 Commando Brigade and the British Army’s Ranger Regiment.
The wider Land Mobility Programme has separately seen the UK select Patria and Babcock’s Common Armoured Vehicle System for elements of its heavier vehicle requirements, a decision announced in September 2025 that also brought Norway into that program.

Zaporizhzhia’s largest mall closes as Russia’s attacks seek to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:46:28 UTC
21:46:28 KST

Zaporizhzhia’s largest shopping and entertainment complex, City Mall, will remain closed throughout September following a Russian drone strike on a neighboring hypermarket last week.
Russia’s attacks are increasingly disrupting the basic civilian life of Ukrainian cities, as strikes on shops and other commercial facilities make it harder for businesses to operate and residents to go about their daily lives. The pattern is especially pronounced in cities close to the front, where Russia is unable to seize territory but can continue attacking from the air.
City Mall announced the closure on 1 September, apologizing to visitors and saying it would provide updates on when operations could resume. The complex did not give an official reason for the decision.
The announcement came four days after a Russian strike hit an Epicentr hypermarket located near the mall on 28 August. The attack sparked a fire covering about 2,000 square meters.
Russia targets Ukraine’s civilian economy
Shopping centers and other commercial facilities have increasingly been caught up in Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian cities.
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up attacks on commercial sites and retail storage facilities, particularly in and around Kyiv, as well as other major cities closer to Russia and the frontlines.
On 21 August, a Russian drone strike on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih killed at least 15 people and injured 130, including 23 children, according to local authorities. A second strike hit emergency responders about 30 minutes later as they worked at the scene.
The attacks have also hit Ukraine’s retail sector financially. As of August, three shopping centers had been destroyed and nine more damaged by Russian attacks since the beginning of 2026, with direct losses to the sector reaching 3.226 billion hryvnias ($72.5 million), according to industry data cited by Censor.NET.
Fear of attacks is also keeping shoppers away. Air raid alerts accounted for 21.8% of shopping centers’ operating hours in August, up from 20.1% in July and 9.4% a year earlier.
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
Zaporizhzhia under Russian attack
For Zaporizhzhia, the pressure is particularly severe. The major city lies close to the front line and has faced sustained Russian attacks throughout the full-scale war.
Unable to seize the city through ground advances, Russia has repeatedly used missiles and drones to strike its infrastructure and civilian areas.
The result is a city where even businesses that survive direct strikes can be forced to close because of the continuing threat.

Ukrainian law enforcement authorities said Wednesday that they foiled an alleged plot by Russia’s FSB security service to assassinate an anti-Kremlin “opposition leader” in the capital Kyiv.
According to Ukrainian media reports, the target of the assassination attempt was Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of combat operations for the Russian Volunteer Corps, a unit of far-right Russians fighting alongside Ukrainian forces.
On Tuesday, the Russian Volunteer Corps said Kaplunov had been abducted outside his home days earlier.
In a statement, Ukraine’s SBU security service said “a group of individuals carried out an armed attack” against its investigators during a search. The agency’s special forces returned fire to subdue the attackers, detaining the assailants and wounding several.
The SBU said that the assailants belong to “one of the units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.” It added that prosecutors have launched an investigation into the attempted murder of law enforcement officials.
Ukraine’s SBU did not identify the Russian opposition figure who was said to have been targeted by the FSB.
That statement came after reports and videos of an alleged shootout in Kyiv between SBU officers and members of Ukraine’s HUR military intelligence agency.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was said to have reprimanded the leadership of both the SBU and HUR for initially keeping silent about the apparent clash between their agencies.
According to Zelensky’s communications adviser, Dmytro Litvin, the president demanded that the two agencies inform the public about what happened.
Russia’s FSB has not responded to Ukraine’s allegations.

Euroclear back in the spotlight: 4 countries eager to use €193 billion in Russian assets after all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:45:33 UTC
21:45:33 KST

The Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden are asking the European Commission, the EU’s executive, to devise a solution that would allow the frozen Russian assets held at Euroclear, the European securities depository, to be used to support Ukraine after all. This brings a matter that seemed to have been settled last December back onto the European negotiating table and puts Belgium back in the grinder.
Euroclear back in the spotlight: 4 countries eager to use €193 billion in Russian assets after all
The four countries raised this request last Thursday in a letter to the Commission. The fact that it is these countries in particular comes as little surprise. The Netherlands, Poland and Sweden were already in favour of this last year. In the Netherlands, the use of the frozen funds is even included in the Jetten government’s coalition agreement.
“These are countries that provide a great deal of support to Ukraine from their own budgets – more than the average,” says VRT’s EU correspondent Rob Heirbaut. “In fact, they would prefer not to have to do so any longer, which is why they are eying those Russian assets.”
It is notable, however, that Spain is on also board. “Spain has always kept a low profile on this issue until now and is certainly no champion when it comes to financial support for Ukraine,” says Heirbaut.
The issue is back on the table, just nine months after European leaders decided not to release the frozen funds. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever (Flemish nationalist) stood his ground at the time. The EU chose instead to borrow 90 billion euros on the capital markets and pass this on to Ukraine as an interest-free loan. That was supposed to suffice for 2026 and 2027.
“That appears not to be the case. That much is already clear,” says Heirbaut. “The war is only intensifying. Moreover, Europe had hoped that non-EU countries such as Canada and Japan would also contribute, but they have contributed less than promised.”
What does this mean for Belgium?
The request from the four countries is not addressed to Belgium, but to the European Commission. They are explicitly asking for a proposal that takes Belgian concerns into account, whereby the risk is spread across all EU Member States. At present, that risk lies largely with Belgium, as the majority of the frozen Russian assets are held at Euroclear in Brussels.
In August, three former senior officials put forward a proposal to this end: Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, the former German Defence Minister; Nathalie Loiseau, the former French European Affairs Minister, and Daleep Singh, who served as Deputy National Security Adviser under President Joe Biden.
‘They say: we can use a European decision to remove that money from Euroclear and transfer it to the EU, and also remove all liability from Belgium,’ explains Heirbaut. ‘They say that is legally possible. I assume those four countries are also in favour of this.’
Meanwhile, the Belgian position remains unchanged. Belgium does not want to bear the burden of legal claims and potential Russian countermeasures alone. It is therefore demanding unlimited solidarity from the other Member States. “At this stage, that is only to be expected,” says Heirbaut. “There isn’t a single proposal on paper yet, so countries are staking out their positions.”
The Belgian government’s hardline stance is partly due to recent developments in Moscow. A Russian court ordered Euroclear to pay damages of over 200 billion euros and upheld that ruling on appeal in July.
Euroclear does not recognise the jurisdiction of that court and has taken the matter to the Commercial Court in Brussels. Belgian PM De Wever fears harsher reprisals if the assets are actually seized.
According to VRT’s Rob Heirbaut, Belgium’s allies are the same countries as in December. France, where several banks also hold Russian assets, and Italy supported Belgium then and continues to do so.
“Who I find to be conspicuously silent is Germany,” says Heirbaut. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a complete U-turn by suddenly advocating the use of the assets. “At the moment, Germany is remaining conspicuously silent.”
What next?
According to Heirbaut, the European Commission is not yet working on a concrete plan. Last year, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that the assets would be used, but she now seems more cautious. “Apparently, they would rather wait until the heads of government have discussed the matter.”
That won’t happen until October, at the European summit. The agenda will include both support for Ukraine and the European multiannual budget. If it proves impossible to find funds for Ukraine through that budget, the Russian assets will once again come in focus.
What is at issue?
Euroclear is a Brussels-based financial institution that holds shares and bonds on behalf of banks and central banks and handles the settlement of stock market transactions. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Russian central bank’s reserves there have been frozen.
Across the EU, this amounts to approximately 210 billion euros in frozen Russian funds. The bulk of this, around 193 billion euros, is held by Euroclear. Russia cannot access these securities, but the money remains legally owned by Russia. Consequently, it cannot simply be seized.
The interest and dividends generated by these assets are paid into a blocked account. Euroclear uses them for reinvestment. The majority of the interest revenue is transferred to the European support fund for Ukraine. In total, Ukraine has already received 6.6 billion euros in interest income.

Germany tests Israeli missile after attempted Russian drone attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, officials said Wednesday, as Western powers race to bolster long-range defenses against what they see as a growing Russian threat.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles, in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 kilometers (310 miles), Germany's Defense Ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defense readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometers, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 kilometers in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defense company MBDA, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges.

Her husband, the prime minister, subsequently denied that there had been any "internal betrayal" on October 7.

Ex-ministers and diplomats urge tougher action against Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:40:24 UTC
21:40:24 KST

Ex-ministers and diplomats urge tougher action against Israel
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More than 230 former Dutch ministers, ambassadors, diplomats and civil servants have called on the cabinet to take far tougher measures against Israel, including a full arms embargo and the suspension of the European Union’s trade agreement with the country.
The appeal comes as the Netherlands prepares to enforce its ban on settlement goods on September 22.
That measure led Israel to expel two Dutch officials from the US-backed Gaza ceasefire centre last week. The signatories say steps of this kind fall far short of what the situation demands.
Those who signed include former Amsterdam mayor Job Cohen, former foreign minister Jozias van Aartsen, former Rotterdam mayor Ahmed Aboutaleb, former development minister Jan Pronk and former defence minister Joris Voorhoeve.
According to NRC, the signatories held office for the Labour party (PvdA), the Christian Democrats (CDA) and the right-wing liberal VVD.
In the letter, the group calls for a complete arms embargo, the suspension of the EU-Israel trade agreement, and an investigation into possible involvement in international crimes by Dutch nationals and by Israelis living in the Netherlands who have served in the Israeli army.
The Netherlands already restricts some military exports to Israel. The signatories want measures that, in their words, match the scale of the violations taking place.
One of the signatories, former diplomat Angélique Eijpe, who left the foreign ministry over its stance on Gaza, said government policy had barely shifted. “We had cautiously hoped the Jetten cabinet would choose a different course,” she told broadcaster NOS in Dutch. “We see steps that mainly have a symbolic impact but do not bring about a change in behaviour.”
It is not the first such appeal – some of the same figures called for international intervention in Gaza a year ago, following a similar call earlier in 2025.
Eijpe said the group did not expect the letter to change policy overnight. “But the situation is so serious that we consider it necessary to keep putting it on the radar,” she told NOS.

21:40:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Tourism Administration recently reminded travel agencies to file reports about groups traveling to China or face fines of up to NT$50,000 (US$1,500), reports said Wednesday.
The warning level for travel to China issued by the Mainland Affairs Council stands at orange, advising against non-essential travel to China. The government recently pointed out the case of a former Amnesty International staffer facing hours of questioning by immigration after his arrival in Shanghai on a business trip.
Despite an official ban on Taiwanese tour groups heading to China, they have been assisting travelers and forming groups, supposedly for research or exchange purposes, per Liberty Times. Even in the event of individuals forming groups to travel in China, Hong Kong, and Macau, the details of the itinerary should be registered, the government said.
New immigration regulations China plans to implement on Sept. 15 will increase the risks of travel to China, according to MAC. Registration before the trip will allow the government to assist in the case of emergencies.
The Tourism Administration sent letters to travel agencies telling them to register groups from Sept. 1. The tour operators also need to remind travelers of the risks.
The administration said it had asked travel associations to tell member agencies about the rules, and the possibility of fines ranging from NT$10,000 to NT$50,000 if they failed to comply, Liberty Times reported.

TEHRAN/KUWAIT CITY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- At least 19 people, including military personnel and civilians, were killed in overnight U.S. strikes across several provinces in Iran, as the country's armed forces retaliated by attacking U.S. bases and assets in the region, Iranian media reported Wednesday.

The report said U.S. strikes on southern Lavan Island killed three members of the Basij volunteer force of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), while four members of the IRGC's Aerospace division were killed in strikes on the western province of Kermanshah.
A commando, identified as Malek Mousavi-Tabar, was killed Wednesday morning during operations to counter the movements of an invading drone in Bahmai County in the western Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad province, it added.
It also cited provincial authorities as saying that four people were killed and 68 others wounded in a U.S. attack targeting a wedding ceremony in Sirik County in southern Hormozgan province. The victims included one four-year-old child, a teenager and two women.
In a post on social media platform X earlier in the day, U.S. Central Command said its forces had "successfully completed a wave of strikes against Iranian military targets," citing "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
In retaliation for the U.S. strikes, Iran's IRGC and army announced that they targeted U.S. bases and assets in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In statements published on its official news outlet Sepah News, the IRGC said its forces shot down a "hostile" U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and launched ballistic missiles toward Camp Titin in Jordan, reportedly killing "a large number of" U.S. troops and destroying several key facilities and combat helicopters.

It noted that its ground forces targeted with drones and missiles the headquarters and accommodation of the U.S. commander at the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, setting on fire a hangar of U.S. drones and a drone deployment ramp and destroying several unmanned aerial vehicles.
Its ground forces also launched a hybrid missile-drone strike on U.S. bases in Erbil, capital of Iraq's Kurdistan region, destroying a maintenance center, technical-equipment warehouses, and a system for guiding espionage balloons, all belonging to the U.S. Army, the IRGC added.
In statements published on its website, Iran's Army said its drone attacks targeted U.S. bases in Bahrain and the UAE.
It said it struck with kamikaze drones U.S. troops and radar facilities at the Shaikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain as well as the Al Minhad and Al Dhafra Air Bases in the UAE.
In a statement carried by Iranian media earlier in the day, Iran's main military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, warned that continued U.S. "malicious" acts in the region would draw "heavier, more extensive and more devastating" responses.
Meanwhile, in a statement on its official X account, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the Iranian attacks, calling them a "blatant violation of its sovereignty" and reiterating its full right to take necessary measures to "protect its security and interests." ■

South Africa could see hottest year on record in 2027 amid strong El Nino: weather service
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
20:38:40 CST
21:38:40 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Africa could face its hottest year on record in 2027 amid an intensifying strong El Nino event, the South African Weather Service (SAWS) has said.
In a statement on Tuesday, SAWS said a strong El Nino had formed in the Pacific Ocean and was likely to intensify during the Southern Hemisphere spring.
"The latest predictions are indicative that the El Nino will likely intensify further to become the strongest event in living memory," it said.
The latest weekly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the eastern central tropical Pacific Ocean have already exceeded the threshold for a very strong El Nino, SAWS said.
A strong El Nino is defined as sea surface temperatures more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above normal, while a very strong event exceeds 2 degrees.
According to SAWS, current forecasts indicate that the anomaly could surpass 3 degrees Celsius.
"Most El Nino events bring conditions of below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures to the southern African region," SAWS said, while noting that not every El Nino event results in drought.
The weather service's October to December 2026 forecast indicates below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures over most of South Africa, with similar conditions expected from November 2026 to January 2027.
"It should be noted that the expected very strong El Nino of 2026/27, in combination with global warming, will likely result in 2027 being the warmest year ever recorded," it said.
SAWS said the 2015/16 El Nino brought unprecedented heatwaves to southern Africa and warned that, if the expected below-normal rainfall occurs, a high frequency of potentially severe heatwaves could accompany the current event.
The agency said uncertainty remained over the eventual strength and regional impacts of the El Nino and that it would closely monitor risks including heatwaves and water scarcity. ■

What is Iran’s Castle Breaker missile, used against US bases?
Kheibar Shekan, Iran’s medium-range missile, is said to play a pivotal role in escalating US-Israel tensions.
Iran’s Kheibar Shekan missile, which means Castle Breaker in Persian, has emerged as one of the most talked-about weapons in the US-Israel war on Iran.
The medium-range ballistic missile has been used by Iran in strikes on US military targets and infrastructure in the Middle East this week, as Tehran aims to demonstrate that its missile arsenal remains well-stocked following six months of intermittent US and Israeli attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Moment US strikes on Iranian port city hit wedding party
- list 2 of 3US launches new strikes on Iran, denies its bases hit in Jordan
- list 3 of 3Top US lawmaker Mike Johnson says lying is part of some Iranians’ religion
The war entered a new phase this week following a lull in fighting for a month, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, close to the country’s strategic port of Bandar Abbas, on Monday. That prompted Iran to strike back at US military assets in Jordan.
Since then, the United States has carried out more attacks on various Iranian targets, with Tehran again responding in kind, targeting several US bases in the region, including in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
So, what is the Castle Breaker, what is it capable of, and what is the latest in the US-Israel war on Iran?
What is the Kheibar Shekan or Castle Breaker missile?
It is a medium-range ballistic missile which has been developed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as part of its wider range of missiles.
It is one of Iran’s newer medium-range missile systems, with a range of roughly 1,450km (901 miles), with a payload range (warhead capacity) of 449kg to 590kg (990 pounds to 1,300 pounds).
In comparison, the US has introduced the Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) during the conflict, described by its producer Lockheed Martin as long-range precision-strike missiles that can hit targets ranging from 60km (37 miles) to more than 499km (310 miles) away.
The US has also used Tomahawk cruise missiles, which are long-range, precision-guided weapons that can fly at low altitudes and hit targets up to 2,500km (1,550 miles) away.
The Kheibar Shekan was unveiled in 2022 and takes its name from Khaybar, the word for a fortified settlement associated with early Islamic history. Shekan means breaker or destroyer.
One of the missile’s key characteristics is its solid-fuel propulsion, which allows it to be launched within minutes during a crisis. Solid-fuel missiles are preloaded with fuel, so they do not need to be fuelled just before launch – a process that can take several hours. This makes them easier and safer to operate, less likely to be detected, and they require less logistical support for the transport of fuel.
The fuel is dense and burns rapidly, producing a brief but powerful thrust. It can also be stored for long periods without degrading or breaking down, unlike liquid fuel, which is more prone to deterioration.
Where has Iran used its Castle Breaker missile?
Iran has repeatedly stated that it has been using Kheibar Shekan missiles against US military positions in the region since the six-month conflict began with US-Israeli strikes on Tehran and other sites around Iran on February 28.
State broadcaster IRIB reported that Iranian forces deployed the missile in retaliatory attacks on US assets in Jordan this week.
On July 20, the IRGC released footage showing Kheibar Shekan alongside Fateh-110, Zolfaghar and Emad ballistic missiles being used in attacks on US military targets.
Four days prior, the IRGC said it had targeted a US jet maintenance facility and a new command-and-control centre in Jordan’s Azraq with Kheibar Shekan missiles.
What other missile systems does Iran have?
Iran has a combination of short-, medium- and long-range missiles at its disposal.
Short-range ballistic missiles, which have a range of roughly 150km to 800km (93-500 miles), are built to reach nearby military targets in rapid regional strikes.
Core systems include the Fateh variants: Zolfaghar, Qiam-1 and older Shahab-1/2 missiles. Their shorter range can be an advantage in a crisis as they can be launched in volleys, compressing warning time and making pre-emption harder.
Medium-range ballistic missiles, with a range of roughly 1,500km to 2,000km (900-1,200 miles), include systems such as Shahab-3, Emad, Ghadr-1, the Khorramshahr variants and Sejjil, alongside newer designs like Kheibar Shekan and Haj Qassem.
These missiles put Israeli targets and US-linked sites in the Gulf states within their range.
Iran also has an arsenal of cruise missiles such as Soumar, Ya-Ali, the Quds variants, Hoveyzeh, Paveh and Ra’ad. The Soumar has a range of 2,500km (1,553 miles).
Former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei had previously limited Iranian missile ranges to 2,200km (1,367 miles) but removed that limit following Israel’s 12-day war on Iran in June 2025.
What’s the latest in the US-Iran war?
The latest escalation has brought a period of relative calm to an end.
The US resumed attacks on Iranian targets on August 31, with US Central Command saying it had struck IRGC sites in southern Iran.
Iran responded with missiles and drones against US forces and military assets located in the region. On Tuesday, the US military said it had completed another wave of strikes against Iranian military targets.
Tehran reported that the US had also struck civilian targets, including a house which was bombed during a wedding celebration in the city of Kuhestak, killing at least five people and injuring 68, including women and children.
Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq’s Erbil in response.
US President Donald Trump previously threatened more attacks if Iran retaliated, while Tehran said it would also respond to US attacks.
The renewed fighting has also put the Strait of Hormuz back at the centre of the crisis as Iranian and US forces vie for control of the critical waterway.
Oil prices rose sharply this week as markets reacted to the renewed US-Iran fighting and the risk to energy shipments through the key waterway, through which 25 percent of the world’s oil and petroleum products are shipped in peacetime.
The US attacks come shortly after Washington announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, declaring that it would target its financial interests across the world.

Andy Burnham blames Tory legacy for leaving UK economy vulnerable

Unknown Publisher

12:38:33 UTC
21:38:33 KST

Andy Burnham blamed the Conservatives’ legacy for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil, in his first prime ministers’ questions clash with Kemi Badenoch, as the UK’s borrowing costs climbed further.
The Conservative leader compared the market pressure on Burnham’s second day to Liz Truss’s mini-Budget. But the prime minister said it was the Tories’ failure to address the UK’s growth and debt which meant the economy was exposed to market shocks.
Badenoch challenged Burnham to be honest over whether tax rises were coming in October’s budget. The prime minister said his first move in office had been to “cut tax”, in reference to VAT on energy bills, but stopped short of ruling out any rises.
UK government borrowing costs rose again at the start of trading on Wednesday, as 10-year bonds jumped by four basis points – the highest since June 2008. The turmoil erodes the fiscal headroom available to the chancellor, John Healey, for the autumn budget.
The rise has been linked by some economists to Burnham’s doubling down on his commitment to public control of utilities in his statement to the Commons on Tuesday, though most market strategists say it is mainly down to a jump in oil prices.
One of Burnham’s close allies, the economist Jim O’Neill, said on Tuesday night that the prime minister’s statement had been “the last thing that investors want to hear on a day where all of this is going on in the background” and said traders were asking: “Who’s going to get real in this country about the challenges of getting our debt down and controlling spending?”
Criticising Burnham’s three-hour statement in the Commons the day before, Badenoch on Wednesday said: “He did not say no to a single spending request … And personally, I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy. But a prime minister needs to be a leader, not a people pleaser.”
She said: “[He] did not rule out tax rises. Instead, what he did was lots of point scoring. He says he wants new politics, he says he wants honesty.
“The fact is, gilt yields now, the cost of borrowing is far more than it ever was under Liz Truss. That budget failed because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now.”
Burnham said his commitments over the summer had been funded and the government would maintain fiscal discipline in the budget.
“The turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they [the Tories] left behind. We’ve had the fastest growth in the G7. Borrowing fell to its lowest level in six years. We’re cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 country. That is problem solving rather than point scoring,” he said.
Asked again to rule out tax rises, Burnham said: “I’ve already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I’m not going to … write the budget here, that will be the matter for my right honourable friend [the chancellor].
“I took a deliberate decision to set an early date for the budget, so that we reduced the period for prolonged speculation of the kind that she is wanting us to indulge in today.”
Burnham, who had said he hoped not to indulge in too much party political attack, criticised Badenoch for her shadow cabinet reshuffle where she sacked the former shadow chancellor Mel Stride and replaced him with Andrew Griffith, a Treasury minister under Truss.
He said Truss’s tenure had been “a short-lived government that crushed confidence in the economy and hammered people’s mortgages. [Badenoch] took a decision at the weekend: she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write it.”
In an attempt to calm the markets, he said his would be a government “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.
“It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents. And that’s the approach that we will take. And that’s the one I would suggest to the party opposite should follow too.”
Later in the session, Burnham was pressed by Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons defence committee, about whether he could commit to defence spending reaching to 3% of GDP by 2030.
Burnham appeared to imply this would happen, saying: “I’ve made that commitment, made it very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time.”
However, this appeared to be a mix-up over dates, as Burnham has thus only pledged to reach 3.5% by 2035, a commitment he reiterated in his exchanges with Badenoch.

British banks in crosshairs as pressure mounts on Burnham to tax profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:38:28 UTC
21:38:28 KST

The countdown is on. Two months out from Andy Burnham’s inaugural autumn budget, bank executives are wringing their hands over whether the government will target their bumper profits with fresh taxes.
The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering a windfall tax on both banks and oil companies in the late October Westminster setpiece.
The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates.
They are now in the crosshairs of campaigners – including the Trades Union Congress (TUC) and campaign group Positive Money – who say a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living.
The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, who has been pushing hard for a new bank tax said: “Britain’s largest banks are making a fortune. Not because they’ve suddenly become more competitive or improved their services to customers, but because high interest rates mean that, right now, they can sit back and watch the money roll in. Inflated mortgages are fuelling record bonus pots.
“With energy bills edging towards record highs this winter, the government is going to need to provide more support for households – and taxing banks’ windfall profits is the obvious way to pay for it.”
Any move in the UK would echo similar efforts in mainland Europe to make lenders pay more tax to help offset surging living costs and higher defence spending. Here are some of the tools different governments used, as well as the benefits and pitfalls of targeting the profits of some of the world’s largest banks.
Spain: taxed and undeterred
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, revealed plans for a windfall tax in 2022 that would raise €3bn from banks over the following two years to help alleviate cost-of-living pressures.
It spooked investors, wiping more than €5bn off the value of Spanish-listed bank stocks, but politicians pushed ahead: putting a 4.8% “solidarity tax” on the domestic revenue of banks whose income passed €800m. That included fees and net interest income, – the amount of money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits.
The €800m threshold and the focus on domestic revenues meant it broadly excluded small local banks and most foreign lenders’ Spanish operations.
Big banks and lobby groups filed legal challenges over the tax, while the European Central Bank (ECB) warned that Spain risked disrupting monetary policy, and damaging lenders’ capital positions, which help to cushion the blow of economic shocks.
Politicians eventually decided to extend the levy a further three years to 2027, after successfully raising €1.3bn in the first year, and €1.7bn in 2024. Banks now face a sliding tax rate of between 1% and 7%, with the highest rate hitting lenders such as Banco Santander whose annual revenue from interest and fees surpassed €5bn.
The extension triggered a fresh spate of legal challenges by banks and lobbyists, and criticism from both the International Monetary Fund and ECB, which warned it could hit bank profits, push up borrowing costs for low-income households, and make Spain’s banks less competitive on the international stage.
Lithuania: a defence spending boost
Lithuania’s government decided to roll out its own windfall tax on banks in 2023, after forecasts showed lenders were due to rake in €1.3bn in net profits that year. That was three times higher than 2022, following a surge in interest rates sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The 60% tax, which applied to any net interest income that was 50% higher than the previous four-year average, was used to fund infrastructure projects and boost defence spending amid Russian threats.
Politicians agreed to exclude income from any newly agreed loans, to prevent a situation where banks stopped issuing mortgages and business loans to avoid paying tax.
The levy helped raise about €250m in 2023 and €247m in 2024, representing 0.3% of the country’s annual GDP, before being extended by an extra year. The European Commission appeared to support the move, saying it helped cut public debt at a time of regional security threats.
But the tax is said to have spooked foreign firms, with the central bank having repeatedly tried to lure new lenders “with no significant success”, according to an EU report.
The banking sector said it also disadvantaged lenders serving local customers, while letting others such as Revolut, which is registered in the country but serves mostly non-residents, off the hook.
Czechia: ‘unrealistic expectations’
Czechia announced its own three-year windfall tax on banks to help cover consumers’ soaring electricity and gas prices in 2022. The temporary measure, lasting from 2023 to 2025, involved a 60% tax on any profits that were more than double (120%) the previous four-year average.
Deeply unpopular with businesses, the tax also caused friction within the far-right ODC civic democratic party, which said it was interfering with the free market and contradicted core conservative values.
Czech finance minister, Zbyněk Stanjura, talked about scrapping the tax a year earlier than planned, but later admitted the levy had not yet covered state costs linked to the energy crisis. While the finance ministry originally hoped to collect more than 30bn Czech koruna from the country’s six largest banks, it quickly became clear they would fall short of those targets.
“It is unclear whether this was due to unrealistic expectations driven by a vision of easy extra revenue and convenient scapegoating of big corporations, or whether the delayed implementation of the tax (from 2022 to 2023) and the behavioural responses by businesses were not duly considered,” the law firm A&O Shearman said in a 2024 report.
The country ended up raising just 1bn Czech koruna, months before the tax expired in December 2025, according to figures reported by local broadcaster Ct24.
Italy: a tax that fell flat
While plans for a windfall tax by prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing government gained international attention, it was one of the least effective levies.
Meloni’s team shocked markets in August 2023 after revealing plans for a 40% tax on banks’ net interest margin. The move drew the ire of banking lobby groups and wiped €10bn off shares in financial services companies, forcing politicians to water down the proposal a day later with a cap that halved the estimated tax takings to €2.5bn, from €4.9bn.
The rules eventually came into force in October that year, but not before being diluted further.
Banks – which are already subject to higher corporation and regional taxes in Italy – were allowed to choose one of two options: pay a tax equivalent to 0.26% of the risky assets on their balance sheets – ensuring those with safer loans paid less – or keeping the money on their balance sheets but putting aside two-and-a-half times that amount into their own reserves to cushion the blow of any economic shock.
Unsurprisingly, all banks chose to put the money in reserve, scuppering original hopes that extra funds could help support mortgage holders and cut taxes.
However, Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has now revived plans for a new tax three-year levy, that would involve a 5% tax on the profits of Italy’s 10 largest banks.
What if the UK followed suit?
If current trends continue, the UK’s four largest banks will rake in £60bn in profits for 2026. Windfall taxes have been used on banks in the UK before, notably in the early 1980s when Margaret Thatcher’s then chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, accused high street banks of escaping the recession and in the 1990s by Labour chancellor Gordon Brown to generate extra revenue.
Calculations by campaign group Positive Money suggest that the UK could raise up to £10.9bn this year from adopting Czechia’s model; up to £6.95bn by following Spain’s sliding tax scale; and £2.2bn by following in Lithuania’s footsteps.
“Plenty of countries have successfully taxed banks’ windfall profits,” the TUC’s Nowak said. “We’re calling for an increase in the bank surcharge to raise billions for the Treasury to cut bills across the country. This is an easy win for government – and the chancellor should ask the banks to pay a fairer share”.
The world’s most powerful banker, JP Morgan boss, Jamie Dimon, has repeatedly warned the UK government against increasing taxes on banks.
The chief executive of lobby group UK Finance, David Postings, said the banking sector “is a major contributor to the public finances, paying over £43bn in tax last year,” a figure which includes income tax payouts on staff salaries.
“Banks based here already pay a corporation tax surcharge and the bank levy, giving them a higher total tax rate than in other major financial centres. Increasing sector‑specific taxes would risk damaging the UK’s international competitiveness and make it harder to attract investment.”

MAPUTO, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- The China (Hunan)-Mozambique Economic and Trade Matchmaking Conference was held in Maputo, the capital of Mozambique, on Tuesday, bringing together more than 180 representatives from over 110 enterprises and business associations, along with government officials and representatives of diplomatic institutions from both countries.
During the event, participants held in-depth discussions on cooperation in areas including cultural and media exchanges, sports, energy and infrastructure, and industrial parks. The two sides signed 11 key cooperation agreements and memoranda of understanding covering four major areas, further advancing economic and trade cooperation between Hunan and Mozambique.
Wang Junshou, a member of the Standing Committee of the Communist Party of China Hunan Provincial Committee and secretary-general of the committee, highlighted Hunan's strong economic performance and industrial foundation, noting that the province's gross domestic product reached 5.53 trillion yuan (about 822.6 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025.
He noted that the China-Africa Economic and Trade Expo has been permanently established in Hunan and that the Pilot Zone for In-depth China-Africa Economic and Trade Cooperation has been approved for development. These national-level platforms, he said, provide new opportunities and stronger support for expanding practical cooperation between Hunan and African countries.
Wang called on Hunan and Mozambique to use the conference as an opportunity to establish regular exchange mechanisms, strengthen strategic alignment, accelerate the implementation of cooperation projects, and promote greater mutual understanding between their peoples.
He added that the two sides should combine Hunan's strengths in technology, equipment and capital with Mozambique's advantages in natural resources, market access and labor, creating a more stable, transparent and predictable business environment for enterprises from both sides and developing more landmark projects featuring mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.
Fredson Bacar, Mozambique's secretary of state of tourism, said Mozambique is seeking to increase the level of local processing of its natural resources while attracting greater investment into manufacturing and digital transformation.
"Strengthening ties with Hunan has significant economic potential," Bacar said, noting that Mozambique's strategic location and transportation corridors could enable the country to serve as an important gateway to markets across Southern Africa.
He added that the country's energy and industrial transformation is also creating new investment opportunities.
Wu Jinjia, charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in Mozambique, encouraged enterprises from both sides to seize opportunities arising from China's zero-tariff policy for African countries and expand cooperation in emerging sectors such as smart agriculture and new energy. ■

Ofer Winter slams rabbi who said it was against Jewish law to vote for party with Arab-Israeli
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:38:18 UTC
21:38:18 KST

People of Israel Party chairman Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter decried on Wednesday statements made by President of the Ateret Kohanim Yeshiva Rabbi Shlomo Aviner, who argued that it was against Jewish law to vote for the party because Arab-Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad is placed second on its Knesset slate.
“When I fought under fire in Lebanon, Gaza, and the West Bank, I served under and personally commanded leaders - commanders and soldiers - who were Druze, Bedouin, and Christian. Through fire and water, I followed my leader and brigade commander, Imad Fares, into battle with complete faith. I knew he would not abandon me in the field, and I trusted his leadership,” Winter stated.
“[Non-Jewish soldiers] were worthy enough to be wounded and even fall for the country. They were worthy enough for us to follow them into battle, and they are worthy enough to lead. Yoseph, my brother, you embody the people of Israel in every sense.
“I am proud of you for having been a commander and leader of soldiers in the Golani Brigade. I am proud that you risked your life for the people of Israel and were wounded in battle. You fought in uniform, and long after your service, you continue fighting to defend the people of Israel everywhere in the world.”
On Tuesday, Aviner was asked whether Jewish law permits voting for a party with a non-Jewish candidate holding the number two position.
“Certainly not,” he answered, arguing that Jewish law distinguishes between the personal treatment of a non-Jew and appointing a non-Jew to a position of national leadership.
“Certainly, a non-Jewish friend should be treated well if he meets the definition of a ger toshav, but he cannot be given positions of leadership over the nation,” Aviner said.
Ger toshav is the term used in Judaism to describe a non-Jewish person living in Israel who will not convert to the religion but observes the Seven Laws of Noah and is therefore considered righteous.
Aviner cited Maimonides’s Laws of Kings, insisting that even a person defined as one of the “righteous among the nations” could not serve as a leader in the Land of Israel.
“He can be a private citizen, yes, but not as a leader,” he said.
Haddad was unveiled as the number two candidate in Winter’s newly established right-wing People of Israel party last week at the party’s launch event.
At the event, Haddad said that entering politics was a continuation of his service to Israel, after years of military service and public diplomacy. He has said he hopes to become Israel’s public diplomacy minister and the first Arab member of the security cabinet.
Tzohar rabbis reject Aviner’s interpretation of the halacha
The Tzohar Rabbinical Organization rejected Aviner’s interpretation, saying leading halachic authorities had already ruled that Jews may vote for non-Jewish candidates for the Knesset.
“Yoseph Haddad is a person who has done, and continues to do, a great deal for the State of Israel, in Israel and around the world, and was even wounded during his military service defending the country,” the organization said.
Tzohar cited the biblical example of King David appointing Ittai the Gittite, whom the organization described as a foreigner, to a senior military command because of his loyalty to the king and kingdom.
“Even today, in the State of Israel, there are non-Jewish citizens who act with devotion for the state, defend it, and contribute to its strength,” Tzohar said.
“The appointment and advancement of such people, when they have the public’s confidence and act loyally toward the state and its laws, does not contradict Israel’s Jewish identity, but is an expression of the state’s strength and its ability to incorporate all its citizens.”
The organization said prominent halachic authorities, including former chief rabbi Isaac Herzog and Rabbi Eliezer Waldenberg, had ruled that non-Jews may be elected to the Knesset and that traditional restrictions concerning the appointment of a king did not apply in the same manner to modern democratic government.
“Accordingly, it is permissible to vote for an Arab candidate who is loyal to the state, and throughout the history of the state, Jews and non-Jews have participated in the Knesset and the government,” Tzohar said.
“Precisely at a time when there are elements among the non-Jewish public who incite against the State of Israel and against the possibility of living together, we must strengthen and empower those Arab citizens who recognize the State of Israel, its Jewish identity, and its sovereignty, and who work for its security and prosperity.”

TALLINN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Ulle Madise, the sole candidate in Estonia's presidential election, was elected president Wednesday during an extraordinary session in the country's 101-member Parliament (Riigikogu).
Madise, Estonia's chancellor of justice, received support from 71 lawmakers, according to the live cast of the parliament session. She needed a two-thirds majority, or at least 68 votes, to be elected in the secret ballot.

Madise replaces President Alar Karis, who said in June that he would not seek a second term. ■
