Trump’s ridiculous bullying of Canada is backfiring | Robert Reich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

What do bullies do when someone stands up to their bullying and punches them in the face? They look for someone weaker to bully who won’t punch back.
Presumably that’s why Donald Trump has now taken on Canada, after Iran punched back so hard in the cage match the US president began more than six months ago as to leave him humiliated and baffled.
Trump wants to be the bully who humiliates others and forces them into submission. Needing to assert his dominance, Trump has now started a trade war with our northern neighbor, friend, second-largest trading partner (after Mexico) and, at least until now, reliable ally.
He’s hammering Canada on his Truth Social and in media appearances, saying Canada has “ripped off” the US for years, and signing an order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.”
This is pure bunk, of course – more empty Trump bravado and ignorant belligerence. Canada? Really? If Mel Brooks were still making movies, this would be a comedy. But as all else with Trump, it’s no laughing matter.
Trump apparently assumed that Canada would quickly surrender because it has more to lose. The tariffs Trump has imposed on Canada – along with those he’s threatening if Canada retaliates – affect a tiny portion of America’s total imports but a huge portion of Canada’s total exports.
Jamieson Greer, Trump’s US trade representative, says the duties are too small to pose a problem for the US and are “more [Canada’s] emergency than ours”.
But bullies like Trump rarely think about the effects of their bullying on the thinking and attitudes of their targets.
Trump’s bullying of Iran has not only reinforced its hardline regime but shown them that control over the strait of Hormuz is an effective means of gaining concessions from other Gulf states as well as the US, and likely strengthened their resolve to build a nuclear weapon.
Trump’s bullying of Canada, meanwhile, is igniting a patriotism that has often eluded that nation, which separatist factions have long threatened to pull apart.
Mark Carney’s decision to stand up to Trump – through “dollar for dollar” retaliation on goods coming from key industries in states including Ohio and Texas with competitive Senate elections – has led to a surge of support for the prime minister’s Liberal party. Liberals won three special by-elections on Monday.
Trump’s trade war with Canada has also dimmed the prospects of Canada’s separatist movements, at least in the short term. A candidate from Carney’s Liberal party edged out a Quebec separatist in one of Monday’s special by-elections, in a district hit hard by US tariffs.
This is a good omen for Canada ahead of 5 October’s vote in Quebec on whether the province’s secessionist party, Parti Québécois, gains additional seats in the province’s legislative body, and 19 October’s vote in Alberta on whether to hold a referendum to secede from the rest of Canada.
Trump may also have underestimated the negative reactions to his trade war at home. According to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans oppose Trump’s moves to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. About 63% oppose his peevish order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.” Only 20% support the higher tariffs on Canadian goods.
The negative response is especially pronounced in border states whose economies are tightly interconnected with Canada.
In Michigan, for example, where overwhelming majorities oppose Trump’s tariffs on Canada, Democrats have launched new attack ads on the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers for refusing to denounce the tariffs. The Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed called Trump an “asshole” for launching the trade war.
There’s still time for the US and Canada to avoid the worst of the economic and political fallout from this. Carney’s “dollar for dollar” retaliation goes into effect on 8 September but Trump’s counter-counter measure – threatened 50% tariffs on autos and auto parts – won’t go into effect until New Year’s Day.
Still, no one should expect an easy resolution to what may go down in history as the stupidest of all the stupid foreign policies Trump has initiated. And given the extent of Trump’s dumb international moves, that is saying something.
- 
  Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

How to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ice-cream – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

With two young kids, we get through a lot of bananas in our household. Perhaps surprisingly, though, most of them are frozen: our daughters eat them straight from the freezer most evenings, with frozen berries and yoghurt, for pudding. We normally order a stack of bananas every Saturday, and before the end of the week they inevitably start to turn brown. At this point, we peel, slice and freeze them for the children’s evening yoghurt, though sometimes, when we have a real excess, I turn them into today’s incredibly satisfying “ice-cream”. Its silky-smooth texture really hits the spot, and satisfies any ice-cream cravings without recourse to added sugar or excessive fat. The trick is to freeze the bananas in a single layer on a flat tray, so they don’t freeze into a homogeneous mass, then transfer to a container to enjoy as and when.
Brown banana ‘ice-cream’
This has to be in my top five everyday desserts, not least because brown bananas are very gooey and sweet, have a rich and creamy texture and a satiating flavour. Portion for portion, it feels luxurious and indulgent, even without the extra sugar, saturated fat, gums and stabilisers found in much commercial ice-cream and other ready-made desserts. Of course, blended fruit is itself a readily absorbable sugar, but the trade-off is worth it for the extra fibre, potassium, manganese and other vitamins. It’s also a fraction of the price of shop-bought ice-cream.
This is best eaten fresh from the blender, but if you need to store a bumper batch, remember to take it out of the freezer at least 10 minutes before you want to scoop it.
1 or more brown bananas
Half the bananas’ weight in liquid – water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative
Toppings, all optional and to taste
Chopped nuts
  Coconut flakes
  Grated chocolate
Peel and chop the bananas into 2cm-thick slices (this makes them easier to blend later), then spread out on a tray and freeze for at least five hours. Once frozen, store in a sealed container in the freezer.
To make the ice-cream, weigh the amount of banana you’ve taken out, then add half its weight in liquid – that is, water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative. Transfer to a jug blender and blitz smooth, but not for too long or the fruit will melt too much; stir, if need be, to get an even blend. Serve immediately as it is, or leave to soften like a Mr Whippy-alike soft serve, or freeze for an hour or more for a firmer, scoopable texture, adding any optional toppings of your choice.

Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.
By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.
“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.
Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.
The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.
For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.
On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediation gigs jump 70% year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.
The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a 2025 study published in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a 2026 study.
Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’s annual report.
But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.
“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.
The rise of the AI cleanup crews
For some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.
Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.
“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”
Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.
For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.
Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.
“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.
But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.
Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.
One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.
Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.
“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”
While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.
What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.
“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.
Slop cleanup jobs may not last
It’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.
Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.
McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.
But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.
“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.
Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.
“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.
But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.
“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.

UK Prime Minister Says Government Will Be ‘Grounded in Fiscal Responsibility’

Armed men abduct Kenyan editor, employer suspects government

Unknown Publisher

Armed men abduct Kenyan editor, employer suspects government
September 2, 2026
An associate editor for one of Kenya's largest news outlets, The Standard, was abducted by armed men overnight and then released near a dam far from the scene around nine hours later, his employer said on Wednesday.
Alex Kiprotich was taken from a car at around 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday on a road near the city of Nakuru.
"The circumstances of Mr Kiprotich's abduction remain deeply troubling, and we will continue to press for full accountability," the government-critical outlet said in a press release after his discovery.
Late on Tuesday the Standard Group's CEO Chaacha Mwita had also said that the "abduction bears all the hallmarks of a targeted attack on a journalist for doing his job."
What do we know about the apparent abduction?
The newspaper released a video overnight of what appeared to be dashcam footage from the car Kiprotich was traveling in when he was abducted.
A white vehicle without any markings apparent in the footage came to a stop in front of the car in an area where temporary barriers created a single-lane bottleneck on the Gilgil-Nakuru highway, and put on its hazard lights.
Four men in civilian clothes and obscuring their faces — some holding firearms and others carrying what appeared to be baseball bats — emerged and converged on the car, soon taking a man back to their vehicle and driving off.
On Wednesday, Standard Group said that Kiprotich had been located near a dam more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) southeast the scene of the abduction roughly nine hours earlier.
"Mr Kiprotich was located by a Standard Group team led by the Group CEO Chaacha Mwita at around 6:30 a.m. near Masinga Dam, after being dumped by his captors in the early hours of the morning," it said.
Kiprotic was "safe, though understandably shaken by his ordeal," his employer said. Kiprotich works for newspaper The Standard, a flagship of the wider media group known for its critical coverage of President William Ruto's government.
Right groups call for investigation, warn of pattern of abductions and intimidation
Police and the government in Kenya did not immediately comment on the incident.
Dozens of government critics and activists have been abducted in Kenya this year alone, according to a report released this week, with the practice becoming more common since widespread anti-government protests in 2024.
Human rights groups have accused state agencies of being responsible, with Standard Group voicing similar suspicions in this case.
Kiprotich had said in June that he narrowly escaped a previous attempt to kidnap him, which came three days after Ruto called out the Standard Group on social media.
Kenya's editors' guild said it was "shocked, outraged and deeply perturbed" by Tuesday's abduction, describing it as "a disturbing escalation in the intimidation and targeting of journalists in Kenya."
Amnesty International Kenya called for an independent investigation, saying the incident raised "serious concerns for media freedom."

Killing at Sea
Three families, two bombings and a hidden war: uncovering the lives behind Operation Southern Spear’s dead.
Since September 2025, the US military has carried out more than 60 strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 people.

In Killing at Sea, Fault Lines investigates the administration’s claims about Operation Southern Spear by uncovering the stories of those targeted and the evidence used to justify lethal military force.

Russia secretly helps Iran develop engines for hypersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:00 EEST
21:00:00 KST

Russia secretly helps Iran develop engines for hypersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
Russia is secretly helping Iran develop a new class of hypersonic cruise missiles.
Source: the Financial Times in an investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, experts' travel data and an analysis of military patents
Details: The FT says the years-long secret programme is codenamed C430L.
"The main purpose of C430L is to help Iran to develop a ramjet propulsion system, an engine that allows a cruise missile to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound," the FT says.
Missile and military experts said the technology is almost certainly intended for anti-ship cruise missiles and cruise missiles for strikes against ground targets. They estimate that such weapons could pose a threat to US aircraft carriers and other warships in the Middle East.
"Iran has built and flight-tested the ramjet propulsion system, although there is no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has yet been deployed," the FT says.
The programme was coordinated by Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport and NPO Mashinostroyenia. The C430L contract with Iran's Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics was signed in November 2023.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received a substantial amount of technical material from Iran on the ramjet engine. Russian engineers analysed data from Iranian flight tests, particularly the performance of the fuel system, combustion stability, air intake and engine nozzle, after which they sent questions and recommendations to the Iranian side.
In April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending around two dozen Russian experts to Iran for technical consultations as part of C430L.
The FT established that senior experts from NPO Mashinostroyenia were involved in the programme, including designers who had worked on naval cruise missiles, ramjet engines and high-speed missile systems.
Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris, said the secret ramjet programme "shows Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres". "Russia doesn't care as much about the red lines in the region," the professor added.
According to the FT, the programme continued in 2026. In June, Rosoboronexport and the Iranian side were still discussing elements of the next stage of development and Russian technical reports. However, the outlet was unable to establish whether the next stage of the programme had begun.
The Kremlin, Rosoboronexport, NPO Mashinostroyenia and the Iranian government did not respond to the Financial Times' requests for comment on the programme.
Background: Earlier, the FT reported that Iran had signed a secret €495 million deal with Russia for the supply of 500 Verba man-portable air-defence systems and 2,500 missiles for them. The contract was also signed through Rosoboronexport.

Sudan: Air attack destroys food aid for families in South Kordofan
Two truckloads of food aid destined for hungry families in South Kordofan state, Sudan, were destroyed in an aerial attack over the weekend, the World Food Progamme (WFP) said on Wednesday.
The UN agency strongly condemned the attack which occurred on 30 August outside the city of Dilling.
The trucks carried 50 metric tonnes of WFP food including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil and salt—enough to provide lifesaving assistance to 5,800 people for one month.
They were heading to Kadugli, where WFP is supporting nearly 58,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or worse, and were clearly marked with its banners and flags.
End ‘unacceptable’ attacks
WFP said the attack was the latest example of the complex operating environment facing it and other humanitarian agencies in Sudan.
The UN has repeatedly called for an end to the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) which erupted in April 2023.
As a result of the conflict, some 30 million people required humanitarian assistance last year.
Since January, WFP has recorded eight aerial attacks that have damaged its premises and disrupted operations.
“Attacks on aid workers and humanitarian operations are unacceptable and must stop,” WFP said, urging all sides to uphold international humanitarian law by protecting civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets.

From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:57:24 EEST
20:57:24 KST

From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs
Kyiv • UNN
From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs.
An academic career can become the foundation for one's own business—especially in finance, where one has to work not only with business models but also with licensing, financial monitoring, data protection, and other regulatory requirements.
Among the Ukrainians creating financial and technology companies in Europe are entrepreneurs with academic backgrounds. Vladyslav Zaporozhchenko and Tetiana Dashevska came to business by different paths: he began with banking research, while she spent years working in banking and fintech.
Vladyslav Zaporozhchenko: from banking research to the payments business
At first, banking was a research subject for Zaporozhchenko. As a student, he studied banking supervision and the payment card market, completed an internship at the NBU's administration, and prepared more than 30 materials on fintech. After his studies, he worked at banks—in lending, payments, and corporate products. His research subject became his daily work: he saw how financial products depend on operations and regulatory requirements.
Later, he says, it became interesting not only to analyze changes but also to create products himself and take responsibility for their operation. His own projects required skills from academic work: working with primary sources, testing assumptions, assessing risks, and documenting decisions.
The next step was the European market: procedures there are more predictable, but they require financial-monitoring, KYC, and compliance policies, risk assessment, and flow planning. In 2018–2021, Zaporozhchenko became the founder of the Czech company AMERO PAY; from 2021, he has been the director of the British QIUNTEXBANK TECHNOLOGY LTD; and in 2022, the Polish company Qiuntex Pay was entered in the KNF register of small payment institutions.
Working in different countries showed how much regulatory approaches can differ: he dealt with the requirements of the Czech National Bank, the UK's FCA, Canada's FinTRAC, Switzerland's VQF, and other regulatory and professional organizations.
In 2022, together with Yulia Raubishke, he founded the British consulting company INTERNATIONAL FINTECH BUSINESS LTD, which provides financial licensing and regulatory support. The company was registered on October 20 of the same year. This was where his previous experience in banking, fintech, and working with regulators found practical application.
Tetiana Dashevska: from a banking career to her own platform
Dashevska's path was different. She entered entrepreneurship after more than twenty years in banking and fintech. With a PhD in economics and an MBA, she spent a significant part of her career launching digital banking products—in other words, she saw from the inside how every new service begins.
Over the years, Dashevska says, she repeatedly ran into the same problem. Every new neobank or payment service had to build a substantial part of its technological infrastructure independently: customer identification, transaction processing, and reporting took months, sometimes years, as well as significant resources. What surprised her most, she says, was the repetition itself—companies were writing things that dozens of companies before them had already written.
Eventually, she decided that this work did not need to be repeated every time—and that is how the idea of a platform made up of ready-made modules emerged, adaptable to the needs of different companies. In 2023, Dashevska and Yevhen Pavlenko founded SoftBees. The company operates in Ukraine and Poland and develops such a platform for launching and developing digital financial services. The model is the same as Zaporozhchenko's: the team remains at home, while the legal entity operates within the European legal framework.
The European market added requirements concerning information security, risk management, personal data protection, and financial monitoring to the technological tasks. In Dashevska's experience, the academic method here means formulating assumptions, checking risks, and documenting decisions. In 2025, SoftBees completed certification of its information security management system under ISO 27001.
What these stories have in common
The stories of Zaporozhchenko and Dashevska do not indicate that an academic degree is a necessary condition for business success. They show how academic and professional experience can find application in entrepreneurship.
In fintech, decisions have to be made while taking technology, finance, and regulatory requirements into account simultaneously. That is why experience working with data, research, and complex documentation becomes a practical tool. For Zaporozhchenko, the journey began with research into the banking system; for Dashevska, it began with many years of work in banks. At first, knowledge helps one understand the problem, and later experience suggests how to turn that understanding into a product or company.

Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:56:00 UTC
20:56:00 KST

Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.
Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
The US attacks on Tuesday ended a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.
Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devestating” retaliation.
Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.
“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.
In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.
Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate.”
It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.
The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. 
 Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

From infrastructure to military drills, China deepens footprint in Egypt as Xi visits Cairo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:53:49 UTC
20:53:49 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s return to Cairo comes as Egypt and China push their relationship beyond infrastructure and trade into technology, defence and a broader strategic partnership with regional implications.
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Egypt on Tuesday for his first visit since 2016, as the two countries mark 70 years of diplomatic ties and push their relationship into new areas in what Beijing has described as a "comprehensive strategic partnership".
Since his last visit, some of Beijing's megaprojects have become part of Egypt’s landscape.
Chinese companies have helped build the central business district of Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. Built by China State Construction Engineering Corporation, it consists of 20 skyscrapers.
At its centre stands the 385.8-metre Iconic Tower, Africa's tallest building.
A light rail system built with Chinese involvement connects Cairo’s eastern outskirts with new urban centres, and a China-Egypt industrial zone near the Suez Canal now hosts more than 200 companies.
The industrial zone created more than 10,000 direct jobs, according to Chinese figures. Chinese reporting puts total investment at more than $4.7 billion (€4.05bn).
The scope is now widening.
AI, advanced manufacturing and technology transfer are increasingly part of the economic agenda, while Chinese and Egyptian fighter aircraft have been training together in the second joint air force exercise between the two countries.
Trade grows, but so does the imbalance
Bilateral trade reached $11.3 billion (€9.75bn) in the first six months of 2026, up 21.5% year on year, according to Egypt's Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics.
Egyptian exports to China almost tripled to $840.8 million (€725.4m), driven by fuel, mineral oil, fruit, vegetables and cotton.
But imports from China reached $10.4 billion (€8.97bn) over the same period — machinery and electrical equipment alone accounting for $4.1 billion (€3.5bn), followed by vehicles, iron and steel, plastics and chemicals.
Egypt wants Chinese investment and technology, but also wants more Chinese companies to manufacture inside Egypt and greater access for Egyptian goods to the Chinese market.
A five-year programme agreed for 2024-2028 calls for local production and technology transfer in electric vehicles, electronics, solar panels, chemicals and modern agricultural technology, with artificial intelligence also listed as a priority.
El-Sisi said ahead of the visit that Egypt wanted to attract Chinese investment in EVs, battery storage, renewable energy and shipbuilding, while expanding technology transfer in telecommunications, AI and space sciences.
Military ties move into view
Defence links are also becoming more visible. China and Egypt are holding the second edition of their Eagles of Civilisation joint air force exercise, running from mid-August into early September at Egyptian air bases. The first was held only last year.
Chinese officials said the 2026 drills would include air combat tactics, air superiority operations, combat search and rescue and joint force deployment.
The US remains Cairo's key longstanding security partner, providing large-scale military assistance and supplying a significant part of Egypt's diversely sourced military equipment.
Washington has not publicly commented on the Chinese exercises. The Pentagon has previously flagged concerns about Chinese military engagement with US partners across the Middle East and Africa.
The exercises fit Egypt's wider policy of diversifying its defence partnerships, a deliberate balancing act that also encompasses its involvement in BRICS, the New Development Bank and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation alongside continued reliance on Western economic and security support.
Next phase of relations crucial
Ahead of the visit, Xi described the country as an important link between the Arab world and Africa and called for deeper China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation through Egypt.
For China, Egypt combines a market of more than 100 million people with a strategic position on the Suez Canal and political weight across the Arab world and Africa.
The two governments have also taken similar positions on several regional issues, including support for a Palestinian state, while Egypt maintains its One China policy.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China in 1956.
El-Sisi has travelled to China eight times since taking office in 2014, most recently in May 2024.
The agreements announced during Xi's visit are expected to provide more detail on newer areas of cooperation, particularly technology transfer and advanced manufacturing, where Egypt has pushed hardest to move beyond the construction and infrastructure model that defined the relationship's first decade.

Ukraine Foils Alleged FSB Terror Plot Against Russian Opposition Leader

Unspecified “terrorist act”

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has told Russian leader Vladimir Putin that Türkiye is ready to exert all kinds of efforts to end the war between Moscow and Kiev, reiterating that the continued armed conflict since 2022 did not benefit either side.
“Türkiye plays a role in the peaceful resolution of conflicts in our region. In particular, it is our expectation, and Mr. Putin’s, that the war between Russia and Ukraine will end peacefully as soon as possible,” Erdoğan told reporters aboard his flight back from Kyrgyzstan on Sept. 2, where he held a bilateral meeting with Putin on the sidelines of a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit.
Describing his meeting with Putin as very fruitful and sincere, Erdoğan said they discussed all the aspects of bilateral ties as well as the ongoing war.
Türkiye’s wish is to see the establishment of peace and stability in the region with the termination of the war, Erdoğan said. “It is obvious that this war does not bring any positive outcome to either side, to the region and the world. Is Mr. Putin happy about this? No, he is not. He, too, is hopeful that the war will end,” he added.
Erdoğan noted that he has “expressed our readiness to do our best for peace. It is a reality that peace will prevail and not war. We are ready to exert efforts to this end.”
Black Sea security is important for Türkiye.
On a question about increased attacks on civilian ships, including those with Turkish flags, Erdoğan underscored the importance of uninterrupted maritime security for Türkiye in the Black Sea.
“The conflict between the warring sides should not escalate to a point where it jeopardizes the safety of civilians and businesses. For these reasons, we are acting with a much broader perspective. We need to solve this problem,” he said.
Erdoğan reiterated the need for the establishment of a new mechanism to secure the shipment in the Black Sea, urging for a speedy resolution before a food security crisis erupts mostly in Africa due to insufficient supply of grain.
Greece should not arm islands.
Another important question Erdoğan answered was on Greece's attempts to arm the Aegean islands with demilitarized status at the expense of ruining ties with Ankara. Greece and Israel have recently signed a multibillion-dollar agreement to bolster the former’s air defense system.
“Greece must reverse the change and course and stop arming islands that have demilitarized status. History is a very good guide for those who learn from it. We will continue to work for peace, security, and stability in our region,” he stated.
Türkiye has always been acting in a constructive way, but it did not receive the same from Greece, Erdoğan said. “Whoever interprets Türkiye’s calm and responsible approach as weakness is making a serious mistake.”
Talks for F-35s continue.
On a question about Türkiye’s plans to return to the F-35 program after transferring its Russian-made S-400 air defense systems, Erdoğan said he discussed all the matters with Putin during their bilateral meeting.
“As you know, Türkiye was part of the F-35 program and delivered an enormous contribution to it. Our talks for Türkiye’s return to the program continue. We think that this issue will be solved following the accomplishment of the processes in the U.S.,” he stated.
Türkiye was expelled from the F-35 joint fighter program in 2019 after it purchased and deployed S-400 air defense systems from Russia. The U.S. laws require that Türkiye end its possession of the S-400 systems to return the purchase of F-35s.
Erdoğan said Türkiye, in the meantime, is accelerating its efforts to create its own jet fighter, Kaan, and other air defense systems. “This is the road map of strong Türkiye,” he added.

“We, as the state, have a road map, a plan, and a timing. Our institutions are working in coordination,” he stated.
“For the law to be implemented, the terror organization must actually lay down its arms and be dissolved. The procedures for this process are well defined. The process is proceeding step by step,” he added.
The president said the state and all other relevant bodies are running the process with care in a bid not to give any room for those who want to ruin it.

‘Not democratically elected’: SC says Manan Kumar Mishra only ‘pro tem’ BCI chairman till fresh election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:51:35 UTC
20:51:35 KST

BCI chief Manan Kumar Mishra only ‘pro tem’ till fresh election, Supreme Court says
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said Bar Council of India (BCI) chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra was only a “pro tem Chairman” until a freshly constituted BCI elects its office-bearers, and directed that major policy decisions be taken in consultation with the Attorney General for India and the Solicitor General, who are permanent ex-officio BCI members.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said Mishra could oversee the BCI's day-to-day functioning but could not be treated as a democratically elected office-bearer once the newly elected state bar councils complete the process of constituting a fresh BCI.“You should also bear in mind that you are like a pro tem chairman till a fresh election of the Bar Council of India, pursuant to the elections already conducted in the state bar councils, takes place,” Justice Bagchi told senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, appearing for the BCI chairman, according to LiveLaw.“So, it is not a situation where he is democratically elected and continues to be so. His term is co-terminus with the elections which are imminent,” the judge said.The court said the existing arrangement could continue for routine administrative work but stressed that institutional checks would apply to policy decisions.“In such situations, day-to-day functioning can be left to the existing arrangement. However, when a policy decision is taken, the participation of a permanent ex officio member acting independently, such as the Attorney General, is necessary,” Justice Bagchi remarked orally, PTI said.
The bench also said it was not endorsing Mishra's continued tenure.“We are not placing any stamp of approval upon the existing arrangement. It is apparent that the present chairperson can continue only until a fresh election to the Bar Council of India takes place pursuant to the state bar council elections already conducted,” it said.The observations came while the court heard pleas challenging Mishra's continued occupation of the BCI chairperson's post and the legal basis for extending his tenure until 2030.Senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the petitioners, said Mishra was unanimously elected chairman for a term from April 17, 2025 to April 16, 2030. She also challenged a resolution extending the tenure of the chairman and vice-chairman from three years to five years despite rules prescribing a two-year term.
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for one of the petitioners, questioned the creation of the Bar Council of India Trust for Promotion of Education, Legal and Professional Reforms and Improvement in Research.Sankaranarayanan alleged that its deed made 11 managing trustees “original and permanent trustees”. The bench questioned how elected members could appoint themselves as perpetual trustees.“The Bar Council of India is a juristic entity. That entity has created a trust from its assets through the elected members who constituted the Council. Can those elected members make themselves permanent trustees of those assets when the composition of the corporate entity that settled the trust is itself determined through elections?” it asked.The court directed the newly constituted state bar councils to elect their office-bearers and representatives to the BCI within three weeks of notification of their composition. The matter will be heard next on September 23.

Death toll from current Ebola outbreak in Congo exceeds 3,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:51:18 UTC
20:51:18 KST

PRETORIA, September 2. /TASS/. The number of laboratory-confirmed Ebola deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is now up to 3,007, the Ministry of Communications and Media said.
The death toll rose by 57 over the past 24 hours, bringing the total number of Ebola cases to 6,186, including 86 identified during that period, while the case fatality rate stands at 48.6%.
About 830 people with symptoms are in hospitals and quarantine facilities. Health authorities are monitoring 88% of the people who had contact with patients infected with Ebola.
The outbreak began on May 15 in the DRC and Uganda and has already become the second deadliest in the history of Ebola surveillance in Africa. The disease has now been reported in six Congolese provinces, with the epicenter located in Ituri Province. On July 28, Ugandan authorities announced the end of the Ebola outbreak in their country. On August 25, the World Health Organization (WHO) confirmed the outbreak’s end in Uganda.
This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which a vaccine is still in the clinical trial stage. Last week, the DRC began vaccinating at-risk groups with a vaccine that has proven effective against another Ebola pathogen, the Zaire ebolavirus.
The largest Ebola outbreak occurred in West Africa from 2014 to 2016, affecting Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. At that time, more than 11,000 people died. The Ebola virus is transmitted to humans from wild animals. The first recorded case of human Ebola infection occurred in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1976. The current Ebola outbreak in the DRC is the 17th on record.

US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:51:15 UTC
20:51:15 KST

Breadcrumb
US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
Iran accused the United States of striking a wedding gathering in the country’s south, killing five people, including a child, and injuring dozens more in an attack on a residential area near the Strait of Hormuz in Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province, on Tuesday night.
The Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile struck the residential property, killing five people and injuring more than 50. Six-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi was among those killed, it said, adding that those wounded had been transferred to hospital in the nearby city of Minab.
Earlier, Reza Shahidiyan, the governor of Sirik county, told the IRIB state broadcaster that 63 people had been injured, including 50 women and children. Other Iranian reporting has cited as many as 68 wounded.
Videos circulated by Iranian rescue workers showed debris scattered across the site and extensive damage to several buildings, including blown-out walls and windows. Another video posted by the Red Crescent showed a large whole on the roof of a residential building, supposedly from the site of the impact.
Kuhestak lies in Sirik county, on Iran’s southern coast along the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil trade passes. The attack came during a large new wave of US strikes across Iran, following more than a month without a direct exchange of fire between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces had launched strikes against targets linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, citing what it called recent attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and on US personnel in the region.
But Washington has not publicly identified the precise target near the wedding site, disclosed the weapon used, or explained how a missile strike came to send lethal shrapnel into a home packed with civilians celebrating a wedding. Earlier reports suggested a telecommunications tower in the Kuhestak area may have been among the targets.
US response
The US did not deny carrying out strikes in the area. Asked about reports of civilian casualties, CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said: "We’re aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media," claiming that "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
The statement does not address whether the strike hit a civilian residence, whether US planners knew a wedding was under way, whether the house was within the expected blast radius of an intended target, or whether CENTCOM is investigating the deaths and injuries reported by emergency workers and local officials.
The US assertion that it does not target civilians sits uneasily alongside mounting reports of civilian harm from its campaign in Iran. On 28 February, a strike on a girls’ school in Minab, also in Hormozgan province, killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to Iranian authorities and rights groups.
Washington has yet to publicly accept responsibility or release a final account of that attack. However, a preliminary US military assessment concluded that US forces were likely responsible and that the school was not the intended target. The reported explanation was that outdated intelligence had wrongly classified the site, or the surrounding area, as associated with an Iranian military installation.
Iranian condemnation
Iranian officials condemned the Sirik attack as an assault on civilians and said the country would respond.
Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would respond "with firmness", while Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker, described the United States as the "Great Satan" and linked the wedding deaths to what he called a broader pattern of US attacks on civilians.
The head of the Iranian Red Crescent Society sent a letter to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday regarding the wedding attack, assuring prosecutors that the organisation was documenting the effects of the attack in order to "collect and record (them) for follow-up through legal and international channels," calling for an independent investigation into Tuesday's deadly incident.
Iranian officials also said electricity and telephone services had been disrupted in the area, amid reports that US strikes had targeted telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan province. Restoration work was under way, according to Iran’s health ministry.
The strike was followed by Iranian missile and drone attacks directed towards US-linked targets and allies across the region, including Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The exchange marked one of the sharpest escalations in weeks in the six-month conflict.

‘A fever dream’: USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:48:48 UTC
20:48:48 KST

At Pattaya’s Hard Rock Cafe and hotel, the city’s mayor and police officials, along with women in traditional Thai dress, wait to greet the sailors who are arriving in civilian clothes, bags slung over their shoulders, off the buses.
The USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew of 5,000 have not been on shore for nearly nine months, a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.
Crew appeared to be told not to speak to the gathered journalists about the reportedly deteriorating living conditions onboard, but said they were looking forward to being on dry land, sleeping and going home.
One sailor, Breese, who didn’t want to give his surname, said “it’s a fever dream right now” and he was looking forward to trying Thai food for the first time and meeting new people.
Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand during the Vietnam war.
At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University.
“In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.
Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.
The Hard Rock hotel is around the corner from the Soi 6 alley, known for its go-go bars, one of the many areas that contribute to Pattaya’s sex tourism industry. Soi 6 and the neighbouring area would be off-limits for crew after sunset, said Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet.
The sailors are being released in staggered groups, so not everyone is out. Shakeira Fairfax, who has travelled all the way from New Jersey, has to wait one more day to be reunited with her daughter, Jada Fairfax.
Fairfax says she is mostly excited: “I just want to pick her up and spin her around. She’s my baby always,” but, she said, “I don’t know who I’m welcoming home.”
Jada finished her basic training last October and was shipped out a month later, two months before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. Jada celebrated her 25th birthday on board in June.
Fairfax says there was an “abrupt” stop to communication when the war broke out, but she has since been able to check in with her intermittently and send care packages.
The ship’s captain, Dan Keeler, acknowledged to the media that the carrier “looks like a dirty car in a parking lot”. As for the reports of the conditions on board, he says: “I don’t know how to say it other than there’s a disconnect between reporting back home and what’s happening on the ship.”
Keeler added: “First-time sailors are going to complain about the food, the living conditions, similar to sending kids off to college for the first time. We did get caught up in an election cycle and got thrown around like a football.”
Keeler said there was plenty of food on the ship but admitted it became hard to get fresh fruit and vegetables, which stopped being served. “I am looking forward to a fresh salad.” They also had to be careful with supplies of soap and toothpaste to ensure every sailor could receive some, he added.
Asked about the reports of attempted suicides onboard the ship, Keeler did not answer, saying there was an open investigation. As for comments from the US president, which included claims that the 270-day deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Keeler told the Guardian “the president speaks for himself”.
Crew from the USS Higgins also arrived at the Hard Rock hotel. When asked about the conditions onboard the two vessels, Ethan Johnson, a cook onboard the Higgins, said: “We joined the military, it’s not a cruise ship.”
Johnson said there was plenty of meat and vegetables onboard the Higgins.
As well as being prohibited from entering certain areas, sailors are also being prevented from doing any water sports in the area, owing to the potential danger.
They will also not be allowed to visit pharmacies as Thai authorities do not want sailors accessing medicines that do not require a prescription in Thailand, but may need a prescription in the US, Poramet said.
Kristopher Robinson, a naval attache with the US embassy, said Pattaya was chosen as the destination for rest and relaxation because the “people of Thailand have a history of being wonderful hosts not just to US sailors but people from all around”.
Robinson said the crew would take as much opportunity for rest as possible and conduct themselves in accordance with US and local laws. “Sailors here, like all tourists, they’re going to enjoy Pattaya’s great food and wonderful culture,” he said.

The Book of Damascus: Stories from a city haunted by its past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:48:46 UTC
20:48:46 KST

Breadcrumb
The Book of Damascus: A journey through a city transformed by war, repression and exile
One of the functions of literature is to capture historical moments from the inside, to describe their social and experiential reality rather than merely listing the external facts. That function is admirably performed by The Book of Damascus – the latest in Comma Press's excellent Reading the City series.
Khaled Khalifa, the greatest Syrian novelist of his generation and a fixture of Damascus literary life, wrote the Preface: "It is true we live in a forsaken land, afraid of the future and the past, afraid of being arrested and 'disappeared', afraid of all forms of annihilation."
Khaled wrote those words – and the contributors wrote their stories – before the collapse of the Assad regime after 14 years of war and more than half a century of tyranny.
His point about annihilation and disappearance still holds, given that sectarian massacres and detentions without due process continue to characterise Syrian political life, albeit on a smaller scale than before.
It's also still true that Damascus is "a city that lives on invisible layers of endless sorrow." But it's no longer true that "What exists today is merely a remnant of a country waiting to breathe its last so it can be buried." That country no longer exists. It was buried on 8 December 2024, when militiamen trained in Idlib arrived in the capital, when the prison gates opened, and when statues of Assad were toppled.
Khaled Khalifa also no longer exists. He died, aged only 59, on 30 September 2023, in the city he loved and refused to leave, whatever horrors it produced. He missed the liberation, the death of the old and the birth of a violently contested new world, with new winners and new victims, a new type of identity politics and a new authoritarianism, and new enthusiasms and possibilities too.
The stories here study that strange extended period when the Assad regime had already died but – its corpse propped up by foreign powers – refused to lie down. They record the city during that long limbo, expressing what it felt like to walk its streets and suffocate in its crushing fear.
Damascus, in this battered but not quite defeated state, is seen through a range of perspectives and filtered through a variety of genres.
Haseeb al-Zainy's The Blacklist is a Kafkaesque story from the depths of the counter-revolutionary war, when the city was characterised by "the sounds of military helicopters overhead, and patriotic songs glorifying the leader blasting" on "a breeze mingled with the smell of car exhausts, gunpowder and burnt corpses."
The narrator does his best to deal with a grotesquely lecherous intelligence officer, but the nightmarishly surreal situation refuses to be so easily dealt with.
In a very different way, The Seven-Gated Girl-Lady by Rasha Abbas recounts nightmares on the way to the shrine of Ruqqayah, stopping at each of the city’s seven gates, each one associated with a planet.
Omar al-Jbaai's brief, sad story In the First Hour of Traffic describes the end of a Damascene type, Mr Kaleh (Kaleh means ‘faded’), whose worn grey suit was purchased with a government voucher, and who won a prize in the 1980s for being "the most productive worker in the public sector."
Odai al-Zoubi's Bitter Hymns is narrated by characters entangled in adultery, deception, and sectarian prejudice. Fares al-Zahaby’s The Curse of Eid Eve, set in Rukn ed-Din, is a tale of haram money and generalised corruption.
Salwa Zakzak's Butterflies in the Sky of Damascus captures the war-ravaged, cannibalised city as experienced by some of its weakest, most overlooked inhabitants: those "silent, terrified girls, searching through rubbish for anything that can be sold or traded, or put to personal use, like childish joy."
There's no room for romanticism in this tale with its simultaneously grim and prosaic ending. Nor in Rawaa Sonbol's A Storyteller for Our Times, whose hero's attempt to supplement his income by reviving a Damascene tradition ends in humiliation and in a deadening and dangerous rather than creative and entertaining form of storytelling.
Some of the stories portray the city from a greater distance, as seen by provincials.
Zaher Omareen's What Only the Chickens and the Donkey Know, for instance, is the story of a conscript from "the open cemetery" of Hama who is first obliged to attend military camp at Dumayr, and then goes looking for debauched delights in Merjeh Square.
The undying tragedy of the 1982 Hama massacre overhangs this otherwise comic tale. In addition to being a contributor, Omareen is also the editor of this collection.
The eponymous Abu Hajal of Abu Hajal and the Magic Lamp is from Deir ez-Zor, but is residing in the capital's Adra Prison on a drug charge.
Abu Hajal’s brother Khalil, a poet, visits the city’s literary hang-outs, like the Rawda and Havana cafés, when he isn’t visiting lawyers and intermediaries on his brother's behalf.
Aboud Saeed, the author of this compact but wide-ranging story, became renowned for his irreverent, tragicomic Facebook updates during the revolution. His book, The Smartest Guy on Facebook, is highly recommended.
The city is seen from the distance of exile too, as so many have been forced to see it.
Alaa Rashidi's Marvellous Musical Memory offers the distanced Damascene a nostalgic tour of the city's musical spots, from the nightclubs of Rabweh to classical performances in Khan Asa'd Pasha, from Sufi chanting at Kaftarou's mosque to the protest songs of Abdul Baset Sarout, not forgetting the Hawasli pirated cassette shop on Sharia al-Hamra.
The narrator once composed his own 'Ultimate Song of Romance and Social Justice', he tells us, his own 'Grand Unification of World Scales', and his own 'Definitive Spirituality-Sensuality Mix'.
He wished to "reconcile" his "completely contradictory tastes in music" but – and this becomes a refrain – "I was displaced," and so "I lost all of my recordings." There’s a powerful metaphor at work here.
In general, there's a lot of power packed into the slim volume of The Book of Damascus, a worthy addition to Comma Press's excellent series, which includes The Book of Cairo, The Book of Khartoum, and The Book of Gaza, among others.
My only complaint is the absence of stories set in the suburbs, in places like Harasta, Muadamiya and Jaramana, that have either been reduced to rubble or crammed with people displaced from elsewhere. But this is less a criticism than a call for another collection of stories – The Book of the Damascus Countryside, perhaps.
Robin Yassin-Kassab co-wrote Burning Country: Syrians in Revolution and War and is the English editor at the ISIS Prisons Museum. His latest book is The Blood Between Us: Syria After the Fall of Assad
Follow him on X: @qunfuz2

Perpetrators behind Tuesday's attempted attack on a power plant in Germany’s Brandenburg state used homemade rockets fitted with copper wires designed to become entangled in overhead power lines and trigger a short circuit, local media reported Wednesday.
The rockets were equipped with copper wires intended to catch on the overhead lines and cause a short circuit, according to German daily Welt.
The devices were reportedly set to be ignited using analog clocks.
The unidentified perpetrators were at least partially successful, as some of the homemade rockets ignited while several others failed to do so, the report said.
The attack reportedly knocked Block B of the Jaenschwalde power plant out of operation for several hours, although the facility was not completely shut down.
German media reported Tuesday that unidentified suspects had attempted to attack electrical infrastructure at the major Brandenburg power plant using explosive devices.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting service. It added that all lines had since returned to operation and the public power supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility is one of Germany’s largest brown-coal power plants and is located in eastern Brandenburg near the Polish border.

Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:47:11 BST
20:47:11 KST

Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
- Published
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.
"That's a secret. A military secret."
Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.
And that, I suspect, is the point.
Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.
It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".
Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.
We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.
But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.
Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".
Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?
Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.
So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.
"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."
Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.
The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.
For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.
Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.
"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.
Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".
"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.
He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.
"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."
There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.
Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?
There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.
But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday that Russia is becoming "increasingly reckless," pointing to a rise in drones and missiles crossing allied airspace and growing malign activities targeting NATO territory.
"Russia has grown increasingly reckless as they continue their terrible war against Ukraine. We have seen more drones and missiles crossing into our airspace along our eastern flank, creating increased risk," Rutte said during a joint news conference with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.
Rutte said NATO and the EU were working "around the clock" to protect their populations against growing threats.
He also cited what he described as malign activities directly targeting NATO territory, including fires allegedly set at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and a Russian "hybrid attack" in Leipzig, Germany.
"The dangers Russia poses are clear," Rutte said, rejecting suggestions that Moscow's actions could divide NATO allies or weaken their support for Ukraine.
Von der Leyen said Germany had identified Russia as being behind an attempt to attack cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport using military-grade material.
"We will not tolerate it. We stand in full solidarity with Germany," she said.
The European Commission chief said the EU was prepared to strengthen sanctions against Russia and close loopholes being exploited by Moscow.
She added that the EU had received a new Ukrainian request worth several billion euros to support air defenses, including advanced Patriot systems, and said member states were considering the request.
Their remarks came after Germany on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said investigators had found the plot was planned by Russian intelligence services and carried out by low-level operatives.
Leipzig Airport is a major freight hub and a key logistics point for military cargo, including Ukrainian Antonov flights.
Russia has rejected claims of assassinations, sabotage, drone incursions, and spying in countries allied with Ukraine, accusing Western governments of stoking "anti-Russian paranoia."

Zelensky, EU warn new parliament blockage has put 3.7 billion euros for Ukraine at risk
The European Commission confirmed on Sept. 2 that the Ukrainian parliament's failure to pass a law on postal packages the day before has put 3.7 billion euros ($4.3 billion) of EU support at risk.
The parliament was supposed to advance new laws to improve Ukraine's tax base on Sept. 1, specifically to eliminate tax exemptions on small packages, but fell 30 votes short of the required majority to advance the key legislation.
The EU intends to give Ukraine 3.7 billion euros under its Macro-Financial Assistance program in the fall, "but there are 12 conditions there, and this law is one of them," European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari confirmed in response to a question from the Kyiv Independent.
"It's a very important law because it plays an important role in mobilizing revenue for the Ukrainian budget. Very much, very much needed," Ujvari said.
"It is important that Ukraine continues with the respective reforms so that we can carry out the disbursements as planned."
President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized lawmakers more forcefully in his evening address on Sept. 1 for failing to advance several reforms that day.
"They may be difficult decisions. They may be unpleasant decisions. They may be unpopular decisions. But they are necessary decisions that help Ukraine get through this time of war," he said.
The president likewise criticized the parliament for blocking EU integration rules, saying that "voting against them, or talking a lot about Europe while not voting for Europe, is dishonest."
"Beyond being dishonest, right now it is also against the state — against the Ukrainian state."
The parliament is also set to consider additional bills on Sep. 2 and 3, many of which are required by the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for Kyiv to unlock financial support.
Zelensky said the government has set a target date of Nov. 1 to implement 44 such reforms.

SINGAPORE, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's economy is expected to grow 5 percent this year, up from the 3.5 percent forecast in the previous survey, with most sectors receiving upgrades, according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's latest survey of professional forecasters released on Wednesday.
The most likely outcome is for the Singapore economy to grow by 5 percent to 5.4 percent, with an average probability of 37 percent, the survey showed.
The most frequently cited downside risks were an escalation or prolonged conflict in the Middle East and a bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, which could trigger spillovers to financial markets.
On the upside, all respondents identified a sustained AI-driven upturn in the technology cycle as a key support for Singapore's economic outlook. Other upside risks included a de-escalation or resolution of the Middle East conflict and stronger-than-expected global growth.
Singapore's economy expanded 5.9 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, significantly exceeding the respondents' median forecast of 4.3 percent in the previous survey.
For the third quarter, respondents expect gross domestic product growth to moderate to 4.6 percent year-on-year. The median forecast for Singapore's economic growth in 2027 is 3.1 percent. ■

In 2024, under the framework of the "Indonesia-China Center for Ocean and Climate," the two countries carried out field research in Cilacap, Indonesia, compiled a manual on mangrove protection and restoration, and brought mangrove science popularization to local schools, according to Deng. ■
