Ukraine's commander-in-chief outlines his principles for leading Armed Forces
Mykhailo Drapatyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has outlined the principles according to which he will lead the Armed Forces.
Source: a document titled "Leadership principles of the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the development of the military in wartime", posted on the website of the Ukrainian Armed Forces
Details: The document sets out a single objective, eight priorities, 14 requirements for commanders at all levels, and eight expectations of headquarters.
The implementation procedure, specific tasks and performance indicators will be defined in separate documents.
The document says that commanders are required to distinguish between resolve and recklessness, since people are the most valuable combat capability in the armed forces.
The first priority on the list is defending the country and those who live in it.
It also emphasises that military service must become predictable.
The document states that changes are to be made to the system of recruitment, training, military service, rotation, retention and discharge of service personnel in order to ensure the armed forces' combat capability while also taking the needs of service personnel and the public into account.
In addition, commanders and headquarters are required to provide honest assessments and not to allow optimism, fear or personal ambitions to distort reality.
Quote: "The standard of conduct is equally binding on generals, officers, sergeants and civilian leaders: there is no place in the Armed Forces for corruption, abuse of power, harassment, discrimination or injustice. A separate requirement for every commander is the responsible use of state resources...
In war, mistakes can cost lives. But a mistake that is acknowledged, analysed and corrected becomes experience. Therefore, I expect every service member to be honest, courageous enough to speak out about problems, and willing to work with others to find solutions."
Details: A separate priority is accelerating adaptation and the introduction of innovations.
Drapatyi also stressed that Ukraine must achieve a lasting and just peace and build its Armed Forces to such a level that no aggressor will consider an attack on Ukraine an acceptable way of achieving its goals in the future.

====================================================================================================

gary chang’s ‘domestic transformer’ makes 32 sqm of hong kong living space work 24 ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:50:06 UTC
19:50:06 KST

Gary Chang’s apartment treats space as a time-shared resource
In Hong Kong, architect Gary Chang’s Domestic Transformer turns a 32 square meter apartment into a series of living environments, using sliding partitions, fold-down elements, and ceiling-mounted tracks to accommodate up to 24 configurations. The project is a long-running experiment in how domestic space can be reprogrammed, asking whether a limited footprint has to mean a limited way of living.
Chang moved into the apartment in 1976, when he was fourteen, sharing the home with his parents, three sisters, and a sub-tenant. The apartment was divided into small bedrooms, a kitchen, bathroom, and circulation space. Without a room of his own, Chang slept in the central passage on a wooden bench after the rest of the family had gone to bed. The experience led him to question the assumption that domestic functions need to occupy permanently defined rooms.
The architect’s design practice has developed this idea through several iterations of the apartment. The space evolved from its original cellular arrangement into an open-plan experiment, then into a version using curtains as partitions before reaching the mechanized Domestic Transformer completed in 2007.
images courtesy of Gary Chang
Sliding walls let the apartment change throughout the day
Chang concentrates services and storage around the perimeter of the apartment and leaves a flexible central area that can be repeatedly reconfigured. The mechanical system is concentrated overhead, with the main sliding partitions suspended from steel tracks fixed to the concrete ceiling. This keeps the floor clear of tracks and allows the storage walls to move across the apartment with relatively little effort. The walls themselves carry much of the apartment’s contents, including appliances, clothing, and media, so moving a partition also changes what is accessible within the space.
Lightweight honeycomb aluminum panels are used for deployable counters and work surfaces, alongside a hydraulic bed that folds away to reveal the living area. Mirrored surfaces and metal finishes create an impression that the boundaries of the apartment are constantly shifting, reflecting light and making the compact interior appear less materially fixed. Among the arrangements are a larger kitchen, a master bedroom, a guest sleeping area, a spa, a cinema and hammock lounge, an enclosed dining room, a walk-in dressing area, and an open studio configuration.
The transformations are particularly revealing because they demonstrate that the project is not organized around a hierarchy of ‘essential’ and ‘non-essential’ domestic functions. The apartment accommodates amenities that might normally be associated with a substantially larger home, including bathing, entertaining, media, storage, work, and overnight guests. When the bed is deployed, the central area becomes a sleeping chamber. When it is folded away, the same floor returns to a living space. Moving storage partitions can create a more enclosed kitchen or open the apartment into a continuous studio. Other configurations turn the interior toward leisure, including a projection setup and a suspended hammock.
Full-height mirrors, aluminum surfaces, and polished metal details reflect light across the interior, making the boundaries of the space less visually apparent. The apartment does not become physically larger, but its surfaces are made to feel less fixed.
yellow-tinted glazing changes the view and atmosphere of the compact interior
DAYLIGHT AND PRIVACY ARE PART OF THE TRANSFORMATION
The flexibility of the apartment extends beyond its walls and furniture. A motorized screen controls the amount of daylight entering through the window, while a yellow-tinted glazing treatment gives the interior a warmer appearance when the screen is retracted. The intervention changes the atmosphere of the room as well as its physical configuration, using light to alter the perception of the compact interior.
Acoustics present a more difficult problem. Moving partitions need enough clearance to slide freely, which makes it difficult to achieve the airtight seals associated with conventional walls. Chang responds by incorporating acoustic isolation into the wet area, where the enclosed steam shower can also serve as a private space for making phone calls.
The compromise points to one of the less visible realities of kinetic architecture: flexibility can come at the expense of some of the qualities provided by permanent construction. The systems have to balance movement, storage, privacy, acoustics, and everyday use within the same small envelope.
movable walls divide the window into changing views of the Hong Kong streetscape
FROM THE SCHRÖDER HOUSE TO HONG KONG’S STREET HAWKERS
Chang’s approach belongs to a longer history of architecture that questions the permanence of the room. Gerrit Rietveld’s 1924 Schröder House used sliding partitions to alter its interior boundaries, while William L. Murphy’s wall-bed system demonstrated how sleeping could be folded into a single-room apartment. Traditional Japanese fusuma and shoji screens offer another precedent for interiors whose boundaries can change according to use.
Chang also draws on a more immediate Hong Kong reference: the city’s street hawkers. Their stalls expand during periods of activity and contract when they are no longer needed, turning limited physical space into a flexible working environment. The comparison is useful because it shifts the idea of transformability away from high-tech novelty and toward a familiar urban practice of making space available only when it is required.
The Domestic Transformer develops this principle at the scale of the home. Its walls, storage units, beds, counters, and screens become components in a larger system of spatial choreography.
with the partitions moved aside, the window opens onto the surrounding city
THE DOMESTIC TRANSFORMER WAS PART OF A LONGER EXPERIMENT
The ideas tested inside Chang’s apartment also appear elsewhere in his work. One important precedent is the Suitcase House at the Commune by the Great Wall near Beijing, completed in 2002. The linear pavilion uses moving and pneumatic elements to change between more open communal arrangements and configurations that provide greater privacy.
Chang later applied related strategies to commercial residential projects in Hong Kong, including serviced apartments where kinetic cabinetry helps make smaller units more adaptable.
The Domestic Transformer therefore represents one stage in a broader investigation rather than a single isolated solution. The apartment allowed Chang to test these ideas at an intimate scale, where questions of movement, storage, privacy, and everyday routines could be experienced directly.
a sliding element reveals storage and hanging space beside the shower
A SMALL HOME THAT ASKS HOW MUCH SPACE WE ACTUALLY NEED
The lasting interest of the Domestic Transformer lies less in the number 24 than in the question behind it. Chang does not make 32 square meters behave exactly like a much larger apartment. Instead, he demonstrates how the same floor area can support a wider range of activities when rooms are no longer treated as permanent entities.
That flexibility is also demanding. The resident has to operate the apartment, move its partitions, deploy its furniture, and accept a degree of mechanical complexity that would be unnecessary in a conventional home. Transformability is therefore not a substitute for space in every sense; it is another way of organizing it.
But in a city where residential space has long been under pressure, the project offers a different measure of domestic capacity. Its architecture is not defined by how many rooms can fit into 32 square meters, but by how many different lives those square meters can accommodate.
The Domestic Transformer ultimately treats the home as something that can change state. A bedroom does not have to occupy the apartment all day, just as a kitchen, dining room, cinema, or workspace does not have to remain permanently assembled. By allowing functions to take turns, Chang turns time itself into part of the floor plan.
a sliding element reveals storage and hanging space beside the shower
a large movable partition shifts across the apartment on its ceiling-mounted track
a suspended hammock transforms the central space into a lounge
the hydraulic bed turns the living area into a bedroom
integrated storage accommodates media and laundry within the apartment’s perimeter
looking out onto Hong Kong’s dense mix of older low-rise buildings and residential towers
when the bed is folded away, the same space becomes a seating area beside the window
the hydraulic bed folds down to create a dedicated sleeping area
sliding partitions close to return the central area to an open configuration
a movable wardrobe opens the apartment’s storage into the living space
a fold-down surface extends the apartment’s kitchen workspace
the compact kitchen sits alongside the apartment’s movable partitions and mirrored surfaces
small fixtures and storage compartments are integrated into the apartment’s perimeter
floor-to-ceiling media shelving becomes part of the apartment’s changing interior system
a projection screen turns the compact interior into a private cinema

Interceptor drone reaching speed up to 1,000 km/h is revolutionary development — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:49:22 UTC
19:49:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. The interceptor drone capable of reaching speeds up to 1,000 km/h, developed by a Tatarstan-based company, is a groundbreaking development in the field of anti-aircraft missile systems, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
Earlier, media reports said that the Tatarstan-based company Aerokon had demonstrated a prototype of an interceptor drone capable of reaching speeds of up to 1,000 km/h. The drone acquires its target using machine vision and a thermal imager.
"This is truly a revolution, in a certain sense, in anti-aircraft missile weapon systems. The first aspect is the high degree of autonomy and the creation of a potentially dead area extending up to 150 km deep. Given that terminal guidance is expected to utilize artificial intelligence algorithms, this significantly streamlines the use of this system, including under conditions of active electronic countermeasures. Most importantly, it ensures a high level of safety for the carriers and delivery systems of such weapons," Stepanov noted.
According to the expert, the use of this drone will help secure maritime areas, paralyze NATO’s air patrols in key zones, and neutralize any aerial target on the front and in the rear.
"I am confident that this concept includes mass production and a relatively low price compared to the expensive missiles of Western systems such as the Patriot. This is an asymmetric response to both the drone wall and the mass deployment of missile defense and air defense systems along our border," concluded Stepanov.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed Sviatoslav Zaiets as commander of the Ground Forces by presidential decree.
Source: presidential decrees No. 853/2026, No. 852/2026l; Armyinform
Quote: "Sviatoslav Anatoliiovych Zaiets shall be appointed as commander of the Ground Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine".
Details: In a separate decree, Zelenskyy relieved Hennadii Shapovalov from his post as Ground Forces commander. Shapovalov was appointed to the role in June 2025.
For reference: Sviatoslav Zaiets comes from the Airborne Assault Forces. In 2014, he commanded a reconnaissance company of the 25th Airborne Brigade during the annexation of Crimea. After the unit was blocked by Russian forces, Zaiets led his personnel out to mainland Ukraine.
He subsequently served as chief of staff and deputy commander of the 8th Airborne Assault Forces Corps.
In April 2026, Zaiets took command of the 20th Army Corps, and in May, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy conferred the rank of Brigadier General upon him.
During his command of the corps, Zaiets focused on the digitalisation of command and control and the development of unmanned systems deployment. He will now lead the Ground Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

This year's conference will bring together representatives from government, industry, academia, and research and application sectors at home and abroad to jointly explore new pathways for intellectual property to serve the country's comprehensive innovation, high-quality development, and high-standard opening-up, according to the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA).

The number of high-value invention patents held on the Chinese mainland had reached 2.29 million by the end of last year, growing at a faster pace than that of overall invention patents, according to data from the CNIPA.
The number of valid invention patents held on the Chinese mainland had reached 5.32 million by the end of 2025. The year-on-year growth rate of high-value invention patents was 2.2 percentage points higher than that of the country's total invention patents last year. ■

Feature: Chinese enterprise deepens roots in Kyrgyzstan, forging new chapter of cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:46 CST
19:48:46 KST

NANNING/BISHKEK, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- In the Tianshan Mountains of Kyrgyzstan, construction is in full swing in August from north to south. At the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway project site, excavators dig through rock and earth while loaders shuttle materials back and forth.
Deep in the Tianshan Mountains, heavy-duty mining equipment operates at an altitude of some 4,000 meters. On the shores of Issyk-Kul, the "Pearl of Central Asia," construction machinery is supporting urban renewal in the eastern city of Karakol.
These steel machines, coming from China's Guangxi Liugong Machinery Co., Ltd. (Liugong), thousands of kilometers away, cross mountains and ascend plateaus to support construction projects across Kyrgyzstan.
BUILDING ACROSS MOUNTAINS
In December 2024, the CKU railway project was officially launched. As one of the main suppliers of engineering machinery for the CKU railway, Liugong is deeply involved in the project.
"Since 2025, we have deployed successive batches of Liugong loaders and excavators to support construction of the CKU railway, undertaking earthwork excavation and material transportation tasks," said Hou Yubo, Industry Customer Director of Liugong Machinery.
He added that this marked the company's first entry into the Central Asian market with electric engineering machinery.
Since September 2025, Liugong, together with local dealers, has been conducting continuous equipment inspections for the CKU railway project, providing maintenance and technical services for loaders, excavators and other machinery to minimize downtime risks and ensure uninterrupted construction of bridges and tunnels at high altitudes.
In November 2025, Liugong officially registered a subsidiary in Kyrgyzstan, advancing its localization strategy. The professional product knowledge and service experience of Chinese staff, combined with local employees' deep understanding of the environment and customers, have proven highly complementary and well-coordinated throughout project operations.
FROM INTERPRETER TO TECHNICIAN
"When I first came to Liugong, I knew almost nothing about engineering machinery," said Marsel Chokoev, a young Kyrgyz man who joined Liugong's team in Kyrgyzstan in February 2026.
What earned him the job was not prior experience in engineering machinery, but his proficiency in Chinese and a strong willingness to learn.
Six months later, he has learned the basics of loaders, excavators, road rollers and bulldozers, and can independently provide basic service consultations to local clients.
As he became more familiar with the equipment, his language skills began to play a vital role in daily operations. He helps relay Chinese technicians' advice on equipment issues to local clients and dealers, while accurately conveying clients' feedback on operating conditions, equipment performance and service needs to his Chinese colleagues.
"Liugong coming to my hometown didn't just give me a stable job. My Chinese mentors taught me their skills without reservation, and we've become like friends. Here, I've not only gained solid professional skills, but also an understanding of sincere friendship that transcends borders," Chokoev said.
From a language interpreter to a skilled technician, this young Kyrgyz man is carving out his own path of growth through each machine, each service call and each conversation.
His journey has also taken him deep into the Tianshan Mountains, where a high-altitude mining site presents a new set of challenges.
Deep in the Tianshan Mountains, a mining site sits at an altitude of around 4,000 meters, where permafrost makes operations extremely challenging. In recent years, Liugong has delivered batches of large-scale mining equipment to the site for loading, excavation and material transport.
Since August this year, Chokoev and other local employees have been stationed there alongside Liugong's mining service personnel, braving extreme cold and oxygen deprivation to help ensure the machinery operates continuously in the rugged mountain terrain.
STRENGTHENING LOCAL TIES
From railway construction sites to high-altitude mines, Chinese equipment has been delivered in successive batches and put to work on the front lines, handling loading, excavation and material transport. As its equipment applications continue to increase, Liugong is also expanding its presence in the local market and broadening its business reach.
On July 1 this year, Liugong delivered its first batch of equipment for municipal infrastructure projects in Karakol, a highland city in eastern Kyrgyzstan.
During the delivery and acceptance process, Liugong and Karakol municipal officials discussed future cooperation, including expanding its product line into more municipal applications. All equipment is expected to be delivered by the third quarter.
As part of Kyrgyzstan's municipal infrastructure upgrade, the equipment will support road maintenance, municipal construction, environmental management and public facility upkeep, providing reliable support for urban operations.
Liugong's experience is but one example of how Chinese equipment manufacturers are strengthening cooperation with Kyrgyzstan and supporting its development.
Rooted in local communities and serving local needs, Chinese enterprises are writing a new chapter of industrial cooperation, joint development and people-to-people connectivity in Kyrgyzstan. ■

Road access to mudslide-hit border port restored in SW China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:36 CST
19:48:36 KST

Rescuers walk towards the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. Road access to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region was basically restored at 10 a.m. Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway. Rescue teams, relief supplies and some rescue equipment have entered the core rescue area via the road, rescuers said. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Road access to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region was basically restored at 10 a.m. on Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway.
Rescue teams, relief supplies and some rescue equipment have entered the core rescue area via this road, rescuers said.
A section of the G216 national highway, the only land route to Gyirong Port, was severely damaged by the mudslide carrying huge boulders, with the restoration of road access critically important in aiding large-scale search operations in the core disaster area.
The repair operation, notably, posed formidable challenges.
"Conditions vary from one section of the road to another," said Zhou Gang from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. The original roadbed remained usable in some sections, but most of it had been severely damaged.
The work zone lay in a narrow mountain gorge, with steep mountainsides on one side and a fast-flowing river on the other. This confined space made it difficult for multiple pieces of heavy machinery to operate simultaneously, severely hampering the work, Zhou added.
An even greater challenge came from the unpredictable conditions inside the gorge, featuring fast-flowing water and lingering risks of rockfalls, landslides and other secondary hazards.
Crews responded by adapting their methods. Along narrow sections, multiple excavators worked in relay, lining up one behind another to dig and pass debris from one machine to the next.
In sections with the strongest currents, excavators pushed into the water to open the way, while crews built diversion structures and used rock-filled steel cages to stabilize the roadbed, advancing section by section.
The mudslide, caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, hit Gyirong Port on Aug. 26, claiming 16 lives and leaving 546 people missing at the border port as of 6 p.m. on Saturday, according to the regional government's latest update.
Following the disaster, Xizang swiftly activated its highest-level emergency response for natural disasters, mobilizing rescue forces from across the region for search and rescue operations, road clearance and other relief work in Gyirong. ■

China Focus: Digital tech, smart gear reshape farming in China's NE granary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:34 CST
19:48:34 KST

HARBIN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Across the fertile black soil of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, data and technology are helping farmers anticipate weather and growing conditions with unprecedented precision, reshaping how food is grown in the country's agricultural heartland.
For 16 consecutive years, the province has ranked first in the country in total grain output. Behind its sustained productivity is a highly mechanized farming system, with the comprehensive mechanization rate for plowing, sowing and harvesting reaching 99.28 percent.
Now, the province is taking the next step toward smarter farming. From AI-powered crop monitoring and drones to upgraded agricultural machinery, technologies are helping farmers make more precise decisions and boost efficiency.
Heilongjiang's transformation offers a glimpse into China's broader efforts to harness technology to safeguard national food security while advancing rural revitalization.
DIGITAL TECH
Inside Beidahuang Information Company in Harbin, the provincial capital, a massive digital map covering 48 million mu (about 3.2 million hectares) of arable land dominates the wall.
Across the screen, data on soil, crop growth and tractor movements updates in real time, as satellite remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) and AI are gradually integrated into every stage of farming, from sowing to harvesting.
"Previously, a farmer could inspect only about 200 mu a day on foot. Now, drones and remote sensing allow us to monitor vast areas and update crop data for the entire reclamation area every five days," said Wang Hao, deputy general manager of the company's market operation center.
Wang noted that such data is now helping shape decisions from field scouting and fertilization to pest control.
The company has developed more than 60 digital systems for farm management. Built on years of agricultural data, its cold-region crop AI model analyzes soil, weather and crop-growth information to generate planting plans and variable fertilization prescriptions.
"Our agricultural service app has improved service efficiency and cut management costs for farmers," Wang said, noting that the app has facilitated online transactions worth over 100 billion yuan (around 14.74 billion U.S. dollars).
"Smart agriculture is moving from validation to acceptance, but large-scale rollout still faces multiple challenges in data, technology fit and adaptability," said Wang, adding that AI models need ample on-site data and repeated verification to overcome environmental variability to actually serve farm production.
In Wuchang, a renowned rice-producing area in Harbin, digital technology is also reshaping the entire production chain.
At Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd., robots stack packaged rice for shipment. Qiao Wenzhi, head of the company, said QR codes on the products provide information such as the production base and nutritional content, allowing consumers to choose rice tailored to their needs.
SMART GEAR
At a planting base in Heilongjiang, a four-wheel laser weeding robot glides along the crop rows. Multi-spectral cameras and sensors on the robots scan the ground, and algorithms instantly distinguish crops from weeds, directing laser beams to precisely eliminate the weeds.
"Weeding used to rely on manual labor or chemicals, which were either costly or harmful to the soil," said Li Yongwei, deputy general manager of Harbin Huagong Zhiyun Technology Co., Ltd. "Laser weeding is a purely physical, chemical-free method."
Li added that this technology, which achieves a weed removal rate of over 95 percent and a crop damage rate of less than 0.1 percent, cuts weeding costs by up to 70 percent compared with manual labor.
Agricultural machinery is also upgrading toward intelligence. At Heilongjiang Dewo Technology Development Co., Ltd., rows of electric-drive precision seeders are lined up on its square. Air pressure and seed spacing, notably, can be monitored and adjusted in real time via smart terminals.
"The system makes adjustments more convenient and can reduce seed damage," said Du Mujun, chief engineer at Dewo, revealing that the seeder operates approximately 50 percent faster than traditional mechanical seeders.
Currently, Dewo's equipment accounts for more than 60 percent of domestic high-end electric-drive seeder sales. The company has also begun exporting its products overseas, helping extend China's intelligent farming tools to global markets.
"Domestic agricultural machinery manufacturing has improved to the point where it can compete with international brands, offering targeted designs at prices roughly one-third lower than comparable foreign products," said He Chunling, international sales manager at Dewo.
Since launching overseas operations in 2019, the company has exported potato mechanization equipment to Russia, Kazakhstan, Peru and Zimbabwe, and seeders to the Republic of Korea.
EMBRACE INTELLIGENT FARMING
In 2025, Heilongjiang recorded its 22nd consecutive bumper harvest, with grain output reaching a record 82 million tonnes. It also had 676,000 intelligent agricultural machines, ranking first nationwide.
The province's agricultural transformation did not happen overnight.
During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the province accelerated the upgrading and intelligent transformation of agricultural machinery, its governor Liang Huiling said earlier this year.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the province plans to foster industrial clusters focused on agricultural robots, intelligent farming equipment and low-altitude economy, Liang said.
In August, construction began on a national AI application pilot base for crop planting, aimed at tackling common technological bottlenecks and developing scalable applications.
Heilongjiang's technological quest aligns with China's broader plans for agricultural modernization.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan calls for improving agricultural efficiency through a combination of high-quality land, superior seeds, advanced machinery and effective methods, while a document issued in February pledged to advance agricultural and rural modernization and promote all-around rural revitalization, expanding the use of drones, IoT and robots in agriculture and rural areas.
"Relying solely on manual labor and farming the land the way our ancestors did is no longer realistic," said Hu Jinyou, a professor at China Agricultural University, noting that while smart agriculture is still being optimized, the deep integration of AI and agriculture is an irreversible trend.
As a new generation of well-educated farmers enters the fields, Hu said, digital management will gradually become the norm. ■

Kazakh president pledges to further consolidate permanent comprehensive strategic partnership with China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:15 CST
19:48:15 KST

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev (2nd L) takes the light rail on the first day of its operation in Astana, Kazakhstan, May 16, 2026. (Kazakhstan's presidential press service/Handout via Xinhua)
BISHKEK, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- As Kazakhstan's relations with China have reached an unprecedentedly high level, his country stands ready to further consolidate the permanent comprehensive strategic partnership with China, enrich the relationship and open up new prospects for cooperation, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said.
In a written interview with Xinhua, Tokayev said the two countries have a long history of bilateral good-neighborly friendship and a lengthy common border.
"As a Kazakh proverb goes, 'Those who walk the same road share a common destiny.' The friendly relations between Kazakhstan and China serve the fundamental interests of the peoples of both countries and are also an important factor in maintaining peace and stability across Eurasia," he said.
"I sincerely thank President Xi Jinping for his friendship toward Kazakhstan. The political dialogue that we have consistently maintained has become a core pillar of Kazakhstan-China relations," Tokayev said.
"Our strategic partnership is comprehensive and covers all key areas -- from trade, investment, energy and transport to industrial cooperation, agriculture, digitalization, healthcare, science and technology, education and culture," he said.
Two-way trade continues to reach new records, with China being Kazakhstan's largest trading partner, he said, branding transport and logistics as strategic areas of cooperation between the two countries.
As a natural link connecting the East and West, Kazakhstan is working with its Chinese partners to build modern transport and logistics infrastructure of regional scale, he said.
Within the framework of Belt and Road cooperation, the two countries are reshaping the transport landscape between Asia and Europe by developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, building new railway trunk lines, expanding dry ports and logistics hubs, and upgrading border infrastructure, he said.
On the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, Tokayev said it holds a priority position in Kazakhstan-China cooperation and is an important transport corridor connecting China and Europe.
The common task of the two countries, he said, is to maximize the route's competitiveness, emphasizing the importance of building smart customs systems, enhancing coordination between information systems, and automating border procedures.
Tokayev said Kazakhstan-China cooperation is moving to a new level, with the scope of cooperation extending from traditional cooperation in the real economy to partnership in the digital economy.
Regarding scientific and technological cooperation as particularly important, he said that China is relatively advanced in such fields as artificial intelligence, digital technologies, robotics, new energy and high-tech manufacturing, while Kazakhstan is also accelerating the implementation of its digital transformation strategy.
"During my recent visit to Shanghai to attend the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, I held fruitful meetings with heads of leading Chinese technology companies. We intend to implement cooperation projects in such areas as the digital economy, smart manufacturing, e-commerce, scientific research and talent development. Scientific and technological cooperation has every possibility of becoming one of the most important directions for the new stage of Kazakhstan-China cooperation," he said.
Artificial intelligence should serve the development of all humanity, and all countries should have fair access to modern technologies, knowledge and computing resources, he said. "On this issue, our position is in line with that of China."
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addresses the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai, east China, July 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Shen Hong)
In the international arena, Tokayev stressed bilateral active cooperation and their similar positions on such issues as strengthening the core role of the United Nations, upholding the principles of international law, pursuing genuine multilateralism and peacefully resolving conflicts.
He reaffirmed Kazakhstan's commitment to the one-China principle and opposition to acts that undermine national territorial integrity.
Kazakhstan will continue to strengthen solidarity and cooperation with China within the frameworks of the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, and will fully support cooperation under the China-Central Asia mechanism, he said.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which, Tokayev said, has successfully upheld the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diverse civilizations and pursuit of common development. These principles can be regarded as a "standard" for international cooperation.
Noting that next year marks the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and China, he said that in addition to political and economic ties between the two sides, people-to-people exchanges have also developed actively -- a trend vividly demonstrated by the 2026 Kazakhstan-China Year of Cultural Exchange.
Highlighting deepening educational ties, Tokayev said that tens of thousands of Kazakh students are currently studying in China, while many Chinese students are choosing to study at universities in Kazakhstan. Branches of renowned Chinese universities and Luban Workshops have been operating in Kazakhstan, while academic exchanges and university cooperation programs continue to expand.
Tokayev pointed to the mutual visa exemption regime as a major driver of tourism between the two countries. He noted that Chinese tourist arrivals in Kazakhstan reached 962,000 last year, an increase of 47 percent from 2024.
He voiced hope to "show our Chinese friends a diverse Kazakhstan -- modern Astana, ancient Turkistan, the mountains of Almaty, the unique natural landscapes of Mangystau, the vast steppe and the heritage of the ancient Silk Road, as well as our music, cuisine and tradition of hospitality."
"At the same time, we are also eager to experience China -- a country with an ancient civilization and remarkable achievements in development," Tokayev said. ■

====================================================================================================

How Turkey-based groups 'hunt' IDF soldiers and build criminal cases against them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:47:49 UTC
19:47:49 KST

A new Israeli government report describes what it says is a systematic effort in Turkey to identify IDF soldiers who also hold Turkish citizenship, map their relatives and military service, and turn information gathered online into criminal complaints.
According to the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry, activists search social media accounts, monitor pages linked to Turkey’s Jewish community, analyze photographs for military insignia and unit affiliations, and pass the information to lawyers for possible legal action.
The report says the campaign is being carried out by a network of anti-Israel organizations in Turkey and alleges that some of the groups involved maintain links with organizations designated or sanctioned by Israel or the United States.
The findings come against a broader backdrop of deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey and increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other senior officials.
But the report argues that the activity now goes well beyond street demonstrations or political rhetoric and has shifted toward identifying individual Israelis, particularly dual Israeli-Turkish nationals who served in the IDF.
At the center of the activity, according to the documents, are the Worldwide Lawyers Association, or WOLAS, and the Freedom Watch Platform, known in Turkish as Özgürlük Nöbeti Platformu.
The two organizations operate in complementary areas, the report says: collecting publicly available information on Israelis, campaigning against Israel, pursuing legal action and trying to convert online information into evidence that can support criminal complaints.
The ministry’s documents also describe a broader network of contacts involving organizations including Al-Haq, IHH, Al-Mezan, Mavi Marmara-linked groups and the Freedom Flotilla movement.
The report characterizes some of those organizations as designated terrorist groups or entities under sanctions, and says activists within the broader network have also expressed support for Hamas online.
From Facebook and Instagram to the courtroom
One of the most detailed sections of the report describes the methods allegedly used by the Freedom Watch Platform.
According to the ministry, activists use open-source intelligence to identify Israelis who served in the IDF and also hold Turkish citizenship.
The first stage is discovery.
Activists monitor followers, posts and other social media activity, with particular attention to pages associated with Turkey’s Jewish community.
Once an individual is identified, the report says, researchers begin mapping that person’s family and social connections.
Photographs and other publicly available material are then examined for military clues, including uniforms, insignia, unit affiliation and the context in which the person served.
In the final stage, the findings are published online and passed to lawyers, who use them to file complaints with Turkish authorities.
The report presents a case from February 2026 involving a former female IDF soldier with both Israeli and Turkish citizenship.
According to the documents, activists identified her through online material that included a post her mother had published on the day she enlisted.
They then analyzed photographs in an attempt to determine her military affiliation, mapped additional relatives serving in the IDF and ultimately published the information before filing a complaint.
From street protest to targeting individuals
The Freedom Watch Platform did not begin as an organization focused on IDF soldiers.
According to the ministry’s documents, it emerged from protests at an Istanbul port in 2024 surrounding delays involving a Gaza-bound aid vessel connected to the Mavi Marmara organization.
It later developed into a broader anti-Israel campaigning platform, including campaigns targeting Israeli companies.
Over time, according to the report, the focus shifted from Israel as a state and Israeli businesses to individual Israelis.
In February 2026, the issue of IDF soldiers holding Turkish citizenship reached the Turkish parliament.
The report also describes cooperation in February and March with HÜDA PAR, including involvement by the party’s legal department.
On March 7, a lawsuit was filed against Turkish citizens with dual nationality who had served in the IDF, according to the report.
After the IDF released information in February 2026 concerning soldiers who hold foreign citizenship, the ministry says the platform intensified its efforts to identify soldiers with Turkish citizenship specifically.
A separate ministry study cited in the report argues that antisemitism, anti-Israel delegitimization campaigns and legal efforts targeting Israelis have become increasingly embedded within Turkish institutions.
The ministry’s research division claims the activity extends from the education and religious systems to organizations operating internationally against IDF soldiers and Israeli civilians, including efforts to accuse them of war crimes.
Turning online material into ‘evidence’
Alongside the Freedom Watch Platform, the report focuses on WOLAS, an organization of lawyers and academics based in Turkey that works internationally on issues of human rights and international law.
According to the documents, one of its methods is to take publicly available information, or information obtained through legal channels, and attempt to convert it into a basis for criminal proceedings against people linked to Israel.
The report says this includes efforts to create a named database of IDF soldiers who hold Turkish citizenship, formalize details in documents intended to serve as “official evidence” in court and transfer the material to law-enforcement authorities in Ankara.
The network map contained in the ministry’s documents suggests the activity extends beyond a single organization.
Alongside WOLAS and the Freedom Watch Platform, the report lists IHH, Al-Haq, Al-Mezan, the Freedom Flotilla movement, Mavi Marmara-linked organizations and other international groups.
The connections described range from joint activism and legal advice to jointly signed international petitions targeting Israel.
The ministry argues that taken together, the activity represents a shift from broad political campaigning against Israel toward a more personalized strategy aimed at identifying, documenting and pursuing individual Israelis through legal channels.

EU eyes additional sanctions on Ukrainian children deportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:45:21 UTC
19:45:21 KST

The EU is preparing new sanctions on 27 Russian individuals and entities involved in the deportation and indoctrination of Ukrainian children, ahead of a September conference in Toronto on their return.
The EU's diplomatic service presented on Wednesday additional listings targeting 27 Russian individuals and entities involved in the forced deportation and indoctrination of Ukrainian children.
EU ambassadors reviewed the new blacklisting at their first meeting since the summer recess. It is expected to be adopted by the end of the month.
It is not the first time Brussels has targeted those responsible for Russia's illegal mass abduction, deportation and re-education of minors from Ukraine's occupied territories. Several individual listings have already featured in previous sanctions packages.
In May, EU countries blacklisted 16 individuals and seven entities to mark the high-level meeting of the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children. A follow-up conference is due to take place in Toronto, Canada, on 28-29 September.
Following Wednesday's presentation, further technical work is required to finalise the listing, as legal checks must ensure the sanctions are robust enough to withstand challenges in court.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) has also shared with member states a list of 1,600 individuals and entities directly contributing to Russia's war effort, part of a broader shift away from large, sector-focused sanctions packages.
Ukraine has verified the deportation of more than 20,500 children to Russia to date. Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab estimates the number may be closer to 35,000, while Moscow has openly suggested it could be as high as 700,000.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) think tank said that the true number of deported children is almost impossible to verify.
Euronews reported earlier that Russia-installed occupation authorities in Ukraine’s regions created an online “catalogue” of Ukrainian children, offering them for coerced “adoption” through the education department.
The minors are reportedly sorted and categorised so users can “filter” them by age, gender, and physical characteristics such as eye and hair colour. The children are also described in terms of personality traits, with some labelled as “obedient” or “calm.”
For Ukraine it can take years to return one child from Russia after abduction, from the beginning of the identification until the return takes place.
Almost every return so far has been mediated by a third state, notably Qatar, South Africa and the Vatican.
In March the United Nations said that the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.

Estonia elects new president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Estonia elects new president
Estonia's parliament elected Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as the country's next president on Wednesday after one round of voting.
In total, 71 votes were cast in favor of Madise in a secret ballot, and 68 were needed for her to become the head of state. There were seven unmarked ballots and none were judged to be invalid.
Seventy-eight members of the 101-seat Riigikogu received ballots, and all 78 took part in the vote.
After the results were read out, Madise told the MPs present: "I will do my best to be worthy of this trust. I hope that through mutual understanding, debating vigorously when necessary while still supporting one another, we can accomplish a great deal together for Estonia, so that life in Estonia is happy, good and safe."
Madise will become Estonia's seventh president and the second female head of state. She will be sworn into office on October 12.
Madise replaces one-term President Alar Karis, who said he would not stand again in June.
Karis congratulated his successor. "Serving as head of state is a great honour and an even greater responsibility. I wish you strength, wisdom and resolve," he wrote on social media.
Congratulations, Ülle Madise, on your election as the next President of Estonia. Parliament has made its choice, and I will soon hand over the office to you. Serving as head of state is a great honour and an even greater responsibility. I wish you strength, wisdom and resolve. pic.twitter.com/ApQFnjHWjj

Who is Ülle Madise?
Ülle Madise (born Ülle Anton on December 11, 1974, in Tartu, Estonia) is an eminent Estonian jurist, legal scholar, and the country's chancellor of justice.
She earned her law degree and master's degree from the University of Tartu. In 2007, she completed her PhD in administrative management at the Tallinn University of Technology
Her career reflects a steady rise through Estonia's public institutions. She held early roles in the Ministry of Justice, served as an adviser to the Riigikogu Constitutional Committee, and worked as chief auditor at the National Audit Office.
From 2009 to 2015, Madise served as the legal adviser to then President of Estonia Toomas Hendrik Ilves. Concurrently, she pursued an academic career, teaching as a professor of public law and constitutional law in several Estonian universities.
On March 31, 2015, Madise assumed office as the chancellor of justice. In this role, she has been advocating for individual liberties, criticizing over-regulation, and maintaining a non-partisan stance.
Beyond constitutional duties, Madise is a passionate champion of the Estonian language. She has strongly advocated for clear public communications.
Madise is widely regarded as one of Estonia's most influential public officials. This standing culminated in the summer of 2026 when she emerged as a leading apolitical candidate for the Estonian presidential election, backed by several major parties.
She is married to Lauri Madise, a judge on the General Court of the European Union's Court of Justice.

====================================================================================================

Xi's Cairo visit tests Egypt's ties with Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:43:11 UTC
19:43:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Xi in Cairo: testing balance between Beijing and Washington
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is holding expanded talks Wednesday, 2 Sep, at the Ittihadiya Palace with Chinese President Xi Jinping, who arrived in Cairo on Tuesday, 1 September, for an official visit, his first in 10 years.
The visit coincides with the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Cairo and Beijing.
The talks with Xi in Cairo come amid an announced focus on advancing the Egyptian-Chinese partnership.
According to the Egyptian presidency, the visit includes "following up on the implementation of the comprehensive strategic partnership agreement concluded between the two countries in 2014, as well as consultations on several regional and international issues of common interest."
Regional and international developments are set to feature on Xi's agenda in Cairo and in his meeting with Sisi, particularly Gaza, the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Nile River.
The future of the international system and relations among countries in the Global South are also expected to be featured.
The timing of the visit is sensitive for Cairo, which is operating in a turbulent regional environment stretching from Israel's war on Gaza and its repercussions to Sudan and the Red Sea, as well as the continuing dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
At the same time, Egypt is seeking to expand its international room for manoeuvre by strengthening its relations with China and other powers, without abandoning its strategic partnership with the United States.
Palestine
The Palestinian issue appears to be the most prominent regional file bringing the Egyptian and Chinese positions together, which will be reflected in Xi's talks in Cairo.
This comes as Egypt has a direct role in mediation and arrangements concerning the Gaza Strip, while China occupies a different position as a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
In an article translated into Arabic and published by Egypt's Al-Ahram newspaper on Tuesday on the occasion of the visit, Xi wrote that "both sides firmly support the just cause of the Palestinian people in restoring their legitimate rights and seek political solutions to hot-button issues and the achievement of peace and stability in the region."
Egyptian sources told The New Arab that Sisi and Xi will discuss developments in Gaza, the future of political and security arrangements in the Strip and reconstruction.
They will also discuss the repercussions of regional conflicts on maritime security and developments related to Iran and the Gulf.
The war in Sudan will also be discussed, as it is a crisis that intersects with the security of the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, according to the sources.
Maritime stability is a direct interest for both countries.
Egypt is concerned with protecting the Suez Canal and its interests in the Red Sea, while China relies on the region as a major route for its trade with Europe.
Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam: A test of China's position
On the Nile and the Ethiopian Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, the issue most directly related to Egyptian national security, Sisi was keen, in an article published in Al-Ahram on Tuesday, to point to the Chinese position calling for the avoidance of unilateral measures.
He wrote that "Egypt highly appreciates China's position, which affirmed its recognition of the vital importance of the Nile River to Egypt as its main lifeline and renewed the importance of refraining from taking unilateral measures and strengthening cooperation in good faith to achieve mutual benefit and win-win cooperation."
The message takes on significance ahead of Xi's talks in Cairo because of China's close relations with Ethiopia.
This makes Beijing an important international party for Cairo in its efforts to establish the principle of not harming the water interests of downstream countries.
Cairo does not appear to be seeking an explicit Chinese alignment against Ethiopia as much as it seeks to strengthen the Chinese position, calling for negotiations, consensus and the rejection of imposing a fait accompli.
This position could provide Egypt with diplomatic leverage in any future move concerning the Nile waters.
Although Sudan does not appear to be a main theme of the visit, its geographic location makes it part of Egyptian and Chinese calculations regarding the Red Sea and Africa.
Egypt is concerned with preserving Sudan's unity and stability and preventing the repercussions of the war from reaching its borders and interests.
China, meanwhile, has economic and political interests in Sudan and the African continent.
Balancing Beijing and Washington
According to experts, Cairo has maintained its strategic relations with Washington in recent years while expanding its relations with Beijing, Moscow, Europe and other powers.
However, Xi's visit to Egypt allows Cairo to strengthen what Sisi calls "strategic balance" by developing deeper relations with a major international power.
It also allows Egypt to benefit from China's permanent membership of the UN Security Council and its economic and political weight.
In his article on Tuesday, Sisi wrote that Egypt had adhered to "a policy of strategic balance as a direction for Egyptian foreign policy at a time when waves of polarisation and competition are rising, affirming its independent foreign policy and calling for the international community to coordinate its efforts to overcome global challenges that have come to threaten the entire world."
Significance of Xi in Cairo
In the same article, Sisi stressed that Egypt and China had become "partners contributing together to strengthening the role of the Global South in the global system in a way that achieves greater justice and fairness for developing countries."
In this regard, the future of the international system is likely to be one of the issues raised during Xi's talks in Cairo.
The issue is important for Cairo because of its membership in the BRICS group, founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China.
Egypt, the UAE, Iran, Ethiopia and Indonesia joined the group during 2024 and 2025.
Cairo is also engaged in various multilateral frameworks, while Beijing sees Egypt as a partner that can help expand Chinese cooperation with the Arab world and Africa.
In this regard, former Egyptian ambassador to Beijing Ali El-Hefny told The New Arab that the importance of the visit and Xi's talks in Cairo was not linked only to the strength of bilateral relations but also to the circumstances facing the region and the world.
He explained that there was a clear convergence between the Egyptian and Chinese visions regarding the importance of stability in the region.
El-Hefny added that the repercussions of wars and conflicts in the Middle East do not stop at the borders of the countries where they take place but extend to the global economy and the interests of international powers, including China.
In his view, Egyptian-Chinese relations can form an important basis for supporting stability.
He noted that the partnership between the two countries should not be limited to the economic sphere, but could be expanded to include technology, industry, investment, infrastructure and other sectors that serve development plans.
El-Hefny stressed that maintaining stability is the condition through which these ambitions can be achieved.
For his part, former Egyptian assistant foreign minister Mohamed Hegazy said the Chinese president's visit to Egypt carries political and economic importance, particularly amid growing international polarisation and rising regional tensions.
He said these circumstances create a need to expand areas of cooperation without becoming involved in specific alliances or blocs.
Hegazy told The New Arab that what distinguishes relations between Cairo and Beijing is their historical foundation, which has allowed them to continue and develop despite changing international circumstances.
He considered China's current rise in influence to be, in part, a return to a global position it had historically occupied.
He added that Egypt's geographic location, political weight and ties with the Arab world and Africa give it a particular ability to develop its partnership with China.
This means the partnership does not have to remain confined to the bilateral framework but can extend to Egypt's regional surroundings.
In his view, the challenge during the next phase is to turn seven decades of trust and understanding between the two countries into more influential practical partnerships.
Such partnerships can offer a more balanced model for cooperation among countries around the world.

Kernel makes world's first sale of low-carbon sunflower oil at sustainability premium
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:42:11 EEST
19:42:11 KST

Kernel agroholding has signed the world’s first deal to sell sunflower oil with a reduced carbon footprint and verified climate impact, the company’s press service reported.
"Despite the war and constant pressure on our operations, we continue working on climate-resilient solutions in the agricultural sector. And this deal proves that we can not only implement the relevant practices in production, but also verify the results through calculations and turn them into commercial value," said Marta Trofimova, Kernel’s head of sustainability.
The buyer was a multinational corporation pursuing a global net-zero carbon strategy, which paid a premium above the market price for verified emissions reductions in the product’s production, the statement said.
The carbon footprint reduction is achieved at three stages: sunflower cultivation, supply chain tracking, and oil production.
The project is based on a system for precisely calculating a harvest’s carbon footprint at the level of individual fields, taking into account soil, weather conditions, crop rotation and cultivation technologies. This makes it possible to identify fields where sunflowers are grown with the lowest climate impact and to build low-carbon supply chains.
The company tracks the entire chain - from the fields with the lowest carbon footprint, through elevators, to the plant - and can confirm exactly which fields the product comes from and the volume of reduced greenhouse gas emissions associated with it.
Kernel’s processing plants use electricity from renewable sources, further reducing atmospheric emissions.
"The global market for low-carbon agricultural products is only just taking shape. The size of the climate premium is calculated based on the volume of verified emissions reductions and the market value of a tonne of carbon, so the price can reach $100 or more per tonne of CO2 equivalent," the statement said.
To further automate calculations, ensure compliance with international standards, and scale up its low-carbon offering, Kernel has begun cooperating with the international technology company Regrow, the statement said.
According to the company, this is the first case on the global agricultural market in which transparency and verified emissions reductions across the entire production chain have created real added value for a product.
Kernel agroholding is the world’s largest producer and exporter of sunflower oil, Ukraine’s largest grain exporter, an operator of an extensive network of logistics assets, and a leading producer of grain and oilseed crops in Ukraine. It is also one of the largest producers and sellers of bottled oil in Ukraine. The company grows agricultural products and sells them.
For the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 (starting July 1, 2025), Kernel’s net profit fell 5% to $208 million, revenue rose 0.4% to $3.092 billion, and EBITDA rose 1% to $403 million.

Estonian PM: Defense minister can decide whether to resign on Thursday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

Estonian PM: Defense minister can decide whether to resign on Thursday
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) bears no personal blame for questionable defense deals, but may still take political responsibility after talks on Thursday.
"This certainly does not look good. As things stand, I do not see any personal fault on the part of the defense minister. But that in no way rules out taking political responsibility. One does not preclude the other. But that is a decision the defense minister himself can make; no one else can make it for him," Michal told ERR.
ERR asked Michal whether he thought Hanno Pevkur should resign.
"The defense minister will come to the government tomorrow and we will make decisions after that," Michal replied.
"The question is more for the former employees and managers of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments [RKIK] who entered into these contracts and made these payments, even in circumstances where they could have resulted in liabilities for the state, and did not report this either, which I find completely incomprehensible. So I am also highly critical of this, which is why I want to get an overview of the situation," he added.
Michal called a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday for Thursday morning, at which he will ask the auditor general to provide an overview of the lack of clarity surrounding accounting in the defense sector. Commander of the Estonian Defense Forces Andrus Merilo, RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher and Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk will also attend.
"I expect to gain an understanding of exactly what the problems are. The broad outlines are already known to the public. But I want to know what plans all those involved have for putting these matters right," Michal said.
"Everyone has their own responsibilities: someone is responsible for procurement and has to conduct background checks — because even Hanno Pevkur's opponents do not think that he personally should have been conducting background checks for procurements; that is RKIK's job — and if someone there failed to do their job, did it inadequately for some reason or provided incomplete information, they will also have to take responsibility for that. I would not rule out civil claims if it emerges that they knowingly provided false information or failed to do something they were required to do," Michal said.
"If goods were ordered that could not be sent to Ukraine because of inadequate quality or because the goods were unavailable, as far as is currently known, there is no way to be satisfied with that situation. And there is even less reason to be satisfied with a situation in which RKIK decided to order additional goods when it appears that the goods previously ordered had not even been received. You can tell from my answers that, to put it mildly, I consider this a very bad situation. It is certainly not satisfactory," the prime minister said.
Asked whether the Estonian state was also prepared to repay €70 million, Michal said RKIK's new director general, Elmar Vaher, should make recovering the money through the courts his first priority.
"I would also like to understand exactly what guarantees were provided by the company or its parent company that they would assume these obligations, but that is something Elmar Vaher and RKIK's new management will have to explain," Michal said.
Michal said he also had questions about why former RKIK Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar left so abruptly.
"Was it already known at that point that there were problems? It seems to me that this is a hot issue on several fronts and we definitely need to take it apart piece by piece," Michal said.
Michal said he had not been in contact with Saar.
"I think the people who are getting to the bottom of this should be the ones communicating with them — whether that is the National Audit Office, the Office of the Prosecutor General or whoever at the Ministry of Defense is investigating the matter," Michal said.
--

====================================================================================================

BIG’s suzhou museum of contemporary art opens to the public as a village of 12 pavilions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:37:51 UTC
19:37:51 KST

BIG’S FIRST COMPLETED ART MUSEUM OPENS TO THE PUBLIC
Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), together with ARTS Group, VIA.inc, and SHUISHI, completes the Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art, a 60,000-square-meter cultural complex on the shores of Jinji Lake in Suzhou, China. Now officially open to the public, the museum is BIG’s first completed art museum and brings together twelve interconnected pavilions beneath a ribbon-like roof. The project draws on the spatial logic of Suzhou’s historic gardens to create a porous network of galleries, gardens, paths, bridges, and public spaces between the city and the lake.
The museum arrives in Suzhou’s rapidly developing lake district as a new venue for contemporary art, design, and public programming. Its opening follows a series of preview exhibitions, including BIG’s Materialism, which remains on view (find designboom’s previous coverage here). The inaugural program of the museum also includes exhibitions spanning modern and contemporary art, technology-driven artistic practices, and exchanges between Eastern and Western artistic traditions.
all images courtesy of Suzhou MoCA
A MUSEUM ORGANIZED LIKE A CHINESE GARDEN
At the center of BIG’s architectural concept is the lang 廊, the covered corridor traditionally found in Chinese gardens. The architects reinterpret this element as a continuous circulation route connecting the twelve pavilions that compose the museum building. Visitors move through galleries and gathering spaces along a main path while smaller routes branch toward individual exhibitions and gardens.
Bridges and tunnels connect spaces above and below ground, allowing the museum to operate less like a sequence of enclosed rooms and more like a landscape of interconnected destinations. The organization also gives the institution flexibility as exhibitions and public programs change over time.
For Bjarke Ingels, the project responds directly to its position between Suzhou’s urban fabric and Jinji Lake. ‘By dissolving the museum into a Chinese garden of interconnected galleries, distributed across the site like pavilions in a park, the museum becomes a connection between the city and the lake, rather than an obstacle,’ he says. The underlying ambition of the proposal is one of urban porosity: visitors can move through sculpture gardens toward the waterfront while water and landscape extend between the buildings.
Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art sits on the shores of Jinji Lake
CONTINUOUS ROOF LINKS 12 PAVILIONS ACROSS SUZHOU’S LANDSCAPE
From above, the looping roof of the museum creates a distinct figure across the site. BIG describes its geometry as recalling an infinity knot, while Catherine Huang, Partner at BIG, compares the aerial composition to traditional papercut patterns framing the gardens below. The roof also responds to the neighboring Ferris wheel, whose elevated visitors overlook the museum. As Ingels notes, this makes the roof surface effectively the building’s ‘fifth facade.’ The project therefore considers two very different experiences at once: a precise graphic composition viewed from above and a more fluid sequence of gardens, art, and architecture experienced at ground level.
‘The gardens begin to flow into one another, unfolding as sequences of spaces, views, art, and nature,’Huang says.‘A composition that appears precise from above’ becomes ‘an experience of exploration and discovery on the ground.’
The strongest idea behind the project lies in its attempt to resist the conventional museum as an isolated object. Spread across twelve pavilions and threaded together by a continuous roof and circulation network, the Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art positions movement through the site as part of the architectural experience. Whether that ambition translates into a genuinely public connection between city and waterfront will depend on how the gardens, galleries, and open routes are used over time.
Among the exhibitions currently presented at Suzhou MoCA is Materialism, BIG’s exploration of the materials used across its architectural projects. The exhibition follows ten materials, from stone to recyclate, through large-scale mock-ups and models. Alongside Materialism, the museum opens with exhibitions dedicated to modern and contemporary art, including a Picasso exhibition and a large survey of contemporary Chinese art.

Six missing after vessel capsizes off South Korea's southeastern coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:37:49 UTC
19:37:49 KST

At least six people were missing after a tugboat capsized off the southeastern coast of South Korea on Wednesday, officials said.
The TNS Catcher, a 286-tonne tugboat, capsized about 9 kilometres southeast of Oryukdo with eight crew members aboard.
The crew comprised six South Korean nationals and two Indonesian nationals. An Indonesian crew member was rescued by a nearby merchant vessel 20 minutes after the accident. He was not in life-threatening condition.
A second Korean crew member was found unconscious inside the capsized tugboat and transported to a hospital aboard a Coast Guard rescue vessel but later died.
The Coast Guard deployed 13 patrol and rescue vessels, aircraft and the Korea Coast Guard Special Rescue Unit. It also requested assistance from the Navy, other government vessels and private boats.
The Coast Guard said waves of 1 to 1.5 metres and strong currents were complicating the operation. Northwesterly winds were blowing at 4 to 6 metres per second.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung directed authorities to “mobilise all available resources for the search and rescue efforts.”
It said a cargo ship passing through the area rescued one crew member, while the second was found unconscious.
At least eight crew members were believed to be aboard the vessel when it capsized.

80-Year-Old Sen. Ed Markey Holds Off Younger Challenger in Democratic Primary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:37:42 UTC
19:37:42 KST

Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts won the Democratic primary race for his seat on Tuesday, fending off a challenge from the decades-younger Rep. Seth Moulton as he seeks another six-year term in the upper chamber.
Running on a progressive platform, Markey adds to a series of primary wins including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, suggesting an appetite among Democratic primary voters for a shift away from the center.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Moulton’s campaign focused largely on affordable housing and health care. His efforts to position himself as a fresh voice in politics ultimately failed against Markey’s decades of experience.
With around 96% of the ballots counted early Wednesday, Markey had 64.9% of the vote to Moulton's 35.1%.
“Massachusetts needs a Senator who stands up and fights back, a Senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey told the crowd during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”
A ‘generational showdown’
Tuesday’s primary was considered by many to be a “generational showdown” between Markey, 80, and Moulton, 47.
During the campaign, Moulton contended that it was time for change in the state's political representation.
“Massachusetts has a choice: settle for the status quo, or demand better,” he wrote in a social media post Tuesday.
The young moderate rose in the polls earlier this year, narrowing the gap between himself and the two-term incumbent. But in the month or so leading up to Tuesday’s primary, polls showed that Markey had regained ground and was holding a comfortable double-digit lead.
This isn’t the first time Markey, who served in the House for nearly 37 years before winning a seat in the Senate in 2013, has held off a younger primary challenger. In his last reelection bid, the then-74-year-old Senator defeated then-Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, who is 34 years his junior, to advance to the November ballot.
Progressives notch another primary victory
Markey has built up a long progressive record over his years in Congress, co-sponsoring the Green New Deal alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and championing left-wing positions on an array of issues. And he made that record—as well as his extensive experience—a focus of his campaign. Markey argued during the primary that Moulton’s stances on various issues don't align with those of their constituents in deep-blue Massachusetts, saying that “there’s only one progressive in this race” and that “we don’t just need a democratic majority in the Senate. We need a progressive majority.”
“It’s not about your age, it’s about the age of your ideas. And I am the youngest guy in this race when it comes to ideas,” Markey told POLITICO. “Democrats want a victory this November. But then they want, beginning next January … a progressive vision turned into reality on the floor of the House and Senate.”
Markey, a staunch and vocal supporter of transgender rights, criticized Moulton for comments he made about transgender athletes in the aftermath of the 2024 election. In an interview with The New York Times in 2024, Moulton said, “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Moulton has since apologized, saying during a debate last month, “If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump Administration and the Supreme Court, you matter.” The Congressman also told POLITICO over the weekend, “I never intended to hurt anybody with my comments,” but went on to say, “I absolutely do not apologize for starting a debate that we need to be willing to have in the Democratic Party.”
Markey is the latest of a number of progressives who have emerged victorious in recent races. Last month, Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, while other progressives earned the party’s nominations in key House races in the state. And Democratic socialists have scored wins in several high-profile contests in the past year, with Zohran Mamdani—who sent shockwaves through the Democratic establishment when he won the New York City mayoral race in November—perhaps most prominent among them.
Markey will next face the uncontested Republican nominee, John Deaton, a lawyer who previously unsuccessfully challenged Sen. Elizabeth Warren for her seat in Congress.
But Democrats are expected to keep the Senate seat in November: The Cook Political Report rates the race as “Solid Democrat,” ranking it among the seats it considers least likely to flip in the upcoming midterms.
