Germany Officially Accuses Russia of Attacking Ukrainian An-124 in Leipzig
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:33:55 UTC
18:33:55 KST

Germany has accused Russia of being responsible for a drone attack on a Ukrainian An-124 aircraft at Leipzig Airport last month.
According to Deutsche Welle, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the attack followed a “well-known pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe.”
He also warned that Germany could be targeted by similar attacks again.
“The methods used, including the drone’s design, its components, the explosives, and the detonation systems, are known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and from Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul added.
Security experts had previously suggested that Russia could be behind the attack, but Moscow has traditionally denied any involvement.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who spoke alongside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn.
In addition, Germany will terminate the agreement concerning the Russian House in Berlin, which many observers believe has been used for espionage and the spread of Russian propaganda.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the Alliance is “fully in solidarity with Germany.”
“The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he wrote on X.
EU foreign ministers will discuss the attack at a meeting in Ireland later on Tuesday.
On August 4, a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 Ruslan cargo aircraft. The drone crashed into the aircraft’s wing but did not detonate. Leipzig Airport was temporarily closed while bomb disposal experts dealt with the device.
According to journalists, the shipment of military equipment and ammunition had arrived in Germany from France and was being prepared for onward transportation.
U.S. intelligence has determined that Russian military intelligence was involved in an attempted act of sabotage involving a drone near an An-124 Ruslan aircraft at Leipzig Airport in early August.
According to the source, the explosives and the drone’s design match equipment used by Russia’s Main Directorate of the General Staff.
In a statement issued on August 24, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service accused German politicians and European media of “immediately” reaching an “unambiguous conclusion” and blaming Russia for the incident “without even waiting for the preliminary results of the investigation.”
On August 25, German law enforcement officials found a third drone and new evidence in the case involving an attempted attack at Leipzig Airport. In particular, investigators discovered that more drones may have been involved in the hybrid operation than previously believed.
On August 10, German newspaper Die Zeit confirmed the failed sabotage attempt after analyzing video footage.
During the incident, the drone crashed into the wing of the An-124 Ruslan for unknown reasons but did not explode.
A U.S. intelligence source familiar with the investigation told ABC News that the device failed to explode because its triggering mechanism had been disabled.

BNN IN FOCUS | Four years, three governments and the same old problems: where does Latvia stand ahead of the election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:33:50 UTC
18:33:50 KST

Ilona Bērziņa
With one month remaining until Latvia’s 15th Saeima election, BNN is launching a series of articles introducing the political forces that, according to opinion polls, are either expected to cross the 5% electoral threshold or are close to doing so. The remaining parties will be covered in a separate overview, because miracles do happen and, every now and then, “Cinderella” makes it to the ball. But first, we offer a retrospective look at Latvia’s governments over the past four years.
During this period, Latvia has experienced the shock of soaring electricity bills, tax reforms, mortgage support measures, changes to the second pillar of the pension system, billions for Rail Baltica, millions for airBaltic, and special charter flights for the prime minister. Prime ministers, ministers and governing coalitions have changed, yet there has also been remarkable continuity when it comes to the country’s so-called “painful issues”: Rail Baltica still needs rescuing, airBaltic still needs money, healthcare is still underfunded and limping on both legs, while yet another government promises that bureaucracy will be cut any day now.
The Kariņš effect, or the government that dismissed itself
In the 14th Saeima election, New Unity won 18.97% of the vote and secured a convincing first place, the United List received 11.01%, the National Alliance 9.29%, and the Progressives 6.16%. Four years later, what remains of the original political landscape resembles a room after a children’s party: the furniture is more or less the same, only rearranged; some of the guests have fallen out over who should get the bucket and spade; and nobody really wants to admit who broke the vase.
Krišjānis Kariņš will most likely go down in history as an election winner who dismantled his own government. His second government took office in December 2022 with fairly comfortable political capital. The coalition consisted of election winner New Unity, the United List and the National Alliance. It seemed that all the government had to do was get on with governing. That, however, proved to be the hardest part.
The Kariņš cabinet also had undeniable achievements. One of the most significant was the introduction of the State Defence Service at a time when Russia’s war against Ukraine had made the issue of Latvia’s security considerably more tangible than the traditional election slogan of “strengthening national defence”.
The traditional problems that had plagued more than one previous government continued to roll along as if on rails. In the spring of 2023, teachers went on strike. Ahead of the strike, Kariņš declared that it would “change nothing”, because striking would not somehow produce additional money for teachers’ salaries. Summer brought the shock of higher electricity distribution tariffs, while inside the government a months-long debate began over whether the coalition should be expanded.
Meanwhile, the new electricity distribution tariffs punched a hole in household budgets, while the government sought to calm public concern by arguing that without its intervention the increase would have been even greater. In political marketing terms, that is roughly equivalent to responding to a flood-producing downpour by telling people to be grateful it was not a hurricane…
While people were trying to make sense of their electricity bills, the government was consumed by internal disagreements. So many pots and pans were smashed in the political kitchen after Kariņš demanded that the coalition be expanded to include the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) and the Progressives that Kariņš eventually resigned. There is another telling detail: in July 2023, New Unity was supported by 12.6% of respondents in an SKDS poll. By September, that figure had fallen to just 7.7%.
Evika Siliņa’s government: achievements and obvious chaos
If the Kariņš government could never quite decide which political partners it actually wanted to work with, Evika Siliņa solved the problem simply: she removed the United List and the National Alliance from the coalition and gave their seats at the decision-making table to ZZS and the Progressives.
People may like or dislike this government, but the Siliņa cabinet cannot be accused of having done nothing. Mortgage refinancing was simplified and competition between banks was strengthened. Support was introduced for borrowers during the period of high EURIBOR rates. As a result of the prescription medicine price reform, the prices of around 90% of prescription medicines fell, while the tax reform increased the monthly tax-free allowance for pensioners to EUR 1,000.
There was, however, a fly in the ointment. Since money does not multiply by itself, the contribution rate to the second pillar of the pension system was reduced to 5% for four years – from 2025 to 2028 – with one percentage point redirected to the first pension pillar. In the political balance sheet of the tax reform, this is the classic case of “more money today, less money in funded pension savings tomorrow”.
The Siliņa government also faced farmers’ protests. One of the farmers’ main demands was to restore the 5% VAT rate on fresh fruit, berries and vegetables characteristic of Latvia, a proposal strongly backed by ZZS. As a result of a political compromise, a reduced VAT rate of 12% was retained for these products instead of the standard 21%. Once again, the government could pat itself on the back and declare: yes, things got worse, but they could have been even worse.
The chaos surrounding the management of Rail Baltica became visible in all its glory during Siliņa’s time in office. It emerged that the project’s scope had been altered without a unified approach, decisions were difficult to trace, the Cabinet of Ministers had been insufficiently involved in overseeing the project, and estimated construction costs for Latvia’s main Rail Baltica route had increased sevenfold.
Admittedly, all of this was the joint achievement of several governments. But it was during Siliņa’s government that the infamous Rail Baltica pile was concreted into the Daugava River – a structure that came to symbolise the absurdities surrounding the entire project. For the government, it proved easier to “swallow the lump” than to undertake a serious reassessment of the project.
Overall, the Siliņa government also failed to convince the public that the country was moving in the right direction. After just its first three months, 33% of respondents believed the government had performed worse than expected, while only 5.3% thought it had done better. By October 2025, 56% of respondents in an SKDS poll believed the government should fall before the next Saeima election, while only 27.9% wanted it to remain in office until the election.
In May 2026, Defence Minister Andris Sprūds resigned following a drone incident. The Progressives announced that they would no longer support the Siliņa government. Criminal proceedings were launched against ZZS Agriculture Minister Armands Krauze in the so-called timber industry case, and Siliņa dismissed him from office. On 14 May, Siliņa herself resigned.
Andris Kulbergs’ government is gaining popularity faster than it is delivering results
With Andris Kulbergs’ government – consisting of the United List, the National Alliance, New Unity and ZZS – Latvia has finally acquired an impressive parliamentary majority of 66 votes. Yet of the 61 priority measures included in the government’s action plan, only seven had been fully completed as of 12 August.
Kulbergs has also inherited Rail Baltica and airBaltic, and it is precisely here that the prime minister’s desire to demonstrate a new style of government runs head-first into the reality of Latvia’s state-owned companies.
The Saeima vote on the possibility of pouring up to another EUR 30 million into airBaltic’s seemingly bottomless pocket and extending the repayment deadline for a previously issued loan showed that this coalition, too, is stable only until the moment MPs actually have to press the voting buttons. Even coalition member ZZS voted against the additional support.
Voters, however, seem to like Kulbergs – at least for now. In May, the United List was supported by 6.8% of respondents. In June, support rose to 9.8%, in July to 12.2%, and in August to 15.2%. Such a rapid political rise in Latvia is usually the result of either exceptionally successful government performance or the fact that a politician simply has not been in office long enough yet.
The picture is considerably harsher for the other parties in Kulbergs’ government. In August, New Unity stood at 4.2%, the National Alliance at 4.5%, and ZZS at 2.8%. Meanwhile, the Progressives, who left the government, were in third place with 8.8%.
Still, let us remember that there is another month to go before the election and, as noted at the beginning, miracles can happen even in politics.

Russia Secretly Helps Iran Develop Supersonic Cruise Missiles, FT Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:32:41 UTC
18:32:41 KST

Russia has secretly helped Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missile technology capable of threatening US warships and other military targets in the Middle East, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The FT said its investigation uncovered a multiyear covert program, codenamed C430L, which began in 2023, and continued into 2026. The program involved Russian missile specialists helping Iran develop a ramjet propulsion system, which can allow cruise missiles to maintain speeds several times faster than sound.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the report, the program was arranged by Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport in cooperation with NPO Mashinostroyenia, a major Russian missile manufacturer. Leaked correspondence reviewed by the FT indicates that Russian engineers travelled repeatedly to Iran and later analyzed data from Iranian flight tests.
“This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades,” Fabian Hinz, an expert on Iranian missiles and senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, told the FT.
Technology that could threaten US warships
Supersonic cruise missiles combine high speed with low-altitude flight, reducing the time available for air-defense systems to detect and intercept them.
The technology could be particularly significant for Iran given the presence of US naval forces and advanced defensive systems in the Gulf.
Fire Erupts at Russian Rocket Engine Plant in Perm
Iran has already built and flight-tested a ramjet propulsion system, but the FT found no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has yet been deployed.
“For the Iranians, this would give them a qualitatively new strategic weapon system that could threaten US Navy vessels,” Jim Lamson, a former CIA military analyst focused on Iran, told the FT.
The leaked documents reportedly show Russian specialists examining the performance of an Iranian propulsion system and questioning Tehran about its fuel system, combustion stability, air intake, and engine nozzle. They also sought clarification about telemetry from an Iranian flight test.
In April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending around two dozen Russian specialists to Iran for technical consultations under the C430L program.
Program continued during war with US and Israel
The reported cooperation continued even after the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in 2026.
A June 2026 Rosoboronexport letter showed that Moscow and Tehran were still discussing the next stage of the program and Russian technical reports, according to the FT.
The cooperation represents a deeper form of military assistance than simply supplying weapons, with Russia reportedly helping Iran acquire the expertise needed to develop an advanced strategic weapon domestically.
“The secret ramjet program shows Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres,” Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris, told the FT.
Russia and Iran have already developed close military ties during Moscow’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
Tehran supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones and helped establish their production inside Russia. Western and Ukrainian officials have also accused Moscow of providing Iran with battlefield assistance, including satellite imagery, drone support, and weapons components.
Senior Russian missile specialists involved
The FT identified several senior NPO Mashinostroyenia specialists who travelled to Iran in connection with the program.
Among them was Alexander Dergachev, the company’s chief designer for sea-launched missiles and cruise missile complexes. Along with this, Alexander Chebakov, who headed the company’s air-breathing propulsion design department, reportedly visited Tehran three times in 2023.
Russian patents reviewed by the FT identify Chebakov as an inventor on patents involving supersonic ramjet engines for cruise missiles.
Another specialist, Yuri Prokhorchuk, was reportedly involved in high-speed missile systems and named as an inventor on a patent for a ramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missile designed to strike ships and land targets.
The FT reported that Rosoboronexport’s Vladislav Kuzmichev also travelled to Iran in 2023 and later negotiated the C430L contract with Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics.
Neither the Russian government, Rosoboronexport nor NPO Mashinostroyenia responded to the FT’s requests for comment. The Iranian government also did not respond.
Iran seeks to close a major technological gap
Iran has developed increasingly sophisticated ballistic missiles and produces turbojet and turbofan engines for slower cruise missiles. However, developing a sustained-flight supersonic cruise missile powered by a ramjet has remained a significant technological challenge.
Iran’s efforts to develop the technology date back decades.
In 2016, Iran’s then-defense minister said the country planned to develop supersonic anti-ship missiles. In 2018, two Iranian diplomats were arrested in Ukraine while allegedly attempting to procure components and documentation for the Soviet-era Kh-31A supersonic anti-ship missile.
In 2019, Iran publicly displayed a domestically developed ramjet engine. In August 2023, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had begun testing a prototype supersonic cruise missile.
Fabian Hinz said Russian assistance could be particularly valuable because developing a functional ramjet-powered weapon is technically difficult.
“People often think about technology transfers as being solely about sending blueprints, parts, or entire missiles,” Hinz said. “But getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable.”
If successful, the program could eventually allow Iran to develop different weapons around the ramjet technology, improve subsequent generations of missiles, and reduce its dependence on foreign suppliers.

A Prop 65 Crash Course: What You Need to Know (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.
I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.
California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.
So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.
Proposition 65, Explained
In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.
It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.
“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.
The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.
And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.
Prop 65 Is Everywhere
Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.
The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.
Chemicals can be added to the Prop 65 list through four mechanisms: through California’s Labor Code; through evaluations from California’s Carcinogen Identification Committee (CIC) or Developmental and Reproductive Toxicant Identification Committee (DARTIC); through identification by certain authoritative bodies, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA); or through identification by a state or federal agency.
Mariana C. Stern, cancer epidemiologist and member of the CIC, says the committee includes epidemiologists, toxicologists, molecular biologists, and cancer scientists who review the available literature before deciding whether a chemical belongs on the list.
“We may spend the whole day trying to dissect one chemical,” Stern says. “It’s not uncommon that we end up deciding we don’t have enough evidence to add this compound to the list.”
But seeing a warning doesn’t necessarily mean a product contains a dangerous amount of a chemical, or even that the product itself has been tested. According to Schwarzman, “some companies have opted to warn rather than test or reformulate, but from our research, I believe that is much less common than when companies post a warning because of the actual presence of the chemical above a certain threshold.”
From a consumer standpoint, the ubiquity of Prop 65 labels also means that it can be harder to prioritize which ones actually warrant attention. “We definitely have a concern with over-warning,” says Tina Cox, section chief of the OEHHA’s Proposition 65 Implementation Program. “Any unnecessary warnings do make it difficult for consumers to identify where the real exposures are, and it does dilute the value of Prop 65 warnings.”
As a result, California has started trying to make them more useful by requiring short-form warnings to name at least one chemical, rather than relying on the generic “may cause cancer or reproductive harm” language. Businesses have until January 2028 to fully comply with the new requirement. The state is also conducting more outreach to help companies understand when a warning is required and when it is not.
The Warning Isn’t a Verdict
Prop 65 was meant to inform consumers, not to tell them which products to buy. By the same token, a product without a warning isn’t necessarily free of hazardous chemicals.
“You’re never going to be zero exposure, even if you avoid all Prop 65 labels,” says air pollution scientist Shahir Fouad Masri. “If you have a product that doesn’t have a label, it’s one of two things: It was tested and it didn’t exceed Prop 65, and therefore it’s safe, or simply nobody ever sent it to the lab.”
That said, a Prop 65 warning is still useful information, and there are ways to reduce your exposure to these harmful chemicals. “Everybody has different risk tolerances and different priorities,” says Schwarzman. Consider how frequently you use the product and at what dose.
“Exposure from that one product, in many cases, is not going to cause cancer,” adds Cox, “but maybe over a lifetime of exposure, or exposure to similar products that have the same chemical, will increase your risk for cancer or reproductive toxicity.”
One example is holiday lights. Flexible plastic components can contain phthalates, which are added to PVC (polyvinyl chloride) to make it more pliable. Those chemicals migrate out of the plastic and come into contact with your hands or enter household dust. “My own choice around that is to handle them briefly and wash my hands,” says Schwarzman. “I don’t have my kids handle them, and I do make a different decision about that than something I’d be consuming on a daily basis.”
On a similar note, if you’re concerned about a warning on a tool, Masri suggests wearing gloves to reduce direct skin contact. There’s also a difference in dermal absorption rate. The skin on your hands, for example, is generally thicker and more calloused than the skin on your face, which means less absorption. So you might think differently about a screwdriver you occasionally handle with gloves than an LED mask you put directly on your face every day, where the potential for absorption is higher.
TL;DR
If you’re considering a product with a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Instead, look for more information.
- Determine what chemical triggered the warning, if identified.
- Check whether the manufacturer provides testing or contaminant information. Look for credible third-party certification, where appropriate.
- Consider how frequently you’re using the product and how extensively. Occasional exposure is different from using something every day.
- Don’t assume the absence of a Prop 65 label means the product is free of contaminants.
- For consumers who want to dig deeper, P65warnings.ca.gov has information about individual chemicals and ways to reduce exposure. There’s also a dedicated Help Desk for Prop 65, along with an email and phone line for specific inquiries.
- If you’re pregnant, trying to become pregnant, taking medications, or managing a medical condition, talk to a qualified health professional.
Prop 65 is a right-to-know law meant to raise awareness and ensure that we, as consumers, have an impact on the type of products we’re exposed to in our daily lives. As Schwarzman puts it, “I want to encourage us all not to feel like the toxic things are inevitable, and there’s nothing we can do, because there often is something we can do.”
Meet the Experts
- Tina Cox, senior environmental scientist (supervisory) and section chief of the Proposition 65 Implementation Program at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)
- Mariana C. Stern, PhD, a cancer epidemiologist and professor of preventive medicine and urology at the University of Southern California, Keck School of Medicine
- Megan Schwarzman, MD, a physician and environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health
- Shahir Fouad Masri, ScD, an air pollution scientist at the University of California, Irvine

Ukrainian War Documentary ‘Brace For Oblivion’ Wins in Ireland, Comes to Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:30:43 UTC
18:30:43 KST

An American filmmaker’s nearly four-year journey alongside Ukrainian soldiers has resulted in an award-winning documentary that is now coming back to Ukraine.
“Brace For Oblivion”, directed and produced by Xackery Irving, won the Best International Documentary Award at the Galway Film Fleadh in Ireland. The film will have a special screening at the Odesa International Film Festival in Kyiv on Sept. 4.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The screening will take place at 12:30 p.m. at Zhovten Cinema. Several of the servicemembers featured in the film are expected to attend, military duties permitting.
Trailer:
Four years, seven Ukrainians, one war
Irving began filming in Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, following Ukrainian volunteers as they left civilian life to defend their country.
Over nearly four years, he filmed with them in Kherson, Bakhmut, Andriivka, Vovchansk and other areas along the front, including zero-line combat zones.
The result is an immersive portrait of seven ordinary people whose lives were transformed by the war.
Rather than offering another overview of the conflict, “Brace For Oblivion” focuses on its intimate consequences: what prolonged combat does to the body, mind and soul, and what it takes to return to ordinary life after experiencing war.
The camera follows the servicemembers through the extreme intensity of open-ended combat and back into the everyday world they are fighting to protect.
Vivat Loses 35,500 Books to Russian Strike, Damage Tops $370,000
From active duty to an Irish premiere
The film’s international premiere in Galway brought one of its central figures directly from the war to the festival.
Junior Lieutenant Bohdan Patel, whose journey is featured in the documentary, traveled from active military service in Ukraine to Ireland to attend the premiere and take part in a Q&A with the audience.
The response there exceeded the filmmakers’ expectations.
An audience far removed geographically and personally from Russia’s war against Ukraine connected strongly with the experiences of the Ukrainian servicemembers, Irving said.
That reaction convinced the filmmakers that the story they had documented could resonate well beyond Ukraine.
“I think we stumbled onto something bigger than we anticipated: a deeply Ukrainian story that is reaching people far beyond Ukraine,” Irving said of the experience.
Ireland’s national broadcaster RTÉ also featured Patel and the film in its national news coverage.
A film about what Ukrainians are fighting to preserve
At its center, “Brace For Oblivion” is not only a film about combat. It is about the fragile connection between the front line and the life that exists beyond it.
The servicemembers followed by Irving are fighting to preserve the ordinary elements of life – people, homes, relationships and a sense of a future – even as war reshapes their physical and psychological reality.
The film’s Kyiv screening comes after its international premiere and award in Ireland, giving Ukrainian audiences the opportunity to see a story about their own war through the eyes of a filmmaker who spent years documenting it from close range.
“Brace For Oblivion” will be screened on Friday, Sept. 4, at 12:30 p.m. at Zhovten Cinema as part of the Odesa International Film Festival.
The film’s path from Ukraine’s front lines to an international festival – and now back to Kyiv – is another example of how Ukrainian wartime experiences are finding audiences beyond the country’s borders.

10:30:37 BST

The Ministry of Defence has identified Chinook, Merlin Mk4/4A, Wildcat AH Mk1 and Jupiter HC Mk2 as the helicopter fleets currently able to support casualty evacuation tasks, while stopping short of confirming exactly which platforms will perform the role between 2027 and 2030.
The position was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary, who asked which helicopter platforms would be available to the Armed Forces to perform casualty evacuation between 2027 and 2030. Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said Defence does not treat casualty evacuation, or CASEVAC, as a capability tied to a single aircraft type.
She said: “The Ministry of Defence continually reviews platform capabilities to ensure that current and future Defence requirements are met. Casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) is a military task rather than a capability delivered by a single helicopter type, and Defence maintains a range of rotary-wing platforms that can be employed to support casualty evacuation as required.”
Sandher-Jones then identified the aircraft currently available for the task, saying: “At present, CASEVAC capability is provided by the Chinook, Merlin Mk4/4A, Wildcat AH Mk1 and Jupiter HC Mk2 helicopter fleets. As announced in the Defence Investment Plan, Wildcat AH Mk1 is planned to be withdrawn from service from 2027.”
The answer means the Army’s Wildcat AH Mk1 remains part of the current CASEVAC mix, but is not planned to remain in service across the full period covered by MacCleary’s question. The MOD did not identify a direct replacement platform for Wildcat in the casualty evacuation task, instead saying future decisions would depend on operational and capability requirements.
Sandher-Jones said: “Decisions on the helicopter platforms that will be available to perform the CASEVAC role between 2027 and 2030 will be taken in accordance with Defence capability requirements and operational needs, which are kept under regular review.”
The Chinook fleet provides heavy-lift helicopter support to the Armed Forces, while Merlin Mk4 and Mk4A aircraft are operated by the Commando Helicopter Force in support of Royal Marines and wider maritime operations. Wildcat AH Mk1 is operated by the Army Air Corps, and Jupiter HC Mk2 is used within the military helicopter training system.
The MOD also declined to provide a fixed figure for the number of helicopters that could be made available for casualty evacuation at any one time. Sandher-Jones said availability would depend on the wider demands placed on individual fleets, including maintenance and training as well as operational commitments.
She said: “The number of helicopters available to undertake a CASEVAC task at any given time is not fixed and will vary according to operational commitments, maintenance requirements, training activity and force readiness levels.”
The minister added that more detailed readiness information would not be released publicly, saying: “The Department does not disclose detailed readiness or availability information, as doing so could prejudice the operational effectiveness and security of the Armed Forces.”

Advocacy group urges Hong Kong to let residents tap pension savings for homes
Federation of Public Housing Estates says recent cuts to MPF administration fees make now an ideal time to relax withdrawal restrictions
A Hong Kong advocacy group has urged the government to let residents use a portion of their mandatory pension savings for home purchases, one of several proposals submitted ahead of the policy address later this month.
The Federation of Public Housing Estates noted on Wednesday that recent cuts to administration fees for the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) – the city’s compulsory retirement scheme – would generate higher savings for its 4.8 million members, making this an ideal time to relax withdrawal restrictions.
“Offering flexibility in using the Mandatory Provident Fund will be especially helpful to young families under 40 who wish to buy homes,” chairman Man Yu-ming said.
Vice-chairman Scott Leung Man-kwong, who is also a lawmaker, suggested allowing withdrawal of partial pension savings for buying homes to strike a balance between flat ownership and retirement protection.
“The sum may not cover the down payment, but it can help offset expenses,” he said. “We believe that the proposed measure could help homebuyers, especially those with more pension savings.”
Leung noted that Singapore allowed residents to withdraw a proportion of their pension to buy homes under certain conditions, while requiring them to refund their accounts if they sell their properties.

The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two Brics members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around US$10 billion. 
Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
China has also played a key role in Egypt's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching US$12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.

Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit on Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.

He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the Global South" in an increasingly polarised world. 
Xi's visit is the second leg of his second overseas trip this year, following his participation in a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan where he spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and others.
In commentary published by Xinhua, Xi said the two countries were "close brothers standing by each other" in the face of imperialism and colonialism and that he looked forward to exploring a deeper partnership. (Xinhua/Agencies)

What does Zelensky’s threat to ‘close Russia’s skies’ mean? And what targets could Ukraine hit next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:27:16 UTC
18:27:16 KST

What does Zelensky’s threat to ‘close Russia’s skies’ mean? And what targets could Ukraine hit next?
Ukraine continues its campaign of strikes on Russia’s rear, and its choice of targets keeps growing more varied. In recent days, drones have hit an oil terminal at the port of Ust-Luga on the Baltic Sea, a drone base in Oryol Region, unknown facilities in Tolyatti, a power plant in Belgorod, and air bases in Yeysk and Saratov Region. But the campaign still centers on the same types of targets, which absorb most of the drone stockpile: oil refineries and marketplace warehouses. On September 1, Volodymyr Zelensky warned that civil aviation infrastructure could become a new target as well. How effective are these strikes? Do they bring Ukraine closer to victory? What is the logic behind the choice of targets in the first place? And can that logic help predict what Ukraine’s military will strike next? Finally, is Ukraine capable of intensifying its strikes? Meduza’s Explainer desk looked for answers to these questions.
What logic drives Ukraine’s choice of targets inside Russia?
There’s no precise answer. What’s available are educated guesses and statements from Ukrainian officials that can be checked against the facts and either confirmed or disproven. Those guesses aren’t pulled from thin air — they come from matching the technical specifications of Ukraine’s drones and missiles to the kinds of targets being hit.
- The characteristics and quantity of Ukraine’s strike weapons limit its choice of targets. Not everything Kyiv might want to hit can be struck regularly and systematically with the drones and missiles it currently has.
- The types of targets Ukraine strikes regularly also offer clues to the goals behind its bombing campaigns — an attempt to understand what effect Kyiv is counting on when it picks targets for massed, sustained strikes.
Exactly how these decisions are made matters less than the fact that the target list is approved at meetings of the war council under President Volodymyr Zelensky. Analysts, Western military experts, or a specialized military AI agent can compile that list. Alex Karp, chief executive of Palantir, the American company that leads this industry, says its model helps select targets for Ukraine’s military, a claim Ukraine confirms. Palantir previously did similar work under a Pentagon contract ahead of the war with Iran.
What strike capabilities does Ukraine have?
By 2026, Ukraine had built up large numbers of two types of drones: ones for strikes deep behind the front line, hundreds or thousands of kilometers away, and ones for the medium rear, 20 to 150 kilometers (12 to 93 miles) back.
- With the first type, Ukraine expanded a campaign Kyiv has dubbed “bringing the war home” — onto Russian territory — or “long-range sanctions”. The strikes first hit the country’s largest oil refineries, then warehouses belonging to the e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon.
- Medium-range drones, equipped with video cameras to guide them onto moving targets, have attacked vehicles in the occupied territories — mainly, though not exclusively, on roads connecting the Rostov region with Crimea.
- These drones are hard to use against targets inside Russia proper. Their two-way video link relies on Starlink satellite terminals, most often mounted on so-called “mother” drones that relay a signal to the strike drones — but the Starlink signal is blocked over Russia. Kyiv’s requests to Elon Musk to unblock it for terminals owned by the Ukrainian military haven’t gone anywhere so far.
- Long-range drones are guided to pre-programmed coordinates, so they can’t hit moving targets, and they carry their own drawback: a small “payload,” meaning a warhead that isn’t very powerful. They can reliably destroy only fragile targets — even reinforced-concrete factory buildings are extremely hard to knock out with them. What’s needed are “softer” targets that can be destroyed with just dozens of kilograms of explosives.
- Ukraine still can’t regularly hit more heavily defended targets deep inside Russia — that would require missiles with warheads weighing hundreds of kilograms. The cruise and ballistic missiles Ukraine’s allies supply are limited in number, and using them often requires approval from cautious Western governments. None of these missiles has a range beyond 300 kilometers (186 miles), so they’re used only against targets in occupied and border territories.
- Ukraine’s own production of long-range missiles has clearly fallen behind schedule and hasn’t yet become a decisive factor. Over the past year, Ukraine’s military has carried out dozens of strikes with Flamingo cruise missiles made by Fire Point, the same company that makes the FP-1, the most widely used long-range drone. The results have been mixed at best: there have been clear successes, such as hits on military plants — mostly near the border — but also cases in which missiles were evidently launched yet no documented “impacts” were ever recorded.
- Ukraine likely still has few of these missiles, and they’re a relatively easy target for Russian air defenses. Overwhelming that defense would require much larger salvos — and for Russia to feel the threat in full, those salvos would need to come far more often.
- Ballistic missiles with ranges in the hundreds or thousands of kilometers, which Fire Point announced more than a year ago, still haven’t materialized; the company’s latest stated deadline is fall 2026.
For now, then, Ukraine remains constrained in its choice of targets.
- Every long-range drone costs tens of thousands of dollars, and fewer than half of those launched reach their target — so the target has to be expensive, both in the value destroyed and its impact on Russia’s economy, and hard to rebuild.
- The target should be lightly defended and free of a reinforced-concrete shell; ideally, the sensitive facilities are spread over a large area, which keeps Russia from concentrating its air defenses to protect them.
- The target’s coordinates also need to be known in advance.
Why did Ukraine settle on oil refineries and marketplace warehouses?
The most important reason is that these targets suit the mass strike weapons Ukraine has on hand. Oil-refining units, storage tanks for petroleum products, and warehouses full of goods stacked on wooden pallets all burn well, and none of them are encased in reinforced concrete. They’re also large-area targets, hard to defend against attacks coming from multiple directions.
These facilities are well suited to massed campaigns because inflicting maximum damage requires hitting only a small number of “targets.” Building alternative, distributed, protected, and camouflaged production and storage sites is difficult, and constantly repairing and restoring them is difficult if not impossible. What gets destroyed isn’t just expensive property — production and logistics chains break down too, inflicting harm on society at large, meaning producers, sellers, and consumers of goods, as well as on other sectors of the economy and public finances.
All of this applies above all to oil refining. Strikes on refineries in August triggered a second gasoline crisis, more serious than the one in spring and early summer. Summer vacations and the harvest are driving a seasonal rise in demand that is amplifying the fuel shortage’s effects. It’s hard to gauge the full scale of it, but the impact on public mood is clear.
Repairing refining units will naturally get harder as the campaign continues, but it’s still not easy to knock the industry out entirely with drones alone. That would require strikes to continue almost without pause, destroying facilities faster than they can be repaired.
Before August, though, Ukraine had paused its strikes on refineries, which allowed oil refining to partially recover by midsummer. During that lull, Wildberries warehouses became the main target. The impact of that campaign on Russian society is obvious, but it’s clearly smaller than the impact of strikes on refineries: those trigger a gasoline crisis that directly touches tens of millions of lives, while the Wildberries campaign has hit tens of thousands of sellers and, to a lesser extent, millions of buyers who’ve faced longer delivery times.
Ukrainian politicians and military officials have offered various explanations for targeting the warehouses. The most detailed explanation holds that it could trigger a systemic financial crisis in Russia: Wildberries owes hundreds of billions of rubles to VTB, one of the country’s largest state banks, which itself issued bonds to finance joint projects with the retailer. Under this theory, the retailer’s collapse would cause problems for the bank and for the country’s entire financial system.
But Ukraine’s military undercut that explanation itself by expanding the campaign to Ozon facilities in late August. Unlike Wildberries, which built its warehouses on credit, Ozon leases its space with its own funds — a different business model that means strikes on its infrastructure pose little risk to the banking system.
The impact of both campaigns — the “fuel” one and the “commercial” one — on Russia’s military capabilities, and on the resilience of its economy and budget, remains limited. Russia’s Defense Ministry gets top priority for petroleum products, along with other government agencies, and no reports of fuel shortages at the front have emerged so far — not even from troops stationed in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, where strikes on the medium rear have disrupted logistics along roads running near the Sea of Azov and through Crimea. Complaints so far have come only from agricultural producers, who aren’t first in line for fuel, and, naturally, from private car owners.
The strikes on refineries and warehouses haven’t seriously dented the federal budget either. Russia’s Finance Ministry reported that non-oil-and-gas revenue rose significantly over the first seven months of 2026 compared to the same period last year. Oil and gas revenue fell, but that decline predates Ukraine’s campaign — prices for Russian oil were already low at the start of the year. The budget’s real problems stem from rising spending, evidently mostly military spending, which is widening the deficit. Ukrainian strikes on the rear, and the need to counter them, may account for some of that increase, but the exact share can’t be established since most military budget line items are classified. What’s adding more pressure on the treasury is the need to spend on other war-related priorities — for example, buying drones and missiles for strikes on Ukraine’s own rear.
Kyiv has drawn one clear benefit from its strike campaigns: Russian society has genuinely “felt” the war far more acutely than in previous years. Whether that brings Ukraine closer to victory is hard to say — historical experience with bombing campaigns in other wars suggests that attacks on sensitive industries alone can’t achieve success.
What other targets might Ukraine’s military choose? And what does Zelensky’s threat to ‘close the skies’ over Russia mean?
Until Ukraine gets its hands on mass quantities of cruise and ballistic missiles, its choice of targets will follow the same principles as before: objects relatively vulnerable to small amounts of explosives, but whose destruction causes significant economic and social damage.
Zelensky announced one such broad category of target on September 1: civil aviation infrastructure. Ukraine’s president didn’t disclose details, but addressing foreign airlines that fly to and over Russia, he said Kyiv “isn’t threatening civil aviation as such,” even as drone attacks mean “Russian skies will de facto be closing.” Vladimir Putin has already called Zelensky’s remarks “a bid for state terrorism” and threatened to abandon the negotiating process entirely in response.
Experience with strikes on aviation infrastructure shows this isn’t the easiest target to hit hard. Iran, for instance, repeatedly attacked airports across the Gulf states and the broader Middle East, including Israel, but that produced only brief pauses rather than prolonged closures of the affected facilities and airspace. Even after direct drone hits, airports reopened to flights within a few days.
Ukraine also struck an important node of aviation infrastructure in May — a branch of the “Southern Russia Air Navigation” agency in the Rostov region, home to the “Rostov Control” air traffic controllers who manage airspace over the entire south of the country. That closed several airports, but only for a few hours, an effect not much stronger than the routine precautionary closures that happen whenever air defenses respond to drone attacks. A larger-scale effect would require a long-term campaign of strikes on aviation infrastructure.
It’s possible Zelensky is counting on the statement alone to reduce the intensity of flights to and over Russia. But it’s hard to say how foreign airlines — mainly Chinese, Arab, and Indian carriers — will respond to this threat if regular strikes that “de facto close Russian skies” don’t follow through on it. Today, these airlines profit handsomely from using Russian airspace, which remains off-limits to their competitors from the European Union and the United States.
The power grid is another sector where uninterrupted operation matters not just for public comfort and well-being but for other industries too. For several years running, Russia itself has made Ukraine’s power generation and distribution infrastructure the primary target of its own seasonal strikes each fall and winter.
Experience with these attacks shows that infrastructure — transformers at electrical substations, above all — can be knocked out, if only briefly, even by drones. A large-scale effect requires hitting many substations across different regions, but this kind of damage is repaired relatively quickly, provided there are spare transformers on hand, which Ukraine gets from its Western partners.
Drones with low-powered warheads are less suited to knocking out generation itself — power plants or heat-producing facilities — where a lasting effect requires missiles.
Russia is already preparing for the likelihood that its next campaign of strikes on Ukraine’s power grid will draw a symmetrical response: construction of physical protection for electrical substations has begun in Moscow.
Current Ukrainian drones are even less suited to strikes on military facilities. They lack a powerful enough warhead and the ability to hit mobile targets anywhere except the occupied territories, where Starlink service works — and even there, only for terminals registered with Ukraine’s Defense Ministry.
There have also been success stories. Ukraine’s military hit Russia’s only fiber-optic cable factory, in Saransk, with drones, and the plant was shut down at least through 2027 “due to equipment damage.” Its output is needed to produce fiber-optic drones, one of the most important components of Russia’s battlefield fire systems.
A striking counterexample: the many failed attempts to halt the assembly line for “Geran”-type drones in Alabuga.
Strikes on other targets — airfields hosting Russian tactical aviation, for example — have long produced, at best, isolated successes. Hangars, including reinforced-concrete ones, protect the aircraft, and when slow-moving drone attacks pose a danger, the planes are simply scrambled into the air.
It’s similarly hard to inflict serious damage on “drone ports,” the bases from which Russia’s military launches its own long-range drones. Destroying each launcher requires one drone, and even that doesn’t always succeed without the ability to “home in” on the target via a two-way video link. As a rule, the consequences of these attacks are not critical for the Russian side.
Can Ukraine expand its strike campaigns?
Zelensky said recently that Ukraine plans to increase its daily drone salvo targeting sites deep inside Russia to 1,000, up from an average of 300 currently — though Russia’s Defense Ministry reports “repelling attacks” by 500 or more drones every day. A two- to threefold increase in intensity would naturally give Ukraine’s military far more freedom to experiment with target selection and with its impact on the enemy country’s economy and society.
This expansion comes with major financial and organizational difficulties that officials in Kyiv acknowledge as well. Ukraine’s military has no room for error in planning its bombing campaigns — producing drones for strikes on the deep and medium rear eats up a significant share of a limited military budget that Western donors largely fund.
During a recent conflict between Ukraine’s Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and Oleksandr Syrskyi, the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces — a dispute that ended in both men’s resignation — Syrskyi said his rival had used funds earmarked for troop pay in the second half of the year to buy drones over the winter instead. After Fedorov left his post and announced his political ambitions, Zelensky blamed him for a $27 billion hole that had opened up in the Defense Ministry’s budget. Fedorov himself insists the projected shortfall during his tenure was $5 billion.
Either way, this isn’t the best moment for a multifold increase in strike capacity. The drones Ukraine uses to attack the Russian rear cost around $50,000 apiece on average, so an additional 500 to 700 drones a day would run $25 million to $35 million a day — $10 billion to $12 billion a year, assuming daily mass launches and not counting ground infrastructure, extra personnel costs, or drones lost on the ground to Russian strikes.
Even the lower estimate amounts to roughly 10% of Ukraine’s entire annual defense spending, on top of its current budgets. Such an expansion could well jeopardize not just military salaries but other programs too, including ballistic missile production.

Working Limburg windmill opens as guesthouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:25:55 UTC
18:25:55 KST

Starting this week, guests can check in for a night spent in the historic De Hoop windmill in Elen (Dilsen-Stokkem - Limburg). The windmill, which is still used to grind grain to this day, will now also serve as a guesthouse. The people behind the project explain the accommodation is needed to ensure this gem of Limburg heritage can be preserved for the future.
Windmill De Hoop was built in 1870 and remained in use until 1968. The mill is now a listed building and has been fully restored. A young miller recently resumed flour production, whilst guests are now given the chance to stay overnight at the mill.
“People are increasingly looking for a unique overnight experience,” says Stef van Boekel of Specialstays. “This mill has a rich history, and we’ve reflected that in the interior, with carefully chosen colours and materials.”
Every Saturday afternoon, work at the mill is in full swing. That’s when a miller grinds grain into flour here. “He’s a passionate 23-year-old, the youngest miller in Flanders,” explains Van Boekel. “Among other things, he produces and sells bread and cake flour.”
Guests staying at the mill or in one of the other rooms on this site can watch the entire milling process up close. “That’s what makes a stay here truly special,” explains Van Boekel. “Not only do guests sleep in a unique location, but they also experience a piece of living heritage.”
Guaranteeing a future for Mill De Hoop
The people behind the project say the provision of accommodation gives Mill De Hoop new prospects for the future. “These days, it’s very difficult for a mill to survive financially on the sale of flour alone,” says Van Boekel.
“By combining it with accommodation, we’re creating a sustainable model that helps the mill to survive. That’s not only important for the mill itself, but also for the village. In this way, the familiar silhouette that has defined the local landscape for over a century will be preserved.”

Charlie Kirk’s Murder Case Heads to Trial As Judge Rules Defendant Could Face Death Penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:25:18 UTC
18:25:18 KST

Almost a year after the killing of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk at a Utah college campus, the case against the suspect accused of fatally shooting him is headed for trial.
On Tuesday, Tyler Robinson, 23, pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges related to the shooting of Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025.
But Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled that Robinson should stand trial, siding with prosecutors who argued there was “a mountain of evidence” against the defendant.
Graf also ruled that prosecutors can continue seeking the death penalty against Robinson, which the defense team has tried to remove as an option. Graf said the court found probable cause for an aggravating circumstance involving the alleged risk to other people at the crowded campus event, making Robinson eligible for capital punishment.
The hearing on Tuesday followed prosecutors’ presentation of evidence during a five-day hearing in July. No trial date has been set, but a pretrial conference is scheduled for Oct. 23.
Kirk’s death worsened fears of political violence spreading across the U.S., and prompted condemnation from allies, including President Donald Trump.
In a statement, Kirk’s widow Erika called the ruling “an important step in our family’s pursuit of justice”.
“Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie’s murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father,” the statement added.
Erika Kirk and the defendant were both in court on Tuesday for the hearing in the city of Provo.
Why capital punishment is an option
According to Utah law, aggravated murder can become a capital felony if prosecutors file notice that they intend to seek the death penalty, which prosecutors have earlier done in Robinson’s case.
Graf bound over Robinson on one count of aggravated murder, one count of felony discharge of a firearm causing serious injury, two counts of obstruction of justice, two counts of witness tampering, and one count of committing a violent offense in front of a child.
The judge could have sent the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which has a sentence of at least 15 years and a maximum of life imprisonment. But Graf said in his ruling that it was reasonable to infer that shooting Kirk from a distance, while surrounded by a crowd of thousands of people, exposed at least one other individual at great risk, meriting the aggravated murder charge.
Kirk, 31, was sitting under a tent when he was shot in the neck while speaking at an event at the university in Orem.
Ryan McBride, a prosecutor with the Utah County Attorney’s Office, said in closing arguments to the court that the four rounds found in the alleged murder weapon—a bolt-action rifle—explain that Robinson knew there was an increased risk to others since it showed the suspect was prepared to fire more bullets if he had missed.
Robinson was lying on a rooftop around 400 ft away when he fired at Kirk, and the prosecutors argued that a shot merely a degree off could have a considerable difference in distance and endangered others’ lives.
“There is a mountain of evidence that proves he is the shooter,” McBride told the court.
But Staci Visser, representing Robinson, argued the state failed to prove the shooter “knowingly” risked people’s lives and said the prosecutors were trying to force the aggravated murder charge.
“There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim,” Visser said. “There was no evidence that would suggest that anyone else was threatened.”
Other factors could affect sentencing
Besides the risk to others, prosecutors also alleged that Robinson targeted Kirk for his political expression and that he fired in the presence of children. If prosecutors prove this at trial, it could affect his sentencing.
Kirk and the organization he co-founded, Turning Point USA, were central to the growing young conservative movement that helped elect Trump.
Kirk was also critical of same-sex marriage and transgender rights. Earlier this year, prosecutors alleged that the political commentator’s stances on these issues drove Robinson to target him. “It’s not difficult to understand the motive here,” McBride said.

Nepal flash floods 'wake-up call,’ expert warns, urges stronger monitoring, evacuation drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:23:49 UTC
18:23:49 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
- Beijing says Aug. 26 disaster ‘caused by glacier instability resulting from the long-term effects of climate warming’
The devastating flash floods and mudslides that struck the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China should serve as a “wake-up call” for countries in the region, an expert in critical geography told Anadolu.
The warning came as the death toll from the Aug. 26 disaster rose to 1,130 on Wednesday, while search operations continued for nearly 4,500 missing people a week after the disaster.
“Such a disaster is inevitably coming always in the dynamic glacial and seismically active environment of the high Himalayas and the Karakorams,” Daanish Mustafa, professor of critical geography at King’s College London, told Anadolu.
The disaster struck last Wednesday when a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
The surge of water and mudslides devastated Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Kavre and the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, while also burying the Gyirong border crossing with Nepal in southwestern Tibet, also known as the Xizang Autonomous Region, on the Chinese side.
“This was a most unfortunate incident and sadly it was not preventable,” Mustafa said.
Of the 3,916 people missing on the Nepalese side of the border, 639 are personnel deployed at hydropower projects across the landlocked country.
“Dams in high mountains simply work to amplify and accentuate the damage from such events. It should be a wakeup call to all the countries, especially India, China and Pakistan who are in the process of building large dams in the environment,” Mustafa said.
China’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that the disaster was “caused by glacier instability resulting from the long-term effects of climate warming.”
“An ice-rock avalanche occurred at a glacier in Nepal, rapidly plunging downhill and scouring the mountainside, which triggered the disaster,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Mustafa said: “At this time, we have to go with the official claims by China and Nepal until independent scientific assessments become available — which will be a while.”
“There is not much one can do about them (disasters), except public education, evacuation drills, effective communication infrastructure and monitoring,” the academic said.
“Those dams can cause catastrophe with such events … With the dams on line such events can cause millions of deaths instead of a few hundred they have in Nepal,” Mustafa said, calling on South Asian societies to “heed” the warning.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 2. /TASS/. Russia's gold reserves will allow it to maintain its global leadership in this field for approximately 30 years, Deputy Head of the Federal Agency for Mineral Resources (Rosnedra) Aslambek Germakhanov said at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
He noted that the country holds the world's third-largest gold reserves and ranks as the second-largest producer. "Russia’s current high-grade gold reserves amount to 17,500 tonnes. At current output rates, these reserves will ensure its leadership position for up to 30 years," Germakhanov said.
The country's resource base currently includes 18,000 tonnes of gold in the P1 and P2 categories. The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. Arab American Institute highlights growing anti-Latino attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:21:30 UTC
18:21:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Arab American Institute highlights growing anti-Latino attacks after FBI report
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 2025 hate crime report shows a record number of attacks on Latinos amid a heightened climate of fear in immigrant communities.
While the report doesn’t show an overall increase in hate crime, the current political climate raises questions about underreporting bias incidents at a time when many people, particularly from marginialised communities, do not feel comfortable reporting crime to law enforcement.
"While the overall number of reported hate crimes declined in 2025, this data should not be mistaken for a decline in hate across our communities," said Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, in a public statement in response to the FBI report.
"The increase in anti-Latino hate crimes is particularly alarming, reaching the highest level ever recorded as the Trump Administration targets immigrant and Latino communities with bigoted rhetoric and policy," she said.
The report showed that 10,881 incidents were reported in 2025, the lowest level of hate crime reported in five years. There is a nine percent decrease compared with 2024. There have, however, been changes to reporting practices, placing potential limitations on data collection.
Berry also noted that national hate crime statistics reflect what is reported from state and local authorities, meaning that the politicisation of law enforcement could account for underreporting of bias incidents. The FBI’s report found that while hate crime incidents against Muslims and Jews had declined by over 20 percent between 2024 and 2025, incidents against Christians had increased.
"Hate crime data also reflects only what's reported to law enforcement and passed on to the FBI. Chronic underreporting, uneven participation across jurisdictions, and the politicisation of government data all limit our ability to see the full scope of hate in America," said Berry.
"We would prefer to take comfort in a decline in reported incidents but worry the loss of confidence in government institutions under this administration has become yet another barrier to accurate hate crime reporting," she said, noting that the current administration has gutted the civil rights division of the Department of Justice.
In addition, even with an official decline in hate crime, advocates note that the numbers are still significant and show that minorities remain vulnerable.
"Hate crime data is an essential tool for identifying gaps in protections and holding institutions accountable. A decline in reported incidents that still top 10,000 annually is not a reason to look away—it's an urgent call to strengthen reporting and confront the policies and policymakers that let hate flourish," said Berry.

Belgian firm faces trial over DR Congo passport corruption

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

18:21:11 KST

Belgian firm faces trial over DR Congo passport corruption
A Brussels court has ordered Belgian biometrics company Semlex and 13 other defendants to stand trial over alleged corruption, money laundering, and tax fraud linked to a contract to produce passports for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo).
The Brussels Council Chamber referred the defendants to a criminal court on Monday following an investigation lasting nearly nine years, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and Transparency International said in a joint statement. Both organizations joined the proceedings as civil parties.
A spokesperson for the Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office said Semlex and an unspecified number of its employees have been referred for trial, according to Reuters. No trial date has been announced.
In May 2020, 51 Congolese citizens, supported by the ‘Congo Is Not For Sale’ coalition, filed a civil action to join the Belgian investigation into alleged foreign bribery, money laundering, and tax fraud linked to the Semlex passport contract. The International Federation for Human Rights, the Human Rights League, UNIS, Transparency International, and its Belgian branch later joined the proceedings as civil parties.
Semlex produced DR Congo’s biometric passports between 2015 and 2025. The deal almost doubled the cost of a passport to $185, with $60 from each document allegedly transferred to LRPS Ltd, a Dubai-based company reportedly linked to a relative of then-President Joseph Kabila. Kabila has not been accused in the Belgian proceedings, and the alleged connection between his associate and LRPS has not been conclusively established.
“We have a right to know where our money went,” Congolese activist and claimant Fred Bauma said, adding that “this trial will finally shed light on the matter.”
Semlex has not publicly commented on the court’s decision. The company previously said it was the target of a smear campaign.
The case comes amid criticism from the Paris-based intergovernmental Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development over Belgium’s limited prosecution of companies accused of bribing foreign officials. On Monday, Transparency International Belgium called the court’s decision “historic.” “For far too long, Belgium has fallen short of its commitments to combat international corruption,” the non-profit group said.
In June 2025, the Congolese government replaced the Semlex passport system with a new $75 biometric passport produced by German firm Dermalog.
Passport-related corruption has also caused controversy elsewhere in Africa. Former Comoros President Ahmed Abdallah Sambi was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2022 over the illegal sale of passports under a citizenship program that prosecutors claimed had cost the country more than $1.8 billion.

Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:20:55 UTC
18:20:55 KST

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.
According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.
The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.
The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.
The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.
The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

Taiwan's Tongtai brings machine tool capabilities to wafer processing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:20:26 UTC
18:20:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tongtai Machine & Tool Co. is expanding its presence in the semiconductor industry by bringing together its electronics equipment and machine tool businesses, CTEE reported Wednesday.
The move targets both the wafer industry and the semiconductor equipment supply chain. The company’s electronics unit focuses on wafer processing and advanced packaging, while its machine tool business makes precision-machined components used in semiconductor manufacturing.
In wafer processing, Tongtai offers machinery for grinding and flattening wafers. They are used at multiple production stages, including manufacturing, packaging, and recycling.
Grinding thins wafers and removes minor surface defects from earlier processing. Flattening creates a more uniform surface and reduces the likelihood of particles adhering to the wafer, according to Good Technology and a thesis by National Taiwan University’s Tu Chi-hsu (凃岐旭).
The company has also developed ductile grinding for harder materials such as silicon carbide. The process removes nanometer-scale amounts of material, minimizing damage and reducing the number of steps required in conventional wafer processing.
On the machine tool side, Tongtai uses high-precision turning and milling combined with ultrasonic processing to manufacture components for semiconductor production machinery. These include gas-control systems, wafer carriers used to hold wafers during processing, and chambers where wafers undergo manufacturing processes.
The company is also supplying laser-processing equipment for advanced packaging. Its systems have been used on advanced packaging production lines to process multilayer composite structures, forming micro-holes and openings while limiting the area affected by heat and minimizing damage to surrounding materials.
Tongtai primarily manufactures and sells machine tools, or industrial machinery used to process metal and other materials. Its revenue totaled NT$665 million (US$20.9 million) in July, up 57.06% from the same month a year earlier, according to Sinotrade.
