It also provides a much-needed moment of positivity for JLR, which reported falling profits earlier this year as it counted the cost of Donald Trump’s tariff wars and supply chain disruption after a crippling cyber-attack last year.

The company said the luxury vehicle, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, heralded “a new era of enhanced refinement and capability”.
While the model’s electric powertrain will limit its impact on the environment compared with JLR’s petrol and diesel models, SUVs of its size are consistently linked to higher numbers of road deaths in accidents involving pedestrians.
However, Range Rover’s bespoke commissioning service does mean that buyers have an “extended choice of near limitless paint colours and finishes, elevated materials, tailored colour combinations and personalisation details including unique embroidery”.
Martin Limpert, the managing director of Range Rover, said the vehicle was the end product of a “decade of considered engineering and technological development”.
Production at Solihull will be supported by the automaker’s propulsion manufacturing centre, in Wolverhampton, which makes battery packs and electric drive units, as well as traditional internal combustion engines.

Ryanair cuts passenger target as high fuel costs prompt smaller winter schedule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:07:19 UTC
18:07:19 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
- Sustained fuel costs could materially raise European short-haul fares and threaten less-hedged rivals, company warns
Ryanair lowered its passenger target for the current financial year as soaring jet fuel prices prompted the Irish budget airline to reduce its winter schedule.
The carrier said Wednesday that it now expects to carry 214 million passengers in fiscal 2027, down from its previous forecast of 216 million.
The reduction is intended to limit Ryanair’s exposure to unhedged fuel purchases during its typically loss-making winter schedule from November to March.
Passenger traffic during that period is now expected to remain broadly unchanged from a year earlier.
Ryanair said the one-off schedule reduction could cut its winter losses by between €70 million ($81 million) and €100 million, depending on pricing and passenger demand.
Jet fuel was trading at approximately $140 per barrel, according to the company, as the conflict in the Middle East continued to drive energy prices higher.
Ryanair has hedged 80% of its fuel requirements for fiscal 2027 at around $67 per barrel, providing it with greater protection against elevated spot prices than many competitors.
The airline said it remains well positioned to record another profitable year, although profit after tax is expected to fall below the record level achieved in fiscal 2026. 
It added that it was still too early to provide detailed profit guidance.
Ryanair also warned that European short-haul airfares could rise materially if high oil prices persist into the summer 2027 season, as airlines pass increased fuel costs on to passengers.
Some less-hedged competitors could struggle to maintain capacity or even survive the coming winter, it added.
Despite the revised full-year target, Ryanair remains on course to increase its summer traffic by more than 5% to 145 million passengers from 138 million a year earlier.
The airline carried 22.2 million passengers in August, up 6% from 21 million in the same month last year, while its load factor remained unchanged at 96%.
Rolling 12-month traffic increased 5% to 214.4 million passengers, with the load factor steady at 94%.

====================================================================================================

Chinese researchers crack tough challenge of low-grade iron ore utilization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:06:02 CST
18:06:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- For decades, billions of tonnes of iron-bearing mine tailings in China lay largely unused. Zhu Qingshan, a researcher at the Institute of Process Engineering (IPE) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, once said: "Turning this 'sleeping wealth' into usable high-grade resources is key to solving the country's iron ore supply problem."
That vision has now become reality. On Tuesday, the world's largest iron ore magnetization roasting project, with an annual capacity of 5.56 million tonnes, passed official acceptance tests in Anshan, northeast China's Liaoning Province. It has been operating stably at full capacity, with key performance indicators exceeding design targets. The project marks a major breakthrough in the industrial use of low-grade iron ore.
According to the IPE, the technology is the world's first solution for large-scale industrial processing of ultra-low-grade iron tailings. It can turn tailings with an iron content of just 11 percent into concentrate with a grade of 65 percent.
This breakthrough is expected to enable efficient and green development and utilization of nearly 30 billion tonnes of refractory iron ore and almost 10 billion tonnes of iron-bearing tailings in China, the IPE said.
HALF-CENTURY QUEST
China consumes more than half of the world's iron ore. Although domestic reserves are abundant, most of the country's deposits are low-grade and hard to process with conventional methods. Over the past decade, China has imported 11.3 billion tonnes of iron ore. Tapping underused domestic resources has driven generations of researchers to tackle this long-standing technical challenge.
In the 1950s, the Institute of Chemical Metallurgy, the IPE's predecessor, began exploring ways to make efficient use of low-grade iron ore. Chemical engineer Mooson Kwauk pioneered fluidized-bed magnetizing roasting techniques to convert poor-quality iron minerals into recoverable magnetite.
Although the technology showed promise, its industrialization was interrupted due to the country's weak industrial base and the historical conditions at the time. Researcher Zhu Qingshan later took up the unfinished mission.
In 2004, Zhu began devoting himself to research on refractory iron ore. At that time, the technology still faced major hurdles to industrialization: conventional magnetizing roasting suffered from low reaction efficiency, high energy consumption and costs, and poor operational stability. Zhu's team introduced innovative technical approaches to address these issues and lay the groundwork for practical application.
FROM LAB TO INDUSTRIAL SCALE
For Zhu, successful basic research was not the end, but the starting point for industrial application. To turn research into usable technology, Zhu and his team developed a complete system for fluidized-bed magnetizing roasting, including key equipment and supporting technologies.
The team secured a partner in southwest China's Yunnan Province for a project with an annual capacity of 100,000 tonnes. However, the project stalled in 2008 amid the global financial crisis due to funding shortages. With support from various levels of government, the researchers spent more than a year troubleshooting on site, and the plant achieved continuous stable operation in December 2012.
This experience also exposed new limitations in the technology, prompting the team to further improve the roasting process and energy efficiency. They developed a second-generation magnetizing roasting process with more precise control of particle residence time, which was later introduced to Ansteel Group, one of China's major steelmakers.
At Ansteel, the technology has achieved a 98-percent conversion rate for iron minerals, delivering significant economic benefits. Eleven licensing agreements now cover a combined annual processing capacity of more than 15 million tonnes. The team is also advancing overseas projects, including a limonite upgrading initiative in Laos. Looking ahead, researchers plan to extend the technology to other mineral processing and solid-waste recycling applications. ■

China issues new national safety standard for large-scale fireworks displays
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:28 CST
18:05:28 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- China has issued a revised mandatory national standard for the safe operation of large-scale fireworks displays, with the new rules set to take effect on Sept. 1, 2027, the State Administration for Market Regulation disclosed on Wednesday.
The standard, GB 24824-2026, was revised under the organization of the Ministry of Public Security and sets unified safety requirements for the design, operation and management of large fireworks displays used at major celebrations and cultural and tourism events.
The revised standard introduces a five-tier classification system for large fireworks displays, from Level I to Level V, based on the size and quantity of aerial shells and other professional fireworks used. Each level is matched with corresponding qualifications for operators and technical personnel, making clear who is responsible for the display.
It also specifies minimum spectator safety distances and tightens operating procedures, adding technical requirements for the fixing and installation angles of launch tubes, as well as rules covering installation, wiring checks and ignition.
Emergency provisions are also strengthened. Displays must be suspended or terminated in conditions including winds above Force 6, sudden heavy rain or thunderstorms, or accidents such as shell explosions inside launch tubes or overturned launch equipment.
Temporary storage sites must be staffed around the clock, and personnel may only enter the display area for cleanup 30 minutes after the show ends, according to the new standard.
The market regulator said it will work with the Ministry of Public Security to promote implementation of the standard and regularly assess its effectiveness.
China is the world's largest producer and consumer of fireworks and firecrackers. The revision comes as large-scale fireworks displays are increasingly used at major celebrations, tourism festivals and nighttime cultural events across China, raising demand for more standardized safety management at crowded public venues.
It also reflects a broader push to strengthen safety governance for large public events, with clearer operator qualifications, risk assessment requirements and emergency procedures aimed at reducing accidents and clarifying accountability. ■

Threatened freshwater fish face multiple extinction risks in Australia's Wet Tropics: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:23 CST
18:05:23 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A study of Australia's Tropical North Queensland freshwater fish has found numerous species face severe risks of extinction from multiple threats, including habitat loss, invasive species, and warmer waters.
Led by Griffith University's Australian Rivers Institute, the assessment identified the Daintree rainbowfish, found only in small rainforest streams in the Daintree region of Far North Queensland, as the species facing the highest risk, with up to 10 unique threats to its population, according to a university statement released Wednesday.
"Freshwater fish are also important components of stream ecosystems and are indicators of ecosystem health. Their decline signals broader environmental deterioration," said lead author Kaitlyn O'Mara, research fellow at the Australian Rivers Institute.
"Many are found nowhere else on Earth. If they are lost from the Wet Tropics, they become globally extinct," O'Mara said.
The study, published in Pacific Conservation Biology, assessed 24 threats, including climate change, invasive species, water extraction, habitat degradation and hybridization.
Researchers found invasive species, climate-driven changes to temperature and hydrology, habitat and water quality degradation, and hybridization with translocated native fishes were among the most severe threats, particularly for narrowly distributed rainbowfish and migratory cling gobies.
They called for urgent conservation actions including habitat restoration, invasive species control, improved riparian management and captive breeding. ■

Chinese researchers design AI-driven platform to empower marine materials innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:19 CST
18:05:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A group of Chinese researchers has unveiled the Robotic Marine Materials Scientist Platform, an intelligent fabrication system that dramatically improves materials research and development efficiency over conventional approaches.
Traditional materials research faces two long-standing bottlenecks: valuable marine experimental data from failed trials are often lost, hindering artificial intelligence (AI) model training, while repetitive manual operations consume time and introduce errors.
To address these challenges, researchers at the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering of the Chinese Academy of Sciences developed the Robotic Marine Materials Scientist Platform for severe marine environments: high temperature, high pressure, high speed, high salinity, and high humidity.
The platform, covering a 400-square-meter intelligent laboratory, automates the entire workflow from design and preparation to testing and feedback. Robots act as "materials scientists" and carry out these tasks autonomously, significantly accelerating the material innovation cycle.
Working in synergy with the "MarineMat AI" assistant, the platform creates a closed-loop R&D system spanning AI-driven design, automated fabrication, characterization, and data feedback. The platform automatically records and structures all experimental parameters for model iteration, with AI prediction accuracy exceeding 90 percent.
Using this platform, the researchers have developed a novel multi-component cermet composite with excellent temperature and wear resistance, achieving over 30 percent improvement in mechanical and tribological performance over conventional ternary materials.
The screw drills made from this material have been deployed in the Chuanke-1 scientific exploration well in south China's Shenzhen at depths of 7,500 to 10,000 meters. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Revived wetland breathes new life into north China's green "city of future"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:11 CST
18:05:11 KST

SHIJIAZHUANG, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- On a calm autumn evening, families paddled across Huizhi Lake in Xiong'an New Area's central green valley park, where waterbirds skimmed over reeds and trees lined the shore.
The lake lies within the Baiyangdian wetland in north China's Hebei Province. Once known as the "Pearl of North China" for its vast waterways, the area is now becoming an integral part of a modern city taking shape nearby.
"In many cities, paddleboarding is usually offered on the outskirts, because suitable waters are hard to find in the urban core," said Li Nan, head of a local paddleboarding club. "Here, people can enjoy nature right on their doorstep."
The club opened at Huizhi Lake in June. On peak weekend days, it receives more than 100 visitors, drawn by the sport's low entry barrier and the chance to get close to nature without leaving the city.
The central green valley is also just a short walk from the headquarters of several centrally administered state-owned enterprises. For their employees, the water offers an easy escape from the office.
"Paddleboarding is becoming a new way for some Xiong'an residents to relax and socialize," said Li.
For Xiong'an, often dubbed a "city of the future" being built from the ground up, such easy access to clean water and greenery is more than just a recreational amenity. It reflects an approach to urban development that places the natural landscape at the heart of the city's design.
On April 1, 2017, China announced plans to establish Xiong'an New Area to relieve Beijing of functions non-essential to its role as the national capital and advance the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.
The master plan for Xiong'an calls for green development, controlled development intensity and systematic ecological restoration, with Baiyangdian a key focus. Waterways, wetlands and green spaces are being woven into the urban fabric from the outset.
Since the establishment of Xiong'an New Area, Baiyangdian has undergone the largest systematic ecological restoration in its history, bringing a major leap forward in water quality.
In 2021, Baiyangdian's water quality improved to Grade III under China's national surface-water quality standards, a level it has maintained for five consecutive years. The wetland is now among China's lakes classified as having good overall water quality.
The restored landscape also opens new opportunities for local industries and breathes new life into cultural traditions.
Cattails, once abundant in Baiyangdian, had come to be seen as a nuisance. They could overgrow waterways and required labor-intensive removal, while the traditional craft of weaving cattails had gradually declined.
In 2024, Yangzhuangzi Village in Anxin County opened a workshop offering free cattail-weaving training to villagers. The initiative has helped turn a once-neglected craft into a source of employment and income.
"Water quality has improved in Baiyangdian in recent years, and the cattails have grown stronger and more resilient, making them better suited for handicrafts," said Yang Zhiliang, Party chief of Yangzhuangzi Village.
After visiting other regions to learn from their experience, the village decided to revive this craft.
Zhao Fengrong, 61, was among the workshop's first trainees. In her hands, ordinary cattails are transformed into baskets and other objects of various shapes.
"We used to weave cattails for our own use. We never imagined we could make money from the craft," Zhao said.
The workshop has helped more than 2,000 people in the village and surrounding areas find employment.
Xiong'an is also developing local brands around its cattail and reed weaving handicrafts, while short-video platforms, livestreaming and online stores are helping traditional products reach customers far beyond the wetland.
Revival, however, is not limited to livelihoods.
For generations, Baiyangdian has also inspired Chinese writers and poets. Its waterways, villages and wetlands have left a distinctive mark on local culture and helped nurture a notable community of poets.
At the Baiyangdian Poetry Culture Park in Anxin County, modern buildings blend with pathways and landscaped spaces. Poems are engraved on walls, steps and walkways, turning the park into an open-air cultural landscape.
In May, an exhibition hall for local poetry opened at the park, providing a venue for exhibitions, reading and cultural exchanges.
"Ecological restoration has given culture the soil it needs to thrive," said Ling Zhiqing, director of the exhibition hall and a native of the area.
Poet Lin Mang said the ecological environment of Baiyangdian has helped nurture the local poetry community. Since the establishment of Xiong'an New Area, he said, the landscape had undergone significant changes.
"Urban development and ecological protection can reinforce each other, allowing local culture, the spirit of poetry and the heritage of the water town to live on and flourish," Lin added. ■

Cambodia launches 10-year policy to eliminate landmines, cluster bombs, other ERWs by 2035
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:05:10 CST
18:05:10 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia officially launched the National Mine Action Policy 2026-2035 on Wednesday, establishing a comprehensive 10-year roadmap aimed at eliminating all identified landmines, cluster bombs, and other explosive remnants of war (ERWs) across the country.
Under the policy document, the Southeast Asian nation aims to clear all identified landmines by 2030, and all identified cluster munitions and priority areas containing ERWs by 2035.
According to the policy document, Cambodia cleared 3,541 square kilometers of contaminated land between the start of humanitarian mine action in 1992 and 2025. Over those 33 years, deminers located and destroyed more than 1.2 million anti-personnel mines, 26,700 anti-tank mines, and 3.24 million ERWs.
Despite these significant achievements, critical challenges remain, the policy document said.
A total of 1,749 square kilometers of land is still contaminated, it said, adding that this includes approximately 557 square kilometers contaminated by landmines, 663 square kilometers affected by cluster munitions, and 529 square kilometers by other ERWs.
Ly Thuch, a senior minister and first vice president of the Cambodian Mine Action and Victim Assistance Authority (CMAA), emphasized that the policy provides a definitive roadmap to eradicate all explosive ordnance by 2035.
Cambodia remains one of the world's most severely affected nations regarding landmines and ERWs. According to the CMAA, landmine and ERW explosions claimed 19,852 lives and injured or amputated 45,301 others between 1979 and June 2026. ■

====================================================================================================

No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

Few dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish of tortilla de patatas, which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes?
That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer in Recetas de Guerra (Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939.
In the case of the tortilla de patatas, the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette.
“There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said.
In the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod.
As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory.
“I got the idea for the book when I came across one of my great-aunt’s handwritten recipe books and I noticed that some of the recipes were marked ‘wartime’,” Álvarez said. “That led me to research recipes from other sources such as Ignacio Doménech, who wrote a book during the war about how to substitute ingredients and how to make the most of leftovers.”
She added: “Doménech showed us hundreds of examples of how, with a lot of imagination, we could survive those terrible days of starvation.”
Some of Doménech’s recipes, although born of privation, could well find themselves on the menu of an upmarket restaurant today, such as his rose petals with milk and honey.
Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.”
The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952. In between, starvation stalked the land, especially in areas that supported the losing republican side in the civil war.
According to Miguel Ángel del Arco Blanco, a historian at the University of Granada, between 1939 and 1942 about 200,000 people died of starvation in Spain.
While people in the countryside could to some extent subsist on olives and whatever they could grow, Álvarez said “the hunger in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia was horrific”.
“It may seem implausible,” she said. “But for far too long, food in the postwar period was far worse than during the war.”
Produce previously fed to livestock such as beetroot and turnips found its way to the table while the shortage of protein meant pets, cats in particular, were at risk.
“They were dangerous years for cats,” Álvarez said. “People used to put notices up in the hallway saying ‘please respect your neighbour’s cat’. But the cats lived on rats and were not good to eat.”
Álvarez said that what she learned while researching the book was to make the most of every kind of produce, adding that the book was also a homage to the generation that lived through those grim years. “I think it’s important that everyone knows what our grandparents lived through because it marked them as a generation. They were incredibly strong.”

China's Xi holds talks with Egypt's Sisi
Unknown

Breadcrumb
China's Xi holds talks with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Wednesday received his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region against the backdrop of the US-Iran war.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting Chinese investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two BRICS members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around $10 billion. Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
Beijing has also played a key role in Sisi's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres (30 miles) east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
'Independent foreign policy'
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the global south" in an increasingly polarised world.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Egypt is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Last week, the US Treasury announced sanctions on the Emirati branch of Egypt's Banque Misr for alleged support to Iran.
Egypt—which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers—hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.

An electric substation near the German city of Cologne was the target of a sabotage attack, police said on Wednesday.
“Based on the current state of the investigation, we do not believe this was a technical malfunction, but rather a deliberate act — a criminal offense,” a police spokesperson for the western city of Essen told the German Press Agency.
The cause and circumstances of the incident in the Rhein-Erft district remain unclear. The investigation is in full swing.
According to the spokesperson, the police were called to the substation in the Rheidt district of Bergheim around 8 pm local time (1800 GMT) on Tuesday evening due to a technical malfunction.
A short circuit caused several power lines to fail. Based on current information, there was no outage of the general power supply.
Energy provider confirms incident
The facility belongs to the energy provider Amprion, which confirmed the incident.
“An incident occurred on Tuesday evening in the vicinity of Amprion’s Rommerskirchen substation in the Rhineland that affected the operation of power plant feeders,” the company stated early on Wednesday morning.
This reportedly led to equipment failures at RWE Power.
The Dortmund-based company added: “The general power supply was not affected at any time, and system stability was always ensured.”
Experts from Amprion are working with the relevant safety authorities to clarify the facts as quickly as possible and assess the impact.
Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant
The incidents came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant.
“We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said.
Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded.
Daily Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated.
Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations.

Russia Helps Iran Develop Engines for Supersonic Cruise Missiles — FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:58:04 UTC
17:58:04 KST

Russia is helping Iran develop engines for supersonic cruise missiles as part of a secret program codenamed C430L.
The Financial Times reported this in an investigation.
According to the publication, the program began in 2023 and continued into 2026, after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Journalists uncovered details of the program based on leaked Russian correspondence, travel data, and an analysis of military patents.
The main goal of C430L is to help Iran develop a ramjet for anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles. Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport organized the program and coordinated it with NPO Mashinostroyenia.
Travel records indicate that Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers repeatedly visited Iran before the C430L program contract was signed with Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in November 2023.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received substantial Iranian technical data on the ramjet. Russian engineers analyzed the results of Iran’s flight tests and sent Tehran questions regarding the fuel system, combustion stability, intake, and nozzle.
In April 2025, Rosoboronexport offered to send a delegation of around two dozen Russian specialists to Iran for technical consultations.
Experienced specialists from NPO Mashinostroyenia were involved in the project. Among them was Alexandr Dergachov, then deputy head of the enterprise and chief designer of sea-launched missiles and cruise missile systems.
Alexandr Chebakov, who heads the design department responsible for developing airbreathing jet engines, visited Tehran three times in 2023. Russian patents list him as the inventor of developments related to supersonic ramjet control systems and cruise missile engines.
The delegation also included Yuri Prokhorchuk, head of the aerodynamics and ballistics department at NPO Mashinostroyenia and co-author of a patent for a hypersonic cruise missile with a ramjet designed to strike ships and land targets.
In July 2023, during their third trip, the Russian engineers were joined by Vladislav Kuzmichev, head of Rosoboronexport’s defense technologies and space department. He later signed the contract with Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics on behalf of the Russian state-owned company.
Iran had been trying to master this technology for decades. In 2016, Iran’s then-defense minister announced plans to develop supersonic anti-ship missiles, while in August 2023, Tasnim, an IRGC-affiliated news agency, reported that testing had begun on a prototype supersonic cruise missile.
Experts estimate that Russian assistance could help Iran overcome technical challenges in developing such an engine and eventually use the technology to develop various types of missile weaponry.
In February, Reuters reported that Iran was close to reaching a deal with China to procure CM-302 supersonic anti-ship missiles to counter the U.S. Navy.

Inside Taliban-ruled Afghanistan: Five years after US exit (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:57:10 UTC
17:57:10 KST

Inside Taliban-ruled Afghanistan: Five years after US exit (VIDEO)
Five years after the US withdrawal, Afghanistan is no longer a country at war in the way the world once knew it. The streets of Kabul are busy, markets are open, and the booms of airstrikes have faded away from villages that once shuddered under them. But the country that emerged from two decades of conflict is also more isolated, poorer, and firmly under Taliban rule. 
RT India’s head of news, Runjhun Sharma, travels beyond Kabul to see what the new Afghanistan looks like on the ground – seen through the eyes of the people who survived the war, the farmers adapting to sweeping Taliban restrictions, and officials trying to convince the world that the country deserves recognition. 
One of the most haunting encounters in the documentary comes in a village near a former US base, where Mohammed Saabr returns to the remains of his home and recounts losing seven members of his family in an American military operation. For families like his, the war may have ended, but it is hardly history. 
Sharma and her team also follow Taliban officials into former poppy-growing areas near the Pakistan border. Afghanistan’s once vast opium economy has sharply contracted under the Taliban ban – something that years of American military operations could not achieve. It’s something the movement presents as a major achievement. 
Farmers, however, describe the other side of that change: Crops that replaced poppy bring in far less money at a time when poverty and hunger are already widespread.
And there is another story the camera tells almost through the absence of the characters. Women are barely visible on Kabul’s streets. At one point, even the sight of a female journalist traveling in a Taliban vehicle draws attention. Later, questions over women’s education and public life become central to an interview with the Taliban leadership, yet Afghan women themselves remain largely outside the frame. 
The film’s political centerpiece is a rare interview with the Taliban’s chief spokesperson in Kandahar. He speaks about sanctions, frozen Afghan assets, relations with Washington, closer economic ties with Russia, and the group’s demand for international recognition, while rejecting outside pressure to change Afghanistan’s internal laws. 
The documentary ends back in Kabul, where Taliban supporters mark five years in power with the Islamic Emirate’s flags and the weapons the American left behind, outside the old American Embassy – symbols of a war they believe they won, in a country still working out what comes next.

The Verkhovna Rada introduced a new format for industrial parks in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:55:43 EEST
17:55:43 KST

The Verkhovna Rada introduced a new format for industrial parks in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported Draft Law No. 12117 on eco-industrial parks and industrial symbiosis. The document also changes the requirements for land and participants.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted, in the second reading and as a whole, a bill providing for a number of changes concerning the functioning of industrial parks in Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Draft Law No. 12117 "On Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of Ukraine Concerning the Improvement of the Functioning of Industrial Parks" was supported by 270 members of parliament.
Under the bill, the concept of an "eco-industrial park" is introduced—an industrial park on whose territory the initiator of the establishment of the industrial park, the management company, participants, and other entities of the industrial park conduct activities in the field of industrial symbiosis, implementing the best available technologies and management methods, and which meets the criteria determined by the Cabinet of Ministers, as well as the environmental, economic, and social requirements established by law.
The procedure for obtaining eco-industrial park status and the specifics of its functioning will be determined by the Cabinet of Ministers.
The concept of an "industrial park" itself is also being changed—it is a territory designated by the initiator of the establishment of the industrial park in accordance with urban planning documentation and equipped with appropriate infrastructure, within which the initiator of the establishment, the management company, participants, and other entities of the industrial park conduct economic activities.
The document stipulates that economic activities involving the production of excise goods may not be carried out within an industrial park, except for the production of biofuels, the production of biocomponents, the generation and/or storage of electricity, including from alternative energy sources, the production of passenger cars, bodies for them, trailers and semi-trailers, motorcycles, vehicles intended to transport 10 or more people, and vehicles for transporting goods.
Economic activities involving the issuance and holding of lotteries, the conduct of gambling, and the cultivation of plants included in the List of Narcotic Drugs, Psychotropic Substances and Precursors may also not be carried out within an industrial park.
The concept of "industrial symbiosis within an industrial park" is also introduced— cooperation on a contractual basis between the initiator of the establishment, the management company, participants, and other entities of the industrial park concerning:
-  the production, performance, and supply of goods, works, and services, and the exchange thereof; 
-  the processing of waste generated at one production facility by other facilities (except
for waste disposal); 
-  the use of by-products; 
-  the reuse of water, the treatment of wastewater, and its subsequent
reuse within the industrial park;  
-  the combined production of electricity and heat (cogeneration); 
-  the production and use of energy from renewable energy sources and/or alternative
fuels. 
The draft law introduces amendments to the rules for establishing industrial parks on state- and municipally owned land. In particular, the right to establish parks on such land is granted to executive authorities, local self-government bodies that transfer such land into ownership, as well as lessees of state- or municipally owned land plots who meet the requirements for using them to establish an industrial park.
Restrictions are established concerning the establishment, development, and functioning of industrial parks. In particular, the initiators of the establishment of parks may not be persons who:
-  are ultimate beneficial owners or participants holding 10% or more of the shares and are citizens or entities of the russian federation, belarus, Iran, or North Korea; 
-  are legal entities registered in states classified by the Cabinet of Ministers as offshore zones, or legal entities more than 50% of whose authorized capital is directly or indirectly owned by legal entities registered in such states; 
-  are legal entities established and registered under the laws of the russian federation, belarus, Iran, or North Korea, except where their assets have been transferred for management to the ARMA in accordance with the procedure established by law; 
-  are business entities economically linked to the aggressor state within the meaning of the Tax Code of Ukraine; 
-  are included in the Unified State Register of Persons Who Have Committed Corruption or Corruption-Related Offenses; 
-  are subject to sanctions imposed by Ukraine, the United States and the EU; 
The requirements regarding the land plots on which industrial parks may be located are changing. Currently, the area of a land plot or the combined area of adjacent land plots must be at least 10 hectares and no more than 1,000 hectares. The document removes the 1,000-hectare limit, while retaining the requirement that the area of adjacent land plots must be at least 10 hectares.
Also, under the draft law, office premises, financial institutions, marketing and advertising facilities, catering establishments, hotels, dormitories, hostels, dual-use structures, renewable energy facilities and energy storage systems may be located within an industrial park.
A list of documents that must be submitted to include parks in the Register of Industrial Parks is also being added:
-  a copy of the initiator’s decision to establish the industrial park; 
-  a copy of the industrial park concept; 
-  information from the State Land Cadastre regarding the land plots and from the State Register of Rights to Immovable Property regarding the immovable property located on them (if available); 
-  the names of the management company and participants, other entities of the industrial park, and an extract or statement from the Unified State Register of Legal Entities, Individual Entrepreneurs and Public Organizations (if available); 
-  a copy of the land plot/land plots lease agreement, together with all amendments thereto, and an extract from the State Register of Rights confirming registration of the lease right to the land plot; 
-  a copy of the lessor’s decision approving the industrial park concept; 
-  an extract from the urban planning documentation concerning the territory designated for the establishment of the industrial park; 
-  a copy of a certificate concerning the use of the buildings located on the plot (if available); 
-  documents confirming the possibility of financing the development and/or operation of the park in accordance with the concept. 
In the future, the decision to include an industrial park in the Register will also specify the area of the industrial park.
The list of grounds on which an industrial park may be removed from the Register is also being expanded: if there is no management company after two years; if the area of the land plot or the combined area of the industrial park’s land plots is reduced to less than 10 hectares; if economic activity that may not be carried out within an industrial park is conducted; or if the period for which the industrial park was established has expired.
As reported by one of the draft law’s authors, Dmytro Kysylevskyi, "as of the end of 2025, 37 factories had been built or were under construction in Ukraine’s industrial parks," noting that "manufacturing enterprises in the parks continue to open throughout 2026."
We remind you
The Cabinet of Ministers updated the rules for state incentives so that industrial parks could restore infrastructure damaged as a result of Russian attacks more quickly. The government will cover up to 80% of the cost of restoring the infrastructure.

Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
Iran said the US bombed a wedding near the Strait of Hormuz, before Tehran launched missiles at Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq.
The United States and Iran have exchanged a new round of attacks – the biggest in more than a month – raising fears of escalation into a wider regional war.
The US Central Command said it struck dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Top US lawmaker Mike Johnson says lying is part of some Iranians’ religion
- list 2 of 4US strikes on Iran kill child at wedding ceremony
- list 3 of 4Mark Ruffalo comments spark pushback against anti-Semitism ‘smear campaign’
- list 4 of 4‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Iran will be “totally wiped out” if it retaliates against the US attacks. “If they do respond, they’ll be hit much harder,” he told Fox News in an interview.
Iran has responded by firing ballistic missiles towards Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region. Tehran has accused the US of hitting a wedding party, killing at least four people.
Here is what’s happening in the US-Iran war.
Where did the US attacks hit?
Iran said that the US bombing of a house during a wedding celebration in the city of Kuhestak has killed at least four people. Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called it a “brutal” attack, where more than 68 people, including women and children, were wounded.
Footage published by the Iranian Red Crescent Society showed a building with walls and windows blown out, and debris scattered on the ground.
The humanitarian group also published pictures of several children receiving treatment at a hospital in Sirik, which overlooks the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition to Kuhestak, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported explosions in coastal cities including Konarak, Bandar Abbas, Jask, and Asaluyeh, as well as Qeshm Island.
The second consecutive night of US attacks comes as Washington is jostling to wrest control over the Strait of Hormuz, the global energy chokepoint, which remains under Iranian blockade and has become Tehran’s bargaining chip.
Two locations near the cities of Ahvaz and Aghajari in Iran’s southwestern Khuzestan province were hit in missile attacks, the province’s deputy governor for security affairs said, according to the state broadcaster IRIB.
Seven people were killed at three locations in the province, and eight others were injured in the attacks, the IRIB reported.
In total, at least 18 people have been killed across Iran.
Where did Iran hit back?
Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq’s Erbil.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its forces carried out a combined missile and drone attack on US facilities in Erbil province in northern Iraq in retaliation for the US strike.
Iran claimed it hit the Sheikh Isa Airbase, which hosts US forces, in Bahrain. The IRGC said it launched a “heavy” ballistic missile attack on Prince Hassan airbase and a US Marine base in Jordan, and hit the headquarters and residence of the American commander of the Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait.
Tehran said its attack on Kuwait set fire to a drone hangar and a ramp through which UAVs participated in attacks on Iran, adding that several US drones were also destroyed, and claimed to have killed a number of US soldiers.
Kuwait reported intercepting drones and missiles but did not report any casualties. There was no immediate comment from Washington, either.
Jordanian armed forces said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace earlier, with the remaining three falling in remote areas without causing casualties.
What are US, Iran saying?
Washington and Tehran have upped the ante in attacks and political rhetoric amid a diplomatic deadlock. Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran will reciprocate if the US returns to the terms of the June Memorandum of Understanding that halted the military hostilities. The two sides have failed to agree before the deal expired on August 17.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said his country “has unforgettable lessons for the American enemy”.
Baghaei, the Iranian spokesman, called for global action against the US strike on the wedding function.
“This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it,” he said, pointing to attacks on the city of Minab and Lamerd on the first day of the war.
In Minab, US forces struck an elementary school, killing more than 150 people, and in Lamerd, they hit a sport hall, killing at least 21 people.
“Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness,” Baghaei said. “Still, those governments and international institutions that remain silent in the face of such barbarism, or seek to justify such acts, must understand that their silence is not neutrality.”
In the US, Trump said he is not trying to force Iran back to the negotiating table, dismissing reports that Washington is seeking a new agreement with Tehran.
“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

Alexandru Hudisteanu, a maritime security expert, told Al Jazeera that the recent escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran is unlikely to be a one-off “because this war has not been settled in military terms and both sides have the impetus to go to war from time to time”.

He added, “there are still conditions that create these flare-ups, especially because the US is trying to show that Iran does not have monolithic control over the Strait of Hormuz and on who passes through the strait.”
The talks over the status of Hormuz have been deadlocked, with Washington demanding an end to the Iranian blockade without any conditions while Tehran wants the US to end its naval blockade on its ports.

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Finance Ministry and the US Treasury saw a basis for the further development of bilateral relations, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said in a comment to the Vesti TV program.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stressed the importance of contacts with Russia for resolving the conflict in Ukraine.
The meeting between Siluanov and Bessent took place on the sidelines of the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting, which was held in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 31 and September 1.
TASS has compiled the main information available so far.
Contacts with US Treasury Department
Siluanov noted that this was his first meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent:
"You know, this was our first meeting with Mr. Bessent. It was on the sidelines of the G20. We got to know each other--that's positive."
He stated that the Russian and US financial departments saw a foundation for further development of bilateral relations: "We agreed that there is a basis for developing our financial relations. Clearly, this isn't easy right now. After all, there are certain tensions between our countries. As geopolitical tensions resolve, I'm confident that we will also develop our financial relations."
According to Siluanov, economic cooperation between Russia and the US can help resolve political issues, and the dialogue must continue: "It seems that financiers can always find common ground, perhaps even faster than politicians. Therefore, we must always talk, we must continue the dialogue. If we find strong common ground, that's what we have. We must develop it, and then political issues will be easier to resolve."
US Treasury statements
Bessent emphasized the importance of contacts with Russia for resolving the conflict in Ukraine: "If the sides don't talk, if we are not engaged, how can it be solved?"
He stated that despite the "sour taste" among his European colleagues, interaction with Russia must continue: "I know that some Europeans have a sour taste, but I think it's very important to engage."
The US side considers Bessent's meeting in Asheville to be productive, said Erin Brown, Deputy Secretary of the Treasury for International Affairs. According to her, Bessent assured that the United States wants a peaceful resolution to the conflict in Ukraine.
Brown added that the ministers discussed "[US President Donald] Trump's plan for peace and economic growth."
She noted that the White House had decided to invite Russian representatives to G20 events.
Media and experts on Siluanov-Bessent meeting
As CNBC stated, the meeting between Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the sidelines of the G20 summit highlighted Washington's readiness to re-establish high-level diplomatic channels with Moscow.
According to the channel, Washington's position differs from the views of European administrations, which continue to isolate Russia.
Bessent held a meeting with Siluanov to discuss "US President Donald Trump's peace plan," CNBC journalist Megan Cassella reported, citing a US Treasury Department spokesperson. According to Reuters, Bessent stated at a meeting with Siluanov that agreements between Moscow and Washington are impossible until the conflict in Ukraine is resolved.
Politico noted that Washington's decision not to hinder Russia's participation in G20 events has angered the US’ European allies and heightened tensions in their relations with the US administration.
Siluanov's current meeting with his American counterpart is a signal for the restoration of relations between the countries, Alexander Abramov, head of the Laboratory for Analysis of Institutions and Financial Markets at the Presidential Academy, told TASS.
According to him, channels of interaction between the countries are being re-established, increasing the likelihood of reaching constructive solutions.
Abramov recalled that the last time the Russian Finance Minister met with the US Treasury Secretary face-to-face was in 2019.
In 2022, the Russian Finance Minister participated via videoconference in the meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors. Then representatives of the United States and a number of other countries demonstratively walked out of the meeting during his speech.

Weight-loss pill 'Wegovy' on sale in German pharmacies from 1 September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:53:19 UTC
17:53:19 KST

The weight-loss pill Wegovy is now available in German pharmacies. Its active ingredient semaglutide increases satiety and the adult dose costs 170 to 280 euros.
The Wegovy weight-loss pill from Danish manufacturer Novo Nordisk will be available in German pharmacies from 1 September. Following EU approval in July, Germany is the first country in which Wegovy is being sold. Novo Nordisk described the authorisation as a "milestone".
The prescription-only medicine is intended as an alternative to the weight-loss injection already on the market and works with the same active ingredient: semaglutide. It mimics a gut hormone that is responsible for the feeling of fullness.
The retail pharmacy price of the weight-loss pill is expected to be between 170 and 280 euros, a spokesperson for the manufacturer explained. While the injectable version of Wegovy has already been approved for children aged 12 and over, the tablet form is only approved for adults.
When taking semaglutide tablets, adults with overweight reduced their body weight by an average of around 13.6 percent, according to the OASIS-4 study, which essentially formed the basis for EU approval. It was carried out by an international team of researchers.
In the trial, 205 participants took the drug. A further 102 participants received a placebo. With the injection, the average weight loss was higher, at 19 percent. However, the treatment period in that study was 72 weeks, two months longer than for the tablet (64 weeks).
As with the injection, the oral version also comes with side effects: many patients who use the medicine experience gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea and diarrhoea. It can also lead to inflammation of the pancreas.
Compared with the injection, the tablet has to be taken every day. For the injection, administering it once a week is sufficient. For both products, however, what matters alongside regular use is diet and exercise, said Julia Szendrödi, president of the German Diabetes Association.
100 billion dollar market
"Whether injection or tablet: medicines against obesity are not miracle cures for optimising weight, but components of a therapy for a chronic disease," said Szendrödi.
The use of products such as Wegovy is always part of a broader treatment concept. These drugs do not replace prevention, Szendrödi added. There is a need for better nutrition labelling, quality standards for school meals and restrictions on advertising unhealthy foods to children.
Globally, the market for weight-loss medicines is fiercely contested. According to analysts, by 2030 it could be bringing in 100 billion dollars a year for pharmaceutical companies, business daily Handelsblatt reports. Various products are now available. In the United Kingdom, for instance, the pill "Foundayo" from US manufacturer Eli Lilly will be on sale from the end of August.
These weight-loss medicines are intended for people with obesity, with a body mass index (BMI) above 30. In cases of conditions such as type 2 diabetes or sleep apnoea that are linked to excess weight, they can also be used below a BMI of 30.

The French President and Dutch Premier will meet in Eindhoven to discuss how to strengthen ties, especially concerning the shared priority of bolstering European sovereignty.
According to the Elysée, Macron is set to be accompanied by a delegation of French companies, including Mistral AI — widely viewed as Europe's leading AI champion — during his visit to the headquarters of Dutch semi-conductor company ASML, where he will also meet with leaders in the field of European technology.
Later on Wednesday, Macron will attend the landmark inauguration of the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition at the British Museum in London, before taking part in bilateral talks with Burnham on Thursday.
In recent years, the French president has played an instrumental role in championing the daring gambit to loan the 950-year-old tapestry to the British Museum, which is putting it on display until next July.
The 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry, which famously depicts the conquest of England by William the Conqueror of Normandy, arrived in London in July for the sell-out exhibition, after leaving France for the first time in more than nine centuries.
Experts feared it could be damaged but the French culture ministry insisted it had arrived in good condition.
Macron is "very eager" to see the tapestry displayed "in optimal conditions" laid out flat at full length on a table, the French presidential official said.
On the diplomatic side, Britain's new Prime Minister will be looking for concrete outcomes from Macron, as he eyes closer post-Brexit cooperation with the European Union.
The British leader — who replaced predecessor Keir Starmer in July — has vowed to boost sluggish UK growth and keep pushing France for help stopping migrants crossing the Channel to Britain aboard small boats.
Burnham has largely focused on domestic policy since taking over, but has also appeared eager to project his standing on the international stage, in particular maintaining London's support for Ukraine following Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
Starmer had enjoyed some success in this area, working closely with Macron and winning admiration from allies. Macron built with Starmer the best relationship with any of the five UK premiers he has seen prior to Burnham, during his near decade in office.
The pair adopted lead roles in a so-called Coalition of the Willing of nations supporting Ukraine. The French leader has remained eager to press his vision of European sovereignty not dependent on the United States, where the United Kingdom is seen as having a crucial role to play even after Brexit.
Burnham has so far only welcomed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Downing Street since becoming prime minister and visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip.

UK cancer-therapy company strikes deal to manufacture CAR-T treatment in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:50:52 UTC
17:50:52 KST

A London-listed biotech company Hemogenyx Pharmaceuticals has signed a binding agreement with Cellin Technologies, an Estonian cell-therapy company based in Tehnopol Science and Business Park, to manufacture and roll out its CAR-T therapy, HG-CT-1, for patients with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia, a form of blood cancer that has either returned or never responded to earlier treatment. The deal builds on a preliminary letter of intent signed in September 2025, and the companies say it marks the shift from planning to execution.
The arrangement works because of Estonia’s “Hospital Exemption” pathway, a rule that lets a licensed doctor use an advanced therapy that hasn’t yet received full marketing approval, so long as Estonia’s State Agency of Medicines signs off case by case. For Hemogenyx, that means patients can get access sooner, and the company can start collecting real-world data and revenue well before a full commercial approval would normally come through. Estonia’s national health insurance fund can even reimburse the cost for insured patients, which removes one of the biggest obstacles to actually getting a therapy used.
Under the agreement, Hemogenyx will spend roughly four months transferring its manufacturing know-how to Cellin, which will then produce the therapy at its GMP-certified Tallinn facility and become Hemogenyx’s exclusive Estonian partner for the next five years, handling the regulatory dossier and coordinating reimbursement. Patients, including those traveling in from other countries, will be treated at a Tallinn clinic, Taastava Kirurgia Kliinik AS. Hemogenyx keeps full ownership of the underlying science and manufacturing process, along with the right to develop and sell HG-CT-1 anywhere else in the world, and the two companies will split the net operating margin earned from every patient treated.
Dr Vladislav Sandler, CEO & Co-Founder of Hemogenyx Pharmaceuticals, said: “The signing of this definitive agreement with Cellin transforms our plans in Estonia from intent into execution. Our first priority remains saving the lives of patients with relapsed or refractory AML, for whom treatment options remain scarce. With the framework now in place for manufacturing, regulatory submission and reimbursement, we have a clear, binding path to delivering HG-CT-1 to patients and to generating the Company’s first revenues from the therapy, while gathering valuable real-world data to complement our ongoing Phase I trial.”
Ivari Saar, Board Member of Cellin Technologies, said: “Moving from a letter of intent to a definitive agreement in under a year reflects the commitment of both teams to bringing next-generation CAR-T therapy to patients in Estonia. Cellin’s GMP manufacturing infrastructure and regulatory expertise are now formally engaged to deliver HG-CT-1 under the Hospital Exemption framework, positioning Estonia at the forefront of advanced cell therapy in Europe.”
None of this is guaranteed yet. It still depends on the technology transfer going smoothly, Estonian regulators approving the Hospital Exemption dossier, and the health fund agreeing to reimburse costs – and the companies have been clear that there’s no promised minimum number of patients or minimum revenue attached.
For Cellin, which already runs its own cell therapy through this same regulatory route, the deal is a chance to expand its role as a manufacturing and clinical-delivery partner for international biotech firms. If things go to plan, Estonia would become one of the first places where HG-CT-1 reaches patients outside a formal clinical trial, putting the small Baltic country at the center of a fast-moving corner of cancer treatment.
Source: tehnopol.ee

Ukraine strikes Russian naval drone in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:50:43 UTC
17:50:43 KST

- Ukraine's Navy destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel near Snake Island using a precision strike from a drone.
- The destroyed vessel was likely a Russian KAMA-class drone boat, first unveiled in June 2026 with a stated range of 700 kilometers.
Ukraine’s Navy said it destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel near Snake Island in the Black Sea on Tuesday, according to Militarnyi.
Footage released alongside the announcement shows the drone boat being struck by a precision munition dropped from an unmanned aerial vehicle after being detected. The vessel caught fire and detonated following the strike. Based on the released footage, Ukraine appears to have used a Bayraktar TB2 drone, a Turkish-made system Ukraine has operated since before the full-scale invasion, to carry out the attack.
Ukraine’s Navy said the destroyed vessel was likely a KAMA-class uncrewed boat built by Russian drone maker ZALA, the same company behind the Lancet loitering munition widely used against Ukrainian forces and equipment.
ZALA first unveiled the KAMA publicly in June 2026 at the International Maritime Defense Show “FLOT-2026” in Kronstadt, near St. Petersburg. The company presented two versions of the platform, one with a waterjet propulsion system and one with an outboard motor, both intended for what ZALA described as civilian and dual-use missions, including hydrographic surveys, environmental monitoring, search-and-rescue operations, port and oil platform security, and cargo delivery to islands.
According to specifications ZALA released at the unveiling, the KAMA has a maximum range of 700 kilometers (435 miles) from shore and can carry a payload of up to 600 kilograms (1,323 pounds), allowing for a range of onboard equipment including electro-optical sensors and thermal imaging cameras. The jet-propelled version measures 6.5 meters (21 feet) long and weighs about 1,000 kilograms (2,205 pounds) with a fiberglass hull, while the outboard motor version is slightly larger at 7.9 meters (26 feet) and roughly 1,200 kilograms (2,646 pounds). Both versions reach a maximum speed of around 30 knots and can operate in sea states up to three, according to the manufacturer, navigating using satellite positioning, an inertial navigation system, and marine radar.
Defense analysts who examined the KAMA at its unveiling noted that despite ZALA’s framing of the platform around civilian applications, the design closely resembles other Russian uncrewed surface vessels already documented in offensive roles, including a camera-equipped variant used in a May 2026 attack on Odesa. No dedicated attack or “kamikaze” configuration of the KAMA had been publicly announced by ZALA prior to Tuesday’s strike, though analysts had previously said such an adaptation could not be ruled out given the platform’s modular payload capacity.
Snake Island, a small outpost in the northwestern Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube, has remained a recurring flashpoint throughout the war given its strategic position along shipping lanes used for Ukrainian grain exports. Ukrainian forces have conducted repeated strikes on Russian naval assets and reconnaissance platforms operating in the surrounding waters since retaking the island from Russian forces in 2022.

Wednesday’s High Court verdict against Chung Pui-kei moves a high-profile case towards its resolution after it sparked intense public anger and government warnings, leading the Hong Chi Association to appoint an independent review committee headed by a former Law Society president to overhaul facility oversight.
The jury of five men and two women found Chung guilty of five counts of raping the mentally incapacitated resident who lived at a Tai Po home operated by the association.
The jury rejected the 38-year-old defendant’s contention that the 23-year-old victim might have fabricated the allegations out of grievance or jealousy after her romantic feelings for him went unrequited.
The trial heard that the woman, whose intellectual functioning was equivalent to that of a nine-year-old, considered Chung a “very friendly” warden who often chatted with her, played video games with her, and occasionally gave her marshmallows.
Prosecutors accused the defendant of abusing the woman’s trust and raping her three times in a male staff room and twice in her room between July 13 and August 9, 2024.

President Vladimir Putin has dismissed growing speculation that he plans to announce a new round of military mobilization following State Duma and regional elections later this month.
“It’s complete nonsense. It’s an information attack on Russia,” Putin told reporters late on Tuesday in his first remarks on the rumors.
As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has stalled in its fifth year, questions are once again mounting over whether Putin could resort to a politically costly mobilization to boost his military’s manpower.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected reports of an impending draft, characterizing them as a foreign disinformation campaign.
Last week, Ukrainian intelligence agencies warned that Russia was “drawing up plans” to mobilize 600,000 men this year and in 2027.
Putin declared a “partial” mobilization of 300,000 reservists in September 2022, a move that was similarly dismissed just days before it was announced. That call-up triggered a mass exodus of draft-eligible men from Russia.
Since then, the Kremlin has gradually made legal changes that some observers view as preparations for a fresh wave of mobilization.
The Russian military has moved to a digital draft registry with automatic travel bans, shifted to year-round draft processing, and now allows reservists to be deployed to guard “critical infrastructure” without being formally called up to serve.
However, some experts caution that another mass mobilization would encounter logistical hurdles and fail to address challenges on the front line. At the same time, observers point to the fact that Putin’s “partial” mobilization order remains in effect, suggesting Putin might not need to formally announce a new draft.

World leaders missing in action as UN warns of climate target breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:47:38 UTC
17:47:38 KST

1.5C global warming breach likely as Australia defends Pacific climate talks
In short:
The prime minister has hit back at criticism over the federal government's high-profile climate meeting for world leaders next month.
It comes as a UN report warns the world is unlikely to keep global warming below 1.8C.
What's next?
Pre-COP will be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in early October before COP31 gets underway in November.
The prime minister has defended the number of leaders attending a high-profile climate meeting in the Pacific Islands, as a United Nations report warns the world will breach the 1.5C global warming benchmark within the next five years.
The federal government had initially wanted world leaders to attend pre-COP next month, ahead of the main climate talks in Türkiye in November.
Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting the lead-up event as part of a compromise, after Australia's failed bid to host COP31, the world's largest annual climate summit.
There had been reports Australia was struggling to convince leaders outside the Pacific to attend a special meeting in Tuvalu, before Fiji's foreign minister, Sakiasi Ditoka, gave the first public account of those going.
He said Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, Thailand, Maldives and Timor-Leste had so far agreed to send leaders to the event, and Germany, Mexico and South Korea will send ministers.
When questioned about attendance at the pre-COP while speaking to media at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, Anthony Albanese said the government had always anticipated that a pre-COP event would not attract the same level of patronage as COP itself.
"The fact that the pre-COP is being held in Fiji with a side trip to Tuvalu as well is something that is really welcomed because what it will do is provide a focus on what is happening in the Pacific.
"The entry fee for credibility at the Pacific Islands Forum and for bilateral engagement in the Pacific is taking climate change seriously."
The prime minister also voiced his displeasure with the line of questioning.
"You are being so disrespectful to the Pacific leaders who are here," he said.
"We need to actually have some respect for the process and respect for our Pacific leaders, and Australia has an absolute interest in engaging with the Pacific."
The government pitched pre-COP as an opportunity to show leaders the perils that climate change poses to low-lying island nations in the Pacific, and to drive greater global action on climate change.
However, the nations sending leaders are hardly major polluters, nor do they need reminding of the risks climate change poses to vulnerable countries.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen said pre-COP was a "key opportunity" for the Pacific.
"The Pacific said to us, 'We thought it would be good to invite some leaders.' We've done that," he said.
"There's a very small component in Tuvalu, which is a small country, with limited capacity to host people.
"But that will be important in terms of not only prime ministers, heads of multilateral development banks, cabinet ministers who often don't attend pre-COP either but are coming to this one."
'Every fraction of a degree counts'
The growing climate risks confronting Pacific nations have been underscored by a landmark UN report, which has warned the world will likely pass 1.5C global warming in 2030.
It found that a temperature rise peak of 1.8C above pre-industrial levels was now the best-case scenario and highlights what can be done to return to 1.5C after the overshoot.
Countries have been trying to keep global temperatures to well below 2C as part of the Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty on climate change.
That includes an agreement to "pursue efforts" to limit warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial times.
That target was chosen because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) indicates that crossing that threshold risks unleashing far more severe climate change impacts.
Climate Change Authority chair Matt Kean said urgent climate action remained necessary, despite the likelihood that the 1.5C target would be exceeded.
"Every fraction of a degree that we can limit global warming will reduce the danger and reduce the cost," he said.
"There is a huge reason for Australia and indeed the rest of the world to limit global warming; the economic consequences will be dire if we don't, and the danger to lives and livelihoods will be severe if we don't.
"So the message is very clear: we need to speed up the pace at which we're reducing our emissions."
Malte Meinshausen, professor of Climate Science at the University of Melbourne, said the energy transition means some of the worst scenarios that were possible a few years ago are no longer likely.
But he added that failure to reduce global emissions quickly meant the ideal scenario of limiting warming to just above 1.5C was no longer available.
"Compared with our options five years ago, the new paths are more costly, come with more floods, fires and droughts and the need to draw, at some point, carbon emissions out of the atmosphere that we are currently emitting," Professor Meinshausen said.
"Acting now is still the cheaper option than not acting now, as we can still achieve 1.5C in the longer term."
Calls for Australia to do more
Speaking at the Pacific Islands Forum, Vanuatu's Climate Change Adaptation and Energy Minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said Australia was not doing enough to curb carbon emissions.
"Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels; we all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis,"
"The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that. You need to stop expansion, and you need to start transitioning away."
The comments come a day after Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King helped open a project that will feed gas fracked from the Beetaloo Basin into the Northern Territory's power grid.
Mr Albanese defended Australia's approach to the energy transition, saying the country was "highly regarded" when it comes to climate change.
"The Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we've taken, and they also understand […] because they're dealing with it as well, that the transition can't happen overnight.
"It requires strategies and policies to be put in place, and one of the things that renewables require is firming capacity, and gas has a role to play in firming capacity."

It has sunk to the level of a junta and terrorists: which regimes around the world does Belarus maintain relations with
Kyiv • UNN
According to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, official Minsk is deepening ties with authoritarian regimes against the backdrop of its isolation from the West. In particular, Belarus is preparing a visa-free regime with North Korea and has also received Afghan Taliban members.
The public diplomacy of the Republic of Belarus during Alexander Lukashenko’s presidency has strengthened ties with a number of authoritarian and totalitarian states around the world. These include not only Russia, but also Iraq, Libya, Syria, Venezuela, North Korea, Myanmar, Iran, and Afghanistan after the Taliban returned to power. The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reports this, UNN reports.
Details
At the same time, the FIS noted that Lukashenko’s public friendship with dictators has one interesting pattern: Saddam Hussein, Muammar Gaddafi, the Assad family, Nicolás Maduro, and Ali Khamenei all eventually lost power or died under various circumstances.
Minsk is now drawing closer to North Korea, the Taliban, and Myanmar’s junta—that is, regimes that themselves are under sanctions, international isolation, or accusations of crimes against their own populations. Traditional partners—from the EU to the United States—remain inaccessible to Belarus. Over the past month, this isolation has become particularly noticeable. Foreign Minister Ryzhenkov announced preparations for a visa-free regime with North Korea, calling it “colorful and interesting.” Belarus also hosted a delegation from the Afghan Taliban, while Lukashenko publicly praised the leader of Myanmar’s junta, Min Aung Hlaing
Meanwhile, North Korea is one of the poorest countries in the world. Its GDP per capita does not exceed $1,200, compared with nearly $10,000 in Belarus.
In addition, official Minsk tried not to publicize the Taliban’s visit: some members of the delegation are still listed as belonging to terrorist organizations by the Belarusian KGB.
