Spain sheds almost 163,000 jobs in August as unemployment climbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:44:26 UTC
17:44:26 KST

The Spanish economy lost 162,840 jobs last month with 44,419 registering as unemployed. The drop represents the smallest decrease in August since the Covid-19 pandemic.
August once again brought negative figures for employment in Spain.
Spain's Social Security system lost 162,840 contributors, while unemployment increased by 44,419 people, in a month traditionally marked by the end of the tourist season and a fall in hiring for sectors such as education.
Despite the drop, the loss of contributors is the smallest recorded in an August since the Covid-19 pandemic. On a year-on-year basis, the Spanish labour market has created around 680,000 jobs.
At the end of the second quarter of 2026, the unemployment rate in Spain fell to 9.87%, the lowest since the first quarter of 2008, compared to 10.83% in the previous period and forecasts of 10.7%.
In 2026, the figures are also influenced by the process of regularising foreign workers.
By the end of August, the Social Security system counted 337,917 contributors incorporated through this process, which has helped cushion the seasonal fall in those paying into the system.
In total, foreign workers already exceed 3.5 million contributors and represent 15.9% of the total labour force.
These figures have led Spain's Minister for Inclusion, Social Security and Migration, Elma Saiz, to describe the evolution of the labour market as "historic job growth".
Education accounts for the biggest job losses
Education is once again the sector hardest hit by the seasonal drop in registrations.
More than 78,000 teachers and other education professionals have ceased to be affiliated, coinciding with the holiday period and the interruption of numerous contracts during the summer.
The end of the peak tourist season has also contributed to the drop in registrations and the rise in unemployment.
"As it happens every summer, when the holidays end, unemployment rises because of seasonal work", explained Spain's Second Deputy Prime Minister and Labour Minister Yolanda Díaz.
The increase in unemployment is higher than that seen in recent years for this month.
The figures, however, are again partly shaped by the regularisation of foreign workers, as some of those benefiting from the process have registered as jobseekers.
The total number of unemployed people stands at 2,356,000 which is the lowest level recorded in an August since 2007.

British energy giant BP names Ian Tyler as chair after boardroom turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:42:38 UTC
17:42:38 KST

British energy giant BP has appointed Ian Tyler as its permanent chair following the abrupt removal of his predecessor over governance and conduct concerns in May.
BP has appointed Ian Tyler as its permanent chair after months of upheaval at the top of the British energy giant.
Tyler takes up the position immediately following a search that considered both internal and external candidates, BP said on Wednesday.
BP shares were little changed in early London trading. They have gained around 25% since the beginning of the year, broadly matching the rise in rival Shell’s shares.
Tyler had served as interim chair since 26 May, when BP abruptly dismissed his predecessor, Albert Manifold, after less than eight months in the role.
At the time, BP said the board had identified “governance oversight and conduct issues it deems unacceptable”. Manifold has disputed the company’s account and sought legal advice.
BP shares fell as much as 9% following the announcement of his departure before recovering some of those losses.
Tyler joined BP’s board as a non-executive director in April 2025. He is a former chief executive of construction group Balfour Beatty and currently chairs building materials company Grafton Group.
BP said Tyler had worked alongside more than 15 chief executives during a non-executive career spanning listed and privately owned companies in the oil and gas, natural resources and engineering sectors.
“Ian brings significant experience providing challenge and support to executive teams, while maintaining strong governance and oversight on behalf of shareholders,” said Dame Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director.
Tyler will lead the board as it oversees chief executive Meg O’Neill’s restructuring programme. Her priorities include simplifying BP’s portfolio, strengthening its balance sheet and imposing tighter investment discipline.
BP is seeking to reduce net debt to between $14 billion (€12bn) and $18 billion (€15.4bn) by the end of 2027. The company estimated in July that its net debt stood at between $22 billion and $23 billion at the end of June.
The debt target formed part of a strategic reset announced in February 2025, when BP shifted investment back towards oil and gas, reduced planned spending on low-carbon businesses and promised tighter capital allocation.
BP also announced that Blanc, who oversaw the searches that led to the appointments of both Manifold and Tyler, would not seek re-election at next year’s annual general meeting. She will leave the board once a successor has been appointed.

airBaltic to significantly reduce routes from Riga – destinations being dropped revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:41:54 UTC
17:41:54 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic will offer 57 direct routes from Riga throughout the next summer season, nearly 20% fewer than during this year’s summer season. At the same time, the airline will increase flight frequencies on 12 of its most popular routes, according to calculations by the LETA news agency based on information provided by airBaltic.
The LETA archive shows that during the 2026 summer season, the airline offered nearly 70 direct routes from Riga.
The airline now says that airBaltic will offer 59 direct routes from Riga during the 2027 summer season. However, two destinations – Madeira and Sharm el-Sheikh, which airBaltic will serve during the upcoming winter season – will remain in the route network for only one month, in April. After that, the network will consist of 57 destinations.
During the summer season, airBaltic will operate flights from Riga to Alicante, Amsterdam, Athens, Barcelona, Belgrade, Berlin, Billund, Bucharest, Brussels, Budapest, Burgas, Zurich, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, Hamburg, Helsinki, Heraklion, Catania, Chisinau, Copenhagen, Corfu, Larnaca, Lisbon, Ljubljana, London, Madeira (April only), Madrid, Malaga, Milan, Munich, Naples, Nice, Oslo, Oulu, Palanga, Palma de Mallorca, Paris, Pisa, Porto, Prague, Reykjavik, Rhodes, Rome, Thessaloniki, Sofia, Split, Istanbul, Stockholm, Sharm el-Sheikh (April only), Tallinn, Tampere, Tbilisi, Tel Aviv, Tenerife, Tirana, Tivat, Turku, Vienna and Vilnius.
airBaltic’s Head of Public and Political Relations, Augusts Zilberts, told LETA that all flights for next summer are currently being updated on the airline’s website. The airline confirmed that during the next summer season it will no longer operate flights to Aberdeen in Scotland, Antalya in Turkey, Batumi in Georgia, Bergen in Norway, Dublin in Ireland, Yerevan in Armenia, Faro in Portugal, Gothenburg in Sweden, Malta, Olbia in Italy and Valencia in Spain. Flights to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates are planned for the winter season.
Flight frequencies will be increased from Riga to London Gatwick to up to 14 flights per week, Paris to up to 12 flights per week, Vienna to up to 12 flights per week, Barcelona to up to seven flights per week, Rome to up to seven flights per week, Hamburg to up to seven flights per week, Düsseldorf to up to seven flights per week, Milan to up to six flights per week, Athens to up to four flights per week, Nice to up to four flights per week, Alicante to up to three flights per week and Split to up to three flights per week.
Zilberts stressed that although the number of routes will be lower, the number of seats offered will be comparable to the 2026 summer season.
The airline emphasises that from late March until late October 2027, Riga will continue to serve as airBaltic’s main operational hub and its largest route-network base, offering passengers a broad selection of direct destinations and convenient connections across Europe and beyond.
The 2027 summer flight programme has been developed in line with airBaltic’s new business plan and reflects an optimised, demand-driven route network strategy. The airline is focusing on markets with the highest demand and revenue potential, serving both business and leisure travellers while increasing frequencies on selected routes where passenger demand is growing.
The programme also provides for an improved hub structure in Riga by optimising flight schedules and connection times. According to the airline, this will provide passengers with more convenient travel options both from Riga and via the Latvian capital to destinations across airBaltic’s network. By improving Riga’s connectivity and strengthening its role as a connecting point between the Baltic states and the rest of Europe, the programme is also intended to reinforce Riga Airport’s position as the leading aviation hub in the Baltic region.
The upcoming winter flight season will run from late October 2026 until late March 2027, when the summer season begins. Overall, airBaltic plans to operate flights from the Latvian capital to nearly 70 destinations during 2027.
As previously reported, airBaltic’s Supervisory Board has approved a business plan that, among other measures aimed at improving liquidity, envisages raising EUR 225 million in bridge financing using the existing collateral pool securing the 2029 senior bonds.
In the longer term, the plan envisages recapitalising the company through up to EUR 225 million in new debt and EUR 100 million in new equity. Part of the existing 2029 bonds will be converted into equity, while the remainder will be replaced with new, reduced debt of up to EUR 125 million.
The business plan also envisages the airline operating 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared with 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually increasing to around 40 aircraft by 2031.
As previously reported, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs on Tuesday, 25 August, promulgated the airBaltic Financial Stabilisation Measures Law, which had been adopted by the Saeima under an expedited procedure on 20 August.
The law authorises the government to potentially participate in the purchase of airBaltic bridge-financing bonds worth up to EUR 30 million, alongside private investors and on identical terms. The Cabinet of Ministers will be able to make a separate decision on purchasing the bonds if necessary.
The law also provides for the capitalisation of claims arising from the state loan and bonds already held by the state into the company’s share capital. This means that EUR 50 million worth of state-owned bonds and the remaining loan amount of more than EUR 18 million may be converted into airBaltic shares.
On 25 August, the government also approved extending the repayment deadline for the remaining EUR 18 million principal amount of airBaltic’s state loan until 30 December this year.
This month, airBaltic bondholders supported the capitalisation of the next two bond interest payments, as well as several other measures providing the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders approved adding the interest payments due on 14 August and 14 November this year to the bond principal rather than paying them in cash. They also approved a temporary waiver of minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
Last year, airBaltic Group’s revenue increased by 4.2% compared with 2024, reaching EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, the group posted losses of EUR 44.337 million, 2.7 times lower than in 2024. In 2025, the airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers, 1% more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder. Currently, the Latvian state owns 88.37% of airBaltic shares, Lufthansa holds 10%, Danish businessman Lars Thuesen’s company Aircraft Leasing 1 holds 1.62%, and other shareholders own the remaining 0.01%. The company’s share capital amounts to EUR 41.819 million.
In view of its 2025 financial results and market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its potential initial public offering and does not currently consider an IPO a potential source of capital in 2026, according to airBaltic’s annual report.

17:40:46 KST

A new study has found that non-painful symptoms in young girls, such as fatigue and dizziness, could help predict who is at risk of painful periods later on.
Experiencing non-painful symptoms, such as fatigue and dizziness, before the first period might signal a higher risk of dysmenorrhoea — painful menstruation for the years to come, according to a new study published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.
Many women struggle with period pain, which starts in adolescence and can affect their lives for years after. Researchers hope that addressing some of the symptoms before a person's first menstrual period could reduce the burden of dysmenorrhoea on young women.
“Identifying risk factors for dysmenorrhoea, especially severe dysmenorrhoea, has the potential to improve outcomes for female adolescents through early and more targeted treatment,” the authors wrote.
The researchers analysed data from over 2,000 adolescents and found that non-painful somatic symptoms – such as fatigue, dizziness, gastrointestinal problems, nightmares or sensory changes – and advanced pubertal development at ages nine to ten are strong indicators of future menstrual pain.
Dysmenorrhoea is common in adolescence and is often dismissed as inevitable or left untreated, the authors wrote. It can interfere with daily functioning and lead to other chronic pain conditions; however, little is known about its risk factors, and the lack of research before the first period is hindering efforts to identify those at risk.
Previous research has found that approximately 70% of female adolescents experience menstrual pain, and in 20% of cases it has a significant impact on their daily activities.
The study also found that sleep problems were strongly associated with a greater impact of pain on daily activities. Researchers say that addressing sleep disturbances before the first period could help to reduce the pain burden.
For example, cognitive behavioural therapy targeting this issue in adolescents with chronic pain shows promise for easing both the sleep problems and the resulting pain interference.
“These findings raise the possibility of identifying at-risk individuals before pain becomes a lifelong issue,” the authors wrote.

Sharp rise in utility bills pushes Russia's inflation further off target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:54 UTC
17:34:54 KST

The October increase follows a January rise and is the first double tariff hike in four years. The central bank warned it would push annual inflation further above its 4% target in an economy already squeezed by the costs of its war, sanctions and a 21% key interest rate.
Russia is raising utility tariffs for the second time this year, with an average 15% increase taking effect on 1 October — a move the central bank says will push inflation further above its target in an economy already under severe pressure from war costs and sanctions.
The increase will range from 8% to 22% depending on the region. Residents of Stavropol Krai, Dagestan, and the Tambov and Tyumen regions face the steepest rises, while Moscow tariffs will go up 15% and St Petersburg 14.6%.
An earlier 1.7% increase took effect in January. Raising tariffs twice in a single calendar year is rare in Russia — the last time it happened was in 2022, the first year of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Kremlin has justified the increases by citing ageing communal infrastructure and the need for modernisation.
Utility networks across much of the country date from the Soviet era and have received insufficient investment for decades. Repeated harsh winters and deferred maintenance have accelerated their deterioration.
Sanctions imposed because of Russia's war in Ukraine have restricted access to imported equipment needed for repairs, and the workforce available for infrastructure projects has shrunk as labour has been absorbed by military production and conscription.
The Bank of Russia said the October tariff rise would contribute noticeably to faster annual inflation. Its baseline forecast puts annual inflation in 2026 at 6-7% — well above its 4% target.
Measures affect the small and the poor
After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russia faced a combination of external pressure and internal restructuring.
Western sanctions restricted access to financial markets, technology and equipment. Trade flows were rerouted. State spending rose sharply, concentrated on military procurement and related industries.
The economy avoided deep recession, but the adaptation came at a cost. Growth became increasingly dependent on state contracts and military production, while civilian industries faced labour shortages, expensive borrowing and limited access to technology.
The central bank raised its key interest rate to 21% in late 2024 in response to inflation, making credit extremely expensive for businesses and households. It has kept rates high since.
High borrowing costs have depressed private investment and squeezed smaller companies that cannot access state financing.
Utility bills are a fixed cost that households cannot cut. For lower-income families, a 15% rise in heating, water and electricity charges directly reduces money available for food, clothing and other spending, at a time when food prices have also risen sharply. For higher earners, the same percentage increase matters far less.
Businesses face parallel pressure. Factories, logistics companies, shops and offices all depend on utility services. When costs rise, operating margins shrink, and companies pass costs on to consumers, adding further to inflation.
The Russian economy has relied significantly on domestic demand to sustain growth since 2022.
A squeeze on household spending power from rising mandatory costs works against that dynamic, particularly in regions where wages have not kept pace with inflation and where military contract income is less prevalent than in major cities.

Twelve Israel Prison Service staff indicted over 2023 alleged assault, death of security prisoner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:35 UTC
17:34:35 KST

The prosecution indicted 12 Israel Prison Service (IPS) personnel and former employees on Tuesday over the death of security prisoner Thaer Abu Asab and the alleged assault of eight other inmates at Ketziot Prison in November 2023.
The indictment, filed with the Beersheba District Court, charges all 12 with reckless homicide, aggravated serious bodily harm, and multiple counts of aggravated assault causing bodily harm.
The shift commander and shift sergeant are also charged with obstructing an investigation.
The filing moves a case that began with the questioning of 19 prison personnel nearly three years ago, in formal criminal proceedings.
According to the indictment, the shift commander had earlier shared with some of the defendants his distress over the deaths of Druze soldiers in battle. Later that afternoon, Abu Asab, who was being held with eight other security prisoners, asked the shift sergeant whether there was a hudna (“ceasefire”) in the war. The sergeant relayed the question to the commander.
Commander allegedly led group into cell, ordered attacks
Before the evening count, the commander allegedly told the personnel taking part that they would depart from the normal procedure and enter the cell to show the prisoners that there was no ceasefire.
The indictment alleges that the commander told the group he would take responsibility for whatever happened and said prison management was aware of what was taking place. He also allegedly warned female officers attending the briefing not to enter the cell so that they would not be hurt.
Shortly after 7 p.m., the commander led the group to the cell and began the count. Prosecutors allege that he then ordered the other defendants inside, where they jointly attacked Abu Asab and the eight other prisoners with punches and kicks. Some allegedly used batons.
The commander is accused of directing the assault from inside the cell and personally striking at least one prisoner. After several minutes, he ordered the group to stop, according to the indictment.
None of the defendants reported the alleged assault or recorded any unusual incident during the count, prosecutors said.
Abu Asab collapsed and lost consciousness shortly after the group left. Other prisoners called for help, and medical staff took him to the prison clinic. He had no pulse and did not appear to be breathing. He was resuscitated and transferred to Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba, where he was pronounced dead at 10:22 p.m.
Cardiac, respiratory injuries from beating deemed cause of death
Prosecutors attribute his death directly to the beating. The indictment says he suffered multiple broken ribs and tears in the walls of his heart, causing cardiac failure and bleeding around the organ. His broken ribs also damaged his respiratory system and prevented his lungs from expanding properly.
The combined cardiac and respiratory injuries ultimately caused his death, according to the prosecution. The other prisoners suffered bruising and injuries to their backs, arms, shoulders, and other parts of their bodies.
Early reports following Abu Asab’s death said an autopsy had found extensive signs of violence but had not conclusively established that he died from the blows. The indictment now presents a specific medical account connecting the alleged assault to his death.
The second charge concerns what prosecutors describe as attempts to interfere with the subsequent police investigation.
The shift sergeant allegedly instructed one of the defendants, before he was questioned, to tell investigators that no batons had been used.
The shift commander is accused of contacting another prison officer after his own questioning and asking him to relay instructions to female officers who had not yet been interviewed.
They were allegedly told to say that the defendants entered the cell only after the prisoners caused a disturbance and that any force used was part of a legitimate attempt to regain control.
One of the officers initially gave investigators a false account but later admitted that she had lied and provided her version of the incident, according to the indictment.
Abu Asab, 38, was a Fatah member from the Kalkilya area who had been imprisoned since 2005 following convictions for attempted murder and other security offenses.
The IPS said the incident occurred under the previous prison commissioner.
It added that the current commissioner had ended the service of some of those involved after taking office, saying the organization would not tolerate breaches of the law or its disciplinary rules.

Suspect in Jerusalem baby food contamination case named as Yan Shemla
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:34:31 UTC
17:34:31 KST

Yan Shemla was named on Wednesday as the suspect arrested in connection with the suspected deliberate contamination of baby fruit-puree jars with sedative drugs in Jerusalem.
The Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court extended his detention on Tuesday until September 6 after finding that the investigative material established a “significant” reasonable suspicion of his involvement.
Police suspect Shemla of deliberately inserting sedative substances into jars of Prinok fruit puree sold at two Zol Begadol supermarket branches on Jaffa Street. The offenses under investigation include using poison in a manner that endangers life, theft and negligent handling of medication.
Shemla, a resident of southern Israel, was arrested at his home on Monday after police reported a breakthrough in the investigation. Officers searched the property before taking him for questioning.
The Magistrate’s Court initially allowed his name to be published but temporarily delayed the decision at the request of his attorney, giving the defense time to consider an appeal. His identity was released on Wednesday morning.
Attorney Zecharia Shenkolevsky, who is representing Shemla through the Public Defender’s Office, said his client has a mental-health condition and is in a complex psychological state.
“The investigation is in its early stages, and we expect it to be conducted while protecting his rights, certainly in light of his medical circumstances,” Shenkolevsky said. He added that Shemla was cooperating with investigators.
Several young children hospitalized in Hadassah Medical Center
The case began in June after several young children were hospitalized at Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem with drowsiness, weakness, and apathy after consuming Prinok fruit puree. They were later discharged in stable condition.
Laboratory testing found clonazepam and lorazepam in five jars examined during the investigation. Both are prescription medications from the benzodiazepine family and can cause drowsiness, weakness, and confusion.
The Health Ministry said all five jars appeared to have been opened or tampered with before purchase. Tests of products obtained from the importer found no contamination, and the ministry said it had found no indication of a manufacturing defect.
The findings shifted the investigation toward the possibility that the substances had been inserted after the jars left the importer. No general recall of Prinok products was issued.
Involved Zol Begadol branches close, then reopen with restrictions
The two Zol Begadol branches where the jars were sold were initially closed and later prohibited from selling food and cosmetic products until stricter quality-control measures were introduced.
Shemla’s detention is currently authorized only through September 6. If police want to keep him in custody after that date, they will have to return to the Magistrate’s Court and explain what investigative work remains and why his release could endanger the public or interfere with the investigation.
The court could then extend his detention again, release him under restrictions, or order his unconditional release.

Canterbury has righted the ship since officials have eased off on calling six-agains.
And while Ciraldo won't solely attribute his club's early-season form slump to the changes, he would prefer clearer communication so clubs can plan their conditioning and roster management accordingly.
"If you look at our form at the start of the year you can blame that, but I think there's a lot of factors that went into our results at the start of the year," Ciraldo said.
"We'll look to address those over the next few weeks.
"As the rules came back to what they were last year, we sort of found our rhythm a little bit more, and were able to get back to our style of footy.
"I think it coincides with a number of other things as well.
"I think everyone would like to know what the rule changes are to start the pre-season and not find out about them during the trial period."
Ciraldo said Canterbury had little time to put the trialled kick-off interpretations into practice this week.
"I don't check my emails that often, so someone had to tell me," Ciraldo said.
Canterbury's clash with Brisbane will be the last for Bronson Xerri (Melbourne) and Josh Curran (Perth) before they move on to new clubs in 2027.
Ciraldo paid tribute to the pair for being key parts of the Dogs' revival, and confirmed Sean O'Sullivan had agreed to a contract at Belmore for 2027, despite interest from the Super League.

Sadiq Khan fined by fast-track court over untaxed car City Hall says is not his
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:27 UTC
17:30:27 KST

Sadiq Khan’s office has revealed he was the victim of a scam that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that did not belong to him.
The London mayor was found guilty last month under a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each.
City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London.
The mayor has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge.
The prosecution was undertaken by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which accused Khan of being the keeper of the vehicle when it was spotted as being untaxed on 24 January.
“This is a scam, which is a crime,” said a spokesperson for Khan, whose office said the DVLA had applied to reopen the case and withdraw the prosecution.
“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.”
The DVLA is expected to investigate the false registration.
A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.
PA Media alerted the DVLA to the criminal conviction on Tuesday and its officials confirmed they were reviewing the case and investigating the circumstances of the prosecution.
Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to a Gordon Ramsay restaurant in east London instead of the nearby TfL offices.
The mayor faces the possibility of having to appear in court to try to overturn the conviction.
The single justice procedure was introduced in 2015 as a cheaper method of dealing with low-level criminal cases, allowing magistrates to sit alone and in private.
The system, which is under government review, was criticised in 2024 when about 59,000 train-fare evasion convictions were overturned for being unlawful. It also emerged that children had been wrongly convicted in the secretive courts.
More scrutiny has come over repeated incidents of sick and incapacitated pensioners being convicted for not paying their household bills.
In Khan’s case, court records show he was prosecuted by the DVLA after the annual tax on the Micra, which was first registered in 2002, ran out last September.
The DVLA has been approached for comment.

How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
The SCO’s significance is practical: it gives those who do not want their future defined in Washington a forum to coordinate and hedge
The timing is important. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine remains unresolved, while the war between Iran and the US has turned the Persian Gulf into another theatre of strategic competition, with energy markets again exposed to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The SCO now brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, most of the Central Asian republics and Belarus, alongside partners including Turkey and multiple Gulf states.
Its 10 full members represent more than 3.4 billion people and roughly a quarter of global GDP. However, its growing importance is not simply a matter of size.
Calling the SCO an anti-American alliance is a mistake. Its members have different interests. India and China remain strategic competitors; India and Pakistan have long-standing tensions; and Central Asian governments want room to manoeuvre between Moscow, Beijing, Ankara, Brussels and Washington. Turkey remains a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) member while pursuing a larger Eurasian role.

MOD statistics pre-release access list
The individuals who have 24-hour, pre-release access to Ministry of Defence's key Official and Accredited Official Statistics publications.
Documents
Details
This is a list of the individuals who currently have pre-release access to MOD’s key Official and Accredited Official Statistics. The list includes the titles of the documents which those individuals currently have pre-release access to. This document will be updated as lists are revised, or pre-release access is removed altogether. Publications not included in the lists do not have pre-release access.
Previous pre-release lists can be found in the UK Government Web Archive.

'It’s not 19th century': Kerala CM Satheesan slams cleric over 'women should stay home' remark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.
NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Wednesday rejected Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar’s call for restrictions on women’s participation in public life. He said women must join the mainstream, asserting that such views have no place in a developing Kerala.Speaking to reporters, Satheesan said the state government did not agree with Aboobacker’s position that women should remain at home, adding that even Islam did not require women to be confined to domestic life."We don't agree with his statement that women should stay home. It's not a suitable stand in our developing Keralam. It's not the 19th century that one should make such statements. Even Islam doesn't say that. Women should not stay home, but join the mainstream. That is our stand," he said.Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.Labour minister Bindu Krishna also criticised the cleric, saying such remarks undermined women’s constitutional rights and sought to push them "centuries back".
"Constitution of India assures equal rights to women and men, irrespective of sex. The people have the right to live a free and liberal life. And also, these types of statements push women centuries back. So, we can't accept such statements. Our women are free to move. They are best rulers. Our girls are always coming through this society, and we can't accept such statements," Krishna told ANI.The controversy followed remarks made by Aboobacker at the Hubbul Rasul Conference in Kochi, where he defended recent directives issued by the Kanthapuram faction of Samastha to local Mahalls on women’s participation in religious celebrations.A circular issued by the organisation directed Madrasas not to allow women to be present among unrelated men at religious events. It also advised against displaying young women on public stages and having them participate in road processions alongside unrelated men.
Defending the directives, Aboobacker said women should remain within the home and invoked the Quran to support his position."Women should remain confined within their homes. They should not enter the public sphere. The Holy Quran says so," Aboobacker said, while defending the purdah system as a practice intended to protect women’s dignity.He argued that allowing women into public spaces without restrictions could result in "great destruction", insisting that the measures were intended to honour and protect women rather than diminish them.Aboobacker also said Islam had granted women property and inheritance rights centuries ago to improve their status without requiring them to leave domestic life. He maintained that he was not concerned by opposition or political criticism and said no one could silence him or force him to change Islamic doctrines.

Azerbaijani authorities evacuated 5,000 people after a fire triggered explosions at an ammunition depot overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday, officials said, adding that there were no casualties.

No homes had been damaged and no deaths, injuries or serious losses had been recorded, he added.
Security measures were in force at the entrances and exits of both villages, while evacuees were being accommodated in safe conditions, Nazarov said.

Ed Markey wins: Key takeaways from Massachusetts primary election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:27:35 UTC
17:27:35 KST

Ed Markey wins: Key takeaways from Massachusetts primary election results
Markey secures the Democratic nomination as Massachusetts voters back several of the state’s long-serving lawmakers.
Veteran Democrats defeated younger challengers in Massachusetts’s primary elections on Tuesday, with Senator Ed Markey beating Representative Seth Moulton for the Democratic nomination.
Long-serving representatives Stephen Lynch and Richard Neal also won their races.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
Here are five key takeaways from the Massachusetts primary election results.
Veteran Democrats survive challenges from younger rivals
Several of Massachusetts’s longest-serving Democrats survived challenges in Tuesday’s primaries.
Senator Ed Markey, 80, defeated 47-year-old Representative Seth Moulton to secure the Democratic nomination.
Similar challenges also failed in the House. Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, who has held his seat since 2001, defeated 39-year-old progressive lawyer Patrick Roath in the 8th Congressional District.
In the 1st District, 77-year-old Representative Richard Neal, first elected to Congress in 1988, defeated 39-year-old public school teacher Jeromie Whalen.
All three will now advance to November, with Democrats heavily favoured in Massachusetts.
Markey wins the progressive argument despite his age
Moulton campaigned on the need for a new generation of political leadership, but Markey’s age did not appear to work against him.
Markey, 33 years older than Moulton, ran as the more progressive candidate, with backing from prominent figures on the Democratic left, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and independent Senator Bernie Sanders.
Markey also had the backing of Senator Elizabeth Warren and other members of the state’s congressional delegation, while no member of the delegation endorsed Moulton.
Moulton, a Marine veteran who ran as the more moderate alternative, instead received support from groups including VoteVets and New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill.
Markey also repeatedly attacked Moulton over his comments questioning transgender girls’ participation in girls’ sports. Moulton later apologised and said he supported the transgender community, but Markey continued to raise the issue during the campaign.
“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
However, the opposite dynamic played out in the 8th District, where the younger Roath — unsuccessfully — challenged Lynch from the left.
The results showed that age and ideology did not necessarily go hand in hand in Massachusetts.
“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey said Tuesday. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”
In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”
Progressive challengers make gains but fall short
While younger challengers failed to defeat the state’s veteran Democrats, some still mounted competitive campaigns.
Roath raised about $1.3m compared with roughly $910,000 for Lynch, despite taking on a congressman who has represented the area for more than two decades.
He also significantly narrowed the gap during the campaign. Lynch led Roath by 26 points in a February poll, but by the final stretch of the campaign, his lead had narrowed to seven points.
But Roath ultimately fell short against Lynch.
Whalen also challenged Neal from the left in the 1st District, campaigning on progressive policies including Medicare for All, but fell short against the veteran congressman.
Massachusetts bucks the national trend
The Massachusetts results differed from several Democratic primaries elsewhere in the country, where younger progressive candidates have defeated long-serving politicians.
In Connecticut last month, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin defeated Representative John Larson, 78, who had served in Congress for nearly three decades.
In June, 29-year-old Democratic socialist Melat Kiros defeated Representative Diana DeGette, who had represented her Colorado district for nearly 30 years.
That came a week after two Democratic members of Congress were defeated by left-wing challengers in New York, including five-term Representative Adriano Espaillat.
In Massachusetts, all three major challenges to long-serving lawmakers failed.
But the results were not necessarily a rejection of progressive politics. Markey himself ran from the party’s progressive wing, while Lynch and Neal faced younger candidates running to their left.
Instead, the common factor was the strength of long-serving politicians, regardless of whether their challengers came from the centre or the left.
Biden-backed Dan Koh wins primary for open House seat
Former Biden White House aide Koh won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’s 6th Congressional District, the seat being vacated by Seth Moulton as he ran for Senate.
Koh stood out in the five-way race for openly embracing the former Biden administration. He was endorsed by former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as former Labor Secretary and Boston Mayor Marty Walsh.
Koh will now head into November as the favourite to win the heavily Democratic district.
Democratic primaries may have decided the races
In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primaries may prove to be the biggest electoral hurdle, with Democratic winners heavily favoured to prevail in November’s general election.
Markey will face Republican John Deaton, who ran unopposed in his primary on Tuesday. Deaton previously ran for the Senate against Elizabeth Warren in 2024, losing by about 20 percentage points.
The Democratic nominees in several House districts will also head into November as heavy favourites, meaning Tuesday’s results could in effect determine much of the state’s congressional delegation for the next term.

Which EU countries have the most paid online subscriptions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:27:24 UTC
17:27:24 KST

Nearly one in three Europeans paid for online subscriptions in 2025 according to data from Eurostat, but the continent is deeply split on its digital budget. Subscription services are particularly popular in northern and western households, while parts of Eastern Europe lag far behind.
From binge-watching weekend drama series on Netflix or streaming live football matches on DAZN, nearly one in three people across the European Union now pay a recurring monthly fee just to watch films, series, or live sports online.
New data released by Eurostat shows that 32.7% of internet users across the bloc held a paid streaming subscription in 2025.
But how much Europeans actually open their wallets for digital content varies dramatically depending on the country they call home.
When breaking down the numbers by member state, a stark geographical split emerges: Ireland and Denmark lead the rankings by a wide margin, with 63.9% and 61.1% of internet users respectively paying for video and sports services such as Amazon Prime and Disney+, closely followed by the Netherlands at 59.2%.
At the other end of the spectrum, willingness to pay for streaming services drops significantly.
Bulgaria recorded the lowest adoption rate in the European Union at just 9.3%, followed by Slovenia (13.7%), Latvia (16.7%), and Lithuania (17.4%), creating a massive digital divide across the continent.
Beyond audiovisual entertainment, the data reveals clear differences in the popularity of alternative subscription sectors.
Audio platforms covering music streaming and podcasts on apps like YouTube Premium and Spotify count 23.0% of EU internet users as paying subscribers.
Traditional reads such as online news websites, digital newspapers, and magazines lag far behind at 7.2%, while interactive cloud gaming subscriptions like Xbox Game Pass trail at the bottom with 6.1%.
As digital services continue to anchor modern household routines, these figures highlight a deeply fragmented digital landscape across Europe.
Subscription services hit with lawsuits
Despite their apparent popularity in certain countries, subscription services in the EU have also come under fire from customers in recent months.
A Dutch consumer group is suing Netflix over its subscription price increases of up to 75% since 2017. It put the potential damages at up to €673 million.
It follows similar cases elsewhere in Europe, such as a court in Rome ruling in April that Netflix's price increases in Italy were illegal. The streaming platform is appealing against the decision.
Various courts in Germany have also ruled in favour of consumers in parallel legal battles, while another in Spain is still ongoing and another in Austria concluded in an out-of-court settlement on compensation.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the drone hit the building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, causing a fire and partial structural destruction. Seven people were injured in the attack as of midday, with five hospitalized, Klitschko said.

Emergency crews were working at several impact sites across the capital.
A nearby three-story building also caught fire, while a medical facility in the district was damaged. Some of its windows were blown out, but there were no immediate reports of injuries among patients or staff.
University hit during classes
A Russian drone also struck one of Kyiv’s universities while classes were underway, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Some 160 students were in a shelter at the time of the attack. No injuries were reported.
Another drone impact was later reported in the Holosiivskyi district, where a warehouse building was damaged.
Kyiv Post correspondents in central Kyiv reported hearing multiple explosions during the attack. One correspondent said the blast wave shattered windows in their apartment.
Initial reports on social media claimed that explosions had occurred near Kyiv’s central railway station. Those reports were later not confirmed.
Machine-Gun Pickup Escorts Putin Convoy in Vladivostok
Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, said there had been no strikes on railway infrastructure in central Kyiv.
The latest strike came after Russian attacks overnight and earlier Wednesday morning had already caused fires and damage across the Kyiv region.
In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, debris from a Russian drone fell in an open area and caused a fire, Klitschko said. The same district was targeted during the previous evening’s attack, when falling debris also caused a fire in an open area. A private house in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district was also set on fire.
Two people were wounded in the morning attack in the Kyiv region, according to Regional Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko.
What changed in Russia’s drone war in Ukraine?
Since Thursday, Kyiv has been living under a constant drone siege.
Russia began shifting its long-range drone tactics in Ukraine on Thursday, Aug. 27 – the large swarms once or twice a week that Kyiv residents had become accustomed to have been replaced by near-continuous waves across Ukrainian airspace
As of Tuesday, Sept. 1, there has been no let-up in the strategy, with explosions ringing consistently over Kyiv and other cities, paralyzing businesses nationwide as some major chains were increasingly targeted.
The good news is that the overall number launched stayed relatively consistent and Ukraine’s interception rates remain high – but the bad news is that Russia can likely keep it up for some time.
No major spikes within the same timeframe – but not enough data on daytime launches.
The overall number of drones launched likely increased – though those recorded overnight stayed relatively consistent.
Based on the Ukrainian Air Force’s daily morning briefing, Russia launched an average of around 188 drones per night (6 p.m.-8 a.m.) between Aug. 27-31.
For comparison, the average in July recorded in the same 6 p.m.-8 a.m. window was close to 160 per day, with the lowest on July 21 (58 launched) and the highest on July 2 (496 launched).
The air force did not provide clear data on drones launched and intercepted outside the 6 p.m.-8 a.m. window, though its warnings over the past week suggest they range in the dozens per day.
For context, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said Russia launched 8,653 drones in July – a few thousand more than the 4,955 Kyiv Post calculated based on the air force’s morning briefings.
Recent months also saw a drastic drop in total numbers launched in a single swarm, with Moscow launching a record swarm of over 1,500 drones within 24 hours in May, an attack that coincided with a renewed peace push from Washington and a reiterated hardline stance from Moscow at the time.
The largest number of drones launched in a single attack was on Sept. 7, 2025, when Russia launched 805 drones overnight in an attack that killed at least four civilians.
The known numbers suggest that unless Ukraine could hit Russia’s drone production, Moscow is likely able to sustain the number of launches.

Homemade Rockets Reportedly Hit One of Germany's Largest Power Plants in Sabotage Attempt

Homemade Rockets Reportedly Hit One of Germany's Largest Power Plants in Sabotage Attempt
German authorities reported an attempt to attack energy infrastructure after discovering homemade explosive and incendiary devices near an electrical substation in Turnow-Preilack, located near the Jänschwalde lignite-fired power plant in Brandenburg.
The German newspaper Märkische Allgemeine Zeitung reported on September 1, obtaining a photograph showing what appeared to be an improvised device resembles a small homemade model rocket at the site.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Several improvised devices were found near the site in the Spree-Neisse district, and bomb disposal specialists were deployed to neutralize them.
The targeted substation distributes electricity generated by the 2,000-megawatt Jänschwalde facility—Germany's fourth-largest power station, which includes one 500-megawatt unit kept in reserve.
The plant supplies power to several million households and provides district heating to the city of Cottbus, with the affected substation situated about 5 kilometers away from the main facility.
German media indicated the apparent goal of the action was reportedly to cause a large-scale power outage linked to the nearby coal plant. Police noted that potential damage to a power line was recorded around 8 a.m., though initial reports confirmed no major blackouts occurred.
Brandenburg Prime Minister Dietmar Woidke referred to the event as a "trial attack." He stated, "The alarmingly high frequency of such incidents shows that we must decisively protect our infrastructure."
Woidke added that emergency services and personnel at the substation and power station prevented worse outcomes through timely actions, noting that no injuries were reported.
The event follows a series of sabotage incidents recorded across several European nations since early August. On August 4, an attack attempt targeting a Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft occurred at Leipzig airport using multiple drones, one of which struck a DHL company plane, though none detonated.
Earlier, a deliberate arson attack on a cable bridge connected to the Lichterfelde power station in Berlin damaged five high-voltage and ten medium-voltage power lines, leaving over 35,000 households and nearly 2,000 businesses without electricity and central heating across four districts.
A far-left extremist group known as Vulkangruppe claimed responsibility for the sabotage, prompting law enforcement to open a formal investigation while emergency crews worked to deploy temporary mobile infrastructure and restore full power to the affected areas.

OMA’s taipei housing renewal lets residents shape an alternative to the standard tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:25:35 UTC
17:25:35 KST

RESIDENTS COMMISSION OMA TO RETHINK URBAN RENEWAL IN TAIPEI
The residents of Taipei’s Songshan Yulin Yuan Community appoint OMA to redevelop their aging housing block, proposing an alternative to the standardized residential towers often produced through conventional, sales-led urban renewal. Set within a 1960s planned neighborhood in Taipei, the project asks whether increasing density can preserve some of the spatial habits, greenery, and sense of collective life that residents already value.
The commission arrives at a significant moment for Taipei’s housing stock. More than 70 percent of the city’s housing is now over 30 years old, while many buildings constructed before 1974 do not meet contemporary seismic standards. Taiwan’s Disaster-Prevention Urban Renewal policy, introduced in 2024, offers floor-area-ratio bonuses to encourage the reconstruction of vulnerable structures. The Songshan project responds to these conditions by placing residents themselves at the center of the renewal process. OMA says its proposal grows out of conversations with the existing community. The main challenge of the project is to determine which qualities of the neighborhood should survive the transition.
‘Rather than being commissioned by a developer, we were appointed directly by residents to redevelop their 1960s housing. The neighborhood is characterized by relatively low density, interconnected buildings, and abundant greenery. Through extensive conversations with residents, we learned that these qualities are precisely what they value and want to preserve. Our proposal therefore reinterprets the spatial and social qualities of the existing neighborhood to create a contemporary model of collective living. The aim is to retain a sense of community while accommodating future needs. I believe successful urban transformations grow out of the existing context and aspirations of the community.’ David Gianotten, OMA Managing Partner, tells designboom.
renderings by Stefania Trozzi, Diego Iacono, Nevena Ivanovic, courtesy of OMA
FOUR INTERLOCKING SLABS REPLACE THE AGING WALK-UPS
The architects at OMA transform the existing block into two 24-story residential towers composed of four interlocking vertical slabs. The massing steps and shifts across the site, breaking down the scale of the new development while creating openings between its different volumes. The configuration maximizes north-south facades and introduces vertical openings intended to bring daylight and natural ventilation deeper into the apartments. It also responds to a residential typology found in the original neighborhood, which OMA describes as a ‘front and rear balcony’ arrangement.
Living rooms and balconies face outward, while a central living zone connects to a rear service layer containing kitchens, bathrooms, and utilities. In this way, the project translates an existing domestic pattern into a larger and denser residential structure rather than abandoning it entirely. ‘Songshan Yulin Yuan is part of a 1960s planned neighborhood defined by low density, interconnected building types, and abundant greenery,’says David Gianotten. ‘Through close engagement with residents, we understood that these are qualities that the community wish to retain in the renewed housing.’
the two towers are composed as distinct volumes with stepped and shifted massing
PUBLIC PLATFORMS EXTEND DAILY LIFE INTO THE TOWERS
The spaces between and around the residential slabs become an important part of OMA’s strategy. A network of shared amenities extends through the project at different levels, creating connections between the towers and the surrounding neighborhood. On the second floor, a semi-open platform sits within the surrounding tree canopy and connects with nearby community parks. The space accommodates sports and leisure activities, while the ground floor opens toward nearby schools and the walking track of the park. Here, a receding facade frames the lobby and retail spaces to strengthen the relationship between the new development and its immediate surroundings.
Below ground, a community living room provides quieter leisure spaces. An atrium brings daylight into this lower level while maintaining visual connections between different parts of the building. Rooftop sky gardens occupy the tops of the lower slabs, offering views across Taipei. Together, these shared spaces are intended to form a continuous network for everyday life, extending beyond the individual apartment and into the wider neighborhood.
the proposed towers stand within Taipei’s dense residential landscape
CAN DENSITY PRESERVE A SENSE OF NEIGHBORHOOD?
The Songshan Urban Renewal Residence proposes a different way of thinking about the relationship between density and residential quality. Its architectural argument lies less in rejecting tall buildings altogether than in questioning whether renewal must inevitably produce isolated, repetitive towers. ‘Our aim is to increase density while preserving residential quality through the reorganization of massing, openings, and public spaces, fostering a sense of neighborhood character and domesticity rarely seen in recent renewal projects,’explains Chiaju Lin, OMA Project Director in Taiwan.
The project remains at the schematic design stage, but its commission reflects the active role residents have taken in the redevelopment of their community. The Songshan Yulin Yuan Community selected OMA to rethink their existing housing, drawing attention to the qualities residents hope to retain, including greenery, connected buildings, and familiar patterns of daily life. OMA responds through stepped slabs, balconies, shared platforms, gardens, and communal spaces. While the project is still in its early stages, it presents an approach to urban renewal in which residents take part in shaping the housing that will replace their existing homes.
the redevelopment introduces new housing into Taipei’s existing urban fabric
a shared platform at the base of the towers introduces leisure spaces
OMA’s facade combines deeply recessed windows with balconies and planted outdoor spaces
the two residential towers rise above a landscaped ground level, supported by angled structural elements

His brother died abroad. His boss kept asking when he would return to work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:24:30 UTC
17:24:30 KST

A Thai employee has resigned from his job after what he described as an insensitive response from his manager while he was arranging the return of his younger brother’s body from abroad and preparing for the funeral.
Somsak Butsri shared the story in a Facebook post that quickly went viral.
His brother, a well-known travel YouTuber known as Hlun Solo with millions of followers on social media, died while traveling in Georgia.
In the days that followed, Butsri said he followed company procedures and submitted a written leave request, while also discussing privately how long he would be away.
At the same time, he was coordinating with multiple agencies, handling documents, contacting the embassy and arranging the travel needed to bring his brother’s body home.
He said the process continued late into the night and left him with very little sleep.
According to his post, during that period his manager repeatedly questioned whether his absence was necessary, whether he needed to be physically present, whether the situation was urgent enough to justify leave and whether he could return to work sooner.
Two days after his brother’s body arrived in Thailand, while the family was still holding funeral ceremonies, Butsri received another phone call asking when he would return to work.
He said there were no urgent tasks requiring his presence at the time.
Butsri stressed that he was not asking for special treatment, but for basic judgment and respect.
He said the comments he received reflected a mindset that failed to recognize the human reality of losing a family member.
After the ceremonies ended, he decided to resign.
He returned to the office on Aug. 18 to complete his responsibilities through the end of the month and ensure a proper handover.
On Aug. 23, his birthday, he told his mother and grandmother that he could no longer continue working in an environment shaped by that attitude.
He said he worried they would be anxious because he still needed to contribute to the household income, but their reaction reassured him and allowed him to take a break without overthinking the decision.
Butsri also said he had prepared financially, maintaining an emergency fund that could cover one to two years without work or potentially be used to start a small business.
For now, he said, he has not decided what he will do next because many matters related to his brother remain unresolved.
He also made clear that he did not blame everyone at the company, saying he was sorry to leave supportive colleagues and emphasizing that his decision was not about them.
He ended his post by arguing that leadership should be measured not only by business results, but also by maturity, judgment and respect for people, especially when someone is dealing with one of the hardest moments of their life.

Yandex’s AI assistant could gain expanded permissions on mobile devices, including access to banking apps
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is weighing new rules for preinstalling Russian services on smartphones, tablets, and other devices, a move that could give Alice AI, the assistant developed by Yandex, expanded permissions on users’ devices.
Alice AI could also gain access to banking apps and other applications that collect sensitive data and store it on their own servers, a source told the Russian business daily Kommersant. The source did not specify what kind of data would be involved.
If the new rules take effect, the source said, Yandex’s AI assistant could become a service “with access rights to user data far greater than any preinstalled app on the list.”
The outlet’s sources stressed that the initiative directly targets similar foreign smart assistants and AI models operating in Russia.
The Digital Development Ministry published a draft resolution for public discussion in early August that would update the existing preinstallation rules, referring to an AI assistant “with access to system functions, applications, notifications, authorization, and hardware capabilities.” The ministry has since pulled the document from its website for revision.
The Digital Development Ministry told Kommersant that the proposed changes “are at the discussion stage with the industry.” Yandex had not responded to a request for comment by the time of publication.
Russia has required the preinstallation of Russian software on smartphones, computers, and other electronics since 2021. Alice AI is on the government’s list of mandatory preinstalled apps for 2027.

Fewer foreign-language residents in Finland rely on welfare benefits
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:20:57 EEST
17:20:57 KST

A smaller share of Finland’s growing foreign-language population receives basic social assistance and unemployment benefits than a decade ago, according to figures released by the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela, on Wednesday.
Kela data shows that the number of people whose registered mother tongue is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi rose by more than 70 per cent between 2017 and 2025, from 373,000 to 646,000.
Despite that rise, the proportion receiving several forms of income support fell over the same period.
In 2017, 23 per cent of foreign-language adults received basic social assistance. By 2025, the figure had fallen to 18 per cent. The share receiving labour market subsidy dropped from 24 per cent to 16 per cent.
“The foreign-language population in Finland is larger than before, so their share of Kela benefit recipients has also increased. The development reflects the change in the population structure,” Kela research manager Signe Jauhiainen said in the agency’s release.
The number of foreign-language social assistance recipients still increased as the population grew. Kela recorded 110,000 recipients in 2017 and 137,000 in 2025. Last year’s total included 92,000 adults and 45,000 children.
Jauhiainen said much of the increase in recipient numbers came from Ukrainian speakers after 2023. Ukrainians living in Finland under temporary protection did not qualify for labour market subsidy.
Kela paid €408 million in basic social assistance to foreign-language recipients in 2025, representing 41 per cent of total spending on the benefit. In 2017, the corresponding amount was €172 million, or 24 per cent.
Foreign-language recipients received €597 million in labour market subsidy in 2025, accounting for one-third of total payments under the scheme.
Labour market subsidy and the basic unemployment allowance were replaced by Finland’s new general benefit on 1 May 2026.
Kela paid about €9.2 billion through nine main income-support benefits in 2025. Foreign-language recipients received around €1.8 billion, or 20 per cent. In 2017, they received 15 per cent of €8.6 billion paid through the same benefits.
Kela said the figures differ between benefit categories. Foreign-language recipients accounted for more than 40 per cent of basic social assistance spending in 2025 but less than 5 per cent of national pension payments.
General housing allowance followed a similar trend in recipient rates. Some 26 per cent of foreign-language adults received the benefit in 2017, compared with 18 per cent in 2025.
Their share of housing allowance spending moved in the opposite direction, rising from 19 per cent to 27 per cent. Kela linked part of the change to Ukrainians entering the Finnish social security system and changes to housing support rules.
Students moved from general housing allowance to the student housing supplement in 2025. Owner-occupiers also lost eligibility for general housing allowance during the year, changing the composition of recipients.
Kela said the declining use of unemployment and social assistance among the foreign-language population indicates that a larger share of the group is working or studying.

Erdogan, Putin agree to continue Turkey's nuclear development, improve economic relations

Russian President Vladimir Putin highlighted on Tuesday the recent development of Turkey's first nuclear project, saying that Moscow plans to continue developing the nuclear and economic ties between the two nations.
During a meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, held in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, Putin pointed out the strong relations between his country and Turkey, while also saying that one of the main shared projects between the countries is the construction of the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant.
"Joint projects continue to be implemented. One of them is the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant. You have set a target of commissioning the first unit of the plant this year. This will happen," Putin told Erdogan.
What is Turkey's nuclear project?
Developed by Russian state-owned corporation Rosatom, the plant is located on the Mediterranean coast in Mersin Province. It is Turkey's first and main nuclear project, with the four power units expected to have a total capacity of 4,800 MW using VVER-1200 reactors, which would represent 10% of Turkey's entire energy consumption.
Erdogan also addressed the nuclear project, saying that Turkey plans to build more power plants with Russia in the future. "With the opening of the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant, we will also take steps together to open some new power plants. We are in the midst of these preparations," he said.
According to the statements by the two heads of state, outside of the energy sector, the main focus for developing relations will be on agriculture and tourism, with Russian tourists being among the most important visitors to Turkey, according to Erdogan.
Along with both heads of state, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and the head of Turkey's National Intelligence Organization (MIT), Ibrahim Kalin, also attended the meeting.
Russia expands relations with Iran
During the SCO summit, Putin also met with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who thanked the Russian leader for Moscow's position on the war in Iran and the resulting sanctions.
Both presidents said that together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism."
During the meeting, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow stood in solidarity with the Iranian people in the fight for their interests.
Putin also said that Russia and Iran will maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current military and political environment.
“During this difficult period, we are striving to provide you with the necessary assistance - as we have discussed - and are supplying you with essential goods,” Putin said.
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

The water supply network has also suffered disruption, with 40 schemes currently affected. Hamirpur accounts for 23 of the disrupted schemes, while Shimla has reported 17.
NEW DELHI: Monsoon rains have claimed 259 lives and caused damage worth more than Rs 1,200 crore across Himachal Pradesh in just 64 days, according to State Emergency Operations Centre (SEOC) data. Meanwhile, the latest spell of rain has severely affected connectivity, with 150 roads currently blocked across Himachal Pradesh.Mandi has reported the highest number of closures at 78, followed by Shimla with 30. Fresh rainfall has also disrupted power and water supplies across the hill state.Essential services have also been hit. As many as 374 distribution transformer regions (DTRs) are out of service, affecting power supply across several districts. Mandi has recorded 128 affected DTRs, followed by Shimla with 84 and Kullu with 81.The water supply network has also suffered disruption, with 40 schemes currently affected. Hamirpur accounts for 23 of the disrupted schemes, while Shimla has reported 17.The mounting disruptions come against the backdrop of a deadly monsoon season that has claimed 259 lives between June 30 and September 1. Of the total fatalities, 106 were caused by rain and disaster-related incidents, including 18 deaths in landslides and 13 due to drowning.
Another 153 people died in road accidents during the period.Lahaul and Spiti, the high-altitude tribal district, recorded 15 deaths linked to monsoon-related disasters.The rains have also inflicted extensive damage on public and private infrastructure, with the cumulative losses estimated at Rs 1,202.64 crore. The Public Works Department bore the biggest share of the damage at more than Rs 914 crore, while the Jal Shakti Vibhag reported losses exceeding Rs 258 crore.
The disaster has completely damaged 460 houses and resulted in the deaths of 460 animals, the SEOC data showed.State government departments and field agencies are now carrying out restoration operations in affected districts, working to reopen blocked roads and restore power and water supply.With the monsoon continuing to disrupt normal life, the latest figures underline the scale of the crisis facing Himachal Pradesh, where hundreds of lives have been lost and critical infrastructure has suffered extensive damage in just over two months.

Vaher: Former RKIK director is responsible for failed €70 million shell deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

Vaher: Former RKIK director is responsible for failed €70 million shell deal
The director general of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), Elmar Vaher, told ERR in an interview that former RKIK head Magnus-Valdemar Saar is responsible for the failed €70 million shell deal. RKIK employees failed to follow the necessary financial management principles, he believes.
To what extent, if at all, is RKIK responsible for the fact that the Estonian state may now lose this €70 million?
I will start by saying that one of our main objectives is to help Ukraine – just as we help Moldova and other countries that want to be democratic and are fighting for their freedom. To this end, RKIK carries out a great many procurements, and I want to emphasise that we have actually carried out many, many successful procurements. But indeed, there is one 2024–2025 contract involving advance payments that is now in a situation where the other party has not fulfilled its contractual obligations, and to protect our rights we have now gone to court.
But you made advance payments to a supplier that had never previously supplied this kind of goods, and its background was not checked.
It is difficult for me to comment on that because I was not working at RKIK at the time. That question can certainly be put to RKIK's former management.
I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people's heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were. I can go by what is written down, and I can understand that. And having read those materials, I dare say that I would not have entered into that contract, because in my view it is not right to enter into a contract of this scale and make an advance payment of this size to a company you do not know and which is not itself an ammunition manufacturer.
Have you subsequently been able to establish who was behind that decision?
The decision was made by RKIK's former director general [Magnus-Valdemar Saar].
The National Audit Office also requested those contracts. Do the contracts with this company exist or not? Or why were they unable to be presented to the National Audit Office?
My team tried to locate all the materials from 2024 and 2025 relating to the making of this decision. We have provided all the materials to the National Audit Office, and there are no more materials. The National Audit Office has indeed assessed this as insufficient and said that something is missing. But once again: whatever there was to provide, we certainly provided. RKIK cooperated fully and will continue to do so. I have personally met and spoken several times with Janar Holm and the auditors, so whatever there was to provide, we provided. If something is missing, we are now working to find those missing documents, if that is even possible. I cannot comment on that at the moment.
When did you first realise that the supplier that had been paid was actually unable to deliver the goods?
I can only speak for myself. For me, it became clear in February-March, when we began preparing to terminate the contracts and go to court to protect our rights. That took a little time. And if I remember correctly, in April-May we also filed the relevant claims in court.
Is this €70 million now the final amount, or could it increase or decrease?
That amount is final at present.
You took over as head of RKIK in January this year. Was there already something in the air at that point, or were there already some known problems that could arise?
In my assessment, RKIK's overall financial management principles were not sufficient.
We have made a great many changes and will make more. I became aware of the National Audit Office's conclusions quite early on. I actually wanted to commission a financial audit of RKIK, and I also made that proposal to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur. But we agreed that since the National Audit Office was conducting an audit anyway, we would not duplicate the work and would wait for the final report. I was able to read a draft of the final report materials in June, and since then we have made many changes and will make more to ensure that RKIK's financial management principles are clear and understandable. And most importantly, that RKIK employees also follow them. In my view, the main issue has been that the existing procedures simply were not followed.
So who is responsible now, or what happens next?
The people who signed the contract are responsible. The contract was signed by RKIK's former director general.

Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:14:24 UTC
17:14:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile, officials say
Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, military officials said on Wednesday, as Western powers scramble to acquire long-range weapons to counter what they see as an increased threat from Russia.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system, and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges.
