Drownings in Lake Cauma occurred after normal swimming hours
There have been two fatal accidents while swimming within three days at Lake Cauma in Flims in canton Graubünden. Mayor Christoph Schmidt says he is shocked, but does not want to hear any talk of a ban on swimming outside opening hours.
The latest incident took place on Sunday evening. At around 7:00 pm, a 27-year-old German man was trying to swim to a small island to rescue a friend when he himself got into difficulty. Despite rescue efforts, the young man died at the scene.
Just three days earlier, a 17-year-old tourist from the United Kingdom also had problems swimming and died that same evening in hospital.
The public bathing area at Lake Cauma is open every day during the summer season from 8:30 am to 5:00 pm, according to the Flims-Laax tourist board’s website.
“We are deeply shocked by the two tragic accidents that occurred in such quick succession at this much-loved and popular swimming lake. Both incidents occurred in the evening, after normal opening hours, when there is no guaranteed supervision in the water,” Schmidt told Keystone-ATS news agency.
+ A second young man drowns in same Swiss lake
The last tragic incident took place over ten years ago, in 2016. “Our thoughts are with the families of the victims, and we wish to express our deepest condolences to them for these tragic and painful events,” the mayor added.
Dangers often underestimated
Schmidt does not believe that Lake Cauma is currently particularly dangerous for swimmers. Indeed, it does not present any particular risks in terms of temperature or currents. However, it can generally be observed “that inexperienced swimmers repeatedly underestimate the dangers of open waters such as lakes”. In this regard, the mayor cites distances and temperature.
For Schmidt, “as with many other open bodies of water”, a ban on swimming outside opening hours is not currently under discussion, even following the fatal accidents. For some time now, however, information on the safety plan and bathing rules has been displayed within the bathing area. The safety and rescue plan for the lake and its implementation are refined each year in collaboration with the operator, “where appropriate, with the involvement of the relevant authorities”, the mayor added.

German Navy successfully tests Israeli LORA missile system in the North Atlantic
The German Navy has successfully completed a double test of Israel Aerospace Industries' LORA ballistic missile system, launching the weapon from an operational vessel in the North Atlantic
The German Navy conducted the classified test as part of its OPEX operational testing program, an initiative designed to support the "Marine 2035 and Beyond" program aimed at preparing the fleet for current and future security threats, IAI said in a statement. The missile, launched from a German Navy vessel equipped with the system's command and launcher carriage, successfully navigated its trajectory and struck its target with precision in both test scenarios, meeting all objectives.
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, inspector of the German Navy, called the test a historic achievement. "With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we have made naval history. I am extremely pleased with this achievement," Kaack said, according to Bild and a German Armed Forces Instagram post. "The system can be successfully deployed from our units, and its potential range surpasses anything we have previously known. For the protection of Germany and our allies, this test represents a new chapter in terms of deterrence and readiness at sea."
IAI Chairman Boaz Levy called the test "an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Ministry of Defense," noting it took place in Germany, "the country where the world's first ballistic missile was invented." He said the achievement builds on Israel's Arrow-3 missile defense system already stationed on German soil, further strengthening the countries' defense partnership.
IAI CEO Guy Bar Lev said the naval LORA system was "designed to provide precision strike capabilities at depth, even in challenging operational environments," calling it "one of the most advanced and operationally proven ballistic missile systems in the world."

LORA, which stands for "Long Range Attack," is an Israeli-developed short-range ballistic missile system delivered in a launch container for rapid deployment from naval vessels. According to Bild, two German frigates were deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test, with the missile system offering a range exceeding 500 kilometers (310 miles).
Suggested articles
IAI markets the system as capable of striking "strategic targets deep within enemy territory from mobile or maritime platforms," with the ability to destroy a detected target within ten minutes. The Israeli military has reportedly used the system, including an air-launched version, in strikes in Lebanon and against Iran.
The test comes as Germany moves to expand its long-range precision strike capabilities amid heightened concern over Russian aggression, following recent drone incidents including an attack on Leipzig Airport that Berlin has blamed on Russia. Germany is also finalizing a separate deal to acquire US Tomahawk missiles, with a range of up to 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles), following an agreement reached on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara.

Estonia's defense minister's resignation sought in wake of national defense scandal
Pressure is mounting on Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform Party) to resign after the National Audit Office identified serious problems with financial management in the defense sector, with criticism now coming from both opposition and coalition politicians.
Social Democrat Raimond Kaljulaid said Pevkur had been a hardworking minister and a strong supporter of Ukraine but should consider stepping down voluntarily.
"If Hanno were to ask my opinion today, I would advise him to very seriously consider resigning as defense minister at the earliest opportunity and on his own initiative," Kaljulaid said. "The National Audit Office's repeated criticism, the confusion surrounding procurements and advance payments, and now a criminal investigation — it is simply too much."
Kaljulaid said Prime Minister Kristen Michal should appoint a nonpartisan defense expert with an impeccable reputation to lead the Ministry of Defense for the six months remaining until the elections.
Social Democratic Party leader Lauri Läänemets also called on Pevkur to resign, saying major problems identified at the ministry had remained unresolved for a year.
"We are spending a great deal of money on national defense, and the entire defense sector is under fire today. Hanno Pevkur has become a figure who, in a sense, is undermining trust in national defense," Läänemets told ETV morning show "Terevisioon."
Läänemets said that if Pevkur does not step down voluntarily, the issue could eventually lead to a no-confidence motion against him in the Riigikogu. Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu has also called for Pevkur's resignation.
Pressure on Pevkur increased further Wednesday when Toomas Uibo, chair of coalition party Eesti 200's parliamentary group, said he personally did not see how Pevkur could remain in office if media reports about defense procurement were accurate.
"This is not how things should or can be done in Estonia. I very much hope that the Reform Party makes decisions quickly and takes responsibility," Uibo said. "If the facts reported by the media are true, I personally don't see how the defense minister can continue in office."
The criticism follows a National Audit Office report that found numerous serious problems at institutions under the Ministry of Defense, which auditors said increased the risk of misuse of state funds and assets. Similar problems had been identified a year earlier.
Eesti Ekspress also reported that Estonia paid €70 million in advance to Indian suppliers as part of an effort to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine, despite the suppliers having never previously sold a shell. The promised materiel did not arrive, and the dispute is now in court.
The Prosecutor's Office has since opened a criminal investigation into circumstances covered by National Audit Office audits from this year and last year.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has called a Cabinet meeting for early Thursday, asking Auditor General Janar Holm to provide an overview of accounting irregularities in the defense sector. Michal said he expects Pevkur, Commander of the Estonian Defense Forces Andrus Merilo, Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Elmar Vaher and Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk to present a concrete plan for quickly resolving the problems.

Iceland said ‘No’ to EU membership talks. What does it mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:30:58 UTC
15:30:58 KST

Icelanders voted to keep their stalled EU membership bid on ice, dealing a blow to Brussels' post-Ukraine enlargement drive. Watch the video!
On 29 August, a majority of Icelanders rejected reopening EU accession talks, frozen since 2013, turning down what the government called a "now or never" moment.
The result means no new negotiations with Brussels and no change to Iceland's existing ties: full access to the single market and Schengen area through the European Economic Area, but no seat in the European Parliament or vote in the Council. The referendum was legally advisory, but the government pledged to respect it, effectively shelving the question for years.
Iceland already adopts most EU law through the European Economic Area. Still, it retains unilateral control over its fishing waters, a legacy of the 1970s Cod Wars, which it was not willing to trade for shared quotas under Brussels' Common Fisheries Policy.

Expert: Health Insurance Fund cuts likely to lengthen waiting lists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Expert: Health Insurance Fund cuts likely to lengthen waiting lists
If the Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa) tries to reduce its expenses, it will likely have to do so by cutting services — which means longer waiting lists, says healthcare expert Andres Võrk.
On Friday, the Health Insurance Fund supervisory board approved the draft budget for next year, and Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller said the goal for the coming years is to bring the fund out of its financial crisis so that by 2030 the budget reaches balance — or even a surplus.
University of Tartu econometrics lecturer and healthcare expert Andres Võrk said that there is still little information about Health Insurance Fund's plans, and only one clear measure is known so far — postponing the pay rise for healthcare workers.
"It's clear that this immediately creates significant tension with healthcare workers, who have said during wage negotiations that salaries should rise at least at the pace of average wage growth, if not more," he said.
Võrk added that if the Ministry of Finance forecasts average wage growth of 5.6 percent this year and 4.7 percent next year, it is hard to see where such an increase could come from if it is not reflected in the price component of healthcare services.
"The minister suggested that Health Insurance Fund will not raise wages and that healthcare institutions should find internal buffers for pay increases. But considering that salaries make up a very large share of total costs — about half for hospitals and more than half for family‑doctor centers — finding such a buffer while other input prices rise is unlikely," Võrk said.
He noted that Health Insurance Fund can save costs not only by limiting price growth but also by reducing the number of services. But to assess this, more information is needed: how much the volume of services is expected to change, where reductions might occur, and how this would affect waiting lists.
Although Health Insurance Fund has said that access to healthcare services will not be reduced, Võrk said this may not be enough: the population is aging and demand for healthcare services is increasing. If the number of visits remains at the current level, waiting lists will grow.
"Both the minister and the head of Health Insurance Fund have emphasized the need for greater efficiency in the system — better care pathways. That is always important, whether money is abundant or scarce; efficiency must always be improved," Võrk said.
He explained that when money is lacking, hospitals are forced to become more efficient — but funding must be directed to areas where it creates the most added value.
"This may mean different choices between specialist care and primary care, or between different fields of specialist care — increasing funding in some areas more than others," Võrk said.
As a health economist, Võrk believes Health Insurance Fund should be much better staffed and have significantly stronger analytical capacity. While the fund is proud of its low administrative costs and efficient management, he said it should actually be a stronger negotiating partner for healthcare institutions when discussing prices and the value of services.
Confido CEO: Fund should act like an insurance company
Medical center Confido CEO and general surgeon Edvard Garder said that although little is known about the Health Insurance Fund's budget plans, in general it is certainly possible to achieve accounting balance. The question, however, is how unbalanced Estonia's healthcare system will be afterward.
"Tervisekassa cannot significantly influence its revenue side. Balance therefore means cuts. Budget lines can be renamed or new ones created, but the substance remains cuts," Garder said.
He noted that the think-tank Foresight Center has previously described the deficit as structural — meaning new annual cuts would be needed every year.
"Maintaining the same volume and quality of services without cuts would only be possible if operations were made more efficient. Given the current situation, I do not believe it is possible to achieve tens of millions in efficiency gains year after year when all input prices keep rising," Garder said.
Garder added that Estonia should abandon state‑planned pricing: Health Insurance Fund should not spend time calculating prices itself but should behave like an insurance company — which, in essence, it already is.
"Health Insurance Fund should purchase services based on quality and price from different providers, regardless of ownership form. The market will set the prices," Garder said.
He added that nothing currently forces hospitals within the hospital network development plan (HVA) to operate more efficiently or cheaply, whereas providers outside the HVA are forced to compete on price.
Minister Joller's promise that Health Insurance Fund's budget will reach balance — and hopefully even a surplus — by 2030 sounds very ambitious when stated publicly, Garder said.
"Of course I hope for the best for Estonian health care and I am very interested to see how this surplus will be achieved. But fundamentally, it is wrong to speak of Health Insurance Fund's budget balance as the goal. The goal should be a sustainable healthcare system as a whole, not simply 'Health Insurance Fund at zero by 2030'," Garder said.
He added that without major reforms — such as ownership‑neutral service purchasing or allowing funding to follow the patient to whichever provider they choose — he does not consider the goal realistic.
Health Insurance Fund costs surged after Covid
Võrk said that looking back at why Health Insurance Fund's costs have grown, the rapid surge occurred after the Covid pandemic. In 2023 and 2024, there were large pay increases for healthcare workers and rising input prices across the economy.
"Before Covid, in 2019, Health Insurance Fund's costs made up five percent of GDP; now they are six percent. One percentage point may seem small, but in reality that is nearly 20 percent growth," Võrk said. "Costs grew quickly, and everyone has gotten used to it."
But if the goal is to bring this share back down to pre‑Covid levels — where healthcare costs made up a smaller portion of the economy — the problem is that wages and input prices cannot be reduced. Expectations for the healthcare sector have risen.
"That is very hard to do. It seems the minister and Health Insurance Fund are trying to reduce the fund's role again, but this likely means cuts to services, because I do not believe healthcare workers would accept a decline in real wages," Võrk said.
He added that this means providers will offer fewer services for the price Health Insurance Fund pays and will find work elsewhere in the private sector — funded by individuals or companies. Movement from publicly funded to privately funded health care has increased in recent years.
Some service prices may contain 'air'
Võrk said that in terms of how much public funding goes to healthcare, Estonia is around the European average. Estonia spends 13 percent of public funds on health care, compared to 15 percent in Finland and 17 percent in Norway. This means Estonia does not value health care as highly as wealthier countries — but that is typical, he said: the richer a country becomes, the more it spends on health care.
He pointed out that some services funded by Health Insurance Fund may contain "air" — meaning prices may be higher than necessary. For example, laboratory service prices were cut by 15 percent last year because technological advances allowed a review. Next, diagnostic services such as radiology may be reviewed.
"Looking at the whole picture, hospitals' profits have decreased in recent years — they are not swimming in money. Some services with buffers, like lab or diagnostic services, help subsidize loss‑making services," Võrk explained. "If price lists are reviewed, everything should be reviewed."
How the changes will affect patients is not yet known, because details of how Health Insurance Fund plans to save costs are unclear. Võrk said the fund is right to emphasize that patients do not always need to see a specialist — often advice from a family doctor or nurse is enough, and e‑consultations are widely used.
But overall, as people live longer and have more illnesses, cutting the volume of services or allowing demand to grow faster than supply will lengthen waiting lists.
--
Editor: Karin Koppel, Argo Ideon

Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Wednesday, September 2.
Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
VW reportedly to close four Germany plants
It's only media reports, but if they're to be trusted then Germany's car giant Volkswagen has made up its mind to shut down four of its German production sites.
According to business magazine Wirtschaftswoche, a leaked paper from VW says that the Emden and Zwickau sites are to close in 2031, Hannover in 2032 and Neckarsulm in 2034.
There's been no official VW comment on this but Germany's powerful IG Metall union has dismissed the reporting, saying that any such big decisions would need broad approval.
But the report comes at a time where tension at VW are already at boiling point. The company faces — much like most of Germany's car industry — a deep structural crisis because of pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to EVs, rising production costs and steep US tariffs.
Ukraine says it's ready to ink drone deal with Germany
Ukraine is close to finalizing a drone deal with Germany, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Zelenskyy also warned a surge in Ukrainian drones in Russia's skies meant Russian airspace would be "effectively" closed.
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
A German frigate has tested the Israeli Lora missile system in the North Atlantic in an undisclosed operation, the country's navy said on Wednesday. Berlin is now considering buying the missiles which have a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Germany is in the process of modernizing and expanding its military in response to what it sees as a growing threat from Russia.
The missile test came just hours after Germany said it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
"In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness," navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said.
The Lora missiles are designed for rapid deployment from ships at sea. Germany’s own Taurus missiles also have a range of more than 500 kilometres, but are launched from fighter jets.
At the same time, Germany is working with its European allies to develop its own long-range weapons that would fly further than both the Lora or the Taurus missiles.
Germany identifies suspects behind Leipzig drone attack
German investigators have reportedly identified two suspects behind the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
According to reports on Wednesday from Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, and public broadcasters NDR and WDR, one suspect is an ethnic Russian holding a Latvian passport. The second is a man from Belarus that holds a Russian passport.
On Tuesday, Germany said it believed that Russia was behind the attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian transport aircraft at the airport in early August.
Berlin said there would be strong consequences for the hybrid attack and has announced the closure of Russian consulate in Bonn and of the Russian House in Berlin, a cultural center that Germany believes to be inolved in in spying activity.
Russia denies any involment in the Leipzig attack and on Wednesday summoned the German ambassador because of what it says are anti-Russian actions by Berlin.
EU approves Germany's power capacity program
The European Commission approved Germany's electricity supply support scheme. It is estimated to cost between €15.6 billion and €35.2 billion ($18.1 billion and $40.8 billion).
Germany's plans to increase its electricity capacity by up to 11 gigawatts over five years required approval of the European Commission to ensure they do not distort competition within the bloc.
The plan aims to ensure Germany has enough electricity capacity to meet rising demand.
Contracts in the state aid plan can last up to 15 years and are open to existing and new providers with electricity delivery beginning in 2031.
The energy companies receiving long-term contracts must be "hydrogen-ready" and must operate in a "climate-neutral" way by 2045.
Germany set a goal of having at least 80% of its electricity come from renewable sources by 2030.
Sabotage probe opened in second power station attack near Cologne
North Rhine-Westphalia’s Interior Minister Herbert Reul on Wednesday said an incident at a power station in Bergheim near Cologne is preliminarily being investigated as an act of "anti-constitutional sabotage," using a German legal term applied for criminal acts aimed against the order of the state.
On Tuesday night, police were called to the Amprion substation in Bergheim after bright flashes of light were reportedly visible. A short circuit affected several power lines, but officials said power supply to citizens was not affected.
It was the second incident involving attempts at damaging electricity infrastructure in 24 hours. On Tuesday morning, power lines at a substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg hundreds of kilometers away were damaged by a projectile.
Officials have yet to identify potential suspects involved in either incident.
Based on the investigation so far, Reul said the investigation is looking at whether the sabotage attackoriginated from abroad or had a far-left extremist motive.
Last year in Berlin, a far-left extremist network known as the "Vulkangruppe" carried out multiple sabotage attacks on power grids and energy infrastructure in and around Berlin, leaving thousands without power for nearly a week in the middle of winter.
"Now we need to investigate," Reul said. "This was intentional; it was a crime," Ruel said.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks ... interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country," he added.
Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage
Police in the eastern German state of Brandenburg on Wednesday said they were investigating the possible formation of a terrorist organization in connection with an attack on a power plant and substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg.
According to officials, on Tuesday morning, a projectile managed to carry a cable into the extra-high-voltage power line at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant, creating a conductive connection to the ground that caused a brief outage.
On Wednesday, Brandenburg's state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said "we were damn lucky" that only one of more than a dozen "rocket-like objects equipped with a propellant charge" reached its target.
He added the suspects had positioned the projectiles directly beneath the power lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation on the border with the state of Saxony.
The search for suspects continues, and an investigation is looking into all possibilities.
Brandenburg police said their investigation also includes disruption of public services, the causing of an explosion and the destruction of important equipment.
"At this point, we must assume that the perpetrators had been on the scene for several days beforehand and had installed the necessary equipment," Redmann said.
The construction and installation of the devices required a considerable amount of "technical expertise," he added.
ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h
A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday.
The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes.
There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door.
The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main.
Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m.
According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train.
German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally.
"Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency.
"The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added.
Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete.
IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin
After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled.
The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.
Augsburg station reopens after police give all clear
Augsburg train station reopened after police sealed off the area while investigating an early morning blast that left two passers-by aged 17 and 18 with minor acoustic trauma.
According to the Bild tabloid, police said a hand grenade exploded outside a jewelry shop next to the station, causing minor damage to the facade. Police have not immediately confirmed the report of a grenade.
Police had completely shut down the station after a bomb sniffing dog uncovered a second "suspicious object," which turned out to be fragments of the grenade, Bild reported.
There was no further information available on suspects or a motive.
German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Wednesday said that the European Union is working on imposing more sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks, a day after Germany said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4.
"Russia has escalated and must live with the consequences," Wadephul said at a gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said, without sharing further details on what the new measures would entail, other than they would target "a large number" of individuals.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said that the Leipzig incident had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." adding that the EU was working on sanctions targeting 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry.
Officials had discovered a drone between Ukrainian cargo aircraft fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism, triggering speculation over who could have been responsible.
On Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that although the devices required "a high degree of technical expertise," the plan appears to have been carried out by "low-level" agents.
The ministers said the Russian consulate general in Bonn would be closed, along with the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.

Window panes were also reportedly damaged by the explosion, which occurred in a building passageway.
No information is yet available regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Parts of the station were closed off as police continued investigating the scene. The State Criminal Police Office (LKA) is on the scene with an explosive-disposal robot, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported.
Police first responded to the incident at around 5 a.m. local time.
Augsburg is a regional transport hub around 55 kilometers (35 miles) west of Munich.
Police label power station disruption in Bergheim a 'deliberate act'
Police are investigating a disruption at a power station in the town of Bergheim in western Germany, near Cologne.
On Tuesday evening, several power lines failed following a short circuit at the power station.
"Based on the current status of the investigation, we do not believe this was caused by a technical malfunction, but rather by a deliberate act, a criminal offense," a police spokesperson said on Wednesday morning.
The spokesperson did not initially provide any details regarding the damage or the actions of the alleged perpetrators.
Police said the incident on Tuesday evening did not cause a power outage to the surrounding area.
The incident comes as tensions are high after unknown individuals attempted to cause short circuits in extra-high-voltage power lines near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday morning.
Police found explosive devices near the plant are investigating the incident as an act of sabotage.

Germany news: Terror probe opened in power station attack

Germany news: Police probe suspected power station attacks
Published September 2, 2026last updated September 2, 2026
What you need to know
- Minor injuries reported after object explodes near Augsburg train station
- Police are investigating 'criminal act' at power station near Cologne, North-Rhine Westphalia
- Authorities also opened a terror probe over Tuesday's sabotage of a power station in Brandenburg
- Germany is weighing further action against Russia after announcing it was behind the drone incident at Leipzig airport
Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Wednesday, September 2.
Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
VW reportedly to close four Germany plants
It's only media reports, but if they're to be trusted then Germany's car giant Volkswagen has made up its mind to shut down four of its German production sites.
According to business magazine Wirtschaftswoche, a leaked paper from VW says that the Emden and Zwickau sites are to close in 2031, Hannover in 2032 and Neckarsulm in 2034.
There's been no official VW comment on this but Germany's powerful IG Metall union has dismissed the reporting, saying that any such big decisions would need broad approval.
But the report comes at a time where tension at VW are already at boiling point. The company faces — much like most of Germany's car industry — a deep structural crisis because of pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to EVs, rising production costs and steep US tariffs.
Ukraine says it's ready to ink drone deal with Germany
Ukraine is close to finalizing a drone deal with Germany, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Zelenskyy also warned a surge in Ukrainian drones in Russia's skies meant Russian airspace would be "effectively" closed.
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
A German frigate has tested the Israeli Lora missile system in the North Atlantic in an undisclosed operation, the country's navy said on Wednesday. Berlin is now considering buying the missiles which have a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Germany is in the process of modernizing and expanding its military in response to what it sees as a growing threat from Russia.
The missile test came just hours after Germany said it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
"In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness," navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said.
The Lora missiles are designed for rapid deployment from ships at sea. Germany’s own Taurus missiles also have a range of more than 500 kilometres, but are launched from fighter jets.
At the same time, Germany is working with its European allies to develop its own long-range weapons that would fly further than both the Lora or the Taurus missiles.
Germany identifies suspects behind Leipzig drone attack
German investigators have reportedly identified two suspects behind the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
According to reports on Wednesday from Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, and public broadcasters NDR and WDR, one suspect is an ethnic Russian holding a Latvian passport. The second is a man from Belarus that holds a Russian passport.
On Tuesday, Germany said it believed that Russia was behind the attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian transport aircraft at the airport in early August.
Berlin said there would be strong consequences for the hybrid attack and has announced the closure of Russian consulate in Bonn and of the Russian House in Berlin, a cultural center that Germany believes to be inolved in in spying activity.
Russia denies any involment in the Leipzig attack and on Wednesday summoned the German ambassador because of what it says are anti-Russian actions by Berlin.
EU approves Germany's power capacity program
The European Commission approved Germany's electricity supply support scheme. It is estimated to cost between €15.6 billion and €35.2 billion ($18.1 billion and $40.8 billion).
Germany's plans to increase its electricity capacity by up to 11 gigawatts over five years required approval of the European Commission to ensure they do not distort competition within the bloc.
The plan aims to ensure Germany has enough electricity capacity to meet rising demand.
Contracts in the state aid plan can last up to 15 years and are open to existing and new providers with electricity delivery beginning in 2031.
The energy companies receiving long-term contracts must be "hydrogen-ready" and must operate in a "climate-neutral" way by 2045.
Germany set a goal of having at least 80% of its electricity come from renewable sources by 2030.
Sabotage probe opened in second power station attack near Cologne
North Rhine-Westphalia’s Interior Minister Herbert Reul on Wednesday said an incident at a power station in Bergheim near Cologne is preliminarily being investigated as an act of "anti-constitutional sabotage," using a German legal term applied for criminal acts aimed against the order of the state.
On Tuesday night, police were called to the Amprion substation in Bergheim after bright flashes of light were reportedly visible. A short circuit affected several power lines, but officials said power supply to citizens was not affected.
It was the second incident involving attempts at damaging electricity infrastructure in 24 hours. On Tuesday morning, power lines at a substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg hundreds of kilometers away were damaged by a projectile.
Officials have yet to identify potential suspects involved in either incident.
Based on the investigation so far, Reul said the investigation is looking at whether the sabotage attackoriginated from abroad or had a far-left extremist motive.
Last year in Berlin, a far-left extremist network known as the "Vulkangruppe" carried out multiple sabotage attacks on power grids and energy infrastructure in and around Berlin, leaving thousands without power for nearly a week in the middle of winter.
"Now we need to investigate," Reul said. "This was intentional; it was a crime," Ruel said.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks ... interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country," he added.
Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage
Police in the eastern German state of Brandenburg on Wednesday said they were investigating the possible formation of a terrorist organization in connection with an attack on a power plant and substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg.
According to officials, on Tuesday morning, a projectile managed to carry a cable into the extra-high-voltage power line at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant, creating a conductive connection to the ground that caused a brief outage.
On Wednesday, Brandenburg's state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said "we were damn lucky" that only one of more than a dozen "rocket-like objects equipped with a propellant charge" reached its target.
He added the suspects had positioned the projectiles directly beneath the power lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation on the border with the state of Saxony.
The search for suspects continues, and an investigation is looking into all possibilities.
Brandenburg police said their investigation also includes disruption of public services, the causing of an explosion and the destruction of important equipment.
"At this point, we must assume that the perpetrators had been on the scene for several days beforehand and had installed the necessary equipment," Redmann said.
The construction and installation of the devices required a considerable amount of "technical expertise," he added.
ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h
A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday.
The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes.
There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door.
The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main.
Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m.
According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train.
German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally.
"Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency.
"The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added.
Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete.
IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin
After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled.
The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.
Augsburg station reopens after police give all clear
Augsburg train station reopened after police sealed off the area while investigating an early morning blast that left two passers-by aged 17 and 18 with minor acoustic trauma.
According to the Bild tabloid, police said a hand grenade exploded outside a jewelry shop next to the station, causing minor damage to the facade. Police have not immediately confirmed the report of a grenade.
Police had completely shut down the station after a bomb sniffing dog uncovered a second "suspicious object," which turned out to be fragments of the grenade, Bild reported.
There was no further information available on suspects or a motive.
German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Wednesday said that the European Union is working on imposing more sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks, a day after Germany said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4.
"Russia has escalated and must live with the consequences," Wadephul said at a gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said, without sharing further details on what the new measures would entail, other than they would target "a large number" of individuals.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said that the Leipzig incident had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." adding that the EU was working on sanctions targeting 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry.
Officials had discovered a drone between Ukrainian cargo aircraft fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism, triggering speculation over who could have been responsible.
On Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that although the devices required "a high degree of technical expertise," the plan appears to have been carried out by "low-level" agents.
The ministers said the Russian consulate general in Bonn would be closed, along with the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected Germany's accusations and said the punitive measures are a "serious mistake."

During a press conference on Tuesday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul disclosed intelligence findings about the incident in which an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig Airport last month.
Augsburg station closed due to 'suspicious object'
Police in Augsburg have said the city's main train station is now fully shut down as of 8:30 a.m. with rail service suspended, due to a "suspicious object," without sharing further details.
Earlier, one track had been operating as police investigated a blast from an unknown object earlier Wednesday morning.
Unidentified object explodes near Augsburg train station, injuring 2
An unidentified object exploded near a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg early Wednesday morning, with two people sustaining minor injuries due to acoustic trauma, police said.
Window panes were also reportedly damaged by the explosion, which occurred in a building passageway.
No information is yet available regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Parts of the station were closed off as police continued investigating the scene. The State Criminal Police Office (LKA) is on the scene with an explosive-disposal robot, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported.

Augsburg is a regional transport hub around 55 kilometers (35 miles) west of Munich.

Police are investigating a disruption at a power station in the town of Bergheim in western Germany, near Cologne.

MVRDV Reveals WOMA Mixed-Use Development in Miami’s Wynwood Norte
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

MVRDV has revealed the design for WOMA, a mixed-use development planned for Wynwood Norte, Miami, in collaboration with Quito-based developer Uribe Schwarzkopf and Miami-based architect of record Kobi Karp. The development is planned on the site of a former coffee roasting company and takes cues from Wynwood Norte's industrial character and evolving creative community. Located alongside the nonprofit Bakehouse Art Complex, the project is intended to contribute to the area's growing network of spaces dedicated to art, fashion, and making.
The project will comprise 163 residences alongside office, coworking, retail, and cultural spaces, bringing together living and working environments within a series of stacked volumes. Its facades feature textile-inspired patterns and a palette of blue, green, orange, red, and silver, referencing both the area's history in fashion and garment manufacturing and its more recent association with art and street culture. The building is organized as a collection of small blocks stacked above one another, an approach that responds to the predominantly low-rise and fine-grained character of the surrounding neighborhood. Rather than occupying the full edge of the site, the building is set back to create a landscaped public space at street level. Broad staircases pass through the gaps between the volumes, connecting the ground plane with a raised central plaza.
Positioned at the center of the development, the plaza is conceived as a flexible space for exhibitions, fashion shows, fundraisers, and community gatherings. Four atelier apartments directly face the plaza, providing dedicated live-work spaces for artists, designers, and other creatives. Each unit includes double-height street-facing windows intended to allow the occupants' work to be visible from the public realm.
Related Article
OMA/AMO and OPEN Architecture Design Opening Exhibitions for Powerhouse Parramatta in Sydney, Australia
The project's facade treatment further develops its connection to Wynwood's creative and industrial history. Each volume is distinguished by a woven-textile-inspired pattern, while the varied colors create a visual reference to the neighborhood's street art and its ties to the fashion industry. The approach gives the individual blocks distinct identities while maintaining a cohesive overall composition.
Residential units will range from micro-studios to three-bedroom apartments, alongside offices, a coworking business center, and retail spaces. The development will also include a rooftop amenity level with a swimming pool, sports terrace, pet park, and additional landscaped areas. According to MVRDV founding partner Jacob van Rijs, the project's organization aims to support pedestrian movement, a mix of uses, and interaction between residents, workers, and visitors. Uribe Schwarzkopf CEO Joseph Schwarzkopf similarly describes the project as an extension of Wynwood's existing mix of creative practices and communities.
In other recent project announcements, Steven Holl Architects has been selected to lead the renewal of Ida Noyes Hall at the University of Chicago. In Western Sydney, Powerhouse Parramatta, designed by Moreau Kusunoki with Genton and Arup, is set to open on November 7, 2026, with five exhibitions presenting more than 3,000 objects and over 45 new commissions, including exhibitions designed by OPEN Architecture and OMA/AMO. Meanwhile, construction is progressing on Gothenburg Grand Central by Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter, part of Sweden's Västlänken rail project. The new station is scheduled to open alongside the Centralen underground station in December 2026, with the wider rail tunnel expected to be completed by 2030.

KABUL, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- More than 1,750 Afghan refugees returned to their homeland Afghanistan in a single day on Monday, reported the official Radio and Television of Afghanistan (RTA) on Tuesday night.

ISTANBUL, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Two Turkish-flagged commercial ships collided in the Sea of Marmara off Istanbul early Wednesday, leaving 10 crew members missing, Turkish authorities said.
The collision occurred at around 3:00 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) south of Istanbul's Silivri district, the Istanbul Governor's Office said in a statement.
The incident involved the commercial ship Alsu, which was traveling from the northwestern province of Kocaeli to Aliaga district in Izmir province, and the Tugberk Imamoglu, which was sailing from the southern port of Iskenderun to Karadeniz Eregli on Türkiye's Black Sea coast.

SEOUL, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- One sailor was rescued after a tugboat with eight crew members on board capsized off South Korea's southeastern coast, according to Yonhap news agency on Wednesday.
The 286-tonne tugboat overturned in waters off the country's southeastern port city of Busan at about 1:30 p.m. local time (0430 GMT).
Of the eight crew members, one was rescued by a commercial cargo ship that was passing through the area.
The coast guard dispatched personnel and equipment to the scene for search and rescue operations. ■

Feature: Iran women's volleyball makes historic breakthrough amid adversity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:29:32 CST
15:29:32 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Zewei, Yuan Yukuan and Wei Hua
TIANJIN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Thailand defended the Asian Women's Volleyball Championship title in Tianjin but another team also left a lasting impression.
Iran created its best-ever result at the women's Asian Championship, a fourth place finish, to make another major breakthrough for women's volleyball in West Asia. For a team that has long lived in the shadow of its men's counterpart, the breakthrough came amid challenging circumstances.
Iran has long been a force in men's volleyball, while its women's team has remained relatively little known in Asia. Drawn into Pool A with China, Iran beat Chinese Taipei 3-1 and Iraq 3-0 to finish second in the group before coming from behind to defeat Indonesia 3-1 in the quarterfinals.
Although Iran later lost to China in the semifinals and Japan in the bronze-medal match, the team's physical and resilient style proved one of the tournament's biggest surprises.
The breakthrough did not come easily.
"In the past, conditions for Iran's women's team were quite difficult. The support, training facilities and opportunities to compete were not ideal, especially compared with the men's team," said Iran head coach Alireza Toloe Kian.
He said Iran had hosted international men's volleyball competitions, including senior and age-group events, for more than two decades, giving the men's team more opportunities to compete with strong opponents, while the women's team has had far fewer chances to play international events at home and has relied more on overseas training and competitions.
The broader environment has posed an even greater challenge to the players.
"We are going through a difficult period, and some of our cities are still under the shadow of air strikes," Toloe Kian said. "But I always say that our female players are very brave. They are not afraid, and they have strong hearts. Despite the difficulties, they keep training every day and continue to aim high. I want to thank every one of them."
Iran opposite spiker Elaheh Poor Saleh Shahdehsari said the uncertainty outside the team had not disrupted its training.
"We usually get up around 8 a.m. and have breakfast and some coffee at 8:30. Then we train for about three hours in the morning. After lunch and some rest, we train again from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. After that, the rest of the evening is our own time."
Elaheh began playing volleyball at the age of nine under the guidance of her mother, a volleyball coach. She has since developed into one of Iran's key attackers and leading scorers. In Iran's 3-1 quarterfinal victory over Indonesia, she scored a match-high 29 points.
"Reaching the semifinals was a huge achievement for us," Elaheh said. "Everyone gave their best, and that is why we were able to come this far." Both Elaheh and Toloe Kian expressed their gratitude to the Iran Volleyball Federation and its president Milad Taghavi for their support.
In recent years, more resources have been put into Iran's women's volleyball program, including coaching, equipment and overseas training opportunities. Through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment program, Iran has received support for South Korean coach Lee Do-hee as well as equipment and international training opportunities.
The development of Iran's domestic league and youth system has also helped broaden its talent pool. The Iran Women's Volleyball Premier League is an important platform for national-team scouting, while the federation has also stepped up efforts to identify young players. Around 1,000 players registered through the federation's national system for a U16 selection program, and 80 were invited to the first evaluation camp in Tehran.
"Volleyball is one of the most popular sports among girls in Iran, and more and more girls are playing it," said Iran outside hitter Fatemeh Khalili Chermahini.
Khalili started playing volleyball at the age of 10 after initially practicing taekwondo and earning a black belt.
"I fell in love with volleyball after I started playing it. One of the main reasons was that volleyball is a team sport, and I really like team sports."
Iran has also sought to learn from different volleyball traditions. Toloe Kian said Iran tends to study European teams such as Türkiye and Italy because their players are generally taller and have physical attributes closer to those of European sides. At the same time, the team also looks to leading Asian teams such as China, Japan, South Korea and Thailand, especially for their speed and agility.
From a relatively little-known team to a place in Asia's final four, Iran has made a breakthrough, but the players see it as only the beginning.
"Our dream is to qualify for the Olympic Games, experience competition at the highest level and represent our country," Elaheh said. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Climate change-related disasters highlight urgent need for global action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:29:26 CST
15:29:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- The devastating mudslide that struck border areas of Nepal and China serves as a stark warning that climate change-related disasters pose a grave challenge for all humanity, necessitating greater preparedness and global action to tackle global warming.
The Aug. 26 disaster was triggered by a glacier's collapse in Nepal, due to its instability under the long-term effects of climate warming. The massive mudslide has left 1,127 dead and over 4,800 missing in Nepal, and 16 dead and 546 missing in China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Several hundred foreign nationals from dozens of countries and regions are among the missing.
The deadly mudslide revealed that a sudden outburst, large peak discharge, rapid flow speed, a powerful destructive force and wide-reaching impact are the new and prominent features of cryospheric disasters due to global warming, according to Chinese scientists. It reminds us that global efforts must not be delayed to tackle climate change and protect human well-being and planetary health.
Climate change has triggered a cascade of natural hazards, including ice avalanches in high-altitude regions. Low-lying island nations are increasingly threatened by rising sea levels, while extreme weather events -- exemplified by Europe's unprecedented heat waves, estimated to have caused more than 30,000 excess deaths this summer -- have become more frequent and severe. Moreover, complex climate phenomena such as El Niño are creating further uncertainties, compounding risks to human livelihoods and social stability.
An Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report in 2022 indicated climate and weather extremes are increasingly driving displacement in all regions, with small island states disproportionately affected, while flood and drought-related acute food insecurity and malnutrition have increased in Africa.
The need for global action is urgent. A briefing report of the United Nations' Scientific Advisory Board noted in June that the probabilities of the Earth system reaching tipping points rise significantly as global warming increases. Growing scientific evidence indicates several key Earth sub-systems are at increasing risk of reaching (or have already begun crossing) tipping points, it added, citing large polar continental ice sheets that may have begun long-term melting that could raise sea levels by several meters over centuries.
China is a determined participant in, a major contributor to, and a key leader in global climate governance. The country has long placed ecological conservation high on its development agenda, striving to reach peak carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and carbon neutrality before 2060.
To honor its commitments, China has built the largest and the fastest-growing renewable energy system, and achieved the world's largest and fastest promotion of new energy vehicles. In another milestone of green transition, China's installed photovoltaic power capacity has recently surpassed its coal-fired power capacity for the first time.
China has introduced more legislation to advance ecological civilization. The national law on the ecological conservation of the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau and Xizang's regional regulation on glacier protection represented further major ecological and environmental protection efforts on the plateau.
Internationally, China has actively pushed for the signing and implementation of the Paris Agreement and its green technology products, such as electric vehicles and solar panels, have significantly boosted global efforts in tackling climate change.
No corner of the world is immune to climate crises. This is precisely why no country can face it alone. Collective action is an imperative that has never been more urgent. ■

BRI Stories | Tour guide Abbas Sayed: serving as cultural exchange envoy between China and Egypt

Unknown Publisher

Abbas Sayed gives a guided tour to visitors at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, Egypt, July 2, 2026.
Egyptian tour guide Abbas Sayed has been traveling between China and Egypt for more than two decades, dedicated to promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.
His connection with China began in 2002, when he was preparing to enter Ain Shams University. Upon seeing Chinese characters for the first time in the university's Chinese Department library, he made the decision to learn the intriguing and beautiful language. That marked the start of a bond that would span over twenty years.
Having loved ancient Egyptian civilization since childhood, Abbas harbored a dream after learning Chinese: to introduce Egypt to Chinese people in their own language. After graduating from university, he chose to become a Chinese-speaking tour guide.
For Abbas, being a tour guide is more than just a job -- it carries the responsibility of introducing a country and spreading its culture. From the pyramids to temples to museums, he travels through historical and cultural sites, using fluent Chinese to introduce Egyptian civilization to visitors from China.
The Chinese language opened a window and built a bridge. From 2010 to 2013, Abbas worked at the China Cultural Center in Cairo, where he shifted from introducing Egypt to Chinese visitors to introducing China to Egyptians. He helped set up the "Chinese House," an exhibition space bringing together elements including the 12 Chinese zodiac animals, famous Chinese architecture, and images of China's cultural heritage, to introduce China to the Egyptian public.
Through these exchanges, his role has kept expanding. "I am willing to be a cultural envoy between China and Egypt, bringing the hearts of our two peoples closer together," he said. (Xinhua/Xin Mengchen)

Europe jolted by the Kremlin’s ‘hybrid’ escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:28:33 UTC
15:28:33 KST

Hello from Brussels. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today, we bring you an exclusive sit-down interview with the EU’s trade chief on his quest to rein in the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with Beijing. But we start with the escalating tensions between Europe and Moscow.
This morning, there’s a palpable sense here that the confrontation between Russia and European nations has entered a dangerous new phase. Leaders across Europe have issued scathing condemnations after Germany formally concluded yesterday that the Kremlin was responsible for a recent attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Not at war, but…: Announcing fresh sanctions on Moscow in response to the incident – including tighter entry controls on Russian nationals – German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on Tuesday: "Let me be very clear: we are not at war. But we are the target of hybrid attacks on a daily basis.” Germany has also raised its threat level from “general” to “high”.
‘Malign actions’: NATO secretary-general Mark Rutte said that the evidence pointing to Russia was “clear”, adding that the Alliance would “strengthen (its) ability to deter and defend Allies against any threat – including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig”.
VDL pledges response: European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen also promised a "clear response”. She will meet Rutte later today for talks which, according to NATO and EU officials, will be focused on the response to the Kremlin’s hybrid attacks and how the Alliance and the EU executive can work more closely to counter the threat.
Messages of solidarity with Germany have also poured in from European capitals, with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that Europe will “not be intimidated” and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni vowing a “united response”.
While European nations have seen a string of suspected Russian hybrid attacks in recent years – including exploding parcels at a depot site in Germany and an arson attempt at a Vilnius Ikea store – this is the first time that the finger has been pointed so directly at Moscow.
Not so hybrid?: It also comes against the backdrop of mounting speculation that President Putin could be looking to escalate his hybrid offensive against European nations into a more direct confrontation – something NATO and EU officials are pushing back against.
But reports that CIA chief John Ratcliffe’s secret dash to Moscow was intended to dissuade Putin from escalating against the Baltic states have added to the sense of unease across the continent.
The developments in Germany are set to spill into the informal meeting of EU foreign ministers, who gather today in Ireland, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
High Representative Kaja Kallas says the bloc is preparing “the most far-reaching sanctions” against Moscow yet. Over 1,600 companies and individuals are on a draft list under discussion, but the number is likely to go up in light of Berlin’s announcement.
Pressure for Patriots: Support for Ukraine will also be high on the agenda. Member states are scrambling to find ways to provide Kyiv with the air defence systems it desperately needs to repel Russia’s growing waves of ballistic missiles. Kallas says there is “no concrete success” yet in convincing Greece and Spain to donate their Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy’s warning: Meanwhile, in a statement made last night, President Zelenskyy issued a direct warning to “every airline” that “Russian airspace will effectively be closing” due to Ukrainian drone operations. It follows a week of relentless Russian attacks on Kyiv and non-stop air-raid alerts in the capital.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Kyiv did not threaten civilian aviation, but said those continuing to use Russian airspace and the country’s major airports would have to reckon with the growing presence of Ukrainian drones.
“Today we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports — Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous,” Zelenskyy said. “Although the Russian authorities do not report this as they should, Russian skies will de facto be closed.” Our Ukraine correspondent Sasha Vakulina has more.
Cash for Ukraine: Russia’s escalatory tactics, Jorge writes, including non-stop drone attacks aimed at disrupting economic activity, are rapidly increasing the material costs for Ukraine and casting doubt on whether the EU’s €90 billion loan will last until the end of 2027, as originally intended. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence faces a €23 billion deficit.
The European Commission is reluctant to reopen the delicate debate so soon after approving the loan. Politics are fraught, and there’s no clear path forward. For now, the plan foresees disbursing €45 billion this year and €45 billion next year.
“In terms of longevity, that is what is foreseen: that this €90 billion loan should be disbursed (over) the two years,” Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, told Jorge on Tuesday. “We are focused now on what is already a very ambitious disbursement plan, and for the moment that’s where our focus lies.”
Today’s informal meeting will also touch upon the reform of the bloc’s foreign policy, which global turbulence has put under unprecedented strain. A group of 11 countries has joined forces to demand an end to “obstructive” vetoes (remember Viktor Orbán?) by moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting. “We must ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it – otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength,” the signatories write.
Jorge got hold of the letter and broke it down for us.
China must deliver concrete results by October or face ‘harsher measures’, EU trade chief tells Euronews
Beijing must deliver “concrete results” by an October deadline or face “harsher measures” from the EU, Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič has exclusively told Euronews’ Maria Tadeo, as Brussels rushes to rein in China’s record trade surplus with the bloc.
Ongoing talks between Beijing and Brussels are intended to find an agreement to rebalance the trading relationship and deflate the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with China, which currently stands at a staggering €359.8 billion.
The next two weeks are set to be crucial, with Šefčovič set to hold a video call with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao in mid-September.
“This is super political,” Šefčovič told Euronews, stressing that European leaders want to see results by October.
If dialogue does not deliver results, the EU could resort to defensive instruments.
While Šefčovič did not go into detail about what retaliatory measures could look like, he said Brussels is looking to finalise a “diversification instrument” designed with China in mind. He also said the EU is now far more united in its objectives for the negotiations.
“They [EU27] want to see the direction of travel. They want to even have a concept for the solution of this issue, a pilot scheme,” Šefčovič said.
“I’m trying to do it through these negotiations, but they have to bring us very concrete results. Otherwise, of course, there will be a strong political movement to push for, I would say, harsher measures.”

‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:26:18 UTC
15:26:18 KST

‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
An Iranian fisherwoman explains how her idyllic seaside life was shattered when the US and Israel began their bombing.
In this first-person testimony told to Al Jazeera, Khadijeh Bandari, an Iranian fisherwoman from Hengam Island in southern Iran, explains how the United States-Israel war on her country has disrupted her work and the lives of all the people on the island.
I am 28 years old, and for as long as I can remember, I would go out to sea with my mother, who taught me how to fish.
When I was older, I got a boat of my own and started fishing. The sea belongs to us women just as much as it belongs to men. Like my mother, I consider fishing to be a part of my life.
When I married, my husband, who is from northern Iran, was living on nearby Qeshm Island. After we got married, he moved to Hengam Island, and we opened a small guesthouse together. We sold the fish we caught through our Instagram page and delivered it to different Iranian cities. At a seaside restaurant we also owned, my husband and I served tourists fresh fish we had caught ourselves.
We have a three-year-old son named Keyhan, whose name means “the world”. For us, he is our whole world. Sometimes he comes out to sea with me to fish, but other times he stays on the island with his father.
Life started to become difficult for us when for several weeks in January the internet was shut down in Iran. Few tourists visited the island, and the online sale of fish, which was a big part of our business, also stopped. When the internet was restored, we breathed a sigh of relief and thought life had finally returned to normal, but we were wrong.
On Saturday, February 28, my mother was out at sea fishing while I stayed behind at our restaurant on the shore.
What she called out from the water was the last thing I expected to hear. “The war has started,” she shouted. The sound of explosions from the American bombs reached Hengam Island soon after, and then a village near us was hit. Before we could even understand what was happening, a coastguard came to shore and told us to pack up our stalls and stay away from the beach.
In the first few days, everyone expected that, like before, the attacks would be over within a few days or weeks. But that wasn’t the case, and the war continued day and night. Over time, family by family, the residents began to leave Hengam Island.
Due to fears of bombing, the pier was closed, and fishing boats couldn’t go out to sea due to fears they would be targeted by American bombing. Travelling between Hengam and Qeshm was also prohibited due to fears that the passenger boats would be targeted. Fishing, which had always been a part of our lives, suddenly became a dangerous activity.
When the war intensified, the residents of Hengam who lived closest to the pier were asked to leave their homes due to the threat that the structures would be bombed.
The rest of my family went with my mother to my sister’s home on Qeshm Island while my father stayed behind to look after our goats. As our home was away from the pier, we thought we might be safe. But the island still felt dangerous, and I was afraid for my child’s life.
Nightly discussions always focused on how much time we had left on the island. Many people said they would not leave their homes. Some had nowhere else to go, or some simply didn’t want to abandon their homes and their lives on the island. The bombing of Hengam, Qeshm and the entire southern coastline of Iran continues, and we have no idea when it will stop.
One thing was clear: Both the Hengam and Kandaloo piers had been closed, tourists were no longer coming to the island, and fishermen and women could no longer safely go out to sea.
A month had passed since the war began, and it became clear that it would not end anytime soon. For us, keeping our spirits up and caring for Keyhan had become important. Like anyone with children, we started making up stories and playing games to help our child be less afraid of the sound of bombs and missiles.
For those of us still on the island, maintaining a sense of normalcy became very important. My mother, who had gone to Qeshm, called us every day, begging and crying as she tried to persuade us to leave Hengam. The neighbours who, like us, stayed would gather every night at our beachside stall.
We served local sweets and samosas to the few residents and tourists who were still around, and we talked about the war. We kept telling ourselves, “Maybe the war will be over tomorrow.” But the next day, the bombing continued, and “tomorrow” was pushed further and further away.
Eventually, my husband decided to take us away from Hengam for a few days to visit his family.
The day after we left Hengam, the island was attacked again. The pier where we would take food to my father and where our children would play together every day was destroyed in the attack, and three people were killed.
We heard about the attack on the pier that same day, but we didn’t know how bad the damage was or who had been killed. The phones weren’t working either, so we couldn’t reach anyone. It wasn’t until that evening when we began to hear back from people that we realised the extent of the destruction.
The damage to Hengam wasn’t limited to our homes, the pier and the fear we felt. Many people saw all their life savings, usually in the form of a boat, destroyed in the attacks.
Hava Arbabí lost her small boat and her home in the war. Since then, she has been living at her sister’s house. Aref Arbabi also lost his house that he had only recently started building as well as a boat that he had worked hard to buy this year. Soheil Hormozi will have to make repayments for years to come on a marriage loan he took out to buy a boat, even though the vessel was destroyed in the American attacks. Abutaleb Zarei also bought his boat with a marriage loan, and it was also destroyed. Many other homes in Hengam besides these were destroyed or suffered damage.
From the very first days of the war, people’s businesses and livelihoods on the island came to a standstill. No tourists are visiting the island, and the sea is not safe enough for us to go work in.
Still, many people are forced to go out to sea to fish because this is their only source of income. Even my mother and brother are still fishing despite the circumstances. When you have no other way of making a living, you are forced to take risks.
We lost our business and were forced to start from scratch. I started selling handmade jewellery made from seashells while my husband found work in the north. A few months ago, we moved from the southern sea to the northern coast, but our hearts are still in Hengam. Every day, we think about going back.
My mother, who urged us every day in the middle of the war to leave Hengam, has now returned to the island to fish. Every time she goes out to sea, we worry about her and call each other over and over again. We never know when the American bombing might start again.
Yes, we are homeless because of the war, but I don’t want the people of Hengam to be known just for that. We have always made a living through fishing, tourism and the fruits of our own labour. But now we have been deprived of the ability to work on our own land. We need to be able to return to our lives. For that to happen, the boats that were destroyed need to be replaced, the homes and livelihoods people have lost fixed and, most importantly, security needs to be restored so people can return to their ordinary lives.

Yesh Atid’s downfall: Nearly half of Lapid’s lawmakers are heading for the exits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:23:21 UTC
15:23:21 KST

Over the past decade, Yesh Atid became one of Israel’s largest and most stable political parties, including as a contender for the premiership. But ahead of the coming election, it is steadily coming apart. Of the 24 seats the party won four years ago, only 13 lawmakers are expected to remain on its slate for the Oct. 27 election.
The alliance with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, combined with the approaching deadline for unveiling the candidate list on Sunday, has prompted a growing number of lawmakers who realize they are unlikely to receive winnable spots to announce a temporary departure from political life. During the past Knesset term, Yesh Atid faced a wave of departures by senior figures, some of them among the party’s founders.
Orna Barbivai left to run for mayor of Tel Aviv, while former minister Yoel Razvozov departed for a career in the private sector and business. Boaz Toporovsky, one of Yesh Atid’s founders, announced in June that he was leaving political life. Two longtime party figures and close allies of Yair Lapid, Meir Cohen and Mickey Levy, announced Monday that they were stepping aside to make room for younger lawmakers.
Others who left include Elazar Stern, who joined Gadi Eisenkot, and Ron Katz, who returned to civilian life. Idan Roll left Yesh Atid in January 2025, formed the National Majority faction and later announced that he, too, was leaving the Knesset and political life. Yoav Segalovich, considered close to Lapid, left the party to join forces with Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas. On Tuesday morning, lawmakers Tatiana Mazarsky and Debbie Biton also announced that they would not be part of the slate, though both stressed that they were remaining members of the party.
Behind the scenes, pressure is mounting in Yesh Atid ahead of the filing of candidate lists and the allocation of top slots. The slate will be unveiled Sunday, but in recent days lawmakers, particularly those lower down the pecking order, have been receiving subtle signals that their chances of securing a winnable spot in the next Knesset are slim. Many are choosing to step aside before the slate is formally announced. Those departing have published photos with Lapid, who in most cases has also posted farewell messages of his own.
Alongside the long list of serving Yesh Atid lawmakers, Bennett himself has brought 16 new candidates into the joint slate. Some are expected to be placed among the top five, including Keren Turner and Liran Avisar Ben Horin. With the merger creating an unusually crowded field of candidates, party officials said a selection process was necessary. Some of those stepping aside, including Cohen and Levy, are expected to receive symbolic roles within the party apparatus, a move intended to underscore that the departures were amicable.
Yesh Atid entered this election campaign in one of the deepest crises since its founding, with polls predicting it would win only a single-digit number of seats. Bennett and Lapid joined forces in an effort to stop the party’s slide. But the move also halted some of Bennett’s relative momentum, reflecting the difficulty many voters have had accepting the alliance.
