Honduran court drops charges against former president pardoned by Trump
TEGUCIGALPA, Sept 1 - A Honduran court has dropped charges against former President Juan Orlando Hernandez over fraud and money laundering, judiciary authorities said on Tuesday, nine months after he was freed from U.S. prison where he was serving a lengthy sentence for drug trafficking charges.
Judiciary spokesperson Carlos Silva told local media the judge concluded Hernandez was not responsible for budgetary decisions at the time of the crime and it could not be confirmed that embezzled funds had been channeled into his 2013 presidential campaign.
"Of course we expected this outcome because the case had no basis," Hernandez told supporters outside the court. "The ruling is clear. Today, this chapter of political persecution has ended."
"Those who orchestrated this operation not only wanted to see me banished from Honduras forever, never to return, but they were determined to leave my family on the street," he added, pointing to assets seized by Honduran authorities. "It was utter vandalism."
Hernandez spoke alongside his wife Ana Garcia, who sought their party's presidential nomination in 2025.
Even as Hernandez's supporters celebrated the ruling, anti-corruption groups warned the outcome could further erode Hondurans' trust in the courts and pointed to the absence of a key witness for the prosecution whose release from prison was confirmed just hours before the ruling.
Silva said prosecutors could still appeal the case.
Hernandez had returned to the Central American nation in late July, after being extradited to the U.S. in 2022 on drug trafficking charges. Two years later, he was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in U.S. prison, but was then pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump late last year.
Trump's pardon of Hernandez was announced two days before Honduras' November presidential vote, in a move widely seen as an effort to influence the country's election. Trump also said at the time he would cut funding to Honduras should the candidate for Hernandez's right-wing National Party — now President Nasry Asfura — not win the election.
After being freed from U.S. prison, Hernandez continued to face charges of fraud and money laundering in Honduras as part of a sprawling corruption investigation, known as Pandora II.
Prosecutors had accused Hernandez and other high-profile officials of diverting nearly $11 million in state funds to political campaigns between 2010 and 2013. Some of this money allegedly was used for Hernandez's first presidential campaign.
Charges have also been dropped against other high-profile officials, including former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-finance minister Wilfredo Cerrato.
Hernandez led Honduras from 2014 to 2022, a period during which the Central American nation served as a major drug trafficking route, and hundreds of thousands of Hondurans fled drug-related violence and extortion.
During that period, Hernandez abused his position as president and ran the country "as a narco-state," allowing drug traffickers to operate with "virtual impunity," according to U.S. prosecutors.
Hernandez told Reuters in an interview in late July he had no immediate plans to seek public office in Honduras but wanted to support the new government. REUTERS

Dell Technologies shares moved 9% higher in extended trading on Tuesday after the computer maker reported results and a forecast that easily cleared Wall Street expectations.
Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $7.04 adjusted vs. $4.92 expected
- Revenue: $46.97 billion vs. $44.92 billion expected
Revenue came in higher than every estimate, growing about 58% year over year for the fiscal second quarter, which ended on July 31, according to a statement. Net income of $4.13 billion, or $6.34 per share, increased from $1.16 billion, or $1.70 per share, in the same quarter a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude impact from stock-based compensation.
For the fiscal third quarter, Dell called for $6.50 in adjusted earnings per share on $49.0 billion in revenue, which implies 81% growth. Analysts polled by LSEG had anticipated $4.49 per share and $41.42 billion in revenue.
Dell ratcheted up its full-year view. The company now sees $25.50 in adjusted earnings per share on $192 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting $18.92 per share and $172.67 billion in revenue. As of May, the company's 2027 guidance included $17.90 in adjusted earnings per share, with $165 billion to $169 billion in revenue.
Price increases brought on by climbing input costs factor in to the elevated revenue guidance, Jeff Clarke, Dell's operating chief, said on a conference call with analysts.
As of Tuesday's close, Dell shares had gained 236% year to date, while the wider S&P 500 index is up 11% over the same period. The stock has become a popular choice for investors who want to bet on the continuing growth of artificial intelligence infrastructure. In July President Trump, who has bought Dell shares since returning to office last year, again recommended buying Dell computers.
Michael Dell, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, is now the world's fifth richest person, according to Bloomberg calculations.
"There's an old Texas saying I may have just made up...," Michael Dell posted on X after the results became available. "If you keep growing EPS 200%+ y/y something good will happen."
The company's Infrastructure Solutions Group targeting data center hardware posted $31.78 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, up 89% and more than the $29.61 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. In that segment, Dell generated $16.40 billion in revenue from AI-optimized servers. The sum was above StreetAccount's $16.07 billion consensus.
Storage revenue, at $4.85 billion, went up almost 26%. Revenue from traditional servers and networking equipment jumped 122% to $10.53 billion.
"We are seeing a growing trend of customers that require meaningful CPU compute capacity to support AI and agentic workflows," Clarke said. "These workloads are creating incremental demand for traditional servers."
Dell's Client Solutions Group, which sells PCs and accessories to consumers and commercial clients, contributed $15.03 billion in revenue. The number was up 20% but slightly lower than StreetAccount's $15.08 billion consensus.
"One of the things that we did earlier this year is we saw the PC market showing signs of softening in the second half," Clarke said. "We optimized the bits and bytes we have towards the infrastructure business."
During the quarter, Dell received a $9.7 billion contract to provide software to the U.S. military, and AI-centric cloud infrastructure provider Iren said it agreed to buy $1.6 billion in Dell hardware, including servers that contain Nvidia chips.
Dell now foresees $74 billion in AI-optimized server sales for the fiscal year, which would be up 200%. Just six months ago, the company had predicted 103% growth.

Earlier on September 1, Russian forces pounded regions across Ukraine as children across the country headed to school for their first day of classes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has accused security officials of intentionally failing to wake him on the morning of October 7 blitz, a day after his wife claimed an opposition figure had advance knowledge of the blitz.
Netanyahu is heading into tightly contested elections later this year and faces sustained criticism over responsibility for the security failures surrounding October 7, 2023.
While the prime minister previously claimed officials refrained from waking him, he is now alleging the decision was deliberate.
"Why didn't they wake me? Because they knew that I, as prime minister of Israel, would immediately have ordered to put the entire army on alert, to wake up all the towns... This has been hidden from the public," Netanyahu said during an Instagram broadcast.
In a separate interview, Netanyahu blamed the military high command and former Shin Bet head Ronen Bar, asserting they withheld alerts to avoid a military escalation.
Conspiracy row
The remarks followed a television interview by his wife Sara on Channel 14, in which she claimed opposition figure Yair Golan was aware of the blitz plans beforehand.
Golan, who heads the centre-left Democrats party and rushed to southern Israel on October 7, threatened a 2.5-million-shekel ($830,000) defamation lawsuit unless she issues an immediate apology.

Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Rising sea levels, extreme weather and drought all remain concerns, but destabilised ice and snow at high altitudes is increasingly a threat
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Dr Zhengxu Wang is a distinguished professor at the School of Public Affairs, Zhejiang University. 
On August 26, a section of glacier collapsed at an altitude of more than 5,000 metres on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas. The falling ice and rock accelerated down a steep valley at about 50 metres per second, scouring debris and transforming into a high-speed mudslide that slammed into Gyirong Port on the Chinese side just seven minutes later.
The force of the flow largely buried and obliterated the border facilities. Hundreds of people, many of them travellers, remain missing on the Chinese side. Across the border in Nepal, entire villages were swept away, leaving hundreds dead and thousands unaccounted for.
For decades, the defining image of climate vulnerability has been the low-lying island nation, where rising seas threaten to erase entire communities from the map. That threat is real, urgent and unfinished business. However, the catastrophic mudslide that tore through the China-Nepal border forces us to look beyond the waterline and consider a more complex, multidimensional map of climate risk.
The iconic risk remains sea-level rise. It is slow, inexorable and already under way. Coastal megacities from Shanghai to Mumbai to New York are investing heavily in sea walls and surge barriers. Small island states are exploring relocation treaties and purchasing land abroad as a form of climate insurance. The very predictability of this threat has allowed societies to develop institutional responses.
The second most immediately felt climate risk is extreme rainfall and the catastrophic flooding it brings. For several years, traditionally drier places such as Beijing and large swathes of inland China have suffered disastrous floods that overwhelmed infrastructure, affecting millions and exposing the limits of urban drainage systems never designed for the intensity of rain now falling from a warmer atmosphere.
The third risk is drought. This summer, a severe and persistent drought, coupled with record-breaking heatwaves, created a crisis across much of Europe. The prolonged lack of rainfall pushed major waterways, including the Rhine, Danube and Loire, to historically low levels, disrupting river transport and forcing cargo vessels to reduce their loads. France alone faces an estimated €10-15 billion (US$11.6-17.4 billion) in heat-related losses and a projected 35 per cent drop in maize yields.
Across Europe, low river levels and wildfires have exposed unexploded ordnance from World War II that had long been submerged or buried – another stark reminder of how climate change is already profoundly affecting our lives.

Urgent need for access to Iranian sites, cautions UN nuclear watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:28:00 UTC
06:28:00 KST

IAEA calls for access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
UN watchdog says lack of information and access to facilities to verify Iran’s nuclear material is a proliferation concern.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has called for “utmost urgency” to address the lack of access to Iran’s nuclear sites.
In a quarterly report seen by news agencies on Tuesday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog labelled its “lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern”.
The US has claimed preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon – an ambition that Tehran continues to deny – as the motivation for the war that it launched in March. However, Tehran has been successful in shifting the focus of the hostilities to control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway.
In particular, the IAEA report raised concerns over the lack of access to the Isfahan plant, which was targeted several times by the US and Israel over the past year or so.
In the report, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi expressed his “conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement”.
However, Iran has said that access to the sites that have been struck by military action must be arranged via special arrangement.
The head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization, Mohammad Eslami, said on August 26 that the IAEA “cannot seek to inspect these centres until it develops specific criteria and protocols for inspecting sites targeted by military attacks”.
Tehran suspended cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites before saying in September 2025 it would allow the UN agency’s inspectors to return.
However, access to the nuclear sites that have been bombed has not yet been granted. Despite US President Donald Trump having claimed last year that the US had destroyed the facilities and crippled Tehran’s nuclear programme, Iran’s stores of enriched uranium remain unaccounted for.
Tehran has repeatedly denied any military ambition linked to its nuclear programme, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.
However, the IAEA, whose latest report will be discussed at its board of governors meeting from September 21-25, has reported in the past that the level of Iran’s enrichment of its uranium reserves is well above that needed for civilian purposes, although neither is it at the level of weapons grade.

Australians accused of involvement with IS look set to face Iraqi trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:21:05 UTC

Australians accused of involvement with IS look set to face trial in Iraq
In short:
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the failed Islamic State are set to face trial in Iraq.
Local Iraqi authorities say they have finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
What's next?
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the Islamic State group are set to face trial in Iraq, after local authorities said they had finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
The man known as "Dr Jihad", Perth-born paediatrician Tareq Kamleh, is likely among the group, given previous comments by Iraqi authorities about his involvement with Islamic State going beyond providing medical services.
That is despite his insistence in a recently resurfaced interview that he never pledged allegiance to the so-called caliphate.
Another member of the group may be Yusuf Zahab, now in his early 20s, who was taken to Syria at age 12.
He was captured and separated from his family after the battle of Baghuz in March 2019, when he was still a teenager, and disappeared into the Syrian jail system.
Members of his family, including his mother, were among the women who returned home to Australia in May this year, after spending years in the al-Roj refugee camp in north-eastern Syria.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council issued a statement on Tuesday, local time, announcing interrogations of "5,704 defendants who are members of the terrorist ISIS gangs" had been completed.
It said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
Evidence of crimes against Yazidi community
For the first time, the Judicial Council provided a rough breakdown of the nationalities of those involved.
It said there were prisoners from 67 different countries who were being held: 16 were nationals from Arab states, 19 from European Union members and 32 from other countries.
The bulk of the prisoners came from Syria, with 3,497 detained, while there were 474 Iraqis.
"The investigations, evidence collection, and analysis resulted in the identification of several highly dangerous individuals who had held leadership, security, religious, military, media, or other positions, or who had been involved in high-profile operations and crimes of an international dimension, including first-tier leaders within the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said in a statement.
"The investigations also revealed the multiplicity of roles within the organisation, which were not limited to combat activities, but also included military, security, financial, logistical, administrative, medical, technical, and media activities."
Iraqi authorities said it had uncovered evidence of crimes against the Yazidi community, a Kurdish-speaking minority IS has been described as committing genocide against.
"Six defendants were identified whose case files indicated roles directly connected to the enslavement of Yazidi women, or to their detention, transportation, sale, supervision, or benefiting from the system of enslavement established by the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said.
In July, the Albanese government said it would not provide assistance to "any Australian who made the horrific choice to join a dangerous terrorist organisation".
Regarding the reports about Tareq Kamleh, cabinet minister Clare O'Neil said he could "rot in jail".
Diplomats, consular staff allowed to visit citizens
The Judicial Council said it had allowed diplomats and consular staff from "several countries" to visit their citizens in jail during the interrogation process, as well as the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The ABC has contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and the office of Foreign Minister Penny Wong, for details of what contact Australian officials have had with the group.
The ICRC has also been contacted for comment.
The Judicial Council said there had been insufficient evidence in some cases, leading to some prisoners being released: one Finnish national, one American citizen and seven Iraqis.
Another 457 Syrians will also be released, given a lack of evidence tying them to their alleged crimes.
The US military began transferring Islamic State prisoners held in facilities controlled by Kurdish forces in north-eastern Syria to Iraq earlier this year.
It followed moves by Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, to take back control of large swathes of the country which had been controlled by the Kurds for the best part of a decade, during Syria's bloody civil war.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council revealed interrogations began in February this year, and said a special courtroom had been established to allow trials to happen remotely via video link to avoid risks of transporting high-security prisoners.

Sexual choking sparks calls for action
The federal government is currently exploring whether Australians should be able to opt out of algorithmically curated social media feeds, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek told ABC Insider's program on Sunday.
The announcement came after a 16-year-old Sydney girl's death was linked in media reports to a suspected sexual choking act — a behaviour often promoted to teenage boys through pornography and social media content.
Contos will tell the Press Club that, while the change would be positive, harsher crackdowns are needed.
She will suggest feeds should only show posts from people users follow, unless users explicitly opt out, to circumvent harmful content. Such a move would revert social media algorithms to how they were a decade ago.
"(The change) would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," Contos will say.
"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine."
Teach Us Consent has been running a campaign promoting the change since 2025.
An open letter to the prime minister requesting an end to algorithmic feeds without an opt-out choice has been signed by more than 13,000 Australians.

US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children

US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children
- The US State Department plans to require parents to prove their citizenship or immigration status when applying for their children's passports, aiming to enforce President Trump's order on birthright citizenship.
- Trump's order targets "birth tourism" and narrows birthright citizenship, but faces legal challenges after the Supreme Court ruled a previous version unconstitutional.
- Lawsuits seek to block the new order, with a federal judge expressing doubts; the Justice Department argues the challenge is premature as implementation details are still pending.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US State Department has proposed requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status as part of President Donald Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship.
The draft guidance, reviewed by Reuters, is the first detailed look at how the State Department could enforce Trump’s Aug 6 executive order targeting what it calls “birth tourism” and broadening historical exceptions to birthright citizenship.
The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department.
In a statement, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said that “President Trump has been unequivocal that this Administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully reflects that standard.”
Limiting birthright citizenship has been one of the president’s top priorities in his far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The US Supreme Court ruled his previous attempt violated the country’s Constitution.
Trump’s initial executive order would have granted automatic US citizenship at birth only to children with at least one parent who was a US citizen or a lawful permanent resident known as a green card holder.
In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court found the order was unlawful, with a majority finding it violated the Citizenship clause of the Constitution’s 14th Amendment.
Trump’s Aug 6 order was narrower, taking particular aim at “birth tourism,” in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship.
That order could still be blocked in court.
The new directive would withhold citizenship from children with a parent who works for a foreign government in the US, is engaged in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an “alien enemy.”
“The Department will require parental information and evidence of parental citizenship or immigration status as part of its determination whether the applicant is subject to EO 14418,” the State Department draft guidance reads, citing the executive order number.
If implemented, the proposal would require all parents or legal guardians to provide proof of their citizenship, such as a valid US passport or birth certificate, or evidence of their immigration status, such as an I-94 form or a legal permanent residency card, when submitting a passport application for their children.
The information would be used by the government to determine if the child qualifies for citizenship under the new order, the State Department proposal says.
Currently, parents whose children were born in the US only need to prove their parentage and present photo identification during this process.
They are also asked to check a box on the application form indicating if they are US citizens but are not required to file supporting documentation.
Lawyers pursuing class-action lawsuits on behalf of babies who would be deprived of citizenship under Trump’s initial order have asked two different federal judges to prevent his latest order from taking effect.
One of those lawsuits is before US district judge Deborah Boardman, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.
At a hearing on Aug 28 in Greenbelt, Maryland, Boardman voiced scepticism about what she called Trump’s unprecedented order and allowed the plaintiffs to revise their lawsuit so she could consider whether to block it.
Justice Department attorneys have argued that a restraining order would be inappropriate and that the legal challenge was premature, as federal agencies had yet to issue public guidance on how the president’s directive would be implemented. REUTERS

news
Russia’s finance minister walked into a G20 summit for the first time since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But what did he walk out with?
Source: Meduza
- Finance ministers and central bank governors from the Group of 20 (G20) met in Asheville, North Carolina. Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended in person for the first time since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He last took part in a G20 meeting in April 2022, by video link, according to The Washington Post. That appearance drew protests from several Western countries.
- The Trump administration decided to bring the Russian delegation into the meeting, according to Politico. “We like getting along with everybody,” U.S. President Donald Trump said of the move. The U.S. Treasury Department, meanwhile, did not invite South Africa’s delegation. In late 2025, Trump said he would not grant accreditation to South African officials, citing a “genocide” against the country’s white population.
- At the summit, Siluanov met with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The two discussed Trump’s plan for ending the war in Ukraine and economic cooperation between Russia and the United States. Sources told Politico and Reuters that Siluanov tried to raise other areas of mutual interest, but Bessent cut him off and said that “nothing is possible until the war is over.”
- Officials in both countries used neutral language to describe the meeting between Siluanov and Bessent. Erin Browne, the Treasury’s undersecretary for international affairs, told Politico that Bessent “had a productive meeting with the Russian finance minister.” Russia’s Finance Ministry said the two sides had discussed “issues of Russian-American engagement on the financial track.”
- European delegations objected to the Russian minister’s visit. German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that he would not pose for a group photo with Siluanov, and that other European officials sided with him. Among them was Poland’s finance minister, according to Reuters. In the end, Siluanov was left out of the group photo.
- Klingbeil said he had taken the opportunity to tell the Russian finance minister “straight to his face” that Russia must end the war. “People are dying every day, we have just seen another escalation in the attacks,” The Washington Post quoted him as saying. “You cannot simply return to normality.”
- U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, also criticized the decision to invite the Russian minister to the summit. “The Trump Admin needs to pressure Putin and his cronies, not offer them a platform,” she said. Shaheen urged the U.S. House of Representatives to pass a new sanctions bill against Russia that the Senate had already approved.
- Even so, Siluanov’s trip to the summit showed how ready Washington is to reopen high-level diplomatic channels with Moscow, according to CNBC. The Trump administration is willing to do so even over its European allies’ objections.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is speaking at a press conference in Palau.

'Much bigger system at play' than conversations at schools: Contos
Chanel Contos was asked for her reaction to Nationals senator Matt Canavan's claim the "feminisation" of the school curriculum is a reason why young boys are turning to the online manosphere.
The consent advocate reiterates that it's not just that men and boys are seeking this content out, but it's being intentionally served to them.
"There is a much bigger system at play than kind of like the small conversations in school and that sort of thing," she says.
"Then on these online spaces I think is where we really start to get that rhetoric that conversations against about violence against women and children is an attack on men and boys. But it's truly not."
Government must act to turn off automatic algorithms: Contos
The problem, Chanel Contos says, is social media algorithms that dictate the content we see online.
She says the switch to a stream of content with no end point and users being fed content from users they don't follow was part of tech companies' focus on being addictive.
"Big tech's data about us is the basis of their profit model. They need to know our desires, our fears, what makes us aroused and what makes us insecure in order to optimise what will keep us there for longer, and to keep us going back," she says.
The solution? A mandatory "opt-in" feature for algorithms on social media platforms.
"We're not asking them to stop; we're demanding that they are obliged to clearly ask us first. And then, for us to be able to turn our algorithms on and off at will," she says.
Radicalisation of young men online an 'urgent challenge': Contos
Chanel Contos emerged on the national scene five years ago with her campaign for consent to be taught in schools.
The advocate says five years on, she now recognises consent education is "fighting an uphill battle" against an "addictive content-producing machine" preaching a contradictory message.
She calls the radicalisation of young men into misogyny online an "urgent challenge", and without immediate action, Australia risks a "generation of young men being entrenched".
"Young men online seeking community, belonging and self-improvement advice are targeted with content that blames women for their misfortune and reinstates harmful and outdated gender roles," she tells the National Press Club.
The pathway goes from something as harmless as a workout video and then takes boys and men "into the manosphere".
"Boys and men have valid concerns about the economy, and their relationships with partners and friends. From these concerns, an industry has jumped onto a market opportunity, and unfortunately, misogyny is at the heart of its business model," she says.

Consent advocate Chanel Contos is about to stand up at the National Press Club.

'No doubt' tax changes contributed to house price downturn: Labor minister
A Labor minister has admitted there's "no doubt" the government's federal budget changes have contributed to house prices falling.
Matt Thistlethwaite said interest rate hikes were the main factor putting pressure on household budgets, as well as higher living costs stemming from war in the Middle East, but he acknowledged the budget changes were adding to the downturn too.
"There's no doubt that our policies are part of a suite of reasons, but we're confident that we've got balance right because the housing market was out of control and we needed to make housing more affordable," he told News 24.
In the budget, Labor wound back capital gains tax discounts for investors and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds.

Chalmers stands by Treasury house price forecasts amid downturn
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is standing by his department's forecasts about the impact the May budget's tax changes will have on house prices.
The budget wound back capital gains tax discounts for investors and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds. Treasury forecast the measures would reduce house price growth by 2 per cent.
But an uptick in interest rates, paired with the changes, have been credited for prices falling in almost every capital city in August, according to Cotality.
He stressed Treasury's assumptions in the budget were over a couple of years, not a couple of months.
"It would be unusual to compare outcomes or forecasts from the first couple of months and compare that with the Treasury assumptions over a couple of years," he says.

"House prices and auction clearance rates were already softer before the budget. And that's because, as a number of people have pointed out from outside the government, a key driver of that is interest rate movements as well as developments in the economy more broadly."

Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:10:32 UTC
06:10:32 KST

Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
Russian forces have changed how they strike Kyiv, launching nearly continuous waves of drone attacks throughout the day rather than only at night, as they did before. The Russian army is also increasingly using jet-powered Geran drones — Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed — which fly much faster than older, propeller-driven models and are harder to shoot down.
The city has settled into an uneasy new rhythm as a result, The New York Times reported. Shopping centers and stores close several times a day because of air-raid alerts, and a growing number of residents are spending their nights in shelters. Locals believe Russia is trying to “spread chaos.” “They want people to flee Kyiv. They want to interrupt our regular life,” one resident told the newspaper.
“Right now, Russia’s tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians — first and foremost, our people,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said on Monday that Russian forces had launched more than 1,500 drones over the previous four days, about 800 of them — more than half — jet-powered.
By comparison, Russia fired just 300 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in all of June and about 1,500 of them in July, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on technology.
Along with the numbers, Russia has changed the pattern of the attacks themselves, the BBC reported: the drones come in smaller batches than before, but more often. Russia now sends over three or four jet-powered drones, sometimes as many as 10, roughly every half hour, the BBC said.
On August 27 alone, Kyiv recorded 13 air-raid alerts lasting a combined 15 hours — a record since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Jet-powered drones are harder to shoot down because of their speed. In the winter of 2026, Ukraine was shooting down 95–98% of propeller-driven Shaheds. On August 27, Ukrainian forces shot down 88% of all drones, conventional and jet-powered alike; on August 31, just 79%.
An unnamed Ukrainian government official told The Wall Street Journal that Ukraine already has drones capable of shooting down the newest Geran models, but only a few hundred of them — far short of the thousands it needs.
Ukraine is working to develop countermeasures against jet-powered drones, and sources in the country’s defense industry told the BBC they expect Ukraine to have a counter within the next month.
As Russian strikes on Kyiv intensify, Ruslan Horbenko, a lawmaker from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said Kyiv and the Kyiv region could be officially designated front-line areas. The designation brings benefits including war-risk insurance, exemption from mobilization, and wage guarantees for utility workers. A government resolution to that effect has already been drafted, he said.
The war in photographs: Kyiv
Overnight, Russian forces again struck Kyiv and the surrounding region with ballistic missiles and drones, killing 12 people and injuring more than 20 across the region, according to authorities. Six of the dead were employees of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway; they were killed in a strike on a rail depot in Kyiv.

CARACAS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Maiquetia International Airport, Venezuela's main airport serving Caracas, formally resumed commercial operations Tuesday at temporary terminals built after its original infrastructure was damaged by the June 24 earthquakes.
Located about 20 km from the Venezuelan capital, the airport is in La Guaira state, the area hardest hit by the twin earthquakes that killed more than 6,000 people.
Operations resumed with a Conviasa flight to the Andean city of Valera. Flights to other domestic destinations, including Porlamar on Margarita Island and San Antonio del Tachira near the Colombian border, were also scheduled for the day.
International flights were also expected to operate to Miami with Global X, Panama with Copa Airlines and Madrid with Air Europa.
Authorities had previously said Maiquetia's temporary terminals were expected to handle up to 80 percent of pre-quake demand by December.
The international airports in Valencia, in central Venezuela, and Barcelona, in the country's northeast, had served as alternative hubs for air connectivity and are expected to continue handling more flights than usual. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Violence in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is driving fresh mass displacements, complicating the response to the Ebola outbreak, UN humanitarians said Tuesday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the hostilities are forcing people to flee their homes, and the insecurity and movement of people hamper disease surveillance and response efforts.
As of Sunday, national health authorities had reported more than 6,100 confirmed Ebola cases and nearly 2,950 deaths.
OCHA said that in Ituri province, local civil society sources reported that at least 37 civilians were killed and more than 35 people abducted during armed attacks in the territory of Mambasa on Saturday. At least 86 civilians were killed in attacks across the territory last month.
In neighboring South Kivu province, the office said its partners reported that clashes in Walungu territory have displaced at least 15,000 people since Aug. 23. Most of the displaced are sheltering with host families and need food, shelter and health care. Fighting is also forcing displacements in parts of North Kivu province.
"Despite these challenges, the UN and its humanitarian partners continue to support the authorities' response," OCHA said.
The International Organization for Migration said it has conducted nearly 23 million health screenings in the DRC and neighboring countries, helping to monitor people's movements, detect potential cases and reduce the risk of cross-border transmission.
The United Nations repeated its call on all parties to protect civilians and facilitate safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access, noting that maintaining access to communities affected by the outbreak remains critical for delivering life-saving assistance and supporting efforts to bring the Ebola outbreak under control.
UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher said "we cannot respond incrementally to an epidemic which is now growing exponentially."
Fletcher, speaking at a virtual briefing hosted by the World Health Organization, called for a sustained, large-scale operation to get ahead of the Ebola virus, adding that people need functioning health services, clean water, sanitation, food, protection and livelihoods. Above all, he said, they need trust.
"Time is not on our side. We have the experience, the tools, extraordinary people risking their lives to stop this epidemic. What we need now is political will, access, and resources. We have beaten Ebola before. And we can do it again," said the relief chief. ■

Congress advances new bill to give US edge in open-source AI race with China
Legislation to promote adoption of US open-source models while publicising the risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts
3-MIN READ3-MIN
8
 Listen
The US Congress on Tuesday advanced a new bill that seeks to establish American global leadership in open-source artificial intelligence, an area where China currently dominates, by promoting adoption of US open-source models and publicising risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts.
The legislation was one of several proposals marked up in the US House of Representatives targeting China amid escalating tech competition between the two countries.
Congressional committees “mark up” a proposed bill by reviewing it line by line, debating its merits and voting on changes or amendments before deciding whether to send it for a full House or Senate vote.
Introduced last week, the Open-Source AI Leadership Act, H.R. 10152, would direct the US Department of Commerce to identify barriers to adopting US open-weight models and compile data on their adoption relative to Chinese ones.
Open-weight, or open-source, models are AI models that are released freely over the internet, allowing users with the necessary hardware to download and customise them for their own use.
While leading US AI models including OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are mostly closed-source, meaning that they can only be accessed through official channels, most leading Chinese models are released as open-weight models.

Xi arrived in Bishkek on August 30 for a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. The trip marked his third visit to Kyrgyzstan and came as Beijing and Bishkek seek closer coordination between their development programmes.
The Kyrgyzstan visit was followed by Xi’s trip to Egypt, where China and Egypt are marking 70 years of diplomatic relations. Xi travelled to Cairo at the invitation of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. The visit was his second to Egypt as Chinese president.
Together, the two visits presented China’s approach to relations with developing countries through investment, transport links, trade, education and coordination in international organisations.
In a written speech on arrival in Bishkek, Xi described China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation as entering a “golden period” of development. He said the two countries had built their relationship over 34 years of diplomatic ties and had developed a comprehensive strategic partnership.
The economic component formed a central part of his programme.
China has been Kyrgyzstan’s largest trading partner and source of foreign investment for years, according to Xi’s signed article published before the visit. He pointed to the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Bedel border checkpoint and expanding direct flights as parts of a transport network connecting the countries.
The railway has particular importance for Kyrgyzstan. Its construction gives the landlocked country another transport corridor linking it with China and Uzbekistan and, through wider networks, markets beyond Central Asia.
Xi connected infrastructure development with plans for cooperation in the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence.
“China will continue to do its best to support Kyrgyzstan in growing its economy and improving people's lives,” Xi wrote before travelling to Bishkek.
He also called for progress on the railway, modernisation of land ports and measures to make cross-border movement of people and goods easier.
The agenda fits with Kyrgyzstan’s National Development Program until 2030 and China’s 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026-2030.
Kyrgyz officials and economists said investment from China had supported infrastructure, energy and industrial projects. Tolonbek Abdyrov, professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan, said Chinese investment had created opportunities for the country’s modernisation.
The relationship also extends beyond infrastructure.
China has established one Luban Workshop, four Confucius Institutes and 21 Confucius Classrooms in Kyrgyzstan. The two countries have also signed an agreement to establish cultural centres and have worked together on cultural heritage protection.
Two-way visits exceeded 400,000 in 2025, while 30 pairs of provinces and cities have established sister relationships.
Xi used the Bishkek visit to connect bilateral cooperation with the wider role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
The SCO marked its 25th anniversary in 2026. At the organisation’s summit on September 1, Xi proposed a programme centred on development, security, people-to-people relations and global governance.
He called for cooperation in trade, investment, connectivity, energy, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and green industries.
China plans to establish an international cooperation centre for AI applications for SCO countries and a China-SCO port economy cooperation centre in Tianjin. Xi also announced plans for 100 technology cooperation projects with SCO countries over the next three years.
His speech also put education and skills training on the agenda. China plans to establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation centre and continue programmes involving Confucius Institutes and Luban Workshops.
Xi presented dialogue as the basis for managing differences between countries.
The SCO should maintain the principle that countries are equal regardless of size and should address disagreements through consultation, he said.
At the SCO Plus meeting later in Bishkek, Xi expanded that argument to international governance.
“We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth,” he said.
Xi also called for a greater role for developing economies in international institutions and said Global South countries should have greater representation in international affairs.
The SCO now brings together countries accounting for about half of the world’s population and one quarter of the global economy, according to figures Xi cited during the meeting.
His message in Bishkek centred on an organisation based on partnership rather than military alliances.
“We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation,” Xi told participants.
From Central Asia, Xi’s diplomatic programme moved to Egypt.
The Egypt visit carries a different historical context but follows a similar focus on development and trade.
China and Egypt established diplomatic relations in 1956. Egypt became the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China. The two countries are marking the 70th anniversary of those ties this year.
Before his arrival, Xi published a signed article in the Egyptian newspapers Al-Ahram, Al-Akhbar and Al-Gomhuria.
“This time, I look forward to renewing the friendship and working together with President El-Sisi to explore ways of cooperation and map out a new blueprint for deepening the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership,” Xi wrote.
Economic cooperation has expanded through trade, industrial investment and infrastructure.
Egypt is one of China’s trading and investment partners in the Arab world and Africa and was among the earlier participants in Belt and Road cooperation.
One centre of that relationship is the China-Egypt Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, which Xi and El-Sisi promoted during Xi’s previous state visit a decade ago. Chinese companies have also participated in projects including the Central Business District of Egypt’s new administrative capital and the country’s electric light rail network.
Agricultural trade provides another area of cooperation.
Xi pointed to Egyptian oranges entering the Chinese market under China’s zero-tariff policy for African countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Beijing. The measure gives Egyptian agricultural producers access to China’s consumer market while expanding the range of African goods entering the country.
Xi linked future cooperation to Egypt’s Vision 2030 and China’s current five-year development programme.
China has an industrial base, capital, technology and equipment, while Egypt offers resources, a population of more than 100 million and access to markets across Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.
The two governments see those factors as a basis for further cooperation in manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and trade.
“We need to pursue mutual benefit and win-win cooperation and set a benchmark for joint development,” Xi wrote in his article for Egyptian media.
Education and cultural links also form part of the relationship.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to sign a cultural cooperation agreement with the People’s Republic of China. Chinese is now taught in more than 40 Egyptian secondary schools, while vocational education programmes involving China operate in the country.
Tourism has added another link. The Grand Egyptian Museum has become a destination for Chinese visitors, while an Egyptian civilisation exhibition at the Shanghai Museum drew demand for tickets in China.
Xi called for more cooperation in education, tourism, science, technology, health, sport and archaeology.
The Egypt visit also gives Beijing and Cairo a forum for discussion of regional conflicts and international institutions.
China and Egypt support Palestinian national rights and a political settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Both governments also advocate a larger role for developing countries in international decision-making.
Those positions connect Xi’s message in Cairo with the one he delivered in Bishkek.
In Kyrgyzstan, he called for equal participation in global governance and stronger representation for the Global South. In his article for Egyptian media, he called on China and Egypt to coordinate on peace, development and multilateral affairs.
The two visits also show how China is linking bilateral relationships with wider regional frameworks.
Kyrgyzstan occupies a position on China’s western border and forms part of transport routes across Central Asia. Egypt controls the Suez Canal and connects Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.
China’s cooperation with Kyrgyzstan therefore centres in part on overland connectivity. Its cooperation with Egypt includes industrial development, maritime trade and access between Asian, African and European markets.
Xi’s programme also linked Kyrgyzstan with the SCO and Egypt with China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation.
In his Egyptian article, he described Egypt as an important participant in both frameworks and called for further implementation of China-Arab cooperation programmes and China’s partnership actions with African countries.
The state visits come as China places the Global South at the centre of its international agenda.
Xi used his SCO speeches to argue for sovereign equality, multilateral decision-making and development cooperation. He called for technology and development gains to reach countries at different income levels and for work to narrow digital and artificial intelligence gaps.
“We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides,” Xi told the SCO Plus meeting.
The practical measures announced in Bishkek included technology projects, education programmes and new cooperation institutions.
In Kyrgyzstan, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway remains one of the most visible examples of that approach. In Egypt, the Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, transport infrastructure and construction projects provide comparable examples of long-term economic engagement.
Xi placed people-to-people contacts alongside those investments.
In both countries, his statements referred to education, cultural exchange and contacts between younger generations as elements of relations that extend beyond government agreements.
The Kyrgyz and Egyptian visits also have symbolic weight because of their anniversaries.
Kyrgyzstan is marking 35 years of independence. China and Egypt are marking 70 years of diplomatic relations. The SCO is marking 25 years since its creation.
Xi used those milestones to set out the next stage of China’s partnerships.
In Kyrgyzstan, his message focused on closer economic integration, transport links and the SCO’s future. In Egypt, he focused on industrial cooperation, trade, cultural exchange and coordination between China and the Arab and African worlds.
“For 70 years, China and Egypt have stood by each other rain or shine,” Xi wrote before the Egypt visit. He said the two countries were beginning a new stage of cooperation based on their previous agreements and development programmes.
His message in Kyrgyzstan carried the same emphasis on continuity.
China, Xi said, was ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to advance cooperation and create new prospects for bilateral relations.
From Bishkek to Cairo, the agenda puts infrastructure, trade, technology, education and diplomatic coordination at the centre of China’s ties with Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.

House passes stopgap bill that pauses changes to federal science grant-making process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:02:06 UTC
06:02:06 KST

A Trump administration effort to give political figures control over a large swath of U.S. science funding is off the table until at least December.
On Tuesday members of the House of Representatives voted 370-48, with 14 members not voting, to adopt a Senate appropriations bill that will continue funding federal agencies until December 11.
In August, as part of the stopgap measure, the Senate agreed not to adopt proposed rule changes from the Office of Budget Management that would give politically appointed bureaucrats authority over federal research grants. If implemented, these changes would break from the current system, in which independent panels of peer reviewers, experts in the field, assess grant requests for funding from the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and other governmental agencies.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The proposed rule changes have met an outpouring of opposition from the scientific community. Thousands of researchers, including several Nobel laureates, used the public comment period on the proposal to say it would politicize research and destroy U.S. leadership in global science.
The question of whether the proposed rule changes will go further could hinge largely on the outcome of the midterm elections, which will be held in November: Democrats, who are currently favored to win control of the House, have broadly opposed the changes.

US says at UN it will continue facilitating Ukraine-Russia talks
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, U.S. Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations Dan Negrea made the statement on Tuesday during a UN General Assembly meeting on the situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
He said that the United States continued to facilitate negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv in the most constructive manner possible," he said.
Negrea stressed that only diplomacy can stop the destruction and loss of life.
He said that Russia and Ukraine must return to the negotiating table, as it is clear that no military solution can bring an end to this war. He also reiterated the U.S. call for an immediate ceasefire and good-faith negotiations to restore peace and stability in both countries.
Negrea also raised the issue of the safety of shipping and civilian infrastructure, saying that his country supports the ongoing dialogue aimed at ending strikes on vessels and civilian infrastructure in the Black Sea.
He also emphasized the economic and humanitarian consequences of the war.
He said the U.S. was drawing attention to rapidly rising costs, food security concerns and fuel prices.
The UN General Assembly convened on Tuesday for a debate on the situation in the territories of Ukraine temporarily occupied by Russia.
Ukraine is calling on UN member states, international organizations and parliamentary institutions not to recognize the illegal pseudo-elections that Russia plans to hold in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:57:00 UTC
05:57:00 KST

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026
What you need to know
Below is a roundup of the top headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Tuesday, September 1, 2026 and Wednesday, September 2.
- US military says it has launched strikes on Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)
- US President Trump described the strikes as 'large and powerful'
- Iran said the US would 'regret' the latest attacks
- Jordanian military says it intercepted Iranian missiles in Jordanian airspace
- Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq's Kurdistan region also targeted by Iranian attacks
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Iran fires back at US allies Kuwait and Bahrain
Iran launched a retaliatory drone attack against Kuwait and Bahrain on Wednesday.
Both countries successfully intercepted the incoming drones.
The attack followed a US airstrike that hit a wedding celebration, leaving four people dead and several others injured, according to an Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied that civilians were deliberately targeted.
USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after Middle East deployment
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier docked at the port of Laem Chabang in eastern Thailand on Wednesday after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East.
The massive nuclear-powered vessel, carrying some 5,000 American service members, has spent 286 days at sea and was involved in the US naval blockade of Iranian ports as well as combat operations in the Middle East war.
The length of the deployment had raised concerns amid reports about deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies on board.
During the five days in port, many service members are expected to visit the nearby beach resort town of Pattaya. While the stop is likely to boost local businesses, it's also drawn some scrutiny given Pattaya's reputation as a hub for sex tourism.
US service members have reportedly been barred from visiting the most notorious of the city's streets, as well as cannabis shops, and will be unable to engage in water sports such as jet-skiing.
"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of the US Carrier Strike Group 3, said in a statement.
Two tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz — IRCG
Two oil tankers have caught fire after hitting sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement.
The IRGCsaid the tankers were attempting "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the strait before "striking mines and exploding."
It said the vessels had been forced to disembark their crews. The information has not been independently verified.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company Bahri said two sailors were killed in an attack on one of its vessels in the strait on Monday.
It said its oil tanker Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz" on the evening of August 31. Two Filipino crew were killed in the attack, it added.
The Strait of Hormuz was a key waterway for the transport of oil and gas before the Middle East war broke out in February. Iranian attacks on ships have largely brought traffic there to a halt, although some tankers have moved through the strait in recent weeks.
Pakistan says it remains engaged with Iran, US to end conflict
Pakistan said it remains engaged with the US and Iran on talks to end their conflict and was optimistic that the countries "will return to the table for dialogue," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi told the media during his weekly briefing on Wednesday.
 
Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which was held from August 31 to September 1 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
 
The spokesperson added that Pakistan's Chief of Defense Forces Asim Munir's visit to Tehran last week was also part of the country's push to put an end to the US-Iran conflict. 
 
He said the visit "generated momentum" on a range of issues, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran reports 11 civilian deaths in US strikes
Separate US attacks in southwestern Iran have killed 11 people and injured dozens more, Iranian state media reported on Wednesday.
In Hormozgan province, which straddles the Strait of Hormuz, four people, including a child, were killed after shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a residential home in the costal city of Kuhestak where a wedding was taking place, according to the Iranian Red Crescent. More than 50 people were reported injured.
AFP news agency reported a video shared by an Iranian government account showed extensive debris and damage at what it said was the site of the wedding in Sirik country.
"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a statement, pointing to previous attacks including a strike on a girls' school in Minab in February that killed 160 people.
Elsewhere, officials in Khuzestan province further to the north said US missile attacks on three locations in the province killed seven people and injured eight.
US officials did not directly address reports of the strike on a wedding, but US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians."
WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?
Six months into the Iran war, US military leaders are warning of stretched forces and depleted weapons stockpiles. Does the US have the resources to keep fighting?
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched strikes on US bases with drones and missiles in Erbil, Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to state media.
State-run IRNA reported that the IRGC said they had "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" and had destroyed a maintenance facility, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat."
The claims cannot be independently verified. The US military has not yet commented on the matter.
Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones
Sirens warning of potential aerial threats sounded in Bahrain early on Wednesday amid the latest escalation between the US and Iran.
Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said in a post on X: "A danger is present. The Ministry of Interior calls upon citizens and residents to adhere to calm, head to the nearest safe place, and follow the news through official channels, to safeguard public safety.
Bahrain is home to a major US naval base where the 5th Fleet is headquartered and has previously been targeted by Tehran.
Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.
US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.
"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.
It went on to say that the strikes came after "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
CENTCOM said there were currently 50,000 US military personnel operating in the Middle East.
Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted
The Jordanian Armed Forces said that 10 ballistic missiles launched from Iran had been intercepted, while another three landed in remote areas.
"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. Jordan added that no casualties had been reported.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump said that the latest strikes on Iran had been in response to Iranian missile launches at US targets on Monday and attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back
The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."
"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.
Earlier, Trump told US broadcaster Fox News that US forces had struck Iranian radars.
“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump told Fox. “We waited until it was almost built and then we hit it."
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.
Welcome to our coverage
The US military announced it has launched new strikes on targets in Iran. Iran has vowed retaliation.
The Iran war has been fought intermittently for the past 6 months and with the latest round of hostilities, there doesn't appear to be an end in sight to the conflict that is having major global economic repercussions.
Stay with us for updates and analysis on unfolding events in both Iran and the wider Middle East region.

Elsewhere, officials in Khuzestan province further to the north said US missile attacks on three locations in the province killed seven people and injured eight.
US officials did not directly address reports of the strike on a wedding, but US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians."

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched strikes on US bases with drones and missiles in Erbil, Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to state media.
State-run IRNA reported that the IRGC said they had "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" and had destroyed a maintenance facility, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat."

Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.
US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.
"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.
It went on to say that the strikes came after "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
CENTCOM said there were currently 50,000 US military personnel operating in the Middle East.

The Jordanian Armed Forces said that 10 ballistic missiles launched from Iran had been intercepted, while another three landed in remote areas.
"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. Jordan added that no casualties had been reported.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump said that the latest strikes on Iran had been in response to Iranian missile launches at US targets on Monday and attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back
The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."
"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.
Earlier, Trump told US broadcaster Fox News that US forces had struck Iranian radars.
“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump told Fox. “We waited until it was almost built and then we hit it."
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Italian arms dealer sentenced to 18 months in U.S. prison for supplying ammunition to Russia in violation of sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:55:04 UTC
05:55:04 KST

On Aug. 24, a federal court in the Eastern District of New York sentenced Manfred Gruber, a 61-year-old Italian citizen and former commercial director of an Italian arms company, to 18 months in prison for conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws. Gruber pleaded guilty to the charge on March 30.
According to the U.S. Justice Department, Gruber organized the illegal export of more than $540,000 worth of U.S.-made ammunition produced by a Nebraska company and another supplier in Tennessee, routing it through JFK International Airport in New York. The shipments were declared for export to Italy, where the ammunition was required to remain as per official documents. Instead, prosecutors said, the cargo was routed to Russia via Kyrgyzstan.
The case also involved Sergei Zharnovnikov, the owner of a Kyrgyz arms distributor, who previously pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 39 months in prison. A key piece of evidence consisted of correspondence found on Zharnovnikov’s phone in which the men discussed breaking up shipments of 100,000 rounds into smaller orders in order to avoid attracting the attention of customs officials.
Joseph Nocella, Jr., the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said Gruber had been “held accountable for his scheme to send military‑grade ammunition to Kyrgyzstan before reexporting the ammunition to Russia to support its war effort.”
Gruber had served as commercial director of Bignami S.p.A., which bought ammunition for sniper rifles from Nebraska-based Hornady Manufacturing under a U.S. export license, then rerouted the shipments to Russia through Kyrgyzstan, bypassing permit requirements that the ammunition remain in Italy. The Insider previously identified Gruber’s business partners.
From 2022 to 2024, Russian companies including Arsenal, Artemida, Ve-Kasa, Promtekhnologiya, and Tetis received Hornady ammunition. In 2023, Politico Europe found evidence that Hornady ammunition had been used by snipers from the Wagner Group, the Russian state-funded private military company co-founded by the late Yevgeny Prigozhin. The Insider later found that the company’s ammunition was being used by snipers from the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade of Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
Gruber’s case is not an isolated incident. In August 2025, U.S. authorities seized more than $250,000 and dozens of weapons components and accessories after arresting Maxim Larin, a 44-year-old U.S. citizen from Plantation, Florida who owned several small American companies selling firearms parts. On Aug. 25, 2026, the U.S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of New York accepted Larin’s guilty plea on charges of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the attempted violation of the Arms Export Control Act.
According to prosecutors, Larin and an accomplice in Russia organized shipments of weapons components to Kazakhstan, including trigger mechanisms for semiautomatic firearms, charging handles, and laser rangefinders of the sort used by snipers and artillery spotters.
The investigative bureau Tri Trace Investigations found that from 2009 to 2014 Larin had owned the Russian gun store Shooter’s Shop. In 2012, before leaving the Russian business, he also opened a gun store in the United States. Larin’s former Russian store continues to operate under the iShooter brand. The store’s website has an “international shipping” section listing Express Mail Shipping as its logistics partner. The store’s current owner, Albert Goncharov, is also listed as an employee of Larin’s U.S. company.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday warned that Russian airspace was becoming "completely dangerous" amid the ongoing war with Ukraine.

"For now, the skies over Russia are for drones – not for civilian aviation," he said.
