Putin, Xi attempt to rally SCO leaders behind a new multipolar world order in Kyrgyzstan - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:14:54 UTC
04:14:54 KST

Seven years after similar meetings took place in Central Asia, Russian and Chinese leaders are back again for a familiar meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the Russians and Chinese are seeking to push for a post-American world order.
These leaders have been doing this for a while. Back in 2019, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held a summit in Bishkek. At the time, some of the officials flew to Tajikistan’s capital, Dushanbe, for the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia. Taken together, the leaders were lifting the curtain on their push for a multipolar world order.
Much has changed since 2019. Russia had already invaded part of Ukraine in 2014, but in 2022 it launched a major new invasion. The US left Afghanistan. A civil war broke out in Sudan. The Assad regime was overthrown in 2024. Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, creating a multi-front war. The US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026. Russia and China are watching.
The SCO is one vehicle they use to discuss with non-Western powers the new world order that Moscow and Beijing want to create.
Back in 2019, there were eight member countries attending the SCO, and numerous other countries were attending as observers and partners. Russia’s TASS news agency said on Tuesday, “Russian President Vladimir Putin said the potential of the United Nations (UN) remains untapped and called for improving its effectiveness at the SCO Plus meeting.
'Building a fair multipolar world order is irreversible'
China’s President Xi Jinping, who is set to visit Egypt soon, said the world must reject the “law of the jungle.” Clearly, this was a reference to the US war with Iran.
Putin said Russia is not fully satisfied with the UN, but that is nothing new: “We do not always like or are satisfied with everything the UN does. At the same time, I must note that, to be honest, this has always been the case, practically since its creation.”
Putin called for the SCO to work more closely at the UN and also have broader representation from countries of the Global South and East. Overall, the organization should adapt to the changing realities and fundamental shifts emerging in global politics and the economy.
Xi Jinping said the emergence of a multipolar world “is now an irreversible historical process,” TASS noted. Xi said the SCO “has become one of the key platforms for joint development and addressing challenges facing Eurasian countries.”
SCO summit highlights growing challenge to US-led world order
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko also spoke. Tajikistan President Emomali Rahmon said the UN and SCO can play a greater role in building a fair and inclusive world order, TASS noted. Kyrgyzstan’s President Sadyr Japarov also noted this multipolar theme.
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev made an interesting reference to the current world order. He said that it should not be a “cult of force,” essentially arguing that it shouldn’t be one of “might makes right.” He added, “Our common strategic task is to build a world order in which a cult of force and confrontation gives way to mutual responsibility, joint development, and long-term cooperation.”
Photos from the event appeared to show leaders from 25 countries attending. China’s state news agency Xinhua noted that Xi said, “The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO’s commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times.”
He added that there are many changes that are “accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism, and protectionism are resurging against historical trends.” In essence, this was a critique of the US. He argued that the rise of the Global South is reshaping the world order.
“What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How will countries take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history,” Xi said, according to Xinhua.
“Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law and work together to tackle global challenges,” he added.
The SCO meeting matters because it brings together so many countries that apparently agree on confronting the US-led world order that began at the end of the Cold War.
Many of these countries are now advancing new ideas on how to shape the world order. The origins of the SCO date from 1996, when China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan met to discuss closer cooperation. A charter was signed in 2002. As such, the current SCO is very much a legacy of the long-term leadership of Putin, Xi, and several other leaders who have been around for decades.
Much has changed in the last decade. As things change, the SCO continues to expand. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus have joined. More dialogue partners and observer states have also joined. These include Turkey, Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, and others.
'Hide your strength, bide your time'
What matters at the SCO today, as it did in 2019, is that these countries are openly talking about supplanting the US and creating a new world order. What does this mean for countries such as Pakistan, which work with the US but also formed a new alliance with Turkey and Saudi Arabia? Turkey and Saudi Arabia are both close friends of the US.
Turkey is a member of NATO. However, more and more countries want to hedge and keep a foot in several camps. SCO, BRICS, and other groupings provide that opportunity.
India, for instance, has mastered this balancing act. It has been since the era of the non-aligned movement during the Cold War. In those days, some countries wanted to balance between the Soviets and the Americans. Now the game afoot is to balance between the US and the rest. This is because the US remains the most powerful and influential country in the world.
Beijing has pursued a policy of “hide your strength, bide your time.” As China expands globally and increases the size of its navy, it is no longer hiding. It is now taking a more aggressive stance. However, it doesn’t want direct confrontation yet.
Russia has been willing to directly confront the West over Ukraine. This has led to a long and difficult war. It remains to be seen how Russia will behave as the war appears to sap its strength.
However, for now, Putin continues to put on an image of moving forward with his war in Ukraine.
What that means for the Middle East, Asia, and other areas is not yet clear. China’s outreach to Egypt this week, for instance, is a key example of how Beijing is exerting its influence in the Middle East.

Israeli army ‘kills first, then seeks justification’ for Gaza strikes, says veterans group chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:11:53 UTC
04:11:53 KST

The Israeli army “kills first, then thinks and tries to find a reason” afterward to justify strikes on the Gaza Strip, said the executive director of Israeli veterans' group Breaking the Silence.
In an interview Friday with France 24, Nadav Weiman said the army and Israeli authorities seek to “retrospectively” legitimize attacks by attempting to establish links between victims and Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad after strikes have taken place.
“In cases like this Nasser hospital or the 15 paramedics that were killed by IDF (Israeli army) soldiers in Rafah, or air strikes that are killing three-digit numbers of civilians in Gaza ... suddenly the IDF spokesperson in the state of Israel needs to explain to the international community what we did over there and who are the targets for the attack,” Weiman said.
On Aug. 25, 2025, an Israeli attack on the Nasser Medical Complex in the southern Gaza Strip killed at least 20 Palestinians, including patients, health workers, civil defense personnel, and press crews, while several others were injured in the attack, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry.
On March 23, 15 emergency and civil defense workers, who were protected by international law, were killed by the Israeli army in Rafah, southern Gaza.
Weiman said that intelligence personnel compile the names of those killed and then search for evidence that can establish a connection, such as having a relative linked to Hamas or the Palestinian Islamic Jihad movement, being near a building identified as belonging to Hamas or having once been on a payroll.
“Then the IDF (Israeli army) tries to build a case around certain individuals to say we attacked because there were Hamas members over there,” he said.
He questioned how the military could have identified the victims as targets in advance, particularly in the Nasser Hospital attack, where he said a second shell struck the site and killed most of those present.
“This is something that we do after we shoot,” he said, accusing the army of the deadly attacks. “First we shoot, we kill, and then we think and try to find a reason why it happened.”
“I don't think that the tank that fired the tank shells at the hospital had a booklet with 25,000 Hamas members and looked photo after photo and said, 'Ah, there are Hamas members over there,’” he added.
Weiman said the practice was not unique to the Nasser Hospital incident and cited the 2018 Gaza border protests, when more than 200 Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces.
On March 30, 2018, the Great March of Return and Breaking the Siege began with Palestinians gathering along the barrier between the Gaza Strip and Israel to demand the right of return for Palestinian refugees and an end to the Israeli blockade of Gaza. The protests also coincided with the anniversary of Land Day. Israeli forces killed 215 Palestinians.
“Back then it was the same on the evening news in Israel: 'We killed this and that amount of terrorists,’” Weiman added.
He said Breaking the Silence has received testimonies from soldiers in the current Gaza war confirming that “if we shot and killed someone, he would be listed as a terrorist.”
An operations officer from a major battalion that participated in the Gaza genocide told the group that “every night he had to count all of the numbers of the Palestinians they shot at and listed all of them as terrorists. Doesn't matter if they're civilian or not," Weiman said, adding that this happened “because that's the assumption" in the Israeli army.
He also slammed the Israeli army's internal investigations into wrongdoing, saying they rarely result in meaningful accountability.
“Almost none,” he said when asked how often such investigations lead to charges or disciplinary action.
According to Weiman, military investigations generally focus on lower-ranking officers rather than examining who “gave the command, authorized rules of engagement or approved the number of civilian deaths considered acceptable as collateral damage.”
He said the focus should instead be on policy “and that's something that the IDF (Israeli army) cannot investigate because a situation like this where it is out in the world and outside of regulation is wrong, obviously.”
“The problem is what the state of Israel and the IDF (Israeli army) see as legitimate — as okay commands, as crucial commands — and those are the places that we want investigation,” he said.
Israel launched its genocide on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023. More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 wounded, most of them women and children, according to Palestinian figures.
Despite the ceasefire in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel continues to violate the agreement, with attacks that have killed 1,320 Palestinians and wounded 4,385 others, mostly women and children, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Govt Tuesday halved sugar stock holding limit for dealers to 2,000 quintals
NEW DELHI: Govt Tuesday halved sugar stock holding limit for dealers to 2,000 quintals from Sept 15 till Nov 30, in its bid to ensure adequate availability in the domestic market and prevent hoarding and speculative trading. The move comes as retail prices have moderated to around Rs 63 a kg, but still remain elevated even as ex-mill prices have crashed by more than 20% after govt took a series of steps.At present, stock holding limit for sugar dealers across the country is 4,000 quintals. As per the new order, no sugar dealer can hold any stock for a period exceeding 30 days from the date of receipt of sugar consignments and no dealer can keep over 2,000 quintals of sugar at any time.
Govt expects the reduction will facilitate orderly movement of sugar through the supply chain and ensure its continuous availability to consumers at reasonable prices. Meanwhile, govt has undertaken intensive monitoring and physical verification of sugar stocks, covering sugar mills, dealers and traders.

Petraeus says Afghanistan withdrawal was unnecessary
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:50 BST
04:00:50 KST

General David Petraeus has said the United States and its allies did not need to withdraw from Afghanistan when they did, arguing that the Western military commitment had reached a sustainable level and that the loss of coalition support helped undermine Afghan forces, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Petraeus, who commanded NATO and US forces in Afghanistan before later serving as Director of the CIA, made the comments during the Lord Speaker’s Lecture at the House of Lords on 1 September. He rejected the argument that the length of the conflict itself meant involvement had to end, saying the relevant question was whether the continuing human and financial cost remained proportionate to the interests involved.
He said: “And here, allow me an aside to observe that I do not believe we had to leave Afghanistan when we did. Nor do I believe we should have done so.”
Petraeus continued: “For years I disagreed with the increasingly fashionable argument that we simply had to ‘end endless wars.’ That formulation asks the wrong question. The issue is not how long a conflict has lasted. It is whether the commitment required to sustain it remains proportionate to the interests being protected and the costs being borne.”
He contrasted Afghanistan with Vietnam, which he said had become unsustainable in terms of lives and expenditure. Afghanistan, he argued, had by 2020 reached a comparatively modest level of Western involvement.
Petraeus said: “We obviously have to end wars that are not sustainable. But sustainability should be measured principally by the expenditure of our blood and our treasure. Vietnam, by those metrics, clearly became unsustainable. By contrast, the effort in Afghanistan by 2020 had become sustainable at a relatively modest level.”
He cited approximately 2,500 American troops and 8,500 coalition personnel remaining by the time of the final withdrawal and said Western forces were no longer engaged in front-line combat. Their principal role, according to Petraeus, was advising and assisting Afghan forces and providing capabilities which those forces could not yet supply themselves.
He said: “The Taliban controlled no major population centers, and our forces were no longer engaged in front-line combat. Their principal role was to advise, assist, and enable Afghan partners and provide capabilities the Afghan security forces had not yet developed for themselves.”
Petraeus also criticised the requirement for the Afghan government to release Taliban prisoners during the process leading to the withdrawal. He said: “Nor should we have required the Afghan government to release some 5,500 Taliban detainees merely to secure from our adversary an agreement confirming what it already wanted us to do—to leave.”
A central part of his argument concerned the withdrawal of civilian contractors alongside military personnel. Petraeus said more than 15,000 Western contractors departed, removing specialist support required to maintain American-supplied Afghan aircraft and helicopters.
He said: “The consequences of withdrawal should have been foreseeable. It removed not only American and coalition forces, but also more than 15,000 Western contractors who were indispensable to maintaining the sophisticated American aircraft and helicopters we had provided the Afghan forces.”
Those aircraft had provided mobility for around 35,000 Afghan commandos who were used to reinforce conventional forces facing Taliban attacks around the country. Petraeus argued that the disappearance of aviation maintenance support consequently affected the ability of those commandos to move rapidly between areas of fighting.
He said: “As that maintenance capacity disappeared, so did the mobility upon which some 35,000 exceptionally capable Afghan commandos depended to respond to attacks around the country.”
Petraeus continued: “Without that air mobility, those commandos could no longer reinforce front lines held by much less capable conventional soldiers and police. The essence of the Afghan strategy was therefore fatally undermined—and once that capability eroded, the collapse accelerated.”
He used Afghanistan to make a wider point about how military capability should be assessed, arguing that personnel and equipment numbers alone provide an incomplete measure of combat effectiveness.
Petraeus said: “Military effectiveness cannot be measured simply by counting soldiers, aircraft, ships, or weapons. It depends upon the institutions, logistics, intelligence, technology, industrial capacity, and professional relationships that enable those capabilities to function.”

Heavy bond selling sent the interest rate on 30-year UK government bonds to the highest since 1998, while the 10-year yield surged to a level not seen since the global financial crisis of 2007-08.

"The bond sell-off has... been a global affair," said Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid.
He said the "main culprit was the weekend escalation in the Middle East that saw the US and Iran exchange strikes for the first time since late July".
But Patrick O'Hare at Briefing.com pointed to underlying fears about inflation and government deficits.
"The result has been a steady uplift for sovereign bond yields that has stirred competition concerns for stocks, as well as general growth concerns," he said.
Oil prices up as US resumes attacks on Iran
Wall Street's main stock indices were firmly in the red in late morning trading.
European stocks ended lower, with sentiment hit by official data showing that eurozone inflation hit a three-year high at 3.3 percent in August, cementing expectations that the European Central Bank would raise interest rates next week.

1.6M affected, 1,050 killed by devastating flash floods in Nepal

Aamir Latif
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Around 1.6 million people have been affected by the devastating flash floods, which have killed 1,050 people and left nearly 4,000 missing in Nepal, local media reported, citing the government’s preliminary situation report released Tuesday.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) identified Rasuwa and Nuwakot as the worst-affected districts. Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan were listed as moderately affected, the local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.
The highest number of bodies, 321, were recovered in Chitwan, followed by Nawalparasi East with 216, Nawalparasi West with 170 and Nuwakot with 142.
Some 3,916 people have been reported missing from 62 districts across the country.
Of those reported missing, 62% were Nepali nationals traveling in groups, including domestic tourists, while 17% were employees of government agencies and 15% were foreign nationals.
About 43,000 women and girls in Nepal urgently need humanitarian assistance following the flash floods that swept through parts of the country last week, according to UN Women.
The disaster, the UN agency said, has disproportionately affected women and girls, particularly those who were already vulnerable because of poverty, disability, pregnancy, limited access to information and a lack of resources.
“Pregnant women, lactating women, people with disabilities, the people we would normally support – are gone, washed away, because they could not run to higher ground,” one women-led organization working in affected communities told UN Women.
Massive floods have directly or indirectly affected an estimated 157,050 women and girls living in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.
The overall death toll from flash floods and mudslides in the Himalayas reached 1,066 on Tuesday, a week after the disaster struck the border region between Nepal and China, according to official data.
Data from Nepal and China showed that some 4,462 people, including 844 foreigners, remained missing.
Chinese authorities confirmed 16 deaths, while the search continued for 546 people reported missing, including 261 foreigners.

What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:57:32 UTC
03:57:32 KST

What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
Canada has very few similarities with Iran – to Canada’s own shame.
Let’s leave aside the basic differences, such as location, demographics, weather, and cuisine, and focus on the essentials: Historically, Iran is old and firmly based on an ancient civilization; Canada, like the US, is young and a little accidental, a leftover of the British Empire in its settler-colonial-ethnic-cleansing variant.
In terms of religion, Iran is shaped by pious Shia Islam; Canada displays the flaccid mix of an emasculated Christmas-and-jingle-bells-only Christianity and aggressive anything-goes consumerist secularism typical of the contemporary West.
Geopolitically, Iran is a proud and victorious opponent of the US and Israel; Canada is a fairly ordinary vassal in the American empire.
Accordingly, Canada is deeply and proudly involved in the West’s proxy war against Russia by way of using up Ukraine. Indeed, the Canadian contribution is particularly ironic because it also serves a frenetic and powerful nationalist Ukrainian lobby, rooted in deliberately privileged fascist World War Two runaways and Cold War conspirators. Iran, on the other side, has long helped Russia and, for its efforts, been directly attacked by Kiev’s Zelensky regime. In return, Western sources claim, Moscow has been helping Tehran with its ongoing defense against the US and Israel.
Most importantly, Iran is a country on the side of elementary decency, fundamental human ethics, and international law and therefore against the genocide committed by Israel, the US, UK, Germany, and various other Western accomplices against the Palestinian nation. Canada – Israeli murders of Canadian citizens and some cheap and, in effect, empty gestures from Ottawa notwithstanding – has been, at the very best, yet another camp follower of the Western genocide coalition.
And yet, strange as it may be, recent events have produced something that Iran and Canada have in common. Or to be precise, it’s Washington’s bizarre policies that have created this odd overlap: both Canada the long-standing vassal and Iran the steadfast antagonist are currently at the receiving end of both fresh attempts at coercion by economic warfare and escalating rhetoric from Washington.
Of course, there are orders-of-magnitude differences between the Trump administration’s ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ against Tehran and the latest round of tariff and trash-talk launched against Canada.
The ‘Operation’ targeting Iran, according to its mastermind and cheerleader Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, aims to combine a naval blockade, intelligence gathering, “mapp[ing] every node, every facilitator and every network that Iran” is using to trade abroad, and wide-ranging secondary sanctions to, in Bessent words, “asphyxiat[e]” Tehran. The declared end goal is to “collapse” Iran by inflicting an “Economic D-Day,” as President Donald Trump has put it.
There’s no such intention to wage total economic war in the case of Canada. Regarding Ottawa, Washington has merely initiated a pressure campaign within its empire. Its goal is not absolute destruction but the punishment and coercion of a wayward vassal.
In essence, the Canadian government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected Washington’s offer of a crudely disadvantageous and interfering trade deal, featuring, according to the Financial Times, “ludicrous” American demands.
Faced with “clodhopping bullying” so extreme no leader could have submitted – except maybe, say, the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen or Germany’s Friedrich Merz – Carney had an excellent opportunity to make a stand. He declared that Canada is under US attack and, in effect, at war – all restricted to the economy, of course – and that his government will retaliate tit-for-tat, dollar-for-dollar.
Washington is striking at Ottawa with 50% tariffs on Canadian goods worth $20 billion, and, in return, Ottawa will give as good as it gets. That’s the plan at least. But while the Wall Street Journal reports that both sides are getting ready for a long fight, there also is still some time for last-minute off-ramps.
Things need to be kept in proportion: the new US tariffs would affect about 5% of Canadian exports to its overbearing southern neighbor. The Canadian retaliation would target about 6% of what the US sends north. Meanwhile, US rhetoric is surging. Trump has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America and posted an extraordinarily odd AI-generated video about it, featuring (Canadian?) wild geese marching in lockstep under US flags and firing assault rifles. In Canada, for now at least, Carney’s hardline response is popular.
In short, what is really happening between Ottawa and Washington may well seem like a farce if compared to the state of things between Washington and Tehran. Unsurprisingly, the Iranian leadership has declared that it won’t budge. And why should it? It has already won two rounds of war against Washington. While its economy is certainly suffering, the American-Israeli aggression has, in effect, fully immunized Iranian society against any regime-change schemes.
Finally, Washington will not succeed in making key players submit to its secondary-sanctions blackmail. China, now the world’s great oil power, as The Economist concedes, and a crucial partner for Iran not merely in economic terms, has already made that much clear. Russia is very unlikely to be impressed either.
But take a step back and look at the picture as a whole. Here we are: the US is waging economic war – of different intensity – against both opponents and so-called allies. More importantly, it is meeting resistance in both cases. And most importantly, in both cases, there is no reason to assume that Washington will win. All of that is happening against a background of the US escalating its use of brute force: There is the fresh “deal” – really, steal – to siphon off 65 billion barrels of crude from the de facto US protectorate of post-Maduro Venezuela. Regarding the much-disturbed bond markets, meanwhile, Trump has openly threatened to use the US military to shape them to Washington’s advantage.
The idea is about as smart as trying to fix a microchip with a sledgehammer. But, with the US, that doesn’t mean it won’t be tried. For the red thread running through all of the above is a combination of slipping real power, escalating aggressiveness, and rising resistance from others. What makes this so dangerous is that Washington seems to have entirely lost the ability to realistically adjust its aims and demands to its declining capabilities. Think of it as a bully past his prime who is not only very violent but also not smart enough to see when being more flexible would be in his own best interest.

U.S. House votes to avoid government shutdown amid GOP hard-liner resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:54:51 UTC
03:54:51 KST

The U.S. House on Tuesday voted, 370-48, in favor of a stopgap spending measure that is expected to avert a government shutdown this fall ahead of the 2026 midterm election, despite objections from GOP hard-liners.
The legislation, which the Senate passed in August before breaking for its summer recess, would keep the government funded through Dec. 11.
The measure now heads to President Donald Trump's desk for his signature.
Without passage, government funding is set to lapse at the end of the federal fiscal year, Sept. 30. That's a prospect neither party was keen on as lawmakers hope to quickly return to their districts and continue campaigning ahead of the midterms.
House leadership brought the bill to the floor using a process known as "suspension of the rules," which allows consensus measures to circumvent certain procedural hurdles but requires a two-thirds vote. That meant Democratic votes were needed in the narrowly divided chamber. The package ultimately got broad, bipartisan support. Just 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voted against the measure.
"Thanks to the House Republicans' leadership and the foresight back in July, we began the necessary processes to ensure that the government would not be shut down," House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said after the vote. "We are not going to have our troops in harm's way without getting paychecks."
But before the vote, members of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus raised concerns about both the bill and the process. The lawmakers threatened to hold up what Johnson expected would be a quick vote to pass the measure, which extends current government funding levels.
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, sent a letter on Monday to House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole, R-Okla., and House Budget Committee Chair Jodey Arrington, R-Texas, outlining his concerns with the stopgap spending measure, among them its funding for Planned Parenthood and the absence of a ban on hemp products that contain THC, the psychoactive chemical in marijuana.
"I have serious concerns about simply extending the status quo. Members should be clear about what passage of this legislation would mean: Congress would once again affirmatively fund policies we have spent months fighting to change," Roy wrote.
And Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., who chairs the Freedom Caucus, told Punchbowl News he would vote to block the rest of the GOP's agenda for the week over his objection to the spending measure.
But their opposition was not enough to hinder the vote. With Democratic support, Johnson passed the funding measure even with some GOP defections.
Most lawmakers will be eager to get back to their districts this election season, as Republicans strive to overcome Trump's low approval rating and hold on to narrow majorities in the House and Senate. Polling shows Democrats are largely expected to win control of the House, while the GOP is favored in the Senate.
Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Patty Murray, D-Wash., applauded the spending bills' passage in a statement on Tuesday, but said more work is needed to be done to curb the Trump administration.
"We have a lot of work ahead in the coming months to negotiate spending bills that invest in families instead of President Trump's war budget, and I will be pushing at every step of the way to invest in making life more affordable and rein in the corrupt abuses of this administration," Murray said.

Nigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP.
The Reform UK leader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances.
He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election.
However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point.
The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority.
The commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and was first revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit.
At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Farage called a byelection on 7 July and the initial investigation was paused.
However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May.
The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work.
Farage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues.
Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected.
The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry.
If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process.
In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away.
“Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.”
If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection.
As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country.
Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.

Bessent touts bond market as 10-year Treasury yield spikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:53:45 UTC
03:53:45 KST

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent boasted Tuesday that the U.S. bond market has outperformed the rest of the world since President Donald Trump's return to office. But he made his comments as 10-year Treasury yields rose to their highest level in nearly 20 months amid a global bond sell-off that has raised fears about a repeat of the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
"It's been the best-performing bond market among major countries in the world," Bessent asserted during a "fireside chat" with a Fox Business host at the Group of 20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.
The hedge fund veteran and Cabinet secretary chose a starting point for his analysis that downplayed the bond market's reaction to Trump's presidency. Markets anticipate future events, and investors who began to price in the possibility of a Trump victory started selling off U.S. government debt well ahead of his Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration. Accounting for that context, the U.S. bond market has performed in the middle of the pack over the past two years.
Bessent and Trump have repeatedly made assertions about market performance and the U.S. economy that either skirt the truth or defy reason. Trump on Monday told reporters that, if not for the hindrance of too-high interest rates, the U.S. economy could grow at rates as high as 20%. But such a figure has only been reached once since World War II — and that was during the post-Covid rebound that followed a historic economic contraction.
On Monday, Bessent told CNBC's Sara Eisen the benchmark 10-year yield is "flat since President Trump came in," a sign of stability in the market. In reality, the 10-year is up about 18 basis points since Trump's second inauguration.
Bessent has made similar comments throughout the two-day G20 gathering, where he and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh have focused heavily on finding ways to spur economic growth.
To be sure, the shift in the U.S. 10-year yield is smaller than what other top economies, including the members of the G7 alliance, have experienced since January 2025, according to CNBC's analysis.
But U.S. bond yields, which trade in anticipation of future events, had already been on the rise before the 2024 election. The 10-year Treasury rose by nearly a full percentage point from a low in mid-September 2024 until Inauguration Day, as traders priced in the possibility of faster growth, rising inflation and more debt. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Bessent in Tuesday's remarks downplayed short-term bond moves as he touted the U.S. market, saying, "what happens over a month doesn't matter."
"If there were a problem in the U.S. bond market ... then people would be selling U.S. bonds and buying other countries' bonds," Bessent told CNBC on Monday. "But we are the best-performing market."
Government bond yields broadly rose across global markets on Tuesday, with some countries seeing borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.
Uncertainty over the Fed's policy direction dovetailed with increased geopolitical turmoil — especially in Iran, where U.S. military strikes around the Strait of Hormuz recently resumed after a hiatus. The conflict has raised oil prices, stoking inflation concerns and adding upward pressure on bond yields.
Asked during a press gaggle later Tuesday morning about a spike in Japan's 10-year yield, Bessent said it is "difficult to deconstruct all the aspects that are behind any financial market move, since it's such a multivariable market."
"We have seen kind of global the yield rise," he added. But he noted that he has spoken with Japanese finance officials in recent days, and said, "I think that the Japanese are taking the right steps."
Bessent did not respond to a shouted question about the rise in the U.S. 10-year yield.

Burnham promises to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ in first Commons speech as PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:52:32 UTC
03:52:32 KST

Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.
In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.
The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”
The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.
Shortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances.
The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.
Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities.
His plans are set against a tough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn.
In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:
- 
  Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending.
- 
  Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.
- 
  Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”
- 
  Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”
Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.
The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.
“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.
“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.
“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”
He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”
The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.
“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”
In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.
“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”
Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.
Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.
Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.
The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services.
Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.
The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.

The Russian Embassy in Germany on Tuesday rejected as “unsubstantiated, absurd and irrational” Berlin’s allegations over an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport.
The embassy on Telegram accused Berlin of systematically dismantling the framework of Russian-German cooperation.
It said that Russia’s ambassador to Germany was summoned to the Foreign Ministry and presented with a protest over Russia’s alleged involvement in an explosive-laden drone incident on Aug. 5.
It said German authorities blamed Russia without presenting evidence and announced sanctions over what Berlin called Moscow’s “escalating hybrid attacks.”
The measures include closing Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn by Sept. 18 and terminating a 2011 Russian-German agreement covering cultural and information centers, which includes the Russian House in Berlin.
The Russian ambassador rejected the allegations, calling the measures an “unprecedented escalation” in bilateral relations and warning they would have consequences for which Germany would bear full responsibility.
“He emphasized that the hastily concocted provocation at Leipzig Airport serves exclusively the goals of the Kyiv regime, the militaristic wing of the European political class, and the magnates of the military-industrial complex interested in fueling the Ukrainian conflict,” the statement said.
Separately, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Germany would receive a “fitting response” to its decision to close the Russian House and Russia’s Consulate General.
In remarks to state news agency Tass, Zakharova accused Berlin of using a “far-fetched pretext” to further escalate bilateral relations and said Germany had provided no convincing evidence to support its allegations against Russia.
“Both the Russian House and our Consulate General in Bonn have long been harassing the ruling elite. Now they've come up with a pretext. Well, they'll get a fitting response,” she emphasized.
Zakharova also accused Germany of fueling the Ukraine war and participating in what she called terrorist attacks, saying Moscow would respond to all “anti-Russian” decisions.
The statement came after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month and unveiled extensive measures and sanctions against Moscow.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said at a news conference in Berlin that investigators had found the plot was planned by Russian intelligence services and carried out by low-level operatives.
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, speaking at the same briefing, said he had summoned Russia’s ambassador to deliver Berlin’s protest and notify Moscow of the government’s response.
“The Russian Consulate General in Bonn will close on September 18. The agreement regarding the Russian House in Berlin is being terminated,” Wadephul said. The Soviet-era cultural center in the capital has long been viewed by Western officials as a possible cover for intelligence work.

Kabir Adeniyi
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
At least 57 primary schools are currently not functioning in Nigeria’s northeastern Borno State due to insecurity, while about 80 students abducted during attacks on schools remain in captivity, according to local education authorities.
The situation was disclosed by Fasuma Askira, education secretary of Askira-Uba Local Government Area, where only 56 of the 113 primary schools are currently operating.
On May 15, terrorists attacked Mussa Central Primary School and abducted dozens of children. Although the exact number remains disputed, the Borno State Government has more recently put the number of missing pupils at about 44.
On June 29, insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were sitting for a National Examinations Council examination. Some students were subsequently rescued, but 36 students and a teacher remained in captivity.
Combining the latest government estimate from Mussa with the verified Lassa figure puts the number of students still in captivity at about 80.
As of Aug. 31, the children abducted from Mussa had spent 108 days in captivity, while the Lassa students had been held for 63 days.
Simon Waindu, whose daughter is among the Lassa students, said none of the children had returned and that families had received no information about their rescue.
Meanwhile, authorities have closed schools in communities affected by insecurity. Authorities have also proposed the deployment of community vigilantes around schools when classes resume, while soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.
The latest developments come after Anadolu reported in June that terrorists abducted six women and two babies near the scene of a school attack in Borno state.
The incident occurred shortly after suspected insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking examinations, further highlighting the vulnerability of civilians around schools in the conflict-affected region.
Nigeria's northeastern states have faced more than a decade of insurgency, with Boko Haram and ISWAP among the armed groups responsible for attacks, abductions and displacement.
The continued captivity of students and closure of schools raise concerns over the long-term educational consequences of the conflict, particularly for children in communities already affected by displacement and poverty.

A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.
Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.
After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.
“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.
Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.
“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.
Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.
Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.
The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.
A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.

Rescue package to help vulnerable families care for children at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:44:50 UTC
03:44:50 KST

Rescue package for in-home child care to ensure vulnerable families can access support
In short:
The federal government has announced an $11 million rescue package to shore up the in-home childcare sector.
Earlier this year the ABC revealed the sector was on the verge of collapse, with about 1,000 vulnerable children at risk of losing care.
What's next?
The sector says the support package is "monumental" but has warned big challenges remain for it to reach its potential.
Australia's in-home childcare sector has welcomed an $11 million federal government rescue package, but there is criticism some operators will gain more generous support than others.
In-home care is designed to support families who cannot access mainstream child care, because they live in remote areas, work nights or care for children with complex medical needs, serious disability or child protection concerns.
Earlier this year, the ABC revealed anger from vulnerable families as services came close to shutting down.
In an interview with ABC News, Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said in-home care was "an absolutely vital service".
Senator Walsh recently met one-year-old Cece and her mother, Jennifer, who lived south of Sydney.
Cece was diagnosed with a rare medical condition and doctors recommended she avoid mainstream child care.
"Initially, it was like, 'My God, what are we going to do?'" Jennifer said.
"In today's society, my husband and I both need to work and I love my job and I love what I do."
Jennifer described the program as "game-changing", allowing her to return to work while Cece was cared for by a qualified educator at home.
However, the sector has shrunk significantly in recent years, due to higher costs and unique challenges of delivering early learning in family homes, making the program out of reach for many.
The sector was excluded from a government subsidy scheme introduced in 2024 to cover a historic 15 per cent pay rise for long day care workers.
That meant families had to pay more for in-home care to cover the wage increase themselves.
More than 70 per cent of families in the scheme reduced their hours or withdrew because they could not afford to absorb the rising costs.
The federal government has come under pressure in Senate estimates from the Liberals, Greens and crossbenchers who warned children could be put at risk if the in-home care sector collapsed.
Senator Walsh announced the $11 million support package after hearing from many families including Cece and Jennifer's.
The package includes $5 million for Sustainability Support Grants, $3.4 million to deliver a 15 per cent pay rise to in-home care employees and $2.7 million in further grants for operational support for the sector.
"The in-home care sector is quite unique," Senator Walsh said.
"We wanted to make sure that we knew that the pay rise would be able to be passed on and when we were confident about that we extended the pay rise to the in-home care sector."
Relief package 'monumental' but some workers will miss out
Nicole Morgan, president of the Australian Home Childcare Association (AHCA), has been an in-home care provider for 19 years and described the announcement of the sustainability grants as "monumental".
She said she had been on the cusp of closing in June as it was no longer financially viable to continue operating.
"[The grant] meant that I was able to stay in the program. Not only me, but several other in-home care service providers that were going to close as well and not be working in the new financial year, have remained open."
While all have welcomed the sustainability funding, some operators are angry the worker retention payment, to cover pay rises for carers, is not available to contractors, who make up 70 per cent of the in-home care sector.
That means just five of the 21 agencies qualify for the worker retention payment, which has been available to long day care operators since 2024.
Ms Morgan warned the impact could be "catastrophic".
"We feel the inequity has created a division within the sector that is really unfair," she said.
"What we might find is that those educators will leave those providers. Those families will not be able to afford the cost of care and those providers, therefore, will close," she said.
Senator Walsh said providers employing staff as contractors were still being supported.
"Our In-Home Care Sustainability Support Grants provide tailored support to this specialised sector, and can be used, in line with the grant guidelines, to help providers retain contractors.
"The Worker Retention Payment is also available where providers and educators choose to move from a contractor to an employee model."
Long-term future for home care still to be resolved
Ms Morgan said the in-home care program was "massively underutilised", operating at about 35 per cent occupancy due to the extra costs associated with delivering care in the family home.
She said there were currently 1,370 children accessing the program, with the potential for the program to help 3,200, under the government cap.
Over the past decade, the sector has shrunk from about 70 providers to 21.
Three separate reviews from the federal government, Productivity Commission and consumer watchdog have identified affordability as a barrier to access.
Another and wider-ranging federal government review is underway, which the sector hopes will ensure it is "sustainable" and "viable" into the future.
"The childcare subsidy needs to reflect the cost of care for in-home care and the differences that we have," Ms Morgan said.
Senator Walsh foreshadowed the sector receiving further support after the review was completed.
"The Service Delivery Price Project is due later this year and will provide important input into our plans for universal early education and care, including future support for the In-Home Care sector," she said.

Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:43:38 UTC
03:43:38 KST

An explosives-laden drone aimed at a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport was part of a Russian state operation, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on 1 September.
Germany has moved from suspecting foreign sabotage to formally blaming Russia for the Leipzig attack. The finding has prompted diplomatic and security measures against Moscow while the criminal investigation continues.
Police investigations, the attack pattern, and intelligence findings established Russian responsibility, Dobrindt said. The drones' configuration, components, explosives, and detonation systems resembled those used in other Russian hybrid operations—covert sabotage and disruption below the threshold of open war—and in Russia's war against Ukraine, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said.
The first drone, carrying explosives, was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August and defused. Investigators believe a DHL freighter may have collided with a second drone while aborting its landing after the airport closed; that drone was never recovered. A third drone was found on 14 August in a field at Kabelsketal, where investigators subsequently discovered roughly 50 grams of suspected military explosive.
Leipzig/Halle is an international freight hub used by Ukrainian Antonov aircraft and NATO's strategic airlift program, through which allies charter heavy transport aircraft to move oversized military cargo.
Berlin will close the Bonn consulate on 18 September, end the operating agreement for the Russian House, a Moscow-backed cultural center, tighten entry controls for Russian nationals, seek to add more targets to EU sanctions lists, and pressure Russia's shadow fleet—opaquely owned tankers used to move Russian oil outside Western restrictions. Wadephul also summoned the Russian ambassador. Russia's Berlin embassy will remain open.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Interfax that Moscow would respond to Germany's “anti-Russian action,” without specifying how.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance stood in full solidarity with Germany, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described Berlin's measures as a strong response.
Dobrindt said Germany expects further Russian hybrid attacks. The Leipzig incident follows a widening campaign of suspected Russian sabotage across Europe, including a 2024 incendiary-device attack at the same airport that Western security officials suspected Russian intelligence organized.
How the Leipzig attack unfolded
Euromaidan Press reported on 12 August, citing Die Zeit, that footage showed an explosives-laden quadcopter striking the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov An-124 before falling without detonating. The article also noted that a US Defense Department official told CNN that Washington assessed the drone belonged to Russian intelligence.
On 25 August, EP reported, citing Tagesschau’s NDR/WDR/SZ investigation, that investigators had expanded the case to three drones and found the third with suspected military explosive nearby in Kabelsketal, 10 days after the original attempt.

Social media algorithm opt-in would curb 'manosphere', says advocate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:43:18 UTC
03:43:18 KST

Algorithm opt-in best way to stop big tech serving manosphere content to young men, says advocate
In short:
Chanel Contos is warning tech giants could design their way around weaker attempts to rein in harmful social media algorithms.
The Teach Us Consent chief executive used a National Press Club speech to further her push for algorithmic feeds to be "opt-in".
What's next?
The federal government is considering giving users greater control over content served online, while draft digital duty of care laws are due to be released later this month.
Consent advocate Chanel Contos is urging the federal government to pursue an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds because it will be "too easy" for tech giants to design their way around weaker reforms.
Ms Contos made the case for reining in harmful algorithms, which she said were exposing young people to misogynistic manosphere content and fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia, during a speech to the National Press Club in Canberra today.
She laid out a vision where all Australians would be given the "choice" to turn algorithms on in their feeds, but the "default" experience would be akin to retro 2016-era social media.
In this version of the platforms, users would see posts in chronological order, and only from people or accounts they chose to follow.
Explore-type pages that recommend content would be based on a broad national average, rather than hyper-personalised material determined by the individual's scrolling habits.
"I think political will is the only thing stopping us getting over the line,"
Ms Contos said having an on-off switch for algorithms put power into users' hands and could act as a "safety net" for people to fall back on as social media continues to evolve in the future.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has flagged support for giving Australians more control over the content they are served online but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.
"In response to community concern about the impact of algorithms, we are considering options to ensure people have greater control over what they receive on their devices," Mr Albanese said.
In her speech, Ms Contos argued an opt-out system for algorithms would be a "first step" and congratulated the government for seeking to address the issue.
"However, opt-in algorithms would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she said.
"This is crucial, and the detail in any reform will determine its success."
Algorithms are the automated systems used by social media platforms to decide which posts, videos and other content a user sees and in what order, based on factors such as their behaviour and apparent interests.
Ms Contos, who is the founder and chief executive of advocacy group Teach Us Consent, launched the "fix our feeds" campaign, which calls for the government to mandate an "opt-in" for algorithms, in December last year.
Labor has since indicated an interest in addressing the broader issue to further complement its laws banning Australians aged under 16 from holding any social media account.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said "deliberately opaque" algorithmic recommender systems had allowed social media companies to influence Australian culture "for better or worse".
"Online harm has real-world consequences," she said.
"If we want to prevent harm, we must fix platforms that reward it."
Consent education 'not an attack on men and boys'
Asked about the manosphere, Nationals leader Matt Canavan had said he understood the "fury" but suggested boys were driven to that content by the "feminisation" of the school curriculum.
"I think we've got to have a deep, hard look of why young boys are attracted to this stuff online," he said.
"It is terrible. It is toxic. But … a big reason for that, in my view, is they're sick and tired of getting lectures about how bad men are at school, and so they go to other places."
Senator Canavan said a solution might be more male role models in schools, including teachers.
"I just worry some of the solutions here don't really understand what goes in a young boy's mind," he said.
Ms Contos said there was a "missing piece of the puzzle" in Senator Canavan's view, which was that boys and men did not naturally "want" to engage in misogynistic content and were instead pushed there by profit-driven algorithms.
"There is a much bigger system at play than small conversations in school and that sort of thing," she said.
"It is a multi-billion-dollar industry right now profiting off making young boys and men feel like they need to aspire to be something that is almost wholly unrealistic and then telling them the fact you haven't gotten here is because of these issues, usually one of them involves women or misogynistic rhetoric around that."
Ms Contos said the Australian national curriculum in 2022 introduced consent education in a gender neutral way that gave students the opportunity to periodically talk about their own boundaries.
"This content is ultimately to promote healthy intimacy and to reduce violence. It is absolutely not an attack on men and boys at all,"
"But we need to hold all that while acknowledging that sexual violence is majority perpetrated by boys and men and that shouldn't be shameful for the individual, but it should mean they are willing to be part of the system to change that statistic."
Digital duty of care next on Labor's agenda
Ms Wells has been developing a digital duty of care, which would be a legal obligation on online platforms to proactively identify and reduce foreseeable risks of harm to their users.
It reverses the current situation that relies mainly on users reporting harmful content after something has gone wrong.
An exposure draft of the legislation is due to be released later this month, with Ms Contos describing the "overall strength" of those reforms as "critical" to their success.
Loading...
"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine," she said.
In her speech, Ms Contos linked algorithm-driven harm to the "uphill battle" schools are facing in their attempts to teach consent to young students.
Ms Contos said a yearly class had "little hope" of changing the attitudes responsible for the current culture of sexual violence in schools while an "addictive content producing machine" simultaneously targeted teens with a "contradictory message".
How algorithms fuel the manosphere
She outlined how "manosphere" is not simply a broad term describing online communities that hold male supremacy ideologies, but a money-making venture facilitated by algorithms.
Ms Contos said young men online seeking community, belonging or self-improvement advice are "targeted" with content that blames women for their "misfortune".
This content also reinstates "harmful and outdated" gender roles, like the idea women should not leave the house without their male partner, hold jobs or earn their own money.
"Boys and men have valid concerns about the economy, and their relationships with partners and friends," she said.
"From these concerns, an industry has jumped onto a market opportunity, and unfortunately, misogyny is at the heart of its business model."
Ms Contos described how young men engaging in "harmless" workout or motivational videos are "very quickly" served content promoting the idea that emotional control, material wealth and dominance "especially over women" are "markers of male wealth".
She pointed to research showing men who subscribe to those sorts of beliefs are twice as likely to binge-drink, six times as likely to problem gamble and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts.
They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner, according to the Man Box study.

Government agrees €92.5 billion budget with €12.4 billion deficit
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:39:30 EEST
03:39:30 KST

Finland’s government has agreed a €92.5 billion budget for 2027, including a €12.4 billion deficit, tax cuts and about €1 billion in additional spending savings.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the government had completed its final budget negotiations of the parliamentary term in one day and argued that the economy had returned to growth.
“We have now got Finland back on its feet,” Orpo said at a press conference after the talks.
Finance Minister Riikka Purra said the government would continue with spending reductions agreed earlier. Savings next year include cuts to organisation grants, integration spending and public administration.
Total spending cuts included in the budget amount to about €4.8 billion before taking account of other expenditure increases and tax reductions, according to figures presented by Purra.
The government will also proceed with previously agreed tax changes. Corporate tax will fall from 20% to 18%, while income tax for low- and middle-income earners will be reduced. Purra said the combined tax reductions amount to about €1.7 billion.
The government will abandon a planned tax benefit for data centres. It will also allow municipalities to introduce a voluntary tourist tax under new framework legislation.
Debt servicing costs remain a major pressure on the budget. Interest expenditure is expected to reach €4.4 billion next year, compared with less than €1 billion in 2022.
Purra said higher debt levels and increased interest rates had driven the increase. Defence, security and health and social care costs are also adding to spending.
The government also agreed additional funding for shelters, forests, the justice system, sports facilities and measures to combat African swine fever.
Orpo said the government expected employment to improve during the autumn as economic growth continued.
The opposition criticised the package.
Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela said the budget failed to address Finland’s unemployment problem and attacked the corporate tax cut.
She also criticised reductions in funding for social and health organisations and higher health care client fees, arguing that the measures would place more pressure on low-income households.
The government rejected calls for further fiscal tightening during the budget talks. Orpo said the coalition had already agreed almost €1 billion in additional adjustment and wanted to focus on growth and employment.
Purra said further action would follow if required by the European Commission.
