Labor funds post third-largest monthly loss on record in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

Labor funds administered by the Ministry of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Funds reported the third largest monthly losses ever, losing over NT$240 billion in July amid global volatility caused by worries over corporate earnings and geopolitical unease, data released by the bureau showed yesterday.
Citing the data, the bureau said the labor funds incurred NT$246.36 billion in losses in July, after NT$77.1 billion in gains in June.
Due to July’s heavy losses, the bureau said, the accumulated gains in the value of assets in the funds’ portfolios and income on investment totaled about NT$1.96 trillion from January to July, down from about NT$2.20 trillion during January-June.
Photo: Li Ching-hui, Taipei Times
In addition to worries about corporate earnings amid fears over an AI bubble and lingering tensions in the Middle East in July, the bureau said global financial markets were also affected by uncertainties created by U.S. monetary and trade policies.
However, global financial markets still posted significant gains in the first seven months of this year with the Taiex, the Taiwan Stock Exchange’s benchmark index, soaring 48.88 percent and the MSCI World Index rising 11.33 percent. In contrast, the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Bond Index dropped 0.75 percent.
As of the end of July, the combined value of the funds managed by the bureau, including the Labor Pension Fund, the Labor Retirement Fund, the Labor Insurance Fund, and the Employment Insurance Fund, stood at NT$9.08 trillion, according to bureau data.
The seven-month gains translated into a rate of return of 25.03 percent from January to July, down from 28.46 percent during January-June, according to the bureau.
The bureau said 54.63 percent of its investments were made overseas from January to June, while the remaining 45.37 percent were invested in the domestic market.
The labor funds managed by the bureau have various functions, mainly aimed at helping workers. In particular, the Labor Pension Fund, collects contributions from employers and employees every month and is managed by the bureau to boost the asset value, in a bid to help employees save and invest for their retirement.
The value of assets in the Labor Pension Fund, launched in 2015, totaled NT$5.97 trillion as of the end of July, the highest among all labor funds, and its rate of return for the January-July period stood at 24.58 percent, the bureau said.
The Labor Retirement Fund, which has been in place since 1984, had about NT$1.20 trillion in assets as of the end of July, with a rate of return of 35.02 percent for the seven months, the bureau added.
Meanwhile, the Bureau of Public Service Pension Fund said yesterday the Public Service Pension Fund, which the bureau manages, recorded NT$292.49 billion in gains in the seven months, equal to a rate of return of 21.64 percent.

Does inflammation affect mental health?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:33 UTC
01:46:33 KST

Inflammation is the immune system’s response to injury or infection. If you cut yourself and the area becomes red and swollen, that’s inflammation: immune cells are rushing to fight germs and repair tissue.
But inflammation can also occur in the body during illnesses, and a low level of inflammation can arise from obesity or aging.
“A marker of that inflammation tends to be elevated cytokines in people’s blood,” says Daniel M Davis, head of life sciences at Imperial College London and author of Immune Health: A Myth-Busting Guide. “They’re the molecules immune cells use to communicate with each other.”
Photo: Reuters
There are more than 100 types of cytokines in your body, and some affect the brain.
“If you have a fever, it’s not just physical, you’re also mentally affected,” Davis says. “Some cytokines influence how you feel.”
Studies of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have found that cytokine-blocking anti-inflammatory drugs can also improve mood. Scans suggest this may be because blocking cytokines changes activity in the brain.
A study of nearly 5,000 children found that those with higher than average levels of the cytokine IL-6 in their blood at the age of nine, with no sign of depression, were more likely to suffer depression at 18.
Another study, this time of adults, found a correlation between the development of an immune-related disease and a previous diagnosis of psychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety.
Scientists don’t yet know enough to use this knowledge to treat conditions such as depression or anxiety.
“Several lines of evidence point to an overlap of immune and mental health, but we haven’t disentangled this enough to know who could benefit, and exactly what part of the immune system we could safely target to improve people’s mental health,” Davis says.

The number of accounts created to trade in the local stock market continued to hit a new high at the end of last month as the TAIEX staged a significant rebound in the month, the Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) said yesterday.
About 14.70 million trading accounts had been opened as of the end of last month, up 91,429 from the end of July, as the TAIEX bounced back by 3,008.72 points, or 6.98 percent, after slumping 6.52 percent the previous month, data compiled by the TWSE showed.
The local main board fared well last month, returning to the 46,000-point mark as bargain hunters turned active to pick up stocks hammered by concerns over massive artificial intelligence (AI) investments and by deleveraging among tech stocks a month earlier.
Photo: CNA
Of the new trading accounts opened last month, the number owned by investors aged 19 and under totaled 40,214, the highest increase among all age groups, while the number of trading accounts opened by investors aged 20-30 grew 24,032 in the month, TWSE data showed.
Investors aged 30 and under accounted for 70.26 percent of the total new trading accounts opened last month, indicating the local stock market continued to trend toward a younger demographic, especially with many parents starting to help their children set up financial plans in advance.
As of the end of last month, investors aged 19 and under had 868,888 trading accounts, up 40,214 from July, those aged 20-30 had 1.91 million trading accounts, up 24,032, and those aged 31-40 had 2.38 million trading accounts, up 9,989.
Those in the 41-50 age group had 2.73 million trading accounts as of the end of last month, up 9,218 from July, while those aged 51-60 had 2.41 million trading accounts, up 5,401, and those aged 61 and above had 4.28 million trading accounts, up 1,267.

China’s silence after Tibet flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:31 UTC
01:46:31 KST

The devastation in Tibet from flooding caused by a glacial collapse in the Himalayas was immediate and profound. Entire communities were left in shock, families were torn apart and countless lives were disrupted. That was followed by deafening silence from the Chinese authorities. No official tally of the missing, no acknowledgment of the dead — only a void filled with rumor, grief and suspicion.
Disasters demand transparency. The first responsibility of the state is to inform its citizens of the scale of tragedy. By withholding that information, Beijing reduces Tibetan lives to abstractions, erasing their suffering from public record.
The refusal to announce casualties fits a long-standing pattern of Chinese authorities in Tibet suppressing information whenever Tibetans suffer disproportionately. Whether it is uprisings, self-immolations or environmental disasters, the state’s instinct is to conceal rather than confront.
By silencing reports of Tibetan deaths, Beijing avoids international scrutiny and domestic sympathy. To acknowledge Tibetan suffering would be to admit that Tibetans are distinct, resilient and enduring — qualities the state seeks to erase.
Behind the silence are families waiting for word that will never come. Mothers searching for children swept away by icy water, elders mourning neighbors buried under mud. The absence of official acknowledgment compounds the trauma, leaving Tibetans not only bereaved, but also invisible. The invisibility is itself a form of violence — a calculated erasure of Tibetan existence.
The flooding triggered by the glacial collapse is not just a Tibetan tragedy; it is a warning to the world. Tibet’s fragile environment, already destabilized by climate change and reckless development, is a harbinger of crises to come. If the Chinese state refuses transparency in this situation, what hope is there for honest reporting on disasters that affect millions across Asia?
The cover-up in Tibet is a rehearsal for broader denial.

Taiwan’s semiconductor capabilities have helped create networks around the world, allowing countries to leverage their respective strengths and cooperate on research, development and production, he said.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
Such connections can provide mutual support in the face of natural disasters, pandemics and geopolitical crises, he added.
The global semiconductor industry, with a market estimated to be worth more than US$1.5 trillion this year, encompasses IC design, equipment, materials, advanced manufacturing, testing and packaging, requiring investment from businesses and countries across each segment, Lai said.
He said that Nvidia Corp has invested and procured more than NT$3 trillion (US$94.84 billion) of goods and services annually in Taiwan, while Micron Technology Inc has invested more than NT$1.4 trillion and Advanced Micro Devices Inc has expanded its research investment to more than NT$300 billion.

Xi’s agenda prompts law: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:28 UTC
01:46:28 KST

China’s changes to its National Defense Mobilization Law to prepare for a rapid transition to a war footing are aimed at helping Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) fulfill his “historic mission of national unification,” a Taiwanese official said yesterday.
Xi believes in military dominance and is working to improve China’s wartime resilience, said the official, who is familiar with cross-strait relations and declined to be named.
While Taiwan is focusing on whole-of-society resilience, China is building “offensive resilience” to ensure its attacks face no obstacles or international sanctions, and can achieve its war aims, they said.
Photo: AP
Taiwan is unsurprised by China’s war preparations, they said, adding that democratic allies should closely monitor its next moves, particularly its wartime mobilization plans.
Beijing is also continuing its baseless accusations that Taiwan is seeking independence and Japan is reviving militarism, the official said.
Beijing is writing laws and mobilizing national resources to concentrate its strength for major undertakings, but could also “do something foolish” amid nationalist fervor, posing a global and geopolitical threat, they said.
Xi has few achievements to show for his tenure, as China’s economy is struggling, its people are living under difficult conditions and unemployment among young people is high, they said.
The cheapest way to maintain his grip on power is to appeal to nationalism, the official said, warning that excessive nationalism leads to the export of military dominance.
Nationalism cannot “rejuvenate the Chinese nation,” but would only result in tragedy, they said, adding that Taiwan must improve its defenses.
The new version of the legislation is to take effect on Oct. 1, marking the first major revision since it was enacted in 2010.
The amendments define national defense mobilization as measures taken in response to threats to national sovereignty, unification, territorial integrity, security and development interests, including efforts to ensure rapid transition between peacetime and wartime, and convert economic and social resources into national defense capabilities.
The law stipulates that once China declares a “national defense mobilization status,” it can convert peacetime resources, including personnel, transportation, communications, energy, healthcare and media, into wartime resources under strict government control.
The State Council of China and the Chinese Central Military Commission determine the size, type and method of reservist recruitment based on mobilization needs, the revised law says.
Reservists are required to participate in training, while Chinese men aged 18 to 60 and women aged 18 to 55 are required to perform national defense duties, it says.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director of Tunghai University’s Center for China Studies, said that the amendments reflect the concept of “total mobilization,” with China using its legal system to institutionalize its sovereignty claims over Taiwan, the use of force and national mobilization.
The changes could allow Beijing to portray military action against Taiwan as an effort to “safeguard national unification in accordance with the law,” Hung said.
From the perspective of China’s legal warfare, the law was not specifically designed to target Taiwan, he said.
However, by defining “unification” as a national development interest to be safeguarded through defense mobilization, the law has a clear legal warfare dimension for Taiwan, he said.
In assessing whether China is preparing to use force against Taiwan, it is important not to focus solely on military exercises and troop deployments, Hung said.
Signs of wartime mobilization across China’s economy, industries and society could also serve as important early warning indicators, he added.

Nepal needs more giant dams to avert disastrous floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:25 UTC
01:46:25 KST

In the popular imagination, there is only one threat to picturesque mountain landscapes that can compete with the destruction wrought by flood disasters like the torrent that swept through valleys on the Nepalese-Chinese border: dams.
These concrete behemoths replace the occasional catastrophic natural inundation of such regions with one that is permanent and artificial. Pristine river valleys disappear beneath reservoirs. Communities are forcibly relocated, their lives uprooted.
Those criticisms are true. However, the events of the past week, with 955 dead and more than 4,000 still missing, should be a warning that the imagined counterfactual is false. Roads, tourism, trade and settlement are already transforming remote mountain communities.
Meanwhile, warming is destabilizing the very soil on which homes are built, and sparking disastrous floods. The question is not whether such places will change, but whether the development will include the infrastructure needed to manage their increasingly volatile rivers.
The damage caused by some large dam projects is real. India’s efforts to build a string of reservoirs on the Narmada River displaced hundreds of thousands of often poor, tribal and low-caste families. That injustice sparked a protest movement championed by novelist Arundhati Roy, and helped give hydro such a bad name that multilateral development banks largely stopped funding it in the 1990s.
In retrospect, this was a terrible outcome. Hydroelectricity is one of the few forms of generation to match the rock-bottom prices of wind and solar. (In the US and oil exporting countries, gas turbines can achieve similar prices since the fuel is being provided at negligible cost. However, that is not the case in countries that depend on LNG.) When it is built with a storage reservoir, it also provides on-demand, zero-carbon electricity that can be stored from one month to the next. Such dams also help to control the floodwaters that can do such grievous damage to downstream communities.
A potent example happened in 2018 on the other side of the Tibetan plateau. After a landslide blocked part of the upper Yangtze River and formed a vast unstable lake, dam managers at six reservoirs downstream proactively dumped 1.3 billion cubic meters of water so they would have enough capacity to absorb an outburst flood. Along with other measures, that appears to have substantially reduced the damage done.
The same result has shown up in Europe. Storage dams in Austrian river valleys in recent decades have reduced extreme water levels by about one-third relative to their previous peaks, according to a 2022 study.
The withdrawal of funding from aid donors in rich countries did not stop hydro being built. With the World Bank sitting on the sidelines in the 1990s, China self-financed the Three Gorges Dam, the world’s biggest power station. Africa’s largest, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, was also largely paid for out of Ethiopia’s meager domestic budget, amid objections from neighboring countries. Tanzania is now doing the same.
Nepal itself is going through a mini-boom, but it is being driven by private developers building so-called run-of-river generators — a sort of water-wheel on a massive scale that cannot store significant volumes.
About 90 percent of hydro in Nepal is this type, which provides little of the on-demand power or flood-control benefits of storage dams. The workers missing or miraculously rescued from flooded construction tunnels after last week’s disaster were all building run-of-river plants.
The funding drought from multilateral donors has been remarkably persistent. As far back as 2004, the World Bank argued the pendulum had swung too far against hydro and vowed to reverse this trend. Despite that, the sector has failed to benefit from a resurgence in spending on renewable energy.
Commitments for hydro comprised just 2.8 percent of energy funding by major development banks in 2022, the lowest share since 2009. Since the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change, they have promised US$8.67 billion. Even fossil-fuel production and generation have done better, at about US$12 billion.
That is a perverse outcome. Hydro these days is likely being crowded out by more bankable solar, wind and battery plants, but the whole point of development banks is to finance projects that do not pencil out well in raw cashflow terms. It is hard to put a dollar value on the lives saved and livelihoods preserved if a once-in-a-century flood can be prevented by the sort of water engineering rich nations take for granted. The benefits are nonetheless real.
Nepal’s vast natural water resource and relatively small population should be allowing it to earn good money selling electrons to its energy-hungry neighborhood. And yet until 2023, it was importing more power from India than it was exporting. A transmission line to Bangladesh only went into operation last year. Even amid the current building boom, it has completed just 3.4 gigawatts of the 42 gigawatts of hydro that is economically viable, with another 4.3 gigawatts under construction.
The question for the future is not whether Nepal will continue to develop its rivers. It is whether the next generation of hydro projects merely extracts electricity with run-of-river, or builds storage dams to give downstream communities greater protection against the consequences of our increasingly deadly climate.
David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy. Previously, he worked for Bloomberg News, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times. It said it would continue to engage with employees through existing channels while respecting applicable legal processes.
The strike threat comes as booming demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) hardware has tightened global supply and lifted profits across the sector.
Micron, the world’s third-largest memory maker, reported record revenue of US$41.46 billion and net income of US$28.24 billion for its fiscal third quarter ended on May 28, as demand for its products surged. The company’s market value was about US$1.10 trillion yesterday.
A strike at Micron would be highly disruptive because Taiwan is the company’s largest manufacturing base, according to authorities in Taipei. They say Micron has invested NT$1.4 trillion (US$43.9 billion) in the island and produces DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips there.
The government-run Central Taiwan Science Park (中部科學園區)administration said last month it was closely monitoring the dispute and had assigned staff to help facilitate contacts between Micron and the unions.
It said a strike could affect workers’ livelihoods, Micron’s operations and potentially Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain and wider economy, adding that it could launch labor-management negotiations or mediation if needed.
The dispute echoes a showdown at Samsung Electronics Co in South Korea, where a planned 18-day strike involving as many as 48,000 union members was called off in May after last-minute negotiations.
That deal created a special bonus pool worth 10.5 percent of the chip division’s operating profit, subject to profitability targets.
Micron’s Taiwanese unions said profit-sharing arrangements at Samsung and SK Hynix Inc had widened the gap between Micron workers and their South Korean counterparts.
For this fiscal year, the unions are seeking an additional one-off bonus payment, arguing that Micron’s existing Incentive Pay Plan (IPP) does not adequately reflect the company’s profitability.
The unions said their proposal would amount to about 83 months’ salary for each Taiwan-based employee.
From next fiscal year, they want the IPP replaced with a system that allocates 15 percent of operating profit to bonuses and distributes payments quarterly rather than annually.
Micron’s IPP determines annual bonuses using company and individual performance measures. The unions said the company had not fully explained how its company-performance metric was calculated and argued that it appeared to track revenue growth more closely than profit.
The unions said Micron had indicated it would keep the existing IPP for this year’s bonus payments while delaying negotiations.
Micron said its compensation structure differs from the profit-sharing model sought by the unions. According to the company, employee pay packages include base salary, annual performance incentives, operational bonuses and equity programs, including stock-purchase and restricted-stock plans.
Silicon photonics would play a dominant role next year and make chip-level co-packaged optics (CPO) packaging possible, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) said yesterday. “For years, critics questioned the reliability of CPO. The doubts are being thoroughly dismantled by real-world data and market validation,” TSMC vice president of advanced packaging technology development K.C. Hsu (徐國晉) said at a SEMI forum in Taipei. The company is on track to enter production of CPO later this year, Hsu said in another forum arranged by Imec in Taipei yesterday, about four months after TSMC announced its progress in CPO development in May.

Nepal-Tibet floods death toll exceeds 1,000: officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:20 UTC
01:46:20 KST

The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China rose over 1,000 yesterday, authorities said, as rescue teams worked to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Nepal’s disaster agency on Tuesday said that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing, including 261 foreigners.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, Nepalese authorities said. Emergency crews have been using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.
Photo: AP
The disaster that happened on Wednesday last week began with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges, and carried mud and rocks downstream.
Photo: Reuters
Authorities were yesterday still searching for thousands of people who remain unaccounted for. Rescue teams were also working to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes had been damaged or cut off.
For rescuers, the immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.
Nepalese Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said teams assisted by foreign experts were working at several hydropower projects to reach people trapped in blocked tunnels.
Visuals released by the army showed rescue teams entering dark, debris-filled tunnels, wading through mud and water, and climbing over rocks as they searched for signs of life.
Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue missions since the disaster began, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.
“It felt like I was flying over an entirely different landscape,” he said.
Sharma said he has had little opportunity to speak with the people he rescued, but their expressions told him how deeply the disaster had affected them.
“I can see the pain in their eyes. It’s heartbreaking,” he said.
On the Chinese side, rescuers were working in areas affected by the mudslide, particularly in and around the Gyirong Port border crossing, which was completely destroyed.
Some rescuers, aided by search dogs, were looking for any sign of life in gaps among rocks and debris. Other teams were using heavy machinery to try to reopen a major highway leading to Gyirong Port, which would facilitate the delivery of equipment, personnel and supplies to the disaster zone, the Chinese state-run Global Times newspaper reported.

Taitung County Council Deputy Speaker Lin Tsung-han (林琮翰) and six other current and former county councilors were questioned by the Taitung District Prosecutors Office yesterday over allegations that they abused their positions to benefit the family of Taitung County Council Speaker Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華) in the development of the Dongying International Resort.
Independent county councilor Lin Tsan-tian (林參天) alleged during a council interpellation in May that the Taitung County Government had used public funds to build a road to the resort linked to the Wu family. The road, which was originally supposed to be a 3-meter-wide farm road, was expanded to more than 9 meters and also encroached on state-owned land, he said.
Lin said county councilors typically use their discretionary project funds to help local farmers build water tanks or repair small farm roads. However, he said it was highly unusual for multiple councilors to back the same project, raising concerns that the funding was not intended to benefit ordinary farmers but instead amounted to indirect support for a particular family and its related businesses.
Photo: CNA
In July, prosecutors and investigators launched a probe into alleged abuse of office for personal gain. Three county government officials and Wu’s aide have since been detained.
Prosecutors yesterday morning entered the Taitung County Council chambers, where three councilors were asked to report to the prosecutors office, while the others were taken from their residences for questioning, a source said.
Of the seven councilors questioned, six are members of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), while one is a member of the People First Party.
The prosecutors office moved to question the councilors yesterday, a day before the Taitung County Council was due to formally convene, as the start of the regular session could potentially shield councilors from questioning.

Man found guilty of murdering Tupac
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:17 UTC
01:46:17 KST

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was on Monday found guilty by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of chart-topping rapper Tupac Shakur.
Thirty years after the rap legend’s death, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.
“Count one, murder with use of a deadly weapon, guilty of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon,” the foreperson of the jury announced to the court.
Photo: Reuters
Davis, who faces possible life in prison without parole, addressed US Judge Carli Kierny after the verdict was announced and stated his intention to appeal.
The one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips was accused of ordering the Sept. 7, 1996, killing of the hip-hop artist after his nephew had been beaten by members of Shakur’s entourage at a Las Vegas casino.
“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. “So, what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later, prosecutors said.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records cofounder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of the US’ most celebrated cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.
Davis, whose Crips were one of a patchwork of rival gangs that ran parts of Los Angeles in the 1990s, is the only person to have been charged in connection with the shooting of Shakur.
Sentencing is scheduled for Oct. 13.
The investigation into Shakur’s murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis’ memoirs were published in 2019.
Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur’s murder — in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, Compton Street Legend.
He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
Palal played clips from Davis’ various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.
Michael Sanft, Davis’ defense attorney, characterized his client’s confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact,” Sanft told the jury. “But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting.”
Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur’s murder other than his own statements.
In the run-up to the trial, Davis’ lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.
Shakur, who was 25 when he died, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast.
Known for hits such as California Love and All Eyez on Me, Shakur — the son of a Black Panther — was raised in Harlem, New York, and Baltimore, Maryland, but quickly became the epitome of California hip-hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

Doctor accused of defrauding 424 patients of NT$18m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:17 UTC
01:46:17 KST

Weight-loss doctor Wang Ming-yu (王銘嶼) has been indicted for allegedly defrauding 424 patients out of a total of NT$18.02 million (US$569,658) by charging for a surgical device that prosecutors said was never used during their procedures.
The Kaohsiung District Prosecutors’ Office said Wang was indicted on charges including fraud, document forgery and violations of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act (藥事法) and the Medical Devices Act (醫療器材管理法).
From December 2024, Wang was responsible for gastrointestinal surgery, mainly weight-loss procedures, at Antai Hospital in Kaohsiung, and was appointed vice president last year, the indictment said.
Photo: Huang Chia-ling, Taipei Times
Wang allegedly purchased medical devices used for open abdominal surgery for more than NT$450,000 last year without approval from the central health authorities, prosecutors said.
He also purchased five boxes of laparoscopic equipment from a Chinese company for more than NT$200,000 that same year, they said.
Wang allegedly told 424 patients undergoing laparoscopic gastric reduction combined with intestinal bypass surgery that they would need to pay an additional NT$42,500 for a disposable wireless ultrasonic surgical device, known as “Maxima,” if it was required during their procedures, they said.
Wang allegedly had the device listed as a self-paid medical supply item in consent forms and told the hospital that it would be used during surgery, prompting the hospital to add the item to its medical billing system, prosecutors said.
However, investigators found no evidence that the wireless ultrasonic device had actually been used in the patients’ surgeries. Prosecutors therefore concluded that the 424 patients were charged for the device despite it not being used.
The alleged fraud generated about NT$18.02 million in proceeds, based on the NT$42,500 charge levied on each patient, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors accused Wang of taking advantage of patients’ eagerness to lose weight and their trust in medical professionals to convince them to sign the self-paid medical supply consent forms.
The prosecutors’ office said it has asked the court to impose a heavier sentence, citing the number of fraudulent offenses and Wang’s exploitation of patients.
Wang’s medical license was revoked by the Ministry of Health and Welfare in September last year.
He is also being investigated separately in connection with the deaths of two patients who underwent weight-loss surgery at Antai Hospital. That case remains under investigation.

Lai urges Europe to sign investment, tax agreements with Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:16 UTC
01:46:16 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called on European countries to pursue investment and double-taxation agreements with Taiwan, highlighting growing bilateral investment and opportunities to deepen cooperation in semiconductors and other technologies.
Speaking at the EU Investment Forum in Taipei, Lai said Taiwanese investment in the European Union had surged 650 percent over the past decade compared with the previous 10 years, while bilateral trade reached nearly US $75 billion last year.
"Taiwanese companies are not just focused on individual investment projects. More and more, they’re taking an integrated approach to investment in Europe, with a longer time frame and larger scale," Lai said.
Photo: CNA
He welcomed the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association’s (TEEMA, 台灣電機電子公會) recent announcement that it would establish a technology park in Poland, saying the project would make it easier for Taiwanese companies to invest in the EU and cooperate with local industries.
Lai urged European countries to promote agreements on double taxation and investment with Taiwan, saying they would help unlock greater investment and industrial cooperation.
His remarks came as Taiwan and the EU seek to expand cooperation beyond semiconductor trade and build more resilient technology supply chains.
European Economic and Trade Office head Lutz Gullner said the growing European presence at this year’s Semicon Taiwan trade show reflected a relationship that was becoming more interconnected, technological and broader.
"The ambition is much bigger" than simply buying and selling more semiconductors, Gullner said, adding that Taiwan and the EU aim to build ecosystems together by linking research, design, manufacturing and applications.
Gullner said Taiwan’s strengths in semiconductor manufacturing, design, packaging, materials and equipment complemented Europe’s capabilities in research and technology, as well as its strengths in industries including automotive, energy, telecommunications, health care and aerospace.
He said the European Commission’s proposed Chips Act 2.0, announced in June, would create new opportunities for cooperation with Taiwan.
Lai said combining their respective strengths could help Taiwan and Europe build a more secure, diverse and resilient semiconductor ecosystem.

Nvidia Corp’s US$3.5 billion outlay in MediaTek Inc (聯發科), its largest direct investment outside the US, has thrust a little-known Taiwanese chip designer into the center of the global artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom.
Shares for MediaTek gained 10 percent, or US$20 billion, in market value yesterday after Nvidia agreed to buy bonds convertible into MediaTek shares. It reinvigorated a stock that has tripled in value over the past year as it expanded its footprint in the business of designing AI chips for data centers.
MediaTek has emerged as a key beneficiary of a push by technology companies to design custom semiconductors — often called application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), using its expertise in mobile processors to participate in the AI infrastructure rush.
Photo: Bloomberg
“MediaTek is devoted to developing ASICs, a field Nvidia has eyed for AI development. Their cooperation has boosted market sentiment on the AI era,” Hua Nan Securities Co (華南永昌證券) analyst Kevin Su (蘇俊宏) said in an interview.
With a market value of about US$220 billion, the company is Taiwan’s second-biggest firm after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), which overshadows it with a capitalization near US$2 trillion.
Led by former TSMC chief executive Rick Tsai (蔡力行), MediaTek has worked with Nvidia in the past and has committed to using Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion and other technologies for its future data center customers. The company is looking to boost its AI chip business, saying that it should grow to US$2 billion this year and US$12 billion next year.
“There are different customers needing obviously smaller amounts of computing power,” Tsai said in a television interview on Monday. “This NVLink Fusion again will accelerate their go-to-market capability, and that will be beneficial for them, for Nvidia and for MediaTek.”

The goal is to partner with major tech firms seeking to build their own AI chips. MediaTek is helping Alphabet Inc’s Google manufacture and engineer its custom AI chips for data centers, giving the US company an alternative to Broadcom’s chip-design service.
Nvidia’s financial backing helps build its credibility beyond the praise that Nvidia head Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has heaped upon the Hsinchu-based company.
Nvidia’s investment is part of MediaTek’s US$3.9 billion convertible bond sale, according to terms reported by Bloomberg News on Monday. Alphabet and other investors participated in the round, a spokesperson for MediaTek said in a separate statement, without specifying the investment amounts.
“This investment is a significant strategic endorsement of MediaTek,” Indosuez Wealth Management chief strategist Francis Tan (陳達德) said. “It reinforces MediaTek’s evolution from being primarily associated with smartphone chips into a much broader AI semiconductor company.”

MOFA calls for peace ahead of UN meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) yesterday unveiled its three key messages ahead of the UN General Assembly, including a call for preserving peace in the Taiwan Strait as it stressed that any action undermining the “status quo” in the region is a breach of the UN Charter.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly opens at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday next week. Its General Debate is to take place from Sept. 22 to Sept. 26 and on Sept. 28, under the official theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Baushuan Ger (葛葆萱) told a news conference in Taipei that the theme reflects the challenges that the international community is facing: widening divisions among major economies and great powers, and ongoing conflicts that have eroded the public’s trust in multilateral international mechanisms.
Photo: Chang Chia-ming, Taipei Times
Challenges such as the Russo-Ukrainian war, the conflict in the Middle East, threats to energy and global supply chains, and climate change underscore the necessity and urgency of substantive reforms within the UN, he said.
“As a member of the international community, Taiwan faces the same global challenges as other nations in addition to continuous threats from China, which is escalating tensions across the Taiwan Strait and in the region,” Ger said.
Taiwan needs to participate in multilateral mechanisms, not only to safeguard the rights of Taiwanese and national interests, but also because it has the capacity to contribute to the solution of many issues concerning humanity, he said, adding that the nation is willing to share its experiences with the world.
“However, 23.5 million Taiwanese are still excluded from the UN system due to China’s distortion of the UN Resolution 2758,” Ger said.
China claims the resolution equates to its self-proclaimed “One China” principle, attempting to erase that Taiwan is a sovereign country, improperly depriving the nation of its legitimate right to participate in the UN system, he said.
China has increased its threats in the Taiwan Strait and the Asia-Pacific through “gray zone” tactics such as military intimidation, cyberattacks and economic coercion to unilaterally alter the regional “status quo.”
Beijing also enacted the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law in July to extend its long-arm jurisdiction and transnational repression, violating global democratic values and causing serious international concerns, he said.
“Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are crucial to global security and prosperity,” Ger said, adding that Taipei remains committed to safeguarding cross-strait peace, defending its sovereignty, upholding democracy with like-minded partners and pragmatically promoting its international participation.
He said that Taiwan’s three key messages are:
First, the nation’s meaningful participation in the UN system, allowing it to achieve its sustainable development goals, as “the UN 2758 does not preclude Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the UN system,” he said.
Second, Taiwan stresses its firm commitment to “maintaining the status quo and safeguarding peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait,” he said, adding that the international community and democratic partners support maintaining the “status quo,” while the Taiwanese public backs it strongly.
Third, Taiwan is committed to resolving disputes peacefully and upholding the international legal order, he said.
Any “attempt to or action to disrupt the status quo in the Taiwan Strait violates the UN Charter’s principle of prohibiting the threat or use of force, and requires the peaceful settlement of international disputes,” Ger said.
This year, the MOFA would also ask Taiwan’s diplomatic allies’ permanent representatives to the UN to jointly sign a letter to strongly convey Taiwan’s message to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and speak up for Taiwan during the General Debate, he said.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) would submit an op-ed titled: “Restoring Trust: Taiwan’s Rightful Place in the Free World” to global media to explain the nation’s stance, Ger said.
In addition, MOFA would host side events and local promotional campaigns in New York during the UN General Assembly, while the Legislative Yuan would again dispatch a cross-party delegation of lawmakers to demonstrate strong public support for the government’s efforts, he added.

Woman stabs two in Times Square, killing one person
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:12 UTC
01:46:12 KST

A woman on Monday randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, officials said.
The shooting happened just before 4:30pm next to a New York Police Department (NYPD) substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city’s annual New Year’s Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in New York.
The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference.
Photo: Reuters
Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman, also in the abdomen, Tisch said.
Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died, and the man is in stable condition, police said.
Police did not say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents.
Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives.
Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said.
The woman told them: “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” Tisch said.
The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly toward the officers while waving the knives in front of her.
Two officers then shot the woman, police said.
In the video posted by bystanders, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid.
“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said.
The woman has a “documented mental health history with the NYPD,” which include incidents in 2018 and 2019, but no arrest history with the department, she said.
She did not provide additional details.
Police are investigating. There was no evidence suggesting it was a terrorist attack, Tisch said.
The names of the victims have not been released until their relatives are notified, police said.
“We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions.
The NYPD temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby.
Violent crime has fallen sharply in New York City so far this year, with homicides down 24 percent and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. However, this is the second killing this year in Times Square. A man was fatally stabbed in the same area in May.

Appalachian Trail hiker reclaims record at 91
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:11 UTC
01:46:11 KST

More than 14 million older adults fall every year in the US, perhaps none so often as 91-year-old Dale Sanders.
By his count, Sanders fell 71 times while reclaiming his record as the oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail. Six were what he calls hard falls, including one that led to a brief hospitalization and another just 183m from the finish, but none were enough to permanently divert him from the 3,530km trail that runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine.
The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a “thru-hike” as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders started Sept. 6 last year in West Virginia, hopscotched around with some brief breaks and on Monday finished atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit.
Photo: AP
“I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” he said.
Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 at age 82. Four years later, his 83-year-old friend M.J. Eberhart, also known as Nimblewill Nomad, took the title. However, within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan.
While Sanders’ first journey was easier than he expected, the latest was considerably harder. Despite six months of training, he said he was not in the best condition when he returned to the trail.
“And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say: ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’”
In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands.
“Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.”
Weeks later, his left arm went numb, and he ended up at a Maine hospital. What doctors initially feared was a stroke turned out to be a pinched nerve. Although he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he considered giving up.
He returned home to Tennessee in early last month to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, and she convinced him to press on.
Some of Sanders’ best days were in Pennsylvania, where he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels.”
“When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said.
In fact, Sanders has become something of a star among fellow hikers. Thousands more follow him on social media, which surprised Sanders and caused him to expand his mission beyond reclaiming his record.
“I wanna get it back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he said. “Right now, what’s the most important thing — and it’s one of the things that surprised me — is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.”
Meredith Ewenson, who met Sanders in June while leading a hike in New Hampshire for 10 other women, said he embodied not just the idea that anything is possible, but that the journey matters most.
“Seeing it in real life is something that I’ll definitely remember forever,” she said.
Ewenson said her group spotted Sanders early in the morning, but it was not until he blazed by them hours later that they saw the Grey Beard logo on his T-shirt and realized who he was. They caught up with him that night at an Appalachian Mountain Club hut, arriving around 4pm.
“I got here at noon,” he told them.
The next morning, she and others cheered as Sanders performed a “victory dance” before setting off again.
“My first thought was: ‘Wow, his mobility is insane,’” Ewenson said. “His face on that body just doesn’t make any sense. My brain couldn’t compute how he was so impossibly fit for being that age.”
Sanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports such as acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the US Navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation.
Sanders holds numerous other age-related records, including becoming the oldest person to paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday.
On his latest adventure, he tackled obstacles such as downed trees or steep scrambles with vigor, although he started to get a bit wobbly toward the end of one 19km day. He laid down on the trail, said he needed a power nap and briefly fell asleep.
Two minutes later, he got up and kept hiking.

Farce of KMT’s so-called fiscal discipline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) has floated the idea of the party proposing a universal cash payment next year of NT$20,000 to NT$30,000 (US$632 to US$948), greater than the planned NT$10,000 proposed by the government.
What seems like simply advocating for extra cash for the public is turning the cash handouts debate into a bidding war.
The question is not whether cash handouts are popular, but what the KMT is thinking when it comes to national finances. After all, these are the same politicians who have repeatedly accused the government of padding budgets, wasting public funds and leaving debt for future generations. They touted their roughly NT$48 billion in cuts to the central government’s overall budget as a major achievement in protecting taxpayers’ wallets. Yet they now turn around and push for even higher universal cash payments, costing hundreds of billions of New Taiwan dollars.
If bigger payouts are the answer, why not gun for NT$100,000?
Based on a rough population estimate of 23 million, a universal payment of NT$20,000 amounts to NT$460 billion, while NT$30,000 would come close to NT$690 billion. So, just as the KMT congratulates itself on cutting NT$48 billion from the budget, it is proposing a policy 10 to 14 times larger.
Was all the talk about “government waste” really about fiscal oversight, or was it simply about cutting the ruling party’s budget? If the country is so strapped for cash that wholesale cuts are necessary, where is the money for hundreds of billions in universal cash payments coming from? Conversely, if the government can actually find NT$690 billion, why all the fanfare over NT$48 billion in budget cuts and accusations of reckless government spending?
Fiscal discipline cannot exist only when someone else’s budget is being cut, then conveniently disappear when it comes time to make political promises.
The political objective here might be to create the impression that it was the KMT that fought to get money to the people.
However, each dollar that the government distributes comes not from the KMT’s coffers, and certainly not from Fu’s own pocket, but from national public finances.
The Legislative Yuan has the power to scrutinize budgets and oversee the government, but politicians cannot demand that the executive branch take fiscal responsibility while simultaneously calling for enormous new expenditures, packaging the resulting political benefits as KMT-won dividends.
Handouts of NT$20,000 might win applause today, but could another party simply call for NT$30,000 or NT$50,000? If so, politics would become less about who can govern better and more about hollering the highest bid.
A political party that is fiscally responsible would be able to tell the public where the money will come from, whether it requires additional borrowing, what public infrastructure projects or social welfare programs could be crowded out and whether such a massive one-off expenditure is consistent with the country’s long-term fiscal interests. What it should not do is take people’s tax money only to slip it into red envelopes and slap its own party label on them.
If the KMT genuinely believes that the central government has padded its budget and wasted money, it should insist that surplus funds be used to reduce debt or put forward comprehensive fiscal reforms. It should not jump from calling out the government to pushing for a larger universal cash payout in pursuit of a political sugar hit.
This is not about saving money, it is about the KMT ingratiating itself by using public money.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer

Princess Cruises shutters Taiwan sales operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

Princess Cruises has ended local sales operations in Taiwan, but its scheduled sailings this year would not be affected, Taiwan International Ports Corp (TIPC) chairman Chou Yung-hui (周永暉) said yesterday, as the Tourism Administration pledged to attract more international cruise operators.
Princess Cruises announced on Facebook that the Web site, social media platforms and local sales operations of its Taiwan branch — Carnival Taiwan — ceased operations on Monday.
The US company said it would no longer accept new bookings through its local operating entity, but existing reservations, passenger rights and related support services remain unaffected. Travelers needing assistance will be provided with appropriate contact information.
Photo: Taipei Times
The move is part of a policy adjustment by parent company Carnival Corp to halt local sales operations in several Asian markets, including Taiwan, China, Hong Kong and South Korea, while retaining direct operations in Japan and Singapore, sources familiar with the matter said.
Future travelers will need to book cruises through Princess Cruises’ global Web site or other international sales channels, the company added.
Chou said the decision was a business strategy adjustment by the cruise operator and would not affect this year’s scheduled port calls in Taiwan.
TIPC will continue discussions with Princess Cruises over adjustments for next year and 2028, he said, adding that a growing number of cruise operators have made maiden calls at Keelung and Kaohsiung ports this year.
Tourism Administration Deputy Director-General Huang Ho-ting (黃荷婷) said the change would have some impact on cruise operations, but Princess Cruises ships would continue to call at Keelung and Kaohsiung.
The agency will work with TIPC to develop more strategic measures to attract international cruise operators and visitors, Huang said.
Wayne Liu (劉喜臨), a professor at National Kaohsiung University of Hospitality and Tourism, said the impact on Taiwan’s cruise market is likely to be limited.
He said the move was more like a travel agency ending its local cruise sales role rather than a reduction in Princess Cruises’ actual services.
The company could still use local travel agencies for sales and ground services if it wanted to use Taiwan as a home port in the future, he said.

US Supreme Court allows ballroom project to proceed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:09 UTC
01:46:09 KST

The US Supreme Court on Monday allowed US President Donald Trump to continue construction of his White House ballroom, granting him a major victory as he works to leave a permanent mark on Washington.
The conservative-dominated court ruled 5-4 to lift a lower order demanding most construction be halted, saying that the plaintiff in the case likely did not have legal standing to sue.
US Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court’s three liberals in dissenting, writing in an opinion that the major White House overhaul was “likely unlawful” due to the lack of congressional authorization.
Photo: Reuters
The decision means construction can continue for now, while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation remains unresolved in lower courts.
The ballroom project is just one part of Trump’s second term push to reshape the US capital, which also includes renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool and erecting a huge triumphal arch.
Trump celebrated Monday’s decision, saying it meant the project could go forward “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”
However, the Supreme Court’s ruling was on procedural grounds and did not address the legality of the construction.
National Trust president Brent Leggs said “we are deeply disappointed” by the decision, but “it is noteworthy that the majority did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal.”
The National Trust’s case was brought on behalf of member Alison Hoagland, a Washington resident who claims that seeing the finished ballroom would result in damage to her “aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests.”
The Supreme Court majority ruled those claims were likely insufficient to establish standing, citing previous rejections of similar arguments, but made clear they were not making a final ruling on the project’s legality.
Roberts, writing for the dissenters, said that Hoagland clearly had standing under previous Supreme Court rulings.
The project was “likely unlawful,” because “Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’” for the administration to undertake it.
Roberts earlier this month allowed the project to proceed while the full court considered the matter.
While the ballroom has drawn headlines, the project also includes a military bunker.
A district court and, later, an appellate court, halted work on the aboveground ballroom while allowing construction on the military facility to continue.

Jet fuel surcharges to increase: CAA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:09 UTC
01:46:09 KST

Aviation fuel surcharges are to increase for a second consecutive month as oil prices continue to climb, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said yesterday.
The surcharge would rise to US$32.50 from US$30 for short-haul flights, and to US$84.50 from US$78 for long-haul flights, with the new prices taking effect on Monday next week, it said.
The CAA and Taiwanese airlines in 2005 jointly established a fuel surcharge mechanism based on state-run CPC Corp, Taiwan’s (台灣中油) benchmark international jet fuel price. No surcharge applies below US$40 per barrel. Between US$40 and US$50, the surcharge is US$5 for short-haul routes and US$13 for long-haul routes, rising by US$2.50 and US$6.50 respectively for every US$10 increase in fuel prices.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
CPC’s benchmark price for international aviation fuel is currently at US$156.79 per barrel, up from US$147.57, moving from 12th to 13th pricing tier.
It would be the agency’s fifth surcharge adjustment this year. In April, surcharges for short-haul and long-haul flights were raised to US$45 and US$117 respectively as oil prices soared on the back of the conflict in the Middle East.
The surcharges dropped to US$35 and US$91 for short-haul and long-haul flights respectively in June and further to US$27.5 and US$ 71.5 in July as oil prices fell.
Last month, fuel surcharges reversed up to US$30 and US$78 as oil prices rebounded.
The agency has asked airlines to provide clear information on their official Web sites about the surcharge, including fuel costs as a percentage of total operating costs and the calculation method, to address consumer concerns.

Minister thanks Palau over attendance at PIF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:08 UTC
01:46:08 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) yesterday thanked Palau for enabling him to make a rare appearance at a major annual political gathering of Pacific nations on Monday, despite Taiwan not being an official member of the bloc.
“I am very happy to be able to participate in this year’s Pacific Islands Forum [PIF], and I have to give special thanks to the host country Palau for the arrangement,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs quoted Lin as saying in a statement.
Lin did not elaborate on the nature of the arrangement, saying only that Taiwan was honored to be a partner in the Pacific and would continue to work with its partners to promote greater prosperity and peace across the region.
Photo: AFP
Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) on Monday reported that Lin attended the opening ceremony of the 55th PIF Leaders Meeting, which began in Koror on Sunday and runs through Friday.
Although Taiwan is not a PIF member, it has been a “development partner” of the forum since 1993.
Taiwan typically holds the Taiwan/Republic of China Forum Countries Dialogue and other events in conjunction with the PIF’s annual summit, but rarely attends the forum’s official meetings.
Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) expressed Beijing’s opposition to Lin’s presence, telling reporters that Beijing had “serious concerns” about the space being given to Taiwan, ABC reported.
“Taiwan is not a dialogue partner with the forum, so we have serious concerns,” Qian was quoted as saying, referring to the standard official designation for countries that are not PIF members.
“We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he added.
Taiwan and other non-members of the bloc were barred from participating in last year’s PIF summit, which was held in the Solomon Islands and attended only by the forum’s 18 member states.
Partner countries including Taiwan, the US and China did not take part after the host nation barred them from attending, citing an ongoing review of the forum’s partnership arrangements.
Media reports at the time suggested that the Solomon Islands, which established formal diplomatic ties with China in 2019, ending its relationship with Taipei, sought to block Taiwan’s participation under pressure from Beijing.
China has sought to expand its presence in the Pacific while further isolating Taiwan internationally, including by persuading several of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the region to recognize it.
Three of the PIF’s 18 member states have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan — Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu.

THSRC begins static testing of N700ST-model train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:05 UTC
01:46:05 KST

Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) has begun static testing of the first N700ST-model train after it was assembled at the company’s Yenchao (燕巢) Depot in Kaohsiung following its delivery to Taiwan last month. The new train is scheduled to enter service in July next year.
The train is the first of 12 new sets that Taiwan has purchased from Japan. The static testing is scheduled to be completed in November, followed by dynamic testing and final acceptance testing.
A total of 69 items would be verified across the three stages of testing, the high-speed rail operator said.
Photo: Screen grab from THSRC’s Facebook page
The first three trainsets are expected to gradually enter service from July next year, it said.
Static testing is being conducted at the Yenchao Depot, with the train undergoing power-on tests to ensure that all systems are functioning properly.
Low-speed operation tests would also be conducted at the depot to verify system integration and basic operating performance, it said.
Following the static testing, the train would proceed to dynamic testing on the high-speed rail line, with the tests being conducted during overnight maintenance periods.
The high-speed dynamic tests would verify the train’s operating performance, with test speeds gradually increased in stages in accordance with testing protocols.
For the final acceptance tests, the train would undergo comprehensive validation during regular operating hours in coordination with the train service schedule. The tests would verify that the train’s systems, operating performance and stability meet design requirements under actual operating conditions, the company said.
The 69 test items would cover three main areas: performance and safety, train equipment and passenger service facilities, it added.
Performance and safety tests would include traction performance, braking performance at different levels, aerodynamic resistance, running stability, car-body strength, overhead catenary performance, and verification of the automatic train control system, the company said.
Train equipment tests would cover pressure changes in the driver’s cab, wheel bearings, axle-box lubrication, wheel-slip prevention and adhesion performance, auxiliary battery performance, side windows and windshield wipers.
Service facility tests would include washbasins, toilets, lighting, ride comfort and noise levels.
The overall dynamic testing program is scheduled to be fully completed by the end of April next year, it said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

Iran claims attacks on Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq after US strikes kill 11
Kuwait also reports confronting Iranian attacks, as Tehran responds to US attacks that killed 11 people, including 5 at a wedding party.
The United States has launched a new wave of attacks on southern Iran, prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq, amid an intensifying standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
The attacks early on Wednesday marked the heaviest exchange of fire between the US and Iran in more than a month. Kuwait also said its air defences confronted Iranian drones and missiles.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Qatar says efforts under way to end Iran-US war and reopen Strait of Hormuz
- list 2 of 3Iran and Russia vow to stand against US ‘unilateralism’
- list 3 of 3China’s Xi makes first visit to Egypt in a decade, amid regional turmoil
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement that it had struck “Iranian military sites” after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attempted to attack US troops and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Targets included Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications infrastructure, it said.
Iranian media reported strikes on Sirik, Konarak, Bandar Abbas, Jask, Asaluyeh and Ahvaz, as well as Qeshm Island.
Esmaeil Baghaei, spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said one “brutal” attack had hit a residence in Kuhestak as families gathered for a wedding. At least five people were killed, including a child, and 63 were wounded, according to Iranian media.
Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing Khuzestan’s deputy governor Valiollah Hayati, reported that a further seven people were killed and eight wounded in US missile attacks on three other locations in the province.
Attacks on US assets
The IRGC said it responded to the Kuhestak strike with a ballistic missile attack on Camp Titin, a US Marine Corps site near the Gulf of Aqaba in Jordan.
It also said it hit Prince Hassan airbase in Jordan, targeting hangars housing RQ-4 and MQ-9 drones. It claimed that several aircraft were destroyed and a number of US personnel were killed.
Jordan’s military said it had intercepted 10 of 13 missiles fired at the country, with the remainder falling on open ground.
A US official told Al Jazeera there were no injuries or significant damage at Camp Titin.
In Bahrain, Iran’s army said it launched drones at radar installations and parts of the country’s Sheikh Isa airbase, where Tehran says US forces are stationed.
Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior issued repeated alerts instructing residents to take shelter.
The IRGC later claimed a combined missile and drone attack on US facilities in Erbil province, northern Iraq, and said the strikes destroyed a repair centre and warehouses of technical equipment, and set fuel tanks alight.
Al Jazeera could not verify the claims.
Kuwait also said the country’s air defences responded to “hostile drones and missiles” fired by Iran. Tehran has not commented on the Kuwaiti claim.
Stalled diplomacy
The flare-up on Wednesday follows an exchange of attacks on Sunday, when the US military struck Larak Island in southern Iran, and Tehran retaliated with missile launches against a base housing US troops in Jordan.
It comes as the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, enters its sixth month, with diplomatic efforts to end the war at an impasse.
US President Donald Trump denied a report by ABC News that the latest strikes were aimed at forcing Iran back to the negotiating table.
“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table, as ABC Fake News reported,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, adding that he was satisfied with the status quo.
“I couldn’t care less if they [Iran] sign a worthless, to them, agreement,” Trump said. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”
Iranian officials meanwhile signalled further attacks.
In his first message following the US strikes, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the Iranian armed forces have “unforgettable lessons” in store for Washington.
Colonel Ebrahim Zolfaghari, a spokesman for Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, said “the offensive operations against the Americans will continue until they regret their crimes.
“We warn that the continuation of American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences.”
Ebrahim Azizi, head of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, also wrote on X: “Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished.”
Concern in the Gulf
Al Jazeera’s Aksel Zaimovic, reporting from Qatar’s capital, Doha, said there was no independent confirmation of the extent of the damage from Iran’s retaliatory strikes.
“We are seeing a major escalation across the region, with growing concern over whether the conflict will spill far beyond Iran’s borders,” he said.
Earlier on Tuesday, the US State Department had urged Americans in the Middle East to remain alert and prepare for travel disruptions, warning of “the potential for unforeseen escalation”.
Iran, meanwhile, has continued to assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Attacks on ships around the strait have been reported almost daily, despite Trump and his aides saying the US is managing to get millions of barrels of oil through the strait each day, even as Tehran continues to blockade the waterway.
The crisis in the strait has sent energy prices soaring.
The price of a barrel of oil jumped by more than 4 percent after the strikes on Tuesday. In the US, the average cost of one gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol is now more than $4, up from less than $3 before the war.

Guinea-Bissau approves new constitution that expands presidential powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:45:53 UTC
01:45:53 KST

Guinea-Bissau approves new constitution that expands presidential powers
DAKAR, Sept 1 - Guinea-Bissau has approved a new constitution in a referendum, provisional results showed on Tuesday, expanding presidential powers and reshaping electoral rules ahead of a presidential election scheduled for December.
The West African country, led by military officers who seized power in a coup last November, voted on Sunday on reforms allowing the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries and dissolve parliament in the event of a grave political crisis.
Under the current constitution, Guinea-Bissau's legislature names a prime minister who appoints a cabinet.
The result gives the military government backing to reshape Guinea-Bissau's political system before the presidential election, but the main opposition party boycotted the vote.
The new constitution was approved by 70% of voters in favour and 30% opposed, according to the provisional results announced by the National Electoral Commission. It also said some 544,060 people had voted, almost 60% of registered voters.
Polling stations in the capital Bissau were largely empty on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, while some residents told local media they had not known the referendum was being held or did not understand its purpose.
Guinea-Bissau's main opposition PAIGC party urged its supporters to boycott the referendum, saying the process lacked adequate political and institutional safeguards.
PAIGC leader Domingos Simoes Pereira said in a video message that the backers of the referendum sought to "kill our freedom and bury our democracy."
A spokesperson for the military government could not be reached for comment.
The constitution will cut the size of parliament to 65 seats from 102 and reduce the number of electoral constituencies to 12 from 29.
It further requires presidential candidates to have lived continuously in Guinea-Bissau for the preceding five years.
The coup last year was the ninth in West and Central Africa over five years and part of a cycle of instability in Guinea-Bissau. The country is widely known as a cocaine trafficking hub and has a long history of military interventions. REUTERS
