====================================================================================================

Ireland in talks to join British-led naval alliance
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:21:08 BST
00:21:08 KST

High-level talks between British and Irish defence officials have begun on Ireland joining the Joint Expeditionary Force, the ten-nation grouping led by Britain, according to The Journal.
Niall O’Connor reports that the Irish government has directed the Department of Defence to progress the plan, and that Ireland will initially work as an observer.
Dublin would not join the core elements of the force but a wider grouping known as JEF+, according to the report, which says Ireland has ruled out participation in what it describes as the more offensive core elements.
Sources told the outlet the arrangement is seen as an opportunity for practical cooperation with like-minded partners on shared security challenges, complementing Ireland’s engagement at European Union level. The key, The Journal reports, is that Ireland would draw on the force’s maritime security apparatus to respond to hybrid threats such as drone incursions.
Military sources quoted in the report were candid about what Ireland brings. Given the limits of Irish naval capability, the report says, membership would essentially amount to a watching brief, though it would also offer capability building along with information and intelligence sharing. The meetings are examining what practical benefit Ireland can draw from the other nations.
Who is JEF?
The Joint Expeditionary Force brings together Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It was established in 2014 and operates outside the NATO command structure while being designed to complement it.
The First Sea Lord set out the argument for its existence in an interview published last week. General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said the force brings unique freedoms and permissions because it does not require consensus among all ten nations to act, giving political flexibility to respond in a crisis earlier than NATO might be able to mobilise, given the higher bar of consensus the alliance requires. He said NATO commanders welcome it for exactly that reason, because it gives them choice and options in the early stage of a crisis.
That structure is what makes an Irish association possible at all. Ireland is not a NATO member and its policy of military neutrality would make accession difficult, but the JEF is not a treaty alliance with a mutual defence clause, which leaves room for arrangements of the kind now under discussion.
The force is currently running Lion Protector 26, which began on 3 August and continues to 12 October across Northern Europe, the North Atlantic and the Baltic Sea region. Its opening activity involved escorting vessels carrying allied military equipment into Latvian ports and moving it inland.
Why Ireland is moving
Ireland’s National Maritime Security Strategy, published in February, stated that securing Irish waters will require broader international relationships, with Minister for Defence Helen McEntee saying at the time that the State should not be afraid to work with Britain on security matters.
The undersea infrastructure question sits behind much of this. A substantial share of transatlantic data cables pass through or near Irish waters, and Russian vessels have been observed loitering over cable routes on multiple occasions. Ireland’s defence spending is the lowest in the European Union at around 0.2 per cent of gross domestic product, and the Naval Service has struggled with crewing shortages that have left ships alongside.
The First Sea Lord described the Russian undersea programme in blunt terms in the same interview, saying of the organisation Moscow presents as a deep sea research directorate: “Let’s not kid ourselves. It’s not a research agency. It is an independently funded arm of the Russian state, whose sole purpose is to pursue the destruction of critical underwater infrastructure.”
He also said that allies are struggling to contain very capable Russian submarines.
Cooperation already under way
Practical cooperation is running ahead of any formal arrangement. A Royal Navy warship and a Merlin helicopter are operating in the Irish Sea this week providing air defence for the meetings of EU defence and foreign ministers in County Wicklow, at Irish request, with the ship required to remain outside Irish territorial waters on constitutional grounds.
The French air defence frigate Aquitaine performed a similar role off Dublin and County Cork in July.
British involvement in Irish security has drawn political comment at Westminster, with the Conservative MP John Cooper writing to the Defence Secretary last week to complain about the offshore restriction and accusing Ireland of freeloading on defence.

Jerusalem schools strike after Israel enforces curriculum and bans teachers
Private and Christian schools in East Jerusalem have declared an open-ended strike, protesting sudden Israeli permit blockades for West Bank educators and a systematic push to replace the Palestinian curriculum.
The academic year in occupied East Jerusalem began on Tuesday with an open-ended strike by teachers at private and Christian schools after Israeli meddling in students’ curriculum.
All new first and seventh-grade classes at East Jerusalem’s Palestinian-majority municipal schools have been told to exclusively use the Israeli curriculum this year.
Entry permits for West Bank teachers to teach in East Jerusalem schools have also been blocked by Israel, according to Haaretz.
It means that one-in-three Palestinian students in occupied East Jerusalem, more than 45,000 in total, will be enrolled in the Israeli educational programme, a nearly fourfold increase over six years ago.
Jerusalem Governorate spokesman Marouf al-Rifai described the forced integration of Israeli curriculum into Palestinian schools as a cultural and educational crime.
“The adherence of Jerusalem’s people, teachers, and students to the Palestinian curriculum is not merely an adherence to a textbook, but rather a defense of memory, identity, history, and the right to determine the national narrative,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
Israeli forces recently seized educational compounds formerly operated by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, in the Shu’fat refugee camp and Kafr Aqab, to be replaced with Israeli-administered facilities.
Hamas official Haroun Nasser el-Din issued a statement saying that “the school, the book, and awareness are basic pillars in the battle of Jerusalem”. East Jerusalem and the West Bank have been illegally occupied by Israel since 1967.
“The Palestinian identity in Jerusalem is deeper than to be erased by imposed curricula or the occupation’s procedures and its arrogant policies,” he added.
The permit crisis
Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem have already suffered a severe staffing shortage due to Israel effectively blocking teachers from the West Bank from reaching the city’s schools. The General Secretariat for Christian Educational Institutions in Jerusalem announced an indefinite strike in response to the crisis.
“We were surprised, unfortunately once again, by the non-renewal of entry permits for more than 70 teachers and employees from our educational, administrative, and support cadres, in a sudden manner and without prior warning, which hindered their access to their schools and directly affected their readiness for the opening of the school year,” the body said in a statement.
“The absence of this large number of cadres affects various aspects of school work, educational, administrative, and health, in addition to cleaning services and security and safety procedures, which makes it impossible to guarantee a safe and stable start for our students.”
Sylvia Amer, deputy director for academic and administrative affairs at College des Freres Jerusalem, said that the abrupt reversal of dozens of permits just 10 days before schools were due to open forced the suspension of classes.
“The sudden ban came after they had previously confirmed to us in June that all permits would be available for all members of our teaching and administrative staff and employees,” Amer said.
“If this reality continues, it will gradually lead to affecting the independence of schools and their educational and cultural identity”.
Systematic extortion tactics
The staffing crisis at East Jerusalem schools has been worsened by recent Israeli legislation targeting Palestinian schools.
A Knesset law passed earlier this year prohibits the employment of teachers holding academic degrees from Palestinian Authority institutions within the Israeli educational system.
This effectively targets the core of East Jerusalem’s teaching workforce, where approximately 60 percent of the 6,700 Arab educators hold Palestinian degrees, according to the Haaretz report.
Mike Bassam Farraj, general director of Greek Orthodox Patriarchate Schools, told Al Jazeera that the permit denials and legislative hurdles act as a systematic pressure campaign.
“It serves as a systematic pressure method practised on Christian schools in Jerusalem and private schools in general, aiming to reduce the numbers of employees and teachers coming from the West Bank,” Farraj noted.
Israeli authorities have also weaponised budgetary allocations to coerce institutions, he added.
“In reality, there are continuous financial temptations – so as not to use the word ‘blackmail’ – based on the equation: ‘Adopt the Israeli Bagrut curriculum and take whatever budgets you wish,’ where they then grant you much broader spaces and capabilities,” Farraj explained.
To counter this academic siege, Farraj detailed their reliance on the judiciary.
“As for some other professions, we are forced to engage in legal confrontations and relentless follow-ups before responsible and governmental authorities,” he explained.
“The matter often reaches – as in the specialisation of human medicine, for example – obtaining decisions from the Supreme Court to extract and prove the right of our graduates to obtain professional practice certificates according to their specialisations, whether in medicine or law or others.”

‘Not perfectly aligned’ with human values: Anthropic admits security failures behind AI hacking incidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:18:10 UTC
00:18:10 KST

The US startup behind the Claude chatbot has admitted a series of hacking incidents involving its models reflected a “failure of operational security” and said it has tightened its testing procedures.
Anthropic revealed in July that its models had accessed the open internet three times and gained unauthorised access to the systems of three organisations.
In a new blogpost on the incidents, the company admitted its technology was “not perfectly aligned” with human values and goals.
Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company.
As a result, the company said it had initially paused internal and external cybersecurity testing of models to introduce a tighter safety regime.
“We had been largely relying on a single layer of defense … where we needed several,” said Anthropic.
The startup has now put in place extra measures including: an alert system for when a model attempts to break out of a testing environment or gains internet access; walling off its riskiest test environments more effectively; and requiring external testing companies to commit to a set of safety standards, including making explicit instructions to models during testing – such as “you should not access the internet”.
Anthropic said in July that three unnamed organisations had been hacked by three of its models after a “misunderstanding” with the company’s testing partner, a firm called Irregular, that resulted in the models gaining internet access.
Following the implementation of new measures, Anthropic said it had resumed internal and external cybersecurity tests. Like OpenAI, which revealed a testing safety breach in the same month, Anthropic said it had paused some high-risk reinforcement learning – a trial-and-error development technique where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task.
In its latest blogpost, Anthropic said it had found that defective training setups were “disproportionately large contributors” to misaligned behaviour, the term for when an AI fails to adhere to – or “align” with – human values like not committing harm.
The startup said it had found two alignment failures in the testing incidents: “motivated reasoning”, where despite finding evidence they might be connected to the internet, they may still have adhered to the “belief” they were in a simulated environment and thus not breaching their test lab; and a “recklessness” factor where the models were willing to take harmful action on the internet to pursue the narrow goal of passing a cybersecurity test.
Anthropic said it was tackling a phenomenon in AI development known as “reward-hacking”. This is where a model finds ways to game its training process and earn “rewards” without completing a task – an unsanctioned shortcut.
However, Anthropic said, the testing incidents showed it still had some way to go despite trying to limit reward-hacking.
“As evidenced by the incidents … our process isn’t perfect and our models are not perfectly aligned,” the company said.
Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Anthropic has admitted “its factory was running faster than its quality control”.
He added: “Two things outran Anthropic’s controls this spring – the training pipeline and the security. The incidents are what that gap looks like from the outside.”
The company, which is preparing for a stock market flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.47tn), reiterated its call for coordinated action between government and industry on pacing industry development.
“We believe the world would benefit if the industry adopted a lawful, verifiable, effective mechanism for coordinated pacing as soon as possible,” Anthropic said.
The blogpost added: “The July incidents have stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defenses is even higher than we previously believed.”
As well as the similar breach at OpenAI, the Anthropic incidents followed an episode at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which reported in August that OpenAI and Anthropic models had carried out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.
The Guardian also revealed last month that incidents of AIs escaping users’ control have hit a new high, almost doubling in July compared with the previous month to more than 300.

Niger's thwarted mutiny highlights junta's dependence on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:16:08 UTC
00:16:08 KST

Niger's thwarted mutiny highlights junta's dependence on Russia
A failed mutiny in Niger over the weekend shows how important Russia's Africa Corps mercenaries are in the country, according to analysts. They argue that the failed mutiny on Saturday shows how the country's security landscape has worsened and contradicts claims from Niger's junta about the country's independence from foreign powers.
The pivotal role played by Russia's Africa Corps mercenaries in putting down a mutiny in Niger at the weekend has revealed just how dependent on Moscow the west African country's ruling junta has become.
The growing reliance on Russian mercenaries is also at odds with the junta's insistence that its 2023 coup was about reclaiming the nation's sovereignty and independence from foreign powers, according to analysts.
Read moreNiger junta puts down mutiny with help from Russia's Africa Corps
On Saturday, after a night of intense fighting in the capital Niamey, Niger's military government asked for – and obtained – the Africa Corps' help in wresting back control from disgruntled soldiers who had attacked several sensitive sites and hunkered down in a key military base at the airport.
Russia's ambassador to Niamey, Viktor Voropaev, himself boasted on the same day that the intervention helped "repress a mutiny".
"The Africa Corps played a decisive role through the provision of ground and air support to help loyalist forces retake Air Base 101, one of the capital's most strategic sites, from the mutineers and largely eliminated the remaining threat they posed to the government," Charlie Werb, an analyst at Aldebaran Threat Consultants, said.
Werb argued that the mutiny was the consequence of a worsening security landscape in Niger, with the junta having failed to quell a deadly, long-running jihadist insurgency.
Like its paramilitary predecessor, the Wagner group, the Africa Corps is officially in the Sahel region to help tackle that violence.
But for Lou Osborn, co-founder of the collective All Eyes on Wagner, which tracks the mercenary outfit, "what the Russians are promising above all is this praetorian guard service, to protect the regime – and they are keeping that promise".
'Swapped dependencies'
Beverly Ochieng, an analyst at Control Risks, argued that the Africa Corps had an interest in keeping General Abdourahmane Tiani in power against any opposition – not just the jihadists.
"In order to maintain its presence, its foremost mission is to ensure that the government prevails no matter what threats are under way," Ochieng said.
"So it was not choosing a side, it was still fulfilling the obligation of protecting and responding to the government's requirements."
Like its fellow junta-ruled neighbours Burkina Faso and Mali, Niger turned to Russia for security after breaking with France, its historic colonial ruler, in the wake of the coup.
Despite trumpeting pan-African and pro-independence messages, all three have welcomed Russian mercenaries to help fight jihadists loyal to either al Qaeda or the Islamic State group, who have run rampant across the three countries.
In a report on the August 29 mutiny, the Timbuktu Institute argued the junta's rhetoric sits uncomfortably with the reality.
"While Abdourahmane Tiani's government has made security sovereignty one of the pillars of its legitimacy, the intervention of an outside partner to help contain an internal crisis raises a central question: how far can the pursuit of strategic autonomy go when it comes hand in hand with growing dependence on Moscow?" the Dakar-based think tank said.
Werb argued that "outside support does not necessarily contradict the bloc's sovereigntist stance".
But "it nonetheless shows that the three governments have only swapped security dependencies and that the narrative primarily functions to legitimise their rule", the analyst added.
In any case, the mutiny "highlights the fragilities of a regime whose stability increasingly rests on a Russian partnership now liable to extend beyond the sole framework of the fight against jihadist groups", the Timbuktu Institute said.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'In the line of fire'
Ochieng said the mutiny "demonstrates deep divisions and grievances within the security apparatus", in a country whose soldiers are "constantly in the line of fire, fighting militants".
Whether Saturday's events alter the balance of power in the Niger-Russia relationship is another matter.
Niger received no help in fighting Saturday's abortive uprising from its allies in Burkina Faso and Mali, with which it has formed a confederation claiming to maintain a 5,000-strong joint army.
Even the Russians have not managed to end the jihadist problem. Analysts argue that the Africa Corps' failure to prevent the fall of Kidal in northern Mali in April exposed the mercenaries' limitations, while the local soldiers who receive Africa Corps training are still unable to push back the militants.
But Sergei Eledinov, a retired Russian military officer turned African security expert, insisted that the Sahel countries did not have a better choice.
"Judging a military deployment by whether it has solved a political crisis that, by definition, it cannot solve, would be misguided," Eledinov said.
Moscow's growing presence in the Sahel also comes as part of a wider Russian expansion across Africa, jostling for influence with France in Paris's former colonies.
"They're still in the expansion phase," said Osborn, pointing to Madagascar, Guinea-Bissau, Gabon and Congo-Brazzaville as examples.
Niger's state television accused France of being behind the mutiny, repeating the junta's regular talking point that Paris is trying to destabilise its ex-colony.
Those accusations, frequently rejected by France, have been taken up by Russia – with the foreign ministry calling the mutineers "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".

France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:15:57 BST
00:15:57 KST

France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees
- Published
France has started imposing fees on fast fashion items which could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030, as the government tries to curb sales of cheap clothing sold by e-commerce sites.
The levy, which came into force on Tuesday, follows a new law passed in June to regulate so-called "ultra-fast fashion" companies such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.
The e-commerce giants, known for selling large volumes of cheap apparel, have been criticised by French officials for driving a surge in fast fashion.
China's commerce ministry has described the French law as discriminatory and a trade barrier, saying it could violate World Trade Organization (WTO) principles.
French minister Mathieu Lefevre said the "harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion" on the environment and economy were "well known".
In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European companies.
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two factors: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
For 2026, the charges range from a €0.50 (£0.43) levy on underwear to €2 (£1.71) for T-shirts, to €9 (£7.71) for jeans and €12 (£10.28) for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 (£16.71/$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50% of the product's pre-tax price.
The fees come after Shein, a fast fashion retailer founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, was valued at $26.2bn (£19.3bn) on its first day of public trading on the stock market in Hong Kong.
The company was once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn, but has faced heated competition, trade tensions and questions over the ethics of its supply chain.
The BBC has contacted Shein, Temu and AliExpress with a request to comment.
Shein previously told the BBC that the impact of legislation targeting ultra-fast fashion would "worsen the purchasing power of French consumers, at a time when they are already feeling the impact of the cost-of-living crisis".
Temu, a Chinese-owned e-commerce company, has also been widely criticised by politicians in the UK and US alike.
A spokesperson for Temu previously told the BBC that the brand "acknowledges the important environmental concerns addressed by the proposed French legislation", and argued that it does not operate as a fast fashion company because it is a marketplace and does not manufacture its own products.

Austrian gov’t begins work on constitutional ban of ‘Political Islam'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:15:34 UTC
00:15:34 KST

Austria’s government is beginning to work on a proposal to constitutionally ban “political Islam,” after Chancellor Christian Stocker called for the legislation and Integration and Europe Minister Claudia Bauer said she would draw up a proposal for the coalition partners.
ORF first reported on August 30 that Bauer is preparing the proposal and intends to send an outline to SPÖ and NEOS. This was then confirmed by Bauer on social media.
Stocker first raised the possible legislation in an interview with Heute on August 28. The chancellor expressed his intention to implement a constitutional law on political Islam, which he called “incompatible with democracy and Western values.”
In a statement, Stocker said, “I do not want our children and grandchildren to grow up in an Islamic state.”
Stocker argued that everyone in Austria is free to believe whatever they want and to have whatever faith they choose, “But where believers and non-believers are treated differently, where men and women do not have equal rights, and where our institutions, authorities, and courts are not respected, that freedom ends.”
Stoker: “It cannot be allowed to happen...that a preacher dictates things rather than Parliament”
He then claimed that there is a relative majority of Muslim students in Viennese schools, but “The crucial question is: Will these students become democrats who accept and abide by our legal system and live alongside our society? Or will they become Islamists and be politically influenced?”
Here, Stocker cited a recent figure that pupils with an Islamic religious affiliation represented 41.2% in Vienna’s primary and middle schools, constituting a relative majority.
“It cannot be allowed to happen in this country that a preacher dictates things rather than Parliament,” Stocker added. “It must not be the case that morality police in schools determine what girls should wear or how they should behave. Nor can we ignore the foundations of an ‘honor killing’ while punishing only the act itself. That is why I am in favor of regulating this at the constitutional level as well.”
Bauer reposted the statement, adding, “We will fight political Islam with all means available.”
This follows an earlier proposal by the Freedom Party (FPÖ) in March 2026. The proposal would prohibit activity in support of political Islam or its objectives, dissolve mosques and organizations deemed part of political Islam, confiscate their assets, and potentially revoke Austrian citizenship from members/supporters.
Political Islam in Austria
Austria has long been concerned about political Islam, even launching the Documentation Center for Political Islam (Dokumentationsstelle Politischer Islam) in 2020.
The Center defines political Islam as “an ideology of supremacy that aims at influencing or changing society, culture, state, policy, politics, and/or polity according to such values and norms that are declared as Islamic by the actors of Political Islam, but are not shared by the majority of Muslims and are in clear contradiction to the rule of law, democracy, and human rights.”
The aim of the Center is to research, document, and report on possible foreign influences on Islamist associations active in Austria.
Its research has examined the role of the Muslim Brotherhood in Austria, the influence of Turkey’s Directorate of Religious Affairs (the Diyanet), and even the presence of Hezbollah and Hamas.
When the Center was established, then-integration minister Susanne Raab stressed that Austria wanted to distinguish Islam as a religion from what she described as the extremist ideology of political Islam. She specifically said the government was not placing Muslim institutions or Muslims generally under suspicion.
The Austrian Federal Chancellery’s 2025 National Situation Report discusses “Political Islam” as a security threat and distinguishes between violent/hard-power Islamism and “soft power” Islamism, which it describes as attempts to advance Islamist agendas through legal and political means.

ADL affiliate JLens launches tracker ranking 100 US companies on Jewish employee support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:15:19 UTC
00:15:19 KST

JLens, an ADL affiliate and SEC-registered investment advisor, has launched the inaugural JLens Workplace Tracker ahead of the High Holy Days. The transparency tool is designed to assess whether the 100 largest US public companies have adopted the 14 key policies and practices that support Jewish employees.
The tracker evaluates companies across three core categories: Jewish Experience in the Workplace, Religious Accommodations, and Workplace Protections.
Specific metrics include the presence of a Jewish employee resource group (ERG), antisemitism training, protection against ancestry-based and religious discrimination, floating holidays, prayer or reflection spaces, and confidential reporting mechanisms.
Out of the 100 companies evaluated, 30 received medal designations based on publicly available and company-reported information, while the remaining 70 were designated as “Not Rated” due to insufficient public data.
Gold, silver, bronze designations
The recognized companies include Amazon, Bank of America, Cisco, JPMorgan Chase, KKR, Pfizer, S&P Global, Spotify, and Uber in the Gold category.
Silver designations were awarded to Accenture, Coca-Cola, Eli Lilly, GE Vernova, Intuit, Meta, Microsoft, Salesforce, and Thermo Fisher Scientific.
Bronze designations went to AbbVie, Adobe, Alphabet, American Express, Apple, Citigroup, CrowdStrike, Medtronic, Morgan Stanley, Netflix, Palo Alto Networks, and Texas Instruments.
In a press release issued last Wednesday, Ari Hoffnung, managing director of JLens, emphasized the practical challenges faced by Jewish employees during the holiday season and when requesting religious accommodations.
“Asking for religious accommodation is not easy. A new Jewish employee who has not accrued enough time off, facing the Jewish High Holidays a few weeks into the job, has to decide whether to raise it with a manager they barely know,” Hoffnung stated in the release.
“When a company publishes its religious accommodation policy and walks new hires through it at orientation, that employee is asking for something routine rather than something extraordinary.”
JLens Workplace Guide
Alongside the tracker, JLens released The JLens Workplace Guide: Practices that Support Jewish Employees at Work, which highlights examples such as KKR’s Jewish Heritage Network, Alphabet’s holiday scheduling guide, Citigroup’s floating Heritage Day, and Salesforce’s multi-faith prayer space.
The initiative comes amid growing data highlighting workplace gaps and hiring biases. According to Clal’s Jewish@Work 2024 survey, 13% of Jewish employees reported considering leaving a job due to their experiences as a Jew at work.
Furthermore, a field experiment sponsored by the ADL Center for Antisemitism Research claimed to have found that Jewish American and Israeli American job applicants faced measurable disparities in positive response rates compared to peers with Western European backgrounds.
JLens stressed that the Workplace Tracker is an informational tool rather than a ranking or a measure of employee experience. It also noted that companies can submit updated information for review at any time.

More than 10 European Union member states are willing to contribute resources and people to a new military and civilian mission to advise and train Lebanese forces, the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Tuesday.
The proposed mission stems from the EU studying ways to strengthen Lebanese forces to help free up the Lebanese army to focus on disarming the terrorist group Hezbollah.
Western countries have long called for Lebanon to disarm the Iran-backed group, and doing so is a central component of a ceasefire between Lebanon and Israel aimed at ending a war that has run in parallel with the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

"The EU is not seeking to replace UNIFIL," Kallas told reporters in Ireland following a gathering of European defense ministers.
"Our objective is to strengthen the Lebanese armed forces and the ability of the Lebanese state to provide security across its territory," she said, adding that planning is progressing well.
An EU official told Reuters that the bloc aims to establish the mission in mid-October and then deploy personnel in late 2026 or early 2027.
No details on EU countries involved
Kallas did not provide details on which EU countries would be involved.
France has been trying for several months to organize an international conference to strengthen the Lebanese armed forces, and it also proposed creating an international force as part of efforts to replace UNIFIL.
A senior Western diplomat told Reuters on Tuesday there was limited prospect for major decisions on Lebanon's future before Israel's election in late October. The diplomat also said there was little chance of progress without any clear strengthening of the Lebanese armed forces that would enable them to move into areas previously controlled by Hezbollah.

Recent polls had shown that Winter’s new People of Israel party could win five seats, largely at the expense of Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, which would fall below the electoral threshold.
Ben-Gvir rejects alliance
Last week, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who leads the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, to run on a joint list, as they did in the 2022 elections.
Ben-Gvir had openly rejected such an alliance, prompting reports that Smotrich and Feiglin were negotiating a joint run.
Smotrich has stated that he intends to remain part of Netanyahu’s bloc in the upcoming elections.
Netanyahu had also called on voters not to support the small parties on the Right, warning that splitting the right-wing vote could cost his camp the election and allow the opposition bloc to form the next government.
Feiglin previously served in Likud, led by Netanyahu. He resigned after he did not receive a higher slot on the party’s Knesset list after its primaries and founded the Zehut Party in 2015.
Zehut and RZP both advocate for far-right security policies, including the annexation of the West Bank and Gaza. Zehut also supports libertarian economic policies and the legalization of cannabis.
Smotrich stated upon the signing of the alliance that “the upcoming elections are critical to the future of the national camp and to the future of the State of Israel.”
“Security, settlement, the judicial system, preventing the establishment of a Palestinian state, and our ability to continue leading the major changes that Israel needs – everything is at stake,” he added.
Feiglin stated that he and Smotrich were “bringing the news that so many have been waiting for and embarking on a joint effort aimed at maximizing the strength of the national and faith-based camp.”

In the U.S., a Black Hawk Helicopter Deployed a Swarm of Altius-700 Drones for Autonomous Target Detection and Engagement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:13:23 UTC
00:13:23 KST

In the U.S., an H-60M Black Hawk helicopter deployed a swarm of Altius-700 drones, which autonomously detected targets, exchanged data with one another, and engaged them.
Anduril reported this and also released a video.
The demonstration took place during Project Convergence Capstone 6. The Black Hawk crew engaged several Altius-700 drones in a joint mission to test their ability to operate autonomously as a swarm.
This approach lets the drones distribute tasks and share the information they gather with other drones. As a result, the helicopter crew can use the drones as forward-deployed sensors and strike assets without flying directly toward the target.
The Altius-700 can be equipped with various payloads depending on the mission. In particular, it can be used for reconnaissance and electronic warfare. Its strike version, the Altius-700M, is designed to destroy targets, has a range of up to 160 km, and can remain airborne for up to 75 minutes.
The tests are part of the development of the Air-Launched Effects (A-LE) concept—using unmanned systems launched from manned aircraft to carry out missions at a significant distance from them.
During a three-day test phase in the Mojave Desert, H-60M crews launched and controlled several unmanned systems in a networked configuration. The U.S. Army also tested their performance under high-temperature conditions.
The next phase of the program is expected to involve using the Altius-700 alongside an armored unit, allowing testing of the autonomous system as part of a tactical formation.
This is not the first time the Altius-700 has been tested with U.S. Army Aviation. In April 2026, an AH-64E Apache launched an Altius-700 missile for the first time at the Yuma Proving Ground.
Even earlier, in 2024, Anduril released the results of tests of the strike version, the Altius-700M. During tests at the Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, the drone achieved six direct hits across six missions, including a mock-up of an anti-aircraft missile system.
The U.S. Army is also considering the Altius-700M for the LRPM program—a long-range, high-precision weapon system for helicopters. It is designed to let crews engage targets at long range without flying close to them.
The Altius family is also linked to support for Ukraine. The United Kingdom previously ordered Altius-600M and Altius-700M systems for the Ukrainian military under contracts totaling £30 million.

EU’s green fashion rules face test as global emissions rise 6.3%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:12:45 UTC
00:12:45 KST

The findings of a report on fashion data pose a political challenge for the EU, which has made textiles one of the testing grounds for its broader push to move from a linear economy – make, sell and throw away – towards a circular one.
The global apparel and fashion industry is moving in the wrong direction on climate emissions, with greenhouse gas emissions rising 6.3% in 2024 compared to the previous year, despite a growing number of companies investing in renewable energy, cleaner materials and coal phase-outs, according to the Apparel Impact Institute’s latest assessment.
The increase in emissions was driven largely by higher fibre consumption, particularly polyester, putting the European Union's fashion industry further away from its goal of cutting emissions 45% by 2030 from 2019 levels.
Since roughly 80% to 90% of the EU's fashion footprint lies outside of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency, the EU’s sustainability laws are specifically designed to penalise "outsourced" pollution through a few key mechanisms.
Nonetheless, end-of-life products remain in the EU, with roughly 12.6 million tonnes of textile waste generated in the EU per year.
According to the World Integrated Trade Solution, China is the top textile exporter to the EU, with over €26.5 billion in apparel and accounting for roughly one-third of all textile and clothing products sold in Europe. Bangladesh ranks second, followed by Turkey, India, Pakistan, Vietnam and Morocco.
For the EU, which is tightening rules around fashion to make the industry more circular, new data from the Apparel Impact Institute suggests that clothing production will keep rising even if the bloc's laws succeed in cutting emissions.
"Decarbonising apparel requires action on both sides of the equation: reducing the carbon intensity of material production and manufacturing, while also addressing the growth in material volumes that can outpace those gains," reads the report.
In a bid to end the growth in textile waste, Brussels has introduced a package of measures aimed at changing how clothes are designed, sold and eventually discarded. The EU has also moved to make fashion companies financially responsible for the waste they generate.
But the apparel industry's rising emissions suggest that waste policy alone will not solve the climate problem. The industry's biggest source of emissions is linked to the processing of materials.
Polluting non-EU factories
According to the Apparel Impact Institute's report, textile processing accounts for about 51% of apparel emissions, followed by raw-material production at 26%.
That puts the spotlight on the factories producing fabrics and fibres, many of which are outside the EU.
The bloc can regulate what is sold on its single market, but most of the emissions associated with European consumers' clothes occur in global supply chains, resulting in a clash between EU industrial and climate policy.
With this backdrop, European policymakers are under pressure to decarbonise supply chains while simultaneously responding to concerns from industry about regulation, costs and competitiveness.
The same tension arises from the industry's perspective, according to the report. Manufacturers frequently lack the financing to invest in energy efficiency and renewable power, while clean electricity and alternatives to coal can remain unavailable or too expensive in key production countries. In many cases, sustainable materials can also cost more than conventional alternatives.
The report argues that brands need to share the financial and operational burden with suppliers through longer-term purchasing commitments, project financing and closer partnerships.
It also calls for climate targets to be converted into actual factory-level investment, particularly in energy- and heat-intensive textile processing.
"This includes improving access to appropriate finance, sharing project costs and risks, providing stable and longer-term purchasing commitments and aligning commercial relationships with decarbonisation objectives,” reads the report.
More sustainable fashion
Swedish major international fashion retailer H&M reduced the number of supplier factories using on-site coal boilers from 118 in 2022 to just 10 by the end of 2025, the report reveals.
Industrial electrification is also emerging as an alternative. Heat pumps are being deployed for processes such as laundry, dyeing and drying, while Lenzing, a company that produces wood-based cellulosic fibers, and power generation company VERBUND have commissioned a 14 MW power-to-heat facility in Austria that uses renewable electricity to provide industrial heat.
However, under business-as-usual assumptions, apparel emissions could reach 1.277 gigatonnes in 2030, compared with the 489 million tonnes the sector would need to reach to remain on a 1.5°C-compatible trajectory under the UN Paris Agreement.
Even if factories become more efficient and switch to cleaner energy, the report warns, it will not be enough if the industry keeps producing more carbon-intensive materials like fiber.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Uniform orbit inclination for Russian, Indian, US stations to make flights safe — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:11:38 UTC
00:11:38 KST

MOSCOW, September 1. /TASS/. A uniform orbital inclination for the orbits in which Russian, Indian, and US space stations are planned to be deployed could enhance crew safety by enabling flights and exchanges between the stations, Sergey Yazev, a leading researcher at the Institute of Solar-Terrestrial Physics of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences and a professor at Irkutsk State University, told TASS.
He noted that since 1967, Soviet and later Russian manned spacecraft have used orbits with an inclination of 51.6 degrees relative to Earth's equatorial reference plane. The International Space Station (ISS), which is currently operating at the same inclination and is scheduled to be deorbited and crash into the Pacific Ocean in 2030, also travels in that orbit.
"This orbit will continue to be used. By the mid-2030s, at least three national orbital stations are planned to operate in the ‘Russian’ orbit with an inclination of 51.6 degrees: the Russian Orbital Station (ROS), the US commercial Axiom Station, and the Indian space station Bharatiya Antariksh. A uniform orbital inclination will allow, if necessary, for flights and crew exchanges, which will increase the safety of crews in space and expand the potential capabilities of the new space infrastructure," the scientist said in a conversation with TASS.
It became known last week that India has approved the first module of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), a proposed Indian space station planned for completion by 2035. The station is designed as a low-Earth orbit platform and is linked to India’s human spaceflight program under the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO).

GPHG 2026: Our favourite luxury timepieces vying for top watch industry awards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:11:38 UTC
00:11:38 KST

The Grand Prix d'Horlogerie has revealed its much anticipated official nominations for this year's edition and world tour and here are eight models you should be watching out for.
The watch world and its legion of followers found out on Tuesday which 84 timepieces are in the running for the 2026 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève, the industry's top honour.
Spread across 14 categories, each of the shortlisted timepieces are truly remarkable. The nominees include a Moscow workshop taking on the Swiss giants, a wearable solar system, and a 10-kilo clock that winds your watch while you sleep.
Each of the contenders will compete for one of the 19 prizes celebrating contemporary watchmaking creativity, including the prestigious 'Aiguille d'Or' Grand Prix.
The winners will be revealed at a glittering award ceremony in Geneva on Saturday 7 November and you can watch the event live on Euronews Culture. But, before then, here's a look at some of the pieces that have captured our hearts and minds.
Konstantin Chaykin — ThinKing Mystery
Category: Mechanical Exception
Take two credit cards and stack them: 1.65 mm. That's the thickness of this mechanical marvel, which happens to be wearing a mysterious little smile.
Maybe because while the big Swiss houses were busy fighting over the world's-thinnest record, an independent watchmaker landed a serious blow from his workshop in Moscow. The ThinKing Mystery is billed as the thinnest series-produced mechanical watch in the world.
Let’s unravel the mystery: there is no watch inside the case. The case is the watch. It doubles as the movement's mainplate. Two transparent sapphire discs display the time, and you never see what's turning them. 12 pieces. €426,000.
Christiaan van der Klaauw — CVDK Grand Planetarium Eccentric Silicium
Category: Mechanical Exception
A walk under a starry sky will never feel quite the same once you're wearing this. The eight planets of the solar system, hand-painted, light up on your wrist — each one exactly where it sits in the real sky.
The dial is made of iridescent oxidised silicon. The planets orbit across it in real time and at their true speed. Mercury laps the dial in three months. None of us will live to watch Neptune complete its orbit, which takes 165 years. The Dutch house already won the Calendar and Astronomy category in 2021. 6 pieces. €157,000.
Ulysse Nardin X Urwerk — UR-FREAK
Category: Complication
When two of the most explosive names in independent watchmaking finally get together, you end up with a watch that has neither hands nor a crown.
The Freak collection, launched in 2001 and already crowned in the Iconic category in 2023, tore up the rulebook: the entire movement rotates on itself and doubles as the hand.
Urwerk brings its house speciality, the satellite hours: cubes mounted on rotating arms, with the active figure travelling along the minute scale. The movement pivots every three hours around a silicon balance wheel. Two radical grammars in a single watch. It's quite something to say the least. 100 pieces. €115,000.
L.Leroy — Vox Temporis
Category: Artistic Crafts
Napoleon, Marie-Antoinette and Proust all read the time on a watch from L.Leroy, pioneer of French haute horlogerie.
This one you don't only look at. You listen to it. A single hand stays fixed while the dial turns beneath it to show the hour. The minutes are chimed: a minute repeater sounds them out loud. Hence the name, "the voice of time".
Hidden beneath the case, a flying tourbillon improves accuracy. Above it, the rotating dial carries a flinqué soleil decoration finished with translucent dark blue varnish, under a hand-engraved hand. We've been touched. €341,000.
Louis Vuitton × De Bethune — LVDB-03 Sympathique Louis Varius
Category: Mechanical Clock
One GPHG category isn't reserved for wristwatches. It's well worth mentioning one of the competitors.
Imagine if your phone charger turned into a mechanical work of art. You get home, unclip the bracelet, drop your watch into its cradle. Overnight, the clock winds it and resets it to the right time. No electronics involved.
The mechanical wonder stands about 30 centimetres tall and weighs 10 kilos. On a titanium base inlaid with meteorite, three rose gold rings turn slowly around the structure. They're hand-engraved after drawings by Belgian illustrator François Schuiten: a steam train on a viaduct, hot-air balloons over the African savannah, sherpas on a mountain face, all drifting past.
Behind the project: an alliance between French luxury giant Louis Vuitton, whose watchmaking arm sits just outside Geneva, and De Bethune, one of the most prestigious houses on the horological planet and already an 'Aiguille d'Or' winner. 2 pieces. €4,717,000, clock and watch together.
Grand Seiko — Spring Drive U.F.A. Ushio 300 Diver
Category: Sports
Twenty seconds. Whether you’re working, running or diving, that's all this watch is allowed to gain or lose. Not per day, not per month. Per year.
Grand Seiko presents its first diver's watch fitted with a U.F.A. movement, which the Japanese brand describes as the most accurate mainspring-powered movement ever made. The recipe: a quartz oscillator aged for three months to stabilise its precision.
Ushio means "tide" in Japanese — a nod to the waters surrounding the archipelago of the Land of the Rising Sun. The house was already a GPHG winner in 2021. €10,000.
IWC Schaffhausen — Big Pilot's Watch Perpetual Calendar Ceralume®
Category: Sports
This one leads two lives. By day, a white pilot's watch. By night, a glowing blue object. IWC blended ceramic powder with Super-LumiNova pigments to make the case itself. The result: the whole watch glows for more than 24 hours — the hands, the case, the dial, the strap.
Inside sits IWC’s well-known perpetual calendar, a legendary complication which knows the length of every month and every leap year, with no correction needed until 2100. The calendar shows the date, the day of the week, the month and the moon phases across four subdials. The movement offers a seven-day power reserve and can be admired through the sapphire crystal caseback. 250 pieces. €69,000.
SpaceOne × Baltic — Seconde Majeure
Category: Challenge
Is creative watchmaking reserved for six- and seven-figure pieces? The Challenge category, which honors more affordable models, says no.
Two Parisian brands sign the Seconde Majeure, built around a jumping hour module developed by Théo Auffret, a rising star of independent haute horlogerie. It works through three visible components: beneath the minute disc sits the Central Command Mobile, which makes a full rotation every 60 minutes. At the end of that rotation it engages the Hours Star, which is linked to the hours disc. Finally, the Jumper Spring makes the hour jump, once every 60 minutes.
The kind of beauty that usually costs 10 to 50 times more. €3,200.
The independents are on a roll
The 26th awards ceremony will take place on Saturday 7 November 2026 in Geneva. Every shortlisted timepiece is in the running for the coveted 'Aiguille d'Or' Grand Prix, awarded each year since 2001 to the most striking piece of the year.
Each autumn, the timepieces nominated by the Academy – and subsequently the winners – travel around the world as part of a series of exhibitions offering an unrivalled overview of contemporary watchmaking’s creativity.
The GPHG has set out to open the competition to a wider range of houses, from a wider range of countries, with a growing contingent of independents.
Several legendary names, on the other hand, aren't competing at all. While Rolex has never participated, many of the missing brands are past winners: Patek Philippe, Cartier, Vacheron Constantin, F.P. Journe, Richard Mille, A. Lange & Söhne, Greubel Forsey, and Breguet, last year's 'Aiguille d’Or'.
The Olympics of watchmaking are going ahead without several of their record-holding stars. Which leaves the door wide open for the ones they did not see coming.

How flexible education can support professionals through career disruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:11:34 UTC
00:11:34 KST

Career disruption can change priorities faster than a long-term plan can adapt. Redundancy, relocation, caring responsibilities or a move into another sector may interrupt a familiar routine, yet professional development can continue.
When circumstances shift, structured learning can provide direction. Professionals comparing options may review https://ihcl.org.uk/courses while deciding which type of study could help them keep building relevant knowledge through the transition.
Why does career continuity matter during prolonged uncertainty?
A break in employment does not remove previous experience, but it can make ongoing development more important. Employers may want recent evidence that a candidate has kept their knowledge current.
Career continuity does not mean following the same path at any cost. It means maintaining enough professional activity to keep future options open through study, project work, volunteering or other relevant practice.
During a longer transition, this helps people identify changes in their field. They can return to the market with a clearer view of current requirements instead of relying only on older experience.
Which skills travel well between vountries and industries?
Some abilities remain useful even when a person changes country, sector or employer. For international mobility, the most practical ones are:
- negotiation — finding workable agreements when priorities differ;
- research — locating reliable sources and turning unfamiliar information into useful context;
- professional writing — preparing clear briefs, reports or handover documents;
- remote collaboration — working effectively across time zones, platforms or distributed teams;
- cultural awareness — recognising different workplace norms and responding appropriately.
These skills are useful in roles where people regularly work across borders or organisational cultures. They also help professionals transfer their experience into a new environment more convincingly.
Which learning format fits a busy schedule?
A career transition rarely produces a predictable timetable. Interviews, temporary work, family duties or relocation tasks may appear with little notice, so rigid study arrangements can become difficult to sustain.
A better fit is a format built around manageable units, visible milestones and materials available outside fixed class times. This gives learners a clear weekly direction while leaving room for changes in availability.
It is also worth checking how assessments are organised. Practical tasks completed in stages are easier to fit around an uneven schedule than several large assignments due at the same time.
What should learners prioritise when choosing a programme?
Start with the outcome rather than the course title. Check if the curriculum supports the roles you are considering, whether assessments produce work you can discuss in interviews and how much guidance is available when plans change.
Recognition, workload and access also deserve attention if you expect to move between countries. The programme should be understandable to future employers and realistic to complete from wherever you may be based.
During a career transition, progress is easier to maintain when the next task is clear and support is close at hand. IHCL brings this together through its ACEL approach, personal mentorship and custom-made LMS, helping learners keep moving even when work, location or long-term plans are changing.

What Iceland’s snub means for the EU’s place in the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:09:40 UTC
00:09:40 KST

Supporters of the 'No' campaign display a banner during a rally against reopening Iceland's European Union accession negotiations in Reykjavík on August 27, 2026. | Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — For years, Brussels has sold EU membership as a shield against an unpredictable world: safety, stability and strength in numbers.
With Russia’s war in Ukraine raging and Donald Trump upending the global order — and going so far as threatening to invade Greenland — the EU hoped it had been cast in a more appealing light, despite the challenges caused by the rise of the far right, crises on its doorstep, and trade disputes with the U.S. and China.
“At a time when the international security environment has become far more uncertain than it was a decade ago, many expected support for reopening accession negotiations to grow,” said Nicola Procaccini, co-chair of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament. “The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause.”
Reykjavik’s narrow rejection of restarting EU accession talks in a referendum on Saturday is hardly a death blow to the 450 million-strong bloc. With fewer than 400,000 people and a smaller GDP than Estonia, Iceland was never the prize that would make or break Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s European project.
But the result is still an uncomfortable reality check for a Brussels establishment that has spent the past four years betting that a hazardous world would make the EU more attractive — and had taken Iceland’s renewed interest as a flattering signal of its own relevance.
“A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has,” center-right Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola said, “and answered: not enough.”
Vote of (no) confidence
Enlargement is about more than adding countries to the EU. It is also a branding exercise: a way for Brussels to show that its model of democracy, prosperity and predictability remains attractive in a world of hard power politics.
Every country that knocks on the EU’s door gives the bloc a chance to present itself as a desirable club, in contrast to Trump’s claims that the continent is “decaying.” Iceland was unusually useful in that regard: a wealthy democracy that paused its membership bid in 2015, but was coming back and asking to be let in.
Advertisement
In the run-up to Reykjavík’s referendum, the bloc’s enlargement chief, Marta Kos, overtly framed it as a vote of confidence in the EU. “It would confirm our growing attractiveness in a world that is rapidly changing,” she told POLITICO.
The result of the referendum, then, would appear to signal the opposite.
“Iceland was demotivating,” said an EU official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Even a frozen country doesn’t want to be a part of the EU.”
The response from the European Commission has, so far, been a disappointed shrug. A Commission spokesperson gave a clipped statement, saying it “takes note” of the result and would remain a “close partner” of Iceland.
But a diplomat from a candidate country was gloomier, calling the result a huge blow to the bloc’s enlargement ambitions and the EU’s image more generally. Far-right, Euroskeptic leaders — from Marine Le Pen to Nigel Farage — immediately seized on the referendum’s failure, that diplomat pointed out, making the case for enlargement that much harder.
Reykjavik’s return to the negotiating table could have added momentum to the candidacies of Moldova, Ukraine and Albania, all of which are looking to advance their own paths toward membership. And Montenegro, which has closed over half its accession chapters, was eager to join the bloc at the same time as Iceland to help get its bid ratified.
Advertisement
A second diplomat from a different candidate country was more optimistic about the consequences of Iceland’s negative vote, however. While their first reaction was disappointment, that diplomat said they expected Brussels would focus even more on getting the advanced candidate countries that are eager to join, especially Montenegro, over the line.
Security nothingburger
For Icelandic voters, the reasons for saying No boiled down to a few key issues: fishing rights, sovereignty, the economy, and the fact that Iceland is already inside the European Economic Area and Schengen Area, getting many of the benefits of being in the EU without having to bear the full cost of membership.
Yet the biggest draw was supposed to be security. With Trump looming over Greenland, and using trade to coerce allies and enemies alike, safety in numbers inside the bloc suddenly seemed like an appealing prospect for tiny, remote Iceland.
“We are living in a completely different world than just 10 years ago,” Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, who hails from a pro-EU party, told POLITICO before the vote. Ahead of the referendum, a Commission official said Trump had done the bloc a favor.
Yet Saturday’s referendum shows that while the EU’s promise of solidarity remains compelling for poorer, post-communist states on the bloc’s eastern flank, such as Moldova, Montenegro and Ukraine, security alone is not enough to lure richer, already well-integrated countries like Iceland, but also Norway and Switzerland, into the club.
Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, Iceland’s longest-serving president and an opponent of EU membership, said the Trump fear factor was just not a convincing enough argument, given that Iceland is a founding member of NATO and has a long-standing bilateral security agreement with the U.S. “There’s no shred of evidence that President Trump’s administration has any intention whatsoever in weakening that agreement,” he argued.
Advertisement
“We spent 100 years in a struggle against the Danish king and the Danish authorities in order to gain full independence,” Grímsson added, arguing Icelanders were loath to “start sharing that sovereignty in one way or another.”
Gabriel Gavin and Max Griera contributed to this report.

Explosives used in sabotage attack on German power lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:09:37 UTC
00:09:37 KST

Improvised explosive devices were used on Sept. 1 in a sabotage attack near a coal-fired power plant in Germany, with several electricity lines damaged and supply briefly interrupted, officials said.
Several of the devices were found around 8:00 am (0600 GMT) at the Preilack substation, which distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant, a police spokeswoman told AFP.
At least one detonated but others failed to go off, she said, adding that no one was hurt and there was no major blackout in the area about 100 kilometres (60 miles) southeast of Berlin.
It was the latest in a string of arson attacks around the German capital, with far-left militants often claiming responsibility.
Berlin, a key backer of Ukraine, is also on high alert for sabotage plots linked to Russia.
Dietmar Woidke — premier of Brandenburg state, where the incident took place — condemned the targeting of the power lines.
"We take attacks on our critical infrastructure very seriously," he said in a statement, adding there was a "worryingly high frequency" of such episodes.
"Anyone who tries to sabotage our critical infrastructure and paralyse society is attacking all of us. But we will not allow ourselves to be blackmailed or intimidated by criminal activity."
Power plant operator LEAG described the incident as an "attack". Following the incident, there was a "technical failure" in a unit at the power plant, and a possible connection was being investigated, it said.
Grid operator 50Hertz claimed that unidentified perpetrators damaged several lines in its grid.
"There was a brief interruption of service. All lines are now back in operation. The general power supply is currently not affected," it said in a statement.
In further comments to the Focus news outlet, a spokesman for the operator said homemade projectiles, resembling fireworks typically used on New Year's Eve in Germany, were used in the attack.
Local newspaper the Maerkische Allgemeine Zeitung reported they resembled large, homemade model rockets.
The police spokeswoman said an investigation had been launched to determine who was behind the incident.
Among the recent arson attacks, the most serious took place in Berlin in January.
It caused an electricity outage that left tens of thousands of homes and thousands of businesses without power for nearly a week in the middle of winter in the southwest of capital.
The far-left "Vulkangruppe" (Volcano Group) claimed responsibility for the arson attack on high-voltage cables that caused that blackout.
It also claimed to be behind two sabotage attacks targeting a Tesla electric car factory just outside Berlin.

Shein and Temu items could face €20 levy in France’s crackdown on ultra-fast fashion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:08:28 UTC
00:08:28 KST

Imports of small parcels from China have already fallen by up to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy came into force in July.
France is cracking down on ultra-fast fashion with a new fee that eventually reach almost €20 per garment.
The levy, which comes into force on 1 September, targets major e-commerce platforms including Shein.
It follows legislation passed by the French parliament in June to regulate companies known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.
It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years.
"The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented," said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Friday (28 August) as details of the measure were published.
How will France's ultra-fast fashion levy be determined?
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product's pre-tax price.
A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies' own declarations, is under development, Lefevre's office said.
Shein – which on Monday was valued at $26.3 billion (€22.7b) in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering – declined to comment when contacted by news agency AFP.
Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Will European retailers will be exempt from the levy?
The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect.
In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies.
French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion.
The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre's office said those concerns had been "dispelled" and the measure was not expected to be blocked.
China meanwhile warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as "discriminatory" and in violation of trade principles.
Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy on such shipments came into force on 1 July, according to the French government.

Israeli authorities have seized a UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) school in the Shufat refugee camp, leaving Palestinian children in East Jerusalem facing uncertainty as their academic year begins.
RT’s Charlotte Dubenskij reports from the ground, where families say they fear losing access to affordable schooling or being forced to send their children into an Israeli-run system.
Fourteen-year-old Noor and her 11-year-old sister Fatima are among those still without a school just days before the new academic year, Dubenskij reported from Shufat. The sisters fear the disruption could derail their ambitions of becoming a doctor and a dentist.
Their father told Dubenskij that the family cannot afford municipal schools, which could cost thousands of shekels, while UNRWA, which provides education, healthcare, and other services to Palestinian refugees, charged only a symbolic annual fee. Parents are also concerned about their children being transferred to Israeli-run schools and taught a different curriculum.
A local community leader interviewed by Dubenskij said parents fear the Israeli curriculum would exclude subjects previously taught at UNRWA schools, including Islamic education and Arab history. Asked by the RT correspondent whether he feared the children would be “brainwashed,” he replied: “Of course, absolutely, without a doubt.”
UNRWA says personnel linked to the Jerusalem Municipality entered its Shufat facilities without authorization and began work inside, in violation of the agency’s UN protections. The municipality says the sites are privately owned and will be reopened for local residents, although Dubenskij reported that the school remains closed with no reopening date set.
The developments follow Israel’s takeover of UNRWA’s Qalandiya Training Center in East Jerusalem late last month, disrupting vocational education for hundreds of students. During the raid, Israeli forces shot and wounded a Palestinian teenager. UNRWA said more than 50 Israeli security personnel entered the facility while around 20 staff were inside and forced them from the premises.

Lightning density in Switzerland second highest in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:07:00 KST

Lightning density in Switzerland second highest in Europe
Switzerland experienced a summer with a high number of thunderstorms. More than 22,000 cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were recorded between early June and late August. Relative to its land area, it has the second-highest density of lightning strikes in Europe, according to a report by Meteorage published on Tuesday.
In total, the detection network run by the Météo-France subsidiary recorded 22,158 cloud-to-ground lightning strikes in Switzerland during the meteorological summer, which runs from June 1 to August 31, according to a press release. Across Europe, the total number reached 893,458.
Switzerland lags far behind major countries such as Italy, France and Spain in absolute terms. It stands out, however, when lightning activity is measured relative to the country’s surface area. With 2.43 ground strikes per km² per year, it ranks second in Europe, behind Italy (4.73), but ahead of, in particular, the Netherlands (2.39), Belgium (2.20), France (2.09) and Germany (1.30).
August was the most active month of the summer in Switzerland, with 7,993 cloud-to-ground lightning strikes, compared with 7,424 in July and 6,741 in June. Meteorage recorded 27 days of thunderstorms during the month. The peak was reached on August 28, with 1,886 lightning strikes in a single day.

Appenzell village is named ‘lightning capital’ of Switzerland
Bern and Lugano lead the way
Canton Bern topped the list with 3,426 lightning strikes, ahead of Graubünden (2,773), Ticino (2,552), Valais (2,276) and Vaud (2,188). At district level, the Lugano district recorded the highest level of lightning activity, with 570 lightning strikes and a particularly high density.
However, the summer of 2026 is not among the most lightning-prone of recent years, notes Joris Royet, head of weather projects at Meteorage. It stood out more for the intensity of certain episodes.

“The meteorological summer of 2026 was marked by numerous severe thunderstorm episodes across Europe,” he explains. Several factors contributed to the formation of supercells, accompanied by heavy hailstorms, destructive gusts and, locally, tornadoes.
According to Meteorage, thunderstorm activity in Europe was concentrated mainly during the second half of June and throughout a particularly active August. It was significantly higher than that observed during the summer of 2025.
